en: Now follows the section on the requisites for legal procedure, concerning the disputes of all men in this world where dharma has declined.
A definitive conclusion is being established by us, in accordance with reasoning and traditional scripture.

For the purpose of deciding all disputes, the determination of the meaning of the Smṛtis is now undertaken. Regarding this, Nārada [cites] Manu: "At the time when Prajāpati Manu ruled the kingdom, men were devoted solely to dharma and were speakers of truth."
At that time, there was no legal dispute, nor hatred, nor even envy;
when dharma had perished among human beings, legal disputes were set in motion.
And the king has been made the observer and upholder of that principle.

“Devoted solely to *dharma*”: those for whom *dharma* alone is the expansion [of their lives]. Because *dharma* is paramount for all, there was no legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) arising from seeds such as hatred and envy, which are the causes of legal disputes, due to the absence of unrighteousness (*adharma*). Now, in this *kaliyuga*, because unrighteousness is predominant among men due to the defects of the age, the sages (*śiṣṭas*) such as Manu have "set forth" (*pravartita*)—that is, demonstrated—the system of justice known as legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), in order to prevent injustice based upon that [unrighteousness]. The king was appointed by Manu and others as the "upholder of the rod" (*daṇḍadhārayitā*) for those who act unjustly, acting as the observer of that justice. Regarding this, Manu says:
But when desiring to inspect legal cases, the king, humble and accompanied by Brahmins as well as ministers skilled in counsel, should enter the court.
Seated there or even standing, having raised his right hand and wearing modest dress and ornaments, he should attend to the affairs of the litigants.
Day by day, he shall adjudicate legal cases individually according to the eighteen titles of law, using reasons observed in local custom as well as those found in the scriptures.
Having occupied the seat of justice, with his body properly covered and his mind composed,
he should begin the examination of legal cases after bowing to the guardians of the world.
Just as a hunter traces the track of a deer by drops of blood,
so should a king trace the path of dharma through inference.

“Sitting or standing,” he should observe; not while lying down. “Raising his right hand”—this refers to wearing it over the upper garment like the sacred thread (*upavīta*). “By means of reasons” (*hetubhiḥ*)—that is, by means of proofs obtained through local custom and obtained from the scriptures—he should carry out the determination of legal disputes through subtle reasons, just as one infers the track of a deer from its footprints, regarding the eighteen titles of law. On this point, Yājñavalkya says: “The king should examine legal cases together with learned Brāhmaṇas, in accordance with the treatises on Dharma, free from anger and greed.”
The king should appoint as members of his assembly those who are accomplished in learning and study, knowers of the Dharma, speakers of truth, and who are impartial toward both enemy and friend.

By means of the preceding verses, it is established that three Brāhmaṇas, together with the presiding Brāhmaṇa, shall constitute the members of the court (*sabhāsada*). Accordingly, Kātyāyana has shown the members of the court by way of distinction:
"Having entered the court in modest attire, the king, composed and seated facing the east, shall examine the legal cases of the litigants."
He, moreover, was joined by steadfast members of the assembly— foremost among the twice-born, rooted in wisdom,
skilled in the meaning of the treatises on dharma, and experts in the treatises on statecraft.
Accompanied by the chief justice, his ministers, the Brahmins and the domestic priest,
and the members of the court, the king remains in heaven through the practice of dharma as a witness.
The king should not initiate that which is contrary to the Śruti and Smṛti and detrimental to living beings, nor should he allow that which has already been initiated to continue.

In this verse, "saprāḍvivākaḥ sāmātyaḥ," the members of the court (*sabhāsadaḥ*) are shown separately. The time for the examination of legal cases (*vyavahāra*) has also been stated by that same [author]: "Excluding the eighth part of the day, the three periods [of time] that remain are declared in the scriptures to be the supreme time for legal proceedings."

Having divided the day into eight parts, one sets aside the first for the Agnihotra sacrifice and for the satisfaction of Brāhmaṇas; the subsequent three parts constitute the time for legal transactions (*vyavahāra*). Thus says Manu:
"Having offered oblations to the fires and honored the Brāhmaṇas, he should enter the most auspicious assembly hall.
Regarding that location of the assembly hall, Bṛhaspati says:
In the center of the fortress, one should construct separate houses provided with water and trees;
in the eastern direction, one should arrange an auspicious assembly hall facing east.
It should be provided with garlands, incense, and seats, endowed with the seed-syllable and the color red,
joined with deities in the form of images or paintings, as well as fire and water.

"One should imagine [the assembly] as being joined by the deities beginning with the Sun and the Moon," and "one should also imagine it as joined by the world-protectors (lokapālas). Regarding this, Manu states the secondary rule (*anukalpa*):
"When the king himself does not personally oversee legal cases, then he should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa to oversee the legal cases."
Surrounded by exactly three members of the assembly, he should examine his duties,
having entered the foremost court while either seated or standing.

He alone is designated as the *prāḍvivāka*. Thus says Bṛhaspati: "Because he asks the question (*praśna*) and likewise the counter-question (*pratipraśna*) in a dispute, and because he speaks first with kind words (*priyapūrvam*), he is therefore remembered as the *prāḍvivāka*."
And so Vyāsa says:
"Having carefully questioned the litigant who has come into dispute along with the members of the court, he deliberates upon it; for that reason, he is remembered as the *prāḍvivāka* (the judge)."
Self-controlled, of noble birth, impartial, and free from passion and hatred— he,
surrounded by exactly three members of the court, shall examine his legal cases.
Yājñavalkya: When the king, due to the demands of business, is unable to oversee a legal proceeding himself,
he must appoint a Brāhmaṇa who knows all the laws, together with the members of the court.
Vyāsa says: One who subsists merely by his birth may, at will, be called a "pseudo-Brāhmaṇa" (brāhmaṇabruva) and serve as the king's advisor on dharma; however, the other three castes are not so.
This refers to the case of unlearned Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. Likewise, Kātyāyana states:
"In that situation, if there should be no learned Brāhmaṇa, one should employ a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who knows the Dharmaśāstra; one should avoid a Śūdra with great effort."

In the absence of learned Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, Manu has said: "Or one who lives by his caste alone, though he may be called a 'Brāhmaṇa in name,' may at will be the expounder of dharma for the king; but a Śūdra, under no circumstances."

At that moment when men's tasks grow wearying, he should appoint as a minister a man who is foremost among counselors, knows the Dharma, is wise, self-controlled, and of noble birth, upon that very seat.
Kātyāyana says: [One should appoint as a witness] one who is self-controlled, of noble birth, impartial, not causing alarm, steadfast,
fearful of the hereafter, most virtuous, diligent, and free from anger.
On this point, Hārīta says:
Just as a physician should extract a splinter from the body by means of skillful techniques,
so should the judge extract the "splinter" [of injustice] through legal proceedings.

[Kātyāyana states the characteristics of court members: "Kings should appoint as court members (sabhyas) twice-born men who are free from greed, wealthy, knowers of the Dharma, speakers of truth, and proficient in the Dharmaśāstras."

Regarding that, Manu states the characteristics of an assembly: "In whatever place three Brahmins learned in the Vedas sit together with a learned minister of the king, that assembly is equal to a sacrifice."
The term *prākṛta* means a learned man, specifically the judge (*prāḍvivāka*).
The king should sit facing the east, while the members of the court (*sabhyāḥ*) face north;
the accountant (*gaṇaka*) faces west, and the scribe (*lekhaka*) faces south.
Vasiṣṭha says: Whatever merit is gained when a dying Brahmin is rescued from a body of water,
that same merit is gained when a lawsuit involving one who has fallen into doubt is resolved.

Bṛhaspati says: A council where five, seven, or even three eminent Brahmins— learned in the worlds, the Vedas, their auxiliary sciences, and the Dharma— are seated, is equal to a sacrificial assembly.
In brief, the gods know truth, while humans know falsehood;
he whose mind is established in truth attains divinity even in this very world.

He stated that there are four types of assemblies: "The assembly is said to be of four kinds: established, unstable, sealed, and learned; and the members of the assembly are likewise of those same kinds."
He states their explanation:
"Established" refers to [a city] in a town or village; "unestablished" is that which is called mobile (*calā*).
That which is joined with a sealed official (*mudritādhyakṣa*) and associated with the king is "prescribed by the treatises" (*śāstritā*).
The king, the authorized members of the court, the legal codes, the astrologer and the scribe, gold, fire, water, and his own men— these are indeed the ten constituent elements of the means of proof.
Of these, the king is the head; the presiding judge is made the mouth;
the members of the court are the arms; the legal codes are the hands; and the calculator and the scribe are the two shanks.
There, gold, fire, water, and the eyes, as well as the feet and the self-person (svapuruṣa), are present;
and the specific function of each of these ten has been declared separately.
The king is the presiding speaker and the ruler; the court members are the examiners of the case;
the legal tradition (Smṛti) declares the decision, as well as victory, the awarding of wealth, and likewise punishment.
Gold and fire are for the purpose of oaths; water is for those who are thirsty or agitated. The accountant shall calculate the matter, and the scribe shall record the legal decision.
The king’s own officers shall summon the defendant, the members of the court, and the witnesses;
they shall proceed without obstruction and always protect both the plaintiff and the defendant.
That assembly hall, presided over by a king who possesses a disciplined mind and examines legal cases according to these ten constituent factors, is equal to a sacrificial rite.
He himself stated the characteristics of the calculator and the scribe:
"A sacrifice arises from the conjunction of animals, clarified butter, officiating priests, and so forth;
just as it is connected with these, so too is its practical application described."
In sacrifice Viṣṇu is fully honored; in worldly affairs, the lord of the earth is honored.
Therein, the sacrificer is the victor, while the victim is said to be the defeated one.
The prima facie argument and the rejoinder are the clarified butter; wisdom is said to be the oblation.
The three Vedas and the treatises are the members of the assembly, while the officiating priests are self-restraint, which is the sacrificial fee.
He who, having abandoned greed, hatred, and the like, should carry out the determination of a matter according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, shall obtain the fruit of a sacrifice.
In brief, the gods know truth, while humans know falsehood;
he whose mind is established in truth attains divinity even in this very world.

Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says: "The king should appoint as astrologer and scribe those who know the true nature of words and their designations, who are skilled in calculation, pure, and proficient in various scripts."
Kātyāyana states that this other duty must also be performed:
"The [guild] shall be presided over by a few merchants who possess noble lineage, good character, youth, proper conduct, and wealth, and who are free from envy; they shall serve as its foundation."
The phrase "he should prepare the seat of dharma" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. On this point, Nārada says:
"Families, guilds, assemblies, and the authorized king—among these, each subsequent one is more authoritative than the preceding in legal proceedings."
Yājñavalkya: Kings, officials, guilds, then trade associations, and families—
each preceding one is to be understood as more authoritative than each subsequent one in the legal procedure for men.
A debtor, an artisan, a craftsman, a moneylender, members of a guild, dancers, ascetics,
and ferrymen shall deliver a decision according to their own respective rules.
But for those who roam the forest, the ritual should be performed with forest products;
likewise, for soldiers in an army and for merchants on a caravan.
The king should have the affairs of ascetics conducted by those learned in the three Vedas,
as well as by those who know the application of illusion (māyā-yoga), by the guilds, and by appointed officials.
The meaning is: "by means of a reason that is established by one's own convention (*svasamaya*). Regarding this, Vyāsa states:
"Among the affairs of kings, the village, the guild, the corporation, the family, the teacher, the master, the householder, the father, the eldest brother, and the grandfather [are authorized]."
They may also observe the disputes of men regarding matters within their own jurisdiction.
Then Kātyāyana speaks of the *naigamas*:
"A collection of various citizens is proclaimed by the name *naigama*."
These hosts, bearing various weapons, are proclaimed to have assembled together.
A collection of merchants and the like is proclaimed to be a *pūga*;
however, a collection of Brāhmaṇas is called a *gaṇa* by the wise.
The collection of those such as the Sugatas and Arhats is called a *saṅgha*;
the collection of four-footed animals such as cows and the like is called a *vraja*.
A collection of those who have mastered false treatises is called a *puñja*;
a collection of Caṇḍālas, Śvapacas, and others is called a *gulma*.
A collection of artisans, craftsmen, and the like is called a *śreṇi*.
There should be overseers of affairs for groups (*pūga*), guilds (*śreṇi*), assemblies (*gaṇa*), and so forth.
Pure, knowers of the Vedic dharma, skillful, self-controlled, of noble birth,
proficient in all matters, free from greed, aged, and most eminent.
The word of those who speak for the welfare of the community must be carried out;
this same rule applies even to guilds, merchant associations, heretical sects, and monastic orders.
The characteristics of heretics are stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"Those of evil views who do not assert the authority of the Veda—
such as the followers of Baudha, the Arhatas, and others— are proclaimed by the name 'heretics' (*pāṣaṇḍa*)."
Those who have entered the religious life but are heretics are proclaimed as such.
Those, such as the Vaiśeṣikas and others, who assert that the Veda possesses authority because it was composed by a person, are proclaimed as the class known as Naigamas.
Kātyāyana has presented the definition of the *naigama* differently:
"The *naigama* is proclaimed to be an assembly of various citizens.
Likewise, six *samayas* are mentioned in the *Svāyambhuva-āgama*.
The Buddhist, the Jain, the Śaiva, the Pāśupata,
as well as the Kāpāla and the Pāñcarātra— these six are known as the religious systems (samayas).
Regarding this, Vyāsa says:

"In the case of merchants, artisans, and others who subsist by agriculture or crafts, a determination [of the facts] is impossible for others; one should have it made by those who are experts in those very matters."

This is what is meant: in all cases, whether by way of the path taught in the treatises or by one’s own local custom, a legal proceeding that has been determined is finalized. In this regard, each subsequent stage is more authoritative than the preceding one. Therefore, it is appropriate for the king to review a case after it has been seen by the others. Once a case has been reviewed by the king, there is no further possibility of appeal, as there is no higher authority beyond him. And so says Pitāmaha: "A matter decided by the family elders and the rest should be reviewed according to the successive stages;
for one who is dissatisfied, the process must continue until it has been finally decided by the king."

On this point, Gautama states: “In that regard, the means of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) are the Veda, the Dharmaśāstras, the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), the secondary Vedas (*upaveda*), and the Purāṇa. Furthermore, the customs of regions, castes, and families, when not in conflict with the sacred traditions (*āmnāya*), are authoritative. Farmers, merchants, herdsmen, moneylenders, and artisans each belong to their own respective classes. Having ascertained the matters from them according to their respective jurisdictions, the settlement of legal duty (*dharma-vyavasthā*) is established. In another Smṛti it is said: “Having duly considered the laws of castes and localities, the eternal laws of guilds, and the family laws, one should uphold one’s own duty (*svadharma*).”
Whatever has been practiced by the virtuous and by righteous twice-born men,
that one should establish as not contradictory to the customs of the country, the family, and the caste.
Kātyāyana says:

That which is the stability of the lineage for those [ancestors], handed down in succession according to the nature of things (dharmatā), they call the family dharma; one should protect it in that very same way.
Whatever custom has been established in a particular region and persists for all time,
provided it does not contradict the Śruti and Smṛti, that is called a "local practice" (deśadṛṣṭa).
Bṛhaspati says:
Among the twice-born in the South, the daughters of maternal uncles are married;
in the Middle Country, laborers and artisans eat beef.
In the east, men will be eaters of fish, and women will be devoted to infidelity;
in the north, women will be drinkers of liquor and touchable even when they are in their menses.
The Khaśas accept the wife of a brother who is without a husband;
because of this practice, they are not subject to the infliction of penance.
Kātyāyana says: One should not subvert the established duty of those born from inverse unions, nor of those dwelling in difficult regions, even if that duty is endowed with justice.
Now, regarding the determination of legal cases, Vyāsa speaks of those who should not be appointed:
"If one should oversee legal affairs with the assistance of Śūdras, excluding the twice-born,
his kingdom becomes agitated, and his army and treasury perish."
Those who are ignorant of local customs, nihilists, those devoid of scriptural knowledge,
the insane, the angry, and children should not be appointed to a judicial inquiry.
When dharma, pierced by adharma, enters an assembly,
and the members of that assembly do not extract the dart, they themselves are pierced.
One should either not enter an assembly or speak what is just;
for by neither speaking nor speaking falsely, a man becomes a sinner.
Dharma alone is the true friend who follows one even unto death;
for everything else indeed goes to destruction along with the body.
One quarter of the injustice falls upon the perpetrator; one quarter reaches the witness;
one quarter reaches all the members of the court; and one quarter reaches the king.
Manu says:
The king becomes free from sin, and the members of the assembly are also released;
the guilt goes to the perpetrator where one deserving of censure is censured.
But where the members of the court reach a decision by overstepping the science of logic (nyāya), there dharma, being struck down by adharma, destroys [the wrongdoer]; of this there is no doubt.
Kātyāyana says: But the members of the court must not overlook an action that has proceeded contrary to dharma;
by overlooking it, those kings go headlong to hell.
But having recognized that the king’s mind has strayed from the path of justice, the members of the assembly must speak what is pleasing to him there; thus they shall not become guilty of sin.
Regarding this determination of legal proceedings, Nārada states the following sequence:
"Having taken his seat upon the throne of justice, the king, free from malice,
should be impartial toward all beings, upholding the vow of Vaivasvata."
Placing the Dharmaśāstra before him and abiding by the opinion of the judge,
he should examine the legal cases in their proper order with a concentrated mind.
Without contradicting the treatises on Dharma and the treatises on Artha, the king should skillfully examine and direct the course of legal proceedings.
Just as a hunter, when a deer has been wounded, might track the deer's path by the smear of blood on the undergrowth, so too should one track the path of Dharma.
Bṛhaspati says:
Having understood that the mind of the lord of the earth has strayed from the path of justice, one should speak what is pleasing to him there; the member of the court is not guilty in that case.
But the members of the court must not overlook an action that has proceeded contrary to the law;
by constantly overlooking it, they go headfirst to hell.

However, one who reaches a decision on matters through the application of reasoning based on the opinions of the judge and the members of the court, which serve as the basis for livelihood, does not incur punishment.
Nārada states the characteristics of an unseemly member:
"Whether out of passion, ignorance, or greed, he who speaks otherwise [than the truth] is to be known as an unseemly member though he be a member; one should severely punish that sinner."
Where members of an assembly, having entered the court, sit in silence and deep thought,
and do not speak according to what they have perceived, all of them are speakers of untruth.
Regarding punishment for falsehood, Yājñavalkya says:
"Sabhya judges who act contrary to the legal codes out of passion, greed, or even fear, shall each be punished with a fine double that of the litigant."
Furthermore, Nārada shows what kind of members of the court (sabhāsada) should be appointed:
"The king, however, should appoint righteous and well-tested members of the court—
those who are capable of bearing the burden of legal proceedings, like excellent oxen."
The members of the royal assembly should be well-versed in the meaning of the Dharmaśāstras, of noble birth, speakers of truth, and impartial toward both enemy and friend.
Kātyāyana says: One who studies only a single treatise will not know how to determine legal matters;
therefore, kings should rely upon the sacred tradition (brahmāgama) as the highest authority in disputes.
Nārada: One who has not been appointed should not say anything at all in legal proceedings;
but one who has been appointed must speak words that are impartial.
Kātyāyana says: Those who, though not specifically appointed, should carry out the adjudication of legal disputes—
those who are engaged in the duties of the king— one should determine their punishment.
Nārada said:
Whether commissioned or uncommissioned, one who knows the scriptures is fit to speak;
he who lives by the scripture speaks the divine word.
Elsewhere it is said: That is no assembly where there are no elders;
they are not elders who do not speak of the Dharma.
That is not dharma wherein there is no truth; that is not truth which is permeated by deceit.
Now Bṛhaspati states the punishment for the judge and his assessors:
"Assessors who speak unjustly, as well as those who live on bribes,
and those who betray confidence— all of them must be banished."
Kātyāyana: Even if the matter has not been adjudicated, if the presiding judge should converse in private with the plaintiff, he,
along with the members of the court, shall undoubtedly be punished.

In that regard, the king—or even the presiding judge—should commence the investigation of legal cases while surrounded in the assembly hall by Brahmins who are free from passion and hatred, skilled in discernment, and conversant with the sacred mantras; by ministers; by wealthy merchants; and by the family priest and court officials.
Thus ends the second section, the Section on the Preliminaries of Legal Procedure, in the *Vyavahāranirṇaya* composed by the venerable Varadarāja.
Now begins the Section on the Plaint (*Āvedana*).
Now Kātyāyana states the definition of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*):
"In the extensive exposition of justice known as *dharma*, which is to be accomplished through effort and has been interrupted,
that dispute which is rooted in what is to be proven is called legal procedure."
Regarding that, Kātyāyana provides the etymological definition of the term *vyavahāra*:
"The removal (*haraṇa*) of various doubts (*nānārtha-avasandeha*) is called *hāra*;
because it removes various doubts, it is traditionally known as *vyavahāra*."

Nārada: First, the legal source (āgama) must be established; then the subject matter of the lawsuit (vyavahārapada); followed by the investigation (vicāra) and the decision (nirṇaya). Thus, the judicial process (darśana) is fourfold.

*Āgama* is the hearing of the plaintiff’s statement; from that follows the investigation of the claim, the response, and the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and from that, the determination of victory by means of the *pramāṇas*. This is the sequence.
Regarding the section on the formal complaint (*āvedana*), Yājñavalkya states it in the *Vyavahāramātṛkā*:
When one, unassailed by others on a path that deviates from the conduct of mindfulness,
brings a matter before the king, that indeed constitutes a subject for legal dispute.

When one who has been oppressed or harassed by others through an unjust path arrives at the court and, being questioned by the king or the judge (*prāḍvivāka*), reports whatever he seeks regarding his case—that alone constitutes the basis (*āspada*) of that legal proceeding. By the phrase "if he reports," it is meant that the king or judge must examine the case only when the litigant has come of his own accord; it is stated that the king or judge must not, out of greed for fines, location, or bonds, fabricate or instigate a case. And so Manu says:
"The king himself, nor his official, shall initiate a case."
And one should never, under any circumstances, seize wealth that has been acquired by another.

"Unpresented" means not yet brought forward. "Should swallow" means he should accept it. At the time of presentation, whatever was presented that was deficient or excessive must be written down on the ground, on a wooden board, or similar surface. Kātyāyana states:

"If one party, provoked by passion or other motives, speaks falsely during the proceedings, the judge should first write 'om' (so be it) regarding that [statement] of the plaintiff upon the board or other such surface."
In the context of the judicial process, this refers to the stage of formal determination. Accordingly, Bṛhaspati states:
"The judge shall cause the plaintiff's case, as stated naturally, to be written on a wooden board with chalk;
thereafter, once it has been refined, it shall be transferred to the official document."
Kātyāyana says: One should cut away what is excessive and fill in what is deficient;
one should set it down upon the ground until that matter is fully determined.
Prajāpati has stated the manner of filing the plaint:
"It should be faultless, accompanied by a formal declaration, consistent with authoritative sources and tradition,
concise in words yet rich in meaning, free from ambiguity, and coherent."

One who desires a legal dispute, being oppressed by another through injustice, should make a formal complaint (*āvedayet*). Regarding the manner of filing a complaint in cases where a long time has elapsed, Pitāmaha said: "A person, speaking at the outset with reasons for his forbearance and providing supporting arguments..."
The plaintiff, seeking justice, should state the truth, free from deceitful speech.
Kātyāyana says: One who argues while bearing arms, without an upper garment, with his waistband loosened, or sitting upon a seat, or using his left hand, shall incur punishment.

Bṛhaspati states that if a settlement is reached by the members of the court without the presence of the accuser, prior to the formal charge and immediately after the plaint has been submitted, a fine shall be imposed according to the nature of the accusation:
"But those who, after the matter has been submitted, reach a private settlement,
the judge shall impose upon them a fine proportionate to the original accusation."

In that case, if the matter is found to be just following the plaintiff's statement, the examination of the legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) must be carried out; if it is unjust, it must simply be rejected. Regarding this, Prajāpati says:
"A plaint made by one who is an outcaste or the like, one who has not returned to his natural state, and one made by a person lacking independence, is not established."
R̥ṣyaśṛṅga and Yājñavalkya:
A legal proceeding initiated by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted by disease, beset by calamity, a child, or terrified,
as well as one conducted by an incompetent person, does not succeed.
Nārada says: A teacher and a pupil, father and son, husband and wife, or master and servant—
among these who are united as such, a legal dispute is not valid.
Kātyāyana says:
Where both contradictory and non-contradictory claims are seen presented within a single [plaint], one should abandon that plea from afar.
Nārada states the definition of an inadmissible lawsuit:
"A lawsuit brought by one person against many, or involving women and servants,
is declared by those who know the Dharma to be inadmissible."
Bṛhaspati says: But he who has been dismissed by the king, or he who causes opposition among the citizens,
or against the whole kingdom as well as its constituent elements (prakṛtis), [should be punished].
Furthermore, those legal proceedings that cause discord among districts, villages,
or large groups of people are all declared to be inadmissible.
Again, Nārada says:
Whatever act a minor performs, being likewise lacking independence,
that is declared here by those who know the scriptures to be "unperformed" according to the legal treatises.

The dispute involving a single claimant against many is set aside because it involves a contradictory cause. Kātyāyana states the categories of cases that cannot be proven: "The king should reject a plaint that is unestablished, unassailable [by evidence], meaningless, purposeless, impossible to prove, or contradictory."
He himself provides the explanation:
"That which has not been composed by anyone is cited as 'unestablished' (aprasiddha);
it is proclaimed as being 'irrelevant to the subject' (anyārtha), 'devoid of meaning' (arthahīna), and 'unobjectionable' (nirābādha)."
That which involves a minor offense and a minor purpose is known as "meaningless" (nirarthaka);
however, that which is devoid of any obstruction to the task at hand should be understood as "purposeless" (niṣprayojana).
The wise declare that a claim which is improbable or unproven is not a valid plaint,
whether it has been presented before the judge or the king.
If there is a contradiction within a single village, that is called "contradictory" (viruddha).

The examples are as follows: “This garment of mine was not made by anyone; it has been eaten by this [person]”; “And for another purpose”: “An injury was committed by this Devadatta”; “Devoid of meaning”: “My lamp illuminates the house of Devadatta”; “Of slight offense”: “I have been looked upon by him for a moment with a smile”; “Of little significance”: “My seeds of rice have been stolen by him”; “Lacking subversion of the matter”: “He has bathed in the final ablution (*avabhṛtha*) of my sacrifice”; “Impossible”: “A flower from the sky has been stolen by him. A statement that conveys such a matter is inadmissible, because it cannot be proven and is therefore not to be accepted. Furthermore, when a matter is stated that causes conflict with the King or the judge, that too must be abandoned, according to the maxim: “For the sake of one’s self, one may abandon the earth. Likewise, when there is conflict with a city, a kingdom, or a village, that too must be abandoned, according to the maxim: “For the sake of a village, one may abandon a family. Kātyāyana says that a petition should be made only after a complaint has been presented that is free from the aforementioned defects.
At the proper time, he should question the one seeking justice who stands before him with a bowed head:
"What is your business? What is your affliction? Do not fear; speak, O man!"

"By whom, toward whom, when, and for what reason should one question a guest who has arrived? When questioned in this manner, that which he says shall be determined together with the Brahmins present in the assembly."
Having deliberated upon the matter, if it is found to be just, he should thereafter issue a summons; for this purpose, he may deliver a sealed writ, or otherwise command an official messenger.
But if one who is capable should disregard the king's command when summoned,
the king shall determine his punishment in accordance with the nature of the offense.
For a minor offense, the fine shall be fifty; for a middling offense, it shall be at least two hundred;
and for a grave matter, he shall always be fined at least five hundred.

The commentators have stated that this is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) regarding the gradations of fines for failure to appear. In that regard, if one fails to appear once, the fine is one-third; if twice, half; and if thrice, the full amount. Having thus collected the fine, after thirty nights—or after three fortnights—one should take twelve *bandhas* as security and issue a decree of victory (*jayapatra*) on account of the loss. If the defendant appears after this has been done, the trial must be conducted again. Regarding this, there is a specific rule in the *Trairātra-sūtra*: "If he fails to appear for three nights, four *caṇḍyas* [are the fine]; and likewise in the case of fleeing, or upon defeat, four *kārṣāpaṇas*. This refers to cases involving small amounts of property. In such matters concerning a decree of victory due to loss, the summoner should pay wages to the messenger for as long as it takes for the matter to be resolved; so says the text.
For one day, two days, or three days— depending on the place, time, and other factors—
the leader should provide food for the messenger once the mission has been accomplished.

The *netā* is the summoner. Regarding this, Nārada states that if one summoned by means of a seal (*mudrā*) does not come, then the court should issue an injunction (*āsedha*) until the decision of the legal case is reached:
"If a party does not remain when the matter is to be stated, or if he departs from his word, the plaintiff shall have him restrained until the appearance for the summons."

When the matter to be stated is doubtful, he should not only refrain from proceeding toward a definitive conclusion, but he must also "restrain" that speech as it departs; for one being forbidden with the words "Do not go," should not remain [if he intends to leave]. He should restrain him within the boundary, where "as far as" (*yāvat*) denotes the limit of the restriction. Since one is "summoned" (*āhūyate*) therein, it is called "summons" (*āhvānam*), which refers to the judicial proceeding. Therefore, restraint must be maintained until the completion of the judicial proceeding. Regarding this, he states that restraint is fourfold: "Restraint of place, that based on time, likewise from travel, and from activity."
There are four kinds of restraint; one who is restrained must not transgress it.

"Restriction from place" (*sthānāsedha*) means: "You must not move from this spot. "Restriction from time" (*kālāsedha*), however, is: "If you do not perform [the task] within two or three days, then you must pay such-and-such a fine to the king. "Restriction from travel" (*pravāsāt*) means: "If you go to another village or elsewhere, you shall be punished as before. "Restriction from work" (*karmaṇaḥ*) means: "If you perform work such as building a house without having paid [the wages], you shall be punished as before. One who has been subjected to these four kinds of restriction must not violate them. Likewise: "Fields, gardens, houses, and so forth, as well as wealth, grain, and the like..."
And these [grounds] are to be declared as grounds for defeat by the proponent against those who argue unjustly.

These objects, such as fields and the like, which are the subject of dispute, alone are to be restrained, and no others. Furthermore, even regarding fields and the like, the sowing of seeds and other means of producing goods must be prohibited; for it is heard in the scriptures that if the restrainer loses the case, he must pay both the value of the enjoyment and a fine. However, in the case of a false restraint, he shall be made to pay the value of the enjoyment and an equal amount as a fine, provided that the restrainer himself voluntarily relinquishes his restraint.
Thus:
"There is no fault in transgressing that [rule], nor should one impose a fine;
after reporting it to the king, the one who has restrained [the offender] shall not release him on his own."
One who releases [the defendant] after having bound him shall be made to pay a fine; and one who has not yet completed the binding shall not violate the injunction.

Before the formal filing of the suit, the person placing the injunction is not to be punished for releasing [the defendant]; however, after that time, one who releases him is indeed liable to punishment. By the word *dama*, that which is incurred through defeat in a legal dispute is meant. Now, Nārada states those who are not to be placed under injunction:
"In cases such as crossing a river, traversing a wilderness, being in a dangerous place, or during a calamity..."
One who, being unsuccessful, departs from that obstruction would not commit an offense.
One desiring to marry, one afflicted by disease, one wishing to sacrifice, one situated in calamity,
one attacked by another, and likewise one engaged in royal business.
One desiring to settle down is one facing marriage. He states that [certain tasks] cannot be accomplished due to specific times:
"Cowherds [are busy] when cattle graze; farmers at the beginning of the sowing season;
artisans at their respective times; and soldiers during war."
A minor, an envoy, one intent on giving a gift, one observing a vow, and those in a precarious situation must not be obstructed; nor should the king summon them.
Kātyāyana says: Those who have climbed trees or mountains, those situated on elephants, horses, chariots, or boats,
and those standing in celestial palaces— all of them cannot be obstructed by those seeking to accomplish their tasks.

But he who, by restraining the senses through such means as suppressing speech or holding his breath, should constrain those who ought not to be constrained, shall be punished; however, he does not commit a transgression.

Thus, the meaning is that one who refrains from necessary bodily activity is subject to punishment, provided he has not committed a prior offense. As stated in another Smṛti: "Those who are ill, children, the elderly, those whose limbs are impaired, those occupied with urgent tasks, those overwhelmed by business, those addicted to vices, and likewise those engaged in the king’s service."
A king should never summon one who is intoxicated, insane, negligent, or afflicted,
nor a young woman of noble birth who has lost her protector or is recently delivered.
One should not marry a maiden who is the best among all castes if she is under the authority of her kinsmen.
"Under the authority of her kinsmen" means dependent on her kinsmen. Thus it has been said:
"The husband's side is the authority for women; in his absence, it is the father's side."
"He is the master in matters of employment, self-protection, and abduction.
Regarding certain cases, he states an exception to the preceding rule:
"Those whose households are dependent on him—namely, wanton women and courtesans—"
And for those who have been deprived of their families and those who have fallen from their caste, an invitation is appropriate.

The word "by the king" is to be understood as the ellipsis. In that regard, those who are incapable of conducting legal proceedings by their own nature—namely children, the elderly, and women—should proceed with their case by relying on a son or another trusted friend. Regarding this matter, Hārīta states the specific rule:
"He who is neither a brother, nor a father, nor a son, nor an appointed agent, yet speaks on behalf of another while giving false testimony in legal proceedings, shall be punished."
Nārada maintains that the victory or defeat of those [subordinates] is indeed the victory or defeat of the principal party alone:
"Whether appointed by the plaintiff or even sent by the defendant,
whoever litigates on behalf of another, the victory or defeat belongs to those two."

Bṛhaspati: He who states the prior and subsequent claims on behalf of those who are timid, dull-witted, insane, women, children, or diseased, is not liable for fault if he has been duly appointed [as their representative].
In cases of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, violating the teacher's wife,
and other such indecent accusations, no counter-accusation is permitted.
Except in the case of killing a human, theft, violating another's wife,
eating forbidden food, and the abduction or defilement of a maiden.

"In cases of harsh speech, forgery, and likewise treason against the king, the defendant shall not be compelled [to appear]; rather, the perpetrator himself shall plead the case. Thus, when there is an accusation of a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*) or similar offenses, all persons—including those who are unfit [to appear]—must be summoned by their own presence alone.
The king shall cause that very person to be summoned whom the plaintiff brings forward with truth and without suspicion, either by means of a seal or by a messenger.
Nārada said:
Having ascertained the place and the time, as well as the relative strength and weakness of the matters at hand,
the king should gradually cause even those who are unwell and so forth to be summoned by means of vehicles.

The meaning is that even for those who are ill, children, or the elderly, summoning them by their own presence—or by means of vehicles and the like—is required in cases such as treason against the king, Brahmins, or gods. Yājñavalkya states that this must be done only when the opponent is present.
Kātyāyana says: "A surety capable of resolving the matter should be taken from both parties."
If there is no surety for a litigant who is fit to plead,
he, being protected, shall at the end of the day give a fee to the messenger.
One who is capable of determining the legal matter and fit for detention, fines, and other penalties—regarding this, Kātyāyana states:
"A twice-born man who lacks a surety should be guarded by external watchmen;
however, Śūdras and others who lack a surety should be bound with fetters."
In case of transgression or failure to proceed, he should be fined eight paṇas;
however, the obstruction of the daily duties of people of all castes must not be permitted.

Thus ends the third section, the Section on the Plaint (*āvedana-kāṇḍa*), in the *Vyavahāranirṇaya* composed by the illustrious Varadarāja. [Now begins] the Section on the Framework of Legal Procedure (*vyavahāra-mātṛkā-kāṇḍa*).
In the *Vyavahāramātṛkā*, Yājñavalkya states the nature of the formal accusation (*abhiyoga*):
"The claimant must have the written statement prepared in the presence of the defendant,
exactly as it was asserted, marked with the year, month, fortnight, day, names, caste, and other identifying characteristics."

*Artha* means purpose. One who has something he wishes to establish is the *arthin* (plaintiff). One who stands as his opponent is the *pratyarthī* (defendant). Before him, in his presence, the document (*lekhyam*) is to be written. It must be written exactly as it was previously reported by the plaintiff at the time of entering the legal relationship (*saṃbandhapraveśanakāla*), and just as it was recorded then. Otherwise, there would be the risk of defeat on the grounds that he is "speaking otherwise" (*anyavādī*) or "averse to the legal action" (*kriyādveṣī*). Now, one might object: since that which was reported was already written at the time of entering the legal relationship, writing it again is redundant. To this he replies: "The year, month, [and so forth]. Writing it again is not redundant; for previously, the plaintiff reported only the matter to be proven (*sādhya*) without specifying particulars such as the time and so on. For example: "So-and-so, having taken gold and other goods from me, does not give them back even when requested. Now, however, it must be written again on a clean leaf (*śuddhe patre*) before the defendant, marked with specific details such as the year, month, and so on. This is the distinction. By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the quantity, measurement, and other such details of the property are included. Thus it has been stated by Bṛhaspati: [The text continues with the citation from Bṛhaspati.]
A thesis that is devoid of place and time, lacking in substance and number, and deficient in the measure of what is to be proven, is considered unacceptable.
And so says Prajāpati:
Standing before the opponent, one should set forth the proponent's position—
flawless, accompanied by a formal thesis, and endowed with valid means of knowledge and authoritative tradition.
One should record the substance, the number, the origin, the injury, and the evidence of endurance.
Regarding this, Kātyāyana states a specific rule:
"The place, the time, as well as the location and the settlement."
Birth, perception, and habitual tendencies, as well as the measure and the name of the field.
In disputes concerning immovable property, one should cause these ten items to be recorded: [the names of] the father and grandfather, and the proclamation of former kings.

This is the meaning: "Place" (*deśa*) refers to the Middle Country (*madhyadeśa*) and so forth. "Location" (*sthāna*) refers to Vārāṇasī and so forth. "Situation" (*saṃniveśa*) refers to houses, fields, and the like, properly situated there, demarcated by the divisions of the directions such as east and so on. "Caste" (*jāti*) refers to the Brahminhood and so forth of the plaintiff and the defendant. "Name" (*saṃjñā*) refers to Devadatta and so forth. "Neighborhood" (*adhivāsa*) refers to the adjacent area. "Measurement" (*pramāṇa*) refers to the dimensions such as *nivartana* and so forth. "Field-name" (*kṣetranāma*) refers to "rice-field," "betel-nut field," "black soil," or "white soil. Furthermore, there is the mention of the names of the plaintiff's and defendant's father and grandfather, as well as the proclamation of the names of the three preceding kings. The essential point is that in whatever legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) the year, month, and so forth are required, they should be written down to that extent. And thus says Kātyāyana:

One should examine the strength, the region, the territory, the location, the caste, the physical form, the age, the measure of the disease to be treated, the number [of attendants], and likewise one's own name.
One should compose statements indicating forgiveness after having proclaimed one's own side.

The rule is that it is nothing else. Whatever qualification is observed to have utility in a particular context, that qualification alone should be intended there, and not anything else; this is the established rule. In that regard:
"In the case of a gift, a purchase, or a prior [acquisition], the former is more powerful."

According to this statement, the specification of time is useful only in that case; as for place and so forth, they are useful only in transactions involving immovable property, because such matters must be regulated by neighbors. Therefore, one who desires the proof of a claim should state the accusation thus: "At such a place and at such a time, such an amount of such a substance was taken from me by him at such an interest rate, with the promise 'I will give it back at the time of request'; yet now, though requested, he does not pay. Otherwise, if it were merely said that "something was taken by someone," no legal process would proceed. When several cases arise simultaneously, Prajāpati has declared the order of precedence:
Having understood both benefit and harm, as well as merit and demerit in their entirety,
he should examine all the legal cases of the litigants according to the order of their castes.
Regarding this, Nārada states a specific rule:
"To whichever party the greater suffering occurs, or for whom the legal matter is more extensive, to him the *arthavāda* (consolatory statement) should be given; he shall present his case first."

The meaning is that "abhiyogavāda" is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). Bṛhaspati says: "When a dispute between a plaintiff and a defendant occurs through a scramble for priority, the trial should be conducted according to the order of the social classes (*varṇa*), or else by considering the relative suffering."
In another Smṛti:
"Whatever task is more important, that one should not clear first;
rather, one should attend to them either according to the order of social class (varṇa) or again according to the connection of their qualities."
If at that time a fault committed by the king of the gods should occur,
he would not be defeated merely by abandoning his inviolability.
Kātyāyana states that if the plaintiff is incapable, a period of time should be granted for his training:
"If the plaintiff, due to timidity, does not dare to speak,
a period of time should be granted to him in accordance with his capacity for the task."
He may obtain a written document after one day, or after three days, or even after seven days—
so long as it takes for the thought to arise in him who wishes to speak in the dispute.
And so it is stated in another Smṛti:
"One should indeed write upon the ground as long as the matter is not yet settled;
having corrected any deficiency or excess, one should subsequently enter it onto the document."

This is what is meant: at the time of the initial plea (*āvedana*), if something has been stated—either deficiently or excessively—due to passion (*rāga*) and so forth, and has been recorded on the wooden tablet (*phalaka*) or other such medium, nevertheless, at the time of the formal statement (*bhāṣā*), because of the subsiding of anger and other such emotions, one should cause the pure version to be written down on the document (*patra*), having adopted what was intended to be said in the presence of the opponent and having abandoned what was to be discarded. [Objection: But if that which was already stated is altered, would there not be a lack of legal certainty (*avyavasthā*)? [Response: There is no lack of certainty, because Nārada has established the rule. For it is said:
"The defendant (*pratyarthin*) shall not introduce anything until the reply (*uttara*) to the plaintiff’s statement (*bhāṣā*) [is received];
however, the plaintiff (*arthin*) shall write down [his claim] as long as the matter he intends to state remains."
Likewise,
one should examine the plaintiff's claim only until the defendant's reply is seen;
once the claim is countered by the reply, the examination shall cease.

Regarding the subsequent statement, however, because of the dictum that "the purification of a defective plaint consists solely in its withdrawal," it is impossible to alter what has been stated at a later stage; thus, there is no risk of an infinite regress (*avyavasthā*). If the members of the court (*sabhyas*) fail to purify that defective plaint when the defendant's reply is given—whether out of passion, greed, or fear, or by acting contrary to the law of memory (*smṛtyapeta*) and so forth—they are each to be punished individually according to the manner described. Furthermore, the examination of the legal case must indeed be conducted again, preceded by a new formal plea (*pratijñā*).
A prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) that is confused by multiple points is not established.

Thus, if this statement refers to the understanding of different means of proof (*sādhana*), the illustration is as follows: "At one time, gold was stolen by him; I shall prove it by oath. At another time, silver was also stolen; I shall prove it by witnesses. At yet another time, he took from me for the sake of compound interest (*vartulavṛddhi*) but does not give it when requested; that I shall prove by a document. When this has been stated, a sequential determination must be described due to the difference in the means of proof, not simultaneously. Otherwise, there would be a confusion (*saṃkara*) of the eighteen titles of law (*padāni*). Therefore, just as there is a difference in procedure (*kriyābheda*) according to the difference in the persons of the litigants, so too is there a difference in procedure due to a difference in the grounds (*hetubheda*). Consequently, a plaint (*pūrvapakṣa*) involving multiple titles with distinct means of proof cannot be established simultaneously; thus, legal procedure is appropriate through a division of time based on the difference in procedure. However, where even multiple titles are to be proven by a single means of proof, there it is argued that multiple propositions (*pratijñā*) are justified because of the difference in the objects to be proven (*sādhyabheda*).
Even a case involving many assertions that has been well-ascertained in legal proceedings,
the king may certainly take up, out of a desire to discover the truth.

"Thoroughly determined" (sunिश्चितम्) means determined as being fit to be proven by a single means of proof. Regarding that, Nārada states that the formal accusation (abhiyoga) is of two kinds: "The formal accusation is to be understood as twofold: through suspicion (śaṅkā) and through a formal charge based on the facts (tattvābhiyoga).
He states the reason for both:
But doubt regarding the wicked arises from association with them, as seen in the case of the stolen goods and so forth.

Suspicion arises from association with the wicked. *Hoḍhā* means the mark of a thief—that is to say, a portion of lost property; certainty [of guilt] follows from seeing such a portion of the stolen goods. Regarding both of these, the illustration is as follows: through association with thieves, the suspicion arises that "my property has been taken by this man"; this is a charge based on suspicion (*śaṅkābhiyoga*). And that is of only one form. A charge based on reality (*tattvābhiyoga*)—meaning a charge based on certainty—arises from seeing a portion of lost property. Kātyāyana states that this [charge based on reality] is of two kinds, in the form of an injunction (*vidhi*) or a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*).
"He who does not wish to do what is right, or who does what is unjust, and likewise fails to have it recorded in writing—his claim is not established. Thus [it is said].

“Not doing what is right” or “doing what is wrong”—thus, the formal charge (*abhiyoga*) is of two kinds. An example: having said, “I shall give it at the appointed time,” one takes gold or other goods from me for interest, yet when the time arrives and is requested, he does not give; this is a charge that he “does not do what is right. Or, “This man seizes my gold and other goods by force”; this is a charge that he “does what is wrong,” which is a charge of injustice (*anyāyābhiyoga*). Bṛhaspati states that these two types of charges are further divided into eighteen kinds according to the differences in the objects of proof, such as debts and so forth.
Legal procedure consists of two parts arising from wealth and injury;
it has fourteen divisions based on wealth, while that based on injury is fourfold.
And so Kātyāyana says:
"The two categories [of law] become eighteen through the distinction of the objects to be proven;
yet, due to the eighteenfold division of legal actions, they are divided here by the thousands."

The meaning is "in many ways" or "thousands of times" due to the diversity of actions among the disputing parties and their opponents. Now, Nārada states those eighteen titles of law: "Recovery of debts, deposits, partnerships, and likewise the resumption of what has been given, as well as non-compliance after having entered into an agreement."
Non-payment of wages, as well as sale without ownership,
non-delivery after having sold, and likewise rescission after having purchased;
Non-performance of agreements, disputes, and the son born of the field; the union of man and woman, partition of inheritance, and then violence.
Verbal assault, as well as physical assault,
gambling, and miscellaneous matters— these are recorded as the eighteen titles of law.

When the prima facie case (pūrvapakṣa) has been thus stated, Yājñavalkya states the reply in the *Vyavahāramātṛkā*: "The reply of one who has heard the matter should be written down in the presence of the plaintiff (*pūrvāvedaka*). "Heard" means experienced through direct perception by the person regarding the matter stated, and not from the words of another; his reply is to be written down in the presence of the plaintiff, the claimant (*arthin*). Kātyāyana [says]:
But when such a position has been formulated by the proponent,
the opponent should then provide a rejoinder that is connected to that position.

Nārada states that one should provide a reply at a later time that is connected to the plaint and capable of refuting the entire meaning of the claim. Those who know the law recognize such a reply as being comprehensive, essential, free from doubt, unconfused, and intelligible without further explanation.
Wherever one seeks time due to modesty, fear, or confusion regarding the recollection of the opponent's case, there one deserves to obtain this [time].
For one day, or three days, or even five or seven days,
or for a month, three months, or a year, he receives [the fruit] according to his capacity.
If [the child] has passed away, the impurity lasts for one day; if at six years, it lasts for three nights;
if at two years, it shall be exactly three nights; and if at twelve years, it lasts for seven days.
In the ninth year it shall be five days; in the twentieth, ten days;
with twenty-five years, half a month; and even at thirty years, a full month.
For men engaged in a dispute, the case should be decided no later than three fortnights from that time,
after the judge has taken into account the time, the capacity [of the parties], and the relative strength or weakness of the matters at issue.
The lord may grant a period of time, whether short or long, to the defendant.
What need is there for more?
In matters that require immediate action, one should initiate the legal dispute immediately.
Or, when the time has passed, the king shall grant time to the defendant.
In this matter, Prajāpati has declared:
"One day, or two, or three, or five, or seven;
however, in cases such as debt, the time for payment is traditionally held to be more than three fortnights."
Kātyāyana says: If one who is a dwarf, dull-witted, or afflicted by disease travels from another region after a year has passed, he shall have his own case determined according to the facts.
Furthermore, when the appointed time has passed due to a delay caused by the gods or the king, then another time should be granted.
Even when the time has already been granted, it may be granted again if the matter is of great importance.
— Hārīta.
When a case has been brought and the matter is contested, the reply must be given immediately thereafter;
if the time limit has not yet expired, the time for the reply is still granted even if the defendant has arrived later.
Now Bṛhaspati declares the immediate settlement of disputes:
regarding a cow, a bull, a field, women, and procreation;
likewise regarding a deposit, a loan for use, a gift, and similarly in buying and selling.
In cases of defiling a maiden, theft, quarrel, acts of violence,
fraud, and perjury, one should bring a lawsuit for immediate adjudication.

Yājñavalkya: In cases of violence, theft, verbal or physical assault, false accusations, and the violation of women, one should initiate a lawsuit immediately; in other matters, the time for litigation is said to depend on one's own will.
On this point, Kātyāyana provides the following reply: "The reply may be of four kinds: by way of denial, or by way of a counter-attack, or by way of establishing a prior judgment (prāṅnyāya)."

The illustration is as follows: when a charge has been made that "gold and other goods were taken from me," there are four possible types of reply (uttara) for the defendant: first, "It was not taken"; second, "It is true it was taken, but I shall return it"; third, "Having taken it, I gave it back"; and fourth, "In this very dispute, I have already been victorious. Such are the four kinds of replies that are possible. However, a reply such as "Having taken it, I do not give it back" is not possible [as a formal plea]. In that regard, regarding the reply "It was not taken," the claimant (pūrvavādin) must prove the act of taking. Regarding the reply "It is true it was taken, but I shall return it," no formal means of proof (kriyā) is required, because this is an admission (saṃpratipatti). Regarding the reply "Having taken it, I gave it back," since the act of taking is admitted, the defendant must prove the act of restitution. When it is said, "In this very dispute, I have already been victorious," the victory must be established by means of a written judgment (jayapatra) or by the judges (vyavahāradarśibhiḥ). Thus says Vṛddhavasiṣṭha:
Truth and falsehood, the grounds for the claim, the plea of prior judgment, and the various types of replies;
the truthful statement regarding the matter to be proven is declared to be "admission" (pratipatti).
If there should be a reason for an attack [on the defendant], it would be a false concealment of the truth.
Even if one has been defeated by conduct (*ācāra*), if he causes a document to be written again, he is to be declared as previously defeated; that is called *prāṅnyāya* (prior judgment).
Regarding this, Kātyāyana has stated the sequence for the subsequent pleadings:
"In the case of truth, one should employ truth; in the case of falsehood, one should record falsehood;
in the case of a plea based on a legal justification, one should state that justification; and likewise, in the case of a plea of prior judgment, one should state the victory."
Regarding that, Hārīta states the method of proof:

"In a case where the plaintiff’s claim is admitted (*prāṅnyāya*) or where a reason is stated (*kāraṇokti*), the defendant shall point out the means of proof (*kriyā*); but in a case of denial (*mithyokti*), the plaintiff shall do so; however, in a case of admission (*pratipatti*), no such means of proof is required."

And likewise Nārada says: "In a case of denial (*mithyā*), the means of proof lies with the plaintiff; in a case based on a special plea (*kāraṇa*), it lies with the defendant; but when a matter is established by a prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*), the production of a written decree of victory (*jayapatra*) shall take place."
Regarding the fourfold nature of falsehood, Hārīta states:
"This is false; I do not know it; I was not present there at that time;
and I was unborn at that time"—thus falsehood is fourfold.
Kātyāyana maintains that [a plea] is false if there is an absence of application in any way whatsoever; thus, it has the same meaning as [the charge].
Furthermore: "When another, having heard the meaning of the statement, denies it either in substance or in words, that answer should be known as 'false' (mithyā)."
Others also have likewise stated the definition of a false reply (mithyottara) in brief:
"If a defendant should deny the charge brought against him,
one should recognize that as a false reply (mithyottara) according to legal procedure."
Manu: If the defendant admits the matter written by the plaintiff exactly as it is and states a legal justification for it, that is indeed a counter-pleading (pratyavaskandana).

Some say that this alone should be considered a *ādhārya* (a case to be maintained). Vṛddhakātyāyana states: "One should know that a case is *ādhārya* where the action is stated by the plaintiff; it is not otherwise."
But where an action is absent or when it has indeed become subordinate— Hārīta says:
"Even if one has fallen away from right conduct, if he is caused to write [the confession] again..."
That which was previously defeated by him is called *prāṅnyāya* (a prior defeat).

In this context, the *kāraṇottara* (reply based on a reason) is of two kinds: pure (*śuddha*) and that which is accompanied by a denial (*mithyāsahacarita*). An example of the pure kind is as follows: when it is stated, "He took my hundred gold pieces," the respondent says, "It is true he took them, but they were returned. This very same [response] is called *ādārya* (confession), because it is set aside due to its being unprovable, and it is unprovable because of the admission [of the debt]. Furthermore, if the defendant, having admitted the matter exactly as it was written by the plaintiff with all its qualifications, states a reason, that is called *ādārya*. For example: "He took a hundred coins and did not return them; they were taken for the purpose of purchasing gold and other goods. Because of the admission of this fact—that they were taken [for a specific purpose] and not [simply withheld]—it is set aside due to its being unprovable. An example of the one accompanied by a denial is as follows: when it is stated, "My black horned cow was born in my house, it was lost at such-and-such a time, and it was seen in his house," the respondent says, "This is false; she was indeed born in my house, and she has remained in my house even prior to the time you have indicated. This is not a pure denial (*śuddhamithyā*), because of the presentation of a reason. Nor is it a pure reason (*śuddhakāraṇa*), because there is no admission of the claim as originally stated. For Manu, in defining the characteristics of a pure reason, stated: "The matter which was written down by the plaintiff... [and so forth]. Nor is it not a valid reply (*anuttara*), because it is capable of refuting the claim by means of its pervasiveness. This, then, is the reason accompanied by a denial.

Prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*), however, is of three kinds. First: when one who has been defeated in a previous case seeks to establish his claim through the procedure of prior judgment, saying, "I shall prove it by means of a certificate of victory (*jayapatra*)," for there is no certificate of victory in family disputes, according to the statement: "In family disputes, kinsmen are to be known as witnesses; they too are witnesses. Second: when he says, "I shall prove it by those very same judges who witnessed the case," according to the rule: "Whatever has been heard by the king seated on the seat of justice, seeing the truth—no other may be a witness there, except for the sovereign king. Third: [when he says], "I shall prove it by the witnesses who were present at that time. In this matter, the following is the settled rule: "If a debtor denies the debt in court, and the creditor proves it by means of a prior judgment, the king shall cause the denial to be recorded and shall make him pay the debt along with interest. This is the established law regarding prior judgment. Thus ends the section on prior judgment. Now follows the section on witnesses. It is said: "Witnesses are those who have seen or heard the facts of a case; they should be made to speak the truth in accordance with the sacred law. What is the meaning of this? It means that those who have directly perceived or heard the facts of a lawsuit, whether they be outsiders or insiders, should be made to testify to the truth in accordance with the sacred law. Furthermore, it is said: "They should be of good birth, virtuous, and speakers of the truth; they should be examined in the presence of both parties, and they should be made to swear an oath. What is the meaning of this? It means that those who are of noble lineage, endowed with virtue, and speakers of the truth should be examined in the presence of both litigants and made to swear an oath. Furthermore, it is said: "Those who are learned in the Vedas, those who know the Dharma, those who are pure, and those who are free from greed—these should be made witnesses in cases concerning immovable property. What is the meaning of this? It means that those who are proficient in the Vedas, those who know the sacred law, those who are pure, and those who are free from greed should be appointed as witnesses in cases involving land. Furthermore, it is said: "Women should be witnesses for women, Śūdras for Śūdras, Vaiśyas for Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas for Kṣatriyas, and Brahmins for Brahmins. What is the meaning of this? It means that women should be witnesses for women, Śūdras for Śūdras, Vaiśyas for Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas for Kṣatriyas, and Brahmins for Brahmins. Furthermore, it is said: "In cases of theft, adultery, robbery, and defamation, witnesses of any caste may be accepted. What is the meaning of this? It means that in cases of theft, adultery, robbery, and defamation, witnesses of any caste whatsoever may be accepted. Furthermore, it is said: "The king himself, or a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas, or a member of the assembly, or a guild, or a village headman, or a person appointed by the litigant—these are the six types of witnesses. What is the meaning of this? It means that the king himself, a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas, a member of the assembly, a guild, a village headman, or a person appointed by the litigant—these six are the witnesses. Furthermore, it is said: "One should not question a witness who is asleep, intoxicated, insane, distressed, or terrified. What is the meaning of this? It means that one must not examine a witness who is sleeping, intoxicated, insane, suffering, or afraid. Furthermore, it is said: "One should not question a witness who is a friend, an enemy, a relative, or one who has a motive for lying. What is the meaning of this? It means that one must not examine a witness who is a friend, an enemy, a kinsman, or someone who has a reason to lie. Furthermore, it is said: "A single witness is not admissible, except in the case of a woman, a Śūdra, or a child. What is the meaning of this? It means that a single witness is not valid, except when the case involves a woman, a Śūdra, or a minor. Furthermore, it is said: "When many witnesses contradict one another, the majority should be accepted; or else, those who are most consistent with the facts. What is the meaning of this? It means that when numerous witnesses give conflicting testimony, the majority view should be adopted; or alternatively, those whose accounts are most consistent with the actual facts should be accepted. Furthermore, it is said: "If a witness speaks falsely, he shall be punished with the highest fine; if he suppresses the truth, he shall incur the sin of killing all beings. What is the meaning of this? It means that if a witness gives false testimony, he shall be fined the maximum penalty; if he conceals the truth, he shall incur the guilt of having killed all living creatures. Furthermore, it is said: "If a witness dies after giving testimony, or if he is unable to appear, the judge shall summon him again and make him speak the truth. What is the meaning of this? It means that if a witness passes away after testifying, or if he becomes incapacitated, the judge shall call him back and compel him to speak the truth. Furthermore, it is said: "If a witness is summoned and does not appear, he shall be fined one hundred *paṇas*; if he appears and then departs, he shall be fined twice that amount. What is the meaning of this? It means that if a witness is called and fails to appear, he shall be fined one hundred *paṇas*; if he arrives and then leaves, he shall be fined two hundred *paṇas*. Furthermore, it is said: "If a witness speaks falsely out of affection for a friend, he shall be fined five hundred *paṇas*; if out of hatred for an enemy, he shall be fined one thousand *paṇas*. What is the meaning of this? It means that if a witness lies out of favoritism toward a friend, he shall be fined five hundred *paṇas*; if out of malice toward an enemy, he shall be fined one thousand *paṇas*. Furthermore, it is said: "In cases where the truth is obscured by falsehood, the king shall determine the facts by means of ordeals or oaths. What is the meaning of this? It means that in cases where the truth is hidden by lies, the king shall ascertain the facts through tests of divine proof or oaths. Furthermore, it is said: "The king shall protect the witnesses from intimidation; he shall punish those who obstruct them. What is the meaning of this? It means that the king must guard the witnesses against threats and coercion, and he must penalize those who interfere with them. Furthermore, it is said: "If a witness is questioned in the presence of the litigants and the court, and he remains silent, he shall be punished like a liar. What is the meaning of this? It means that if a witness is interrogated before the parties and the court and refuses to speak, he shall be punished as if he had told a lie. Furthermore, it is said: "If a witness is asked about a fact he knows but does not disclose, he shall be liable for the entire debt. What is the meaning of this? It means that if a witness is questioned regarding a matter he is aware of but fails to reveal it, he shall be responsible for the whole of the debt. Furthermore, it is said: "If a witness is asked about a fact he does not know but speaks anyway, he shall be liable for half the debt. What is the meaning of this? It means that if a witness is questioned about a matter he is ignorant of yet still provides an answer, he shall be liable for half the debt. Furthermore, it is said: "If a witness is asked about a fact he knows and speaks the truth, he shall receive a reward equal to the debt. What is the meaning of this? It means that if a witness is questioned about a matter he knows and tells the truth, he shall be granted a reward equivalent to the value of the debt. Furthermore, it is said: "If a witness is asked about a fact he knows but speaks falsely, he shall be punished with the highest fine. What is the meaning of this? It means that if a witness is questioned about a matter he knows and deliberately lies, he shall be fined the maximum penalty. Furthermore, it is said: "If a witness is asked about a fact he knows and speaks the truth, he shall be honored and rewarded. What is the meaning of this? It means that if a witness is questioned about a matter he knows and speaks the truth, he shall be respected and given a reward. Furthermore, it is said: "If a witness is asked about a fact he knows and remains silent, he shall be punished with the middle fine. What is the meaning of this? It means that if a witness is questioned about a matter he knows and stays mute, he shall be fined the intermediate penalty. Furthermore, it is said: "If a witness is
Because of this statement, and because of the absence of witnesses; the third [type of oath] is "I shall cause [the king] to prosper."

In this regard, because of the hearing of the singular number in the statement, "The answer to the subject matter heard [by the court] shall be written down," the confusion of multiple grounds of proof is excluded. For example: when it is said, "Gold, silver coins, jewels, and clothes were taken by him," the reply is, "It is true that gold was taken, I shall return it; the silver coin was given back; the clothes were not taken. Or, when it is said, "Gold and other jewels were taken for the purpose of purchase," in both cases there would necessarily be a legal proceeding (*kriyā*) based on two contradictory grounds of proof (*mithyākāraṇa*), which is impossible, because in a single lawsuit there cannot be two things to be proven (*sādhya*). Kātyāyana has stated all of this.
That which is true in one part of the thesis, a reason in another part,
and false in yet another part, is not a valid rejoinder because of its inconsistency.
Having said this, he stated right there:
"In a single lawsuit, there should not be legal proof for both parties;
there can be no establishment of the matter for both, nor can there be two proofs in one case."
Regarding that, Hārīta states that when there is a confusion [of pleas], one must act as follows:
"If both a false plea (*mithyottara*) and a plea based on a legal cause (*kāraṇa*) should occur in one case,
or if a true plea (*satya*) is combined with another, which plea is to be accepted therein?"
Having said this, it was further stated:
"In a case where the subject matter is extensive, or where the fruit of the legal action resides therein, the reply should be understood as 'unmixed' (asaṃkīrṇa); otherwise, it is the opposite."

In this way, the reply (*uttara*) remains unconfused therein; otherwise, it would be confused and result in a fragmentation of the legal suit (*vādabheda*). This is the meaning. An example: when a charge is brought that "this man, having taken from me one hundred gold pieces and one silver [coin], does not give them back when asked," and the defendant replies, "I did not take the hundred gold pieces, but I returned the single silver coin," there is no fragmentation of the suit. Since the burden of proof (*kriyā*) falls upon the plaintiff regarding the portion of denial (*mithyā*), and because that subject matter is extensive, the plaintiff himself must prove the absence of the return of the silver by means of that very proof; thus, there is no contingency of a fragmented suit. An example of the result of the burden of proof (*kriyāphala*): when a charge is brought that "having taken one gold piece from me, he not only refused to give it back when asked, but even struck me on the head," and the defendant replies, "I did not strike him on the head, and I returned the gold," even though such a reply is given, there is no fragmentation of the suit. Because the burden of proof for the plaintiff entails a heavier penalty, the plaintiff himself must prove both the striking of the head and the non-return of the gold. However, an example where there is a fragmentation of the suit due to equality of purpose and penalty is as follows: when a charge is brought that "having taken two gold pieces from me, he does not give them back when asked," and the reply is, "One was not taken, one was taken, and that was returned," there is a fragmentation of the suit because the purposes and penalties for the two claims are equal.
