Furthermore, when there are both denial (*mithyā*) and a plea of justification (*kāraṇa*) regarding the same thing to be proven (*sādhya*), an example is: "My horned cow was lost in such-and-such a month; it is seen in his house, yet when requested, it is not given. In this charge, the defendant, however, denies that the cow belongs to the plaintiff, asserts his own connection with it by claiming "That cow is mine indeed," and states a justification (*kāraṇa*): "That cow is mine alone; it has been in my house even before the time you mentioned. Thus, when there is a confusion of denial and justification in the reply, the justification itself should be accepted as the basis.
Or, even when there are two false pleas, the defendant's answer must be accepted as the true cause.

Because of this statement; and because of the statement: “When the defendant (*prativādī*) asserts a plea of denial (*abhāvavādin*) based on a cause (*kāraṇa*). [Objection: But is not the statement “A false plea (*mithyā*) involves an action (*kriyā*) in the case of the plaintiff (*pūrvavāda*)” also a scriptural authority? [Reply: True, but that refers purely to the intention of a false plea. [Objection: Why does the phrase “when the defendant asserts a cause” not refer purely to the intention of a valid cause (*kāraṇa*)? [Reply: Not so. By the word “defendant,” only the exclusion of a false plea (*mithyā*) in the case of a mixed reply (*saṃkarottara*) is expressed here. By the statement “A false plea involves an action in the case of the plaintiff,” it is said that he who has something to prove must provide proof. However, in the case of a reply based on a cause (*kāraṇottara*), the burden of proof lies with the defendant alone, according to the statement: “For even the plaintiff becomes the defendant (*uttaratva*) by virtue of the cause. Therefore, since the meaning of “when the defendant asserts a cause” is already established by the fact that “in a false reply, the plaintiff [proves],” it is well said that by the phrase “when the defendant asserts a cause,” only the exclusion of a false plea is intended. Now, Kātyāyana states the definition of fallacious replies (*uttarābhāsa*):
That which is contradictory, other than the subject, too little, or too much;
and that which pervades only a portion of the [opponent's] position—such a response would certainly not be valid.

And so Hārīta says: "A response that has its words transposed, that is non-comprehensive, whose meaning is obscure, that is confused, that can only be understood through further explanation, or that is substanceless— such a reply is not praised by the wise."
Examples—

An ambiguous reply (*saṃdigdha*) is, for example: when it is said, "He took a hundred pieces of gold," the reply is, "It is true he took them, but was it a hundred pieces of gold or a hundred *māṣas*? Or, when accused of a hundred pieces of gold, one says, "I owe a hundred pieces of cloth. An insufficient reply (*aty-alpa*) is, for example: when accused of a hundred pieces of gold, saying, "I owe fifty. An excessive reply (*ati-bhūri*) is, for example: when accused of a hundred, saying, "I owe a thousand. A reply that covers only a part of the claim (*pakṣaikadeśa-vyāpin*) is, for example: when accused of [stealing] gold and clothing, saying, "I owe the gold. A disjointed reply (*vyasta-pada*) is, for example: when accused of non-payment of debt, answering with a different subject, such as when accused of a hundred pieces of gold, saying, "I was beaten by him. An incomplete reply (*avyāpin*) means one that does not cover the specific details of place, location, and so forth; for example, when it is said, "A rice field was stolen from the northern direction in Vārāṇasī in the Middle Country," the reply is, "The field was not stolen. A cryptic reply (*nigūḍhārtha*) is, for example: when accused of a hundred pieces of gold, saying, "Am I the only one who owes it? This is cryptic because the plaintiff, the judge, a court member, or someone else owes it to another, and thus the meaning is hinted at. A confused reply (*ākula*) is one where the prior and subsequent parts are contradictory; for example: when accused of a hundred, saying, "It is true I took it, but I do not owe it. A reply requiring interpretation (*vyākhyā-gamya*) is one understood only through interpretation due to poorly joined case-endings, compounds, or ellipses; or due to using a local dialect, for example: when accused of a debt to a father regarding a hundred pieces of gold, saying, "I know the gold of my father was taken by word. Here, the meaning "I do not know that a hundred pieces of gold were taken" is understood through the interpretation of the phrase "by the word of my father, who took the hundred. A worthless reply (*asāra*) is, for example: when accused of having taken a hundred pieces of gold with interest, and further accused that only the interest was paid and not the principal, the reply is, "It is true the interest was paid, but the principal was not taken. — Kātyāyana.

Those defiled by great sins, whether driven by madness or intoxication; the mentally infirm, the blind, the elderly, women, and children—these should be known as those who are exempt from [legal] censure.
On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
"If the defendant does not provide a truthful answer according to the facts,
he should be compelled to do so by means of conciliation and other such methods."
The characteristics of conciliation (*sāman*) and the others are as follows:
*Sāman* is speech preceded by kindness; *bheda* (dissension) is the instilling of fear;
*daṇḍa* (punishment) is the deprivation of wealth, as well as beating and imprisonment.
But he who, though being urged by various means, does not give an answer after seven nights have passed, is defeated and deserves punishment.
Whether out of delusion or through deceit, that which was not stated by the proponent,
even if it is included within the reply, should be accepted by both parties.
Kātyāyana states: When a statement has been written down by its own nature and the determination of the case has begun,
he who speaks there of something not previously mentioned is defeated on account of that very matter.

This refers to matters other than adultery with another's wife, land disputes, and non-payment of debts, because in those cases there is no loss of wealth. Yājñavalkya concludes the *vyavahāramātṛkā*, which serves as the foundation for the entire system:
"Thereafter, the plaintiff shall immediately have the proof of the matter he has asserted committed to writing;
upon its establishment, he attains success, but otherwise the opposite occurs."
This fourfold judicial procedure has been set forth for the resolution of disputes.

Then, immediately after that subsequent plea (*uttarakāra*), the plaintiff (*arthin*)—the one who possesses the matter to be proven (*sādhyavān*)—should have it written down. One must not wait for a reply to the charge; rather, it should be done at once. That by which something is proven is the "means of proof" (*sādhana*), which is to say, the instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Consequently, the attainment of the characteristics of a document of victory (*jayapatra*) upon the establishment of the matter asserted is expressed by the word "success" (*siddhi*). Conversely, failure is defeat. Otherwise, if that [matter] is not established, there is no success. Therefore, the plaintiff should have the means of proving the matter asserted written down immediately. Here, by the mention of the "plaintiff," there is the inclusion of whoever has the matter to be proven. And this being so, in the case of a prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*) or when a reason is stated (*kāraṇokti*), even the defendant becomes the plaintiff because he possesses the matter to be proven and thus becomes the party of the first instance (*pūrvavādin*). And so says Kātyāyana:
For even the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) attains the status of a conclusion (uttara) by virtue of its logical cause;
therefore, the formal procedure (kriyā) is always said to be that which establishes the prima facie position.

The meaning is that the burden of proof (kriyā) belongs to the proponent of the claim. Bṛhaspati states: "In a plea of prior judgment and when a reason is alleged, the defendant shall indicate the proof;
but in a plea of denial, the plaintiff shall do so, while in a plea of admission, there shall be no such burden."

In that case, since the cause itself is what is to be proven (*sādhya*), its statement constitutes the *pratijñā* (thesis). Therefore, it is indeed appropriate for the opponent (*prativādin*) to provide proof regarding that very matter. As stated by Nārada:
"The essence of legal proceedings is declared to be the *pratijñā*;
if the proponent loses that, he loses the case, while the one who upholds it becomes the winner."

In accordance with the principle thus stated, this four-legged judicial procedure has been demonstrated for the disputes that are about to be described. As for what was previously stated—that "the king shall examine the legal proceedings with learned men"—in the case of *saṃpratipatti* (admission), there is no dispute because it is independent of proof. And so Bṛhaspati says: "In cases of false denial (*mithyokti*) and likewise in a counter-claim (*pratyavaskandana*), the procedure should be known as having four legs; in the case of a plea of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*) and admissions (*saṃpratipattiṣu*), it is known as having two legs."
On this point, Kātyāyana says:
"The plaint, the reply, the rejoinder,
and the stage of proof— this is declared to be the four-limbed [judicial process]."

In that *Vyavahāramātṛkā*, Yājñavalkya states: “The plaint (*pratijñā*) is to be written down in the presence of the defendant”; “The reply (*uttara*) is to be written by one who has heard the matter”; “Then the plaintiff shall cause the rejoinder (*pratyākalita*) to be written”; “The deliberation (*vimarśa*)—whether the proof belongs to the plaintiff or the defendant—is called the rejoinder (*pratyākalita*); “The means of proving the matter asserted (*pratijñātārthasādhana*) is the legal action (*kriyā*); and “Upon its establishment, he obtains success (*siddhi*)”—this is the fruit of the lawsuit (*vyavahāraphala*). Some, omitting the rejoinder, maintain that victory and defeat alone constitute the single limb [of the lawsuit]. That is incorrect, because victory and so forth are the fruits of the lawsuit, and since they exist even in the case of a confession (*saṃpratipatti*), there would be the undesirable consequence of [the lawsuit] having three limbs. But was not the four-limbed nature stated otherwise by Nārada?
“Dharma, judicial procedure (*vyavahāra*), custom (*caritra*), and royal edict (*rājaśāsana*):
this four-legged judicial process is such that each subsequent one sublates the preceding.

This is not so; for “four-legged judicial process” means that judicial process is of four kinds. It is precisely for this reason that it is stated, “each subsequent one sublates the preceding. Now, Kātyāyana speaks of compromise (*saṃdhi*).
But when the plaintiff and the defendant have been written down and the determination of the case has begun,
a reconciliation may occur between the two heated parties, like that of two pieces of iron.
And where there is a disagreement between both parties regarding the witnesses and the members of the court,
and while the case remains wavering, a settlement should be brought about there.
Where there is equality of authority but a difference between the scriptures and the conduct [of the parties], a reconciliation by royal decree is praised for both.
Bṛhaspati:
When a matter of law and a legal dispute are both subject to doubt before a king,
a settlement should be made there, just as with two pieces of iron heated together.
Then a peace should be made on equal terms, but one on unequal terms is withdrawn.
Having stated the manual of legal procedure (*vyavahāramātṛkā*) and analyzed its constituent parts, Yājñavalkya says:
"Without having fully resolved the charge (*abhiyoga*), one should not bring a counter-charge against this person;
nor should one subject the accused to another charge, nor should one alter what has been stated."

One who is being sued (the defendant) shall not, without having resolved the charge against him, bring a counter-charge against the plaintiff; nor shall he sue one who has been sued by another, because two legal proceedings cannot occur simultaneously. Likewise, at the time of the formal plea (*bhāṣākāla*), he must not lead to a change or alteration of what was stated at the time of the initial filing (*āvedanakāla*), for that would result in defeat for the opposing party. Regarding this, Nārada says:
"The man who, having abandoned his original claim, resorts to another, should be known as a loser of the case due to shifting his plea."
Even without having fully resolved the original charge, he states the counter-charge:
"In cases of quarrels and acts of violence, one may bring a counter-charge even without having first completed the formal process of the initial accusation.

In "quarrels and acts of violence," a counter-charge must necessarily be brought even before the original accusation is finalized, on the grounds that "I was previously struck by him" or "I was cursed by him," because the fault of the one who initiated the action first is more serious. And so says Nārada:
He who first utters an accusation will certainly be the one to bear the fault;
he who does so later is also a wrongdoer, yet for the former, discipline is paramount.
Regarding this, Nārada states that the plaintiff's statement should be presented in accordance with the counter-claim:
"To whichever party the greater suffering occurs, or whose case is more substantial,
to him the plaintiff's statement should be granted— not to one who failed to present it first."

Therefore, the plaintiff's statement (*arthivāda*) and the defendant's statement (*abhiyogavāda*) must be given only to the one who makes the counter-charge (*pratyabhiyogakartṛ*), not to the original accuser. And just as in the cases of *ādharya* and *pratyavaskandana*, it should be stated that his burden of proof (*ādharya*) consists of the reply (*uttara*) and the formal proposition (*pratijñā*). However, the status of being the "thing to be proved" (*sādhyatva*) belongs to that which possesses the reply by virtue of the meaning already stated; for since it is the very object of the proposition (*pratijñārtha*) that is to be proved, the plaintiff's statement must be given only to the one who makes the counter-charge, and the defendant's statement not to the original accuser. And just as in the cases of *ādharya* and *pratyavaskandana*, it should be stated that his burden of proof consists of the reply and the formal proposition. The status of being the "thing to be proved" resides in the nature of the reply, because it is precisely the object of the proposition that is to be proved. And so says Kātyāyana:
That which the proponent intends to establish clearly for himself is the *sādhya* (the probandum); by means of that [reasoning], the entire *sādhya* is established.

Now, regarding the *pratijñā* (thesis): it is said that two types of *pratijñā* are appropriate in a single debate; namely, both the form of the reply and the thesis itself. This was clearly stated by Bṛhaspati:
"When a proponent advances a position without stating the reason, that should be known as a *pratipatti* (acknowledgment); the reason, however, is a distinct *uttara* (reply)."

If one accepts [the claim] as independent of a reason (*kāraṇa*), then there is agreement. However, when a reason is stated, the response consists of two other forms: the reason and the proposition (*pratijñā*). Since the reason is itself that which is to be proven, its status as a "proposition" is not contradictory. When one accepts a matter previously denied, it is logical for it to be a "reason" (*hetu*) because it brings about the state of being proven (*sādhyatva*). Therefore, the same principle applies in the case of a counter-accusation (*pratyabhiyoga*), a confession of weakness (*ādharya*), and a defensive plea (*pratyavaskandana*). Yājñavalkya says: "In the case of denial, if one is proven [guilty], he shall pay the wealth to the king and an equal amount [as a fine]."
One who brings a false accusation shall pay double the amount of the claim from his own wealth.

If a defendant denies what has been written by him as false, and is subsequently proven by documents and other evidence to be in the wrong by the plaintiff, he shall pay that amount of money to the king as a fine. If he is unable to prove his case, then the one who brought a false accusation shall pay double the fine to the king. Yājñavalkya states: "If he denies a document, and even if he is proven on one part, he must be made to pay the whole debt by the king; nor should he accept wealth that was not previously declared."

If a defendant denies or disavows everything that has been written down as a claim—whether it be gold, silver, clothing, or other items of various kinds—and the plaintiff subsequently proves through witnesses or other means even a single portion of that claim, such as gold or something else, and causes the defendant to admit it, then the king shall compel the defendant to pay the entire previously written amount to the plaintiff. An object that was not mentioned by the plaintiff at the time of the initial plea (*bhāṣā*), but is later introduced with the claim "I had forgotten it before," is not to be accepted at the time of the plea. And so says Nārada:
When a person charged with multiple matters denies all the charges,
yet only one part of the case is proven against him, he must pay what was claimed against him.
Bṛhaspati:
"If a person, having made a total denial, should then admit even a small portion, he must be made to pay the entire amount; so says Bṛhaspati regarding one who is accused."
As for the statement of Kātyāyana:
"But when there is a lawsuit involving multiple claims,
the creditor recovers from the witnesses only as much wealth as he proves to be due."
Thus, this refers to the subject of debts owed by sons and others to fathers and others;
for there is the statement: "A debt must be paid by sons and grandsons when it has been proven by witnesses despite denial. Furthermore, as for this statement of Kātyāyana:
In disputes concerning debts and the like, which are generally of a stable nature, once a decision has been reached,
the matter cannot be proven even if the amount stated is either less or more than the truth.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: it is certain that when witnesses and other such means, which have been presented as proving every matter (*sarvārtha*), state only a portion or even more than the required portion, the point to be proven (*sādhya*) is not established. However, in cases such as *sāhasa* (violent crime), since the witnesses are designated as proving the entirety of the matter to be proven, even if they establish only a single part, the whole matter to be proven is indeed established. Kātyāyana states:

"When even a portion of the matter to be proven has been declared by witnesses, the whole shall be [considered proven], provided it concerns sexual intercourse, violence, or theft—whatever has been proclaimed as the matter to be proven."
Yājñavalkya:
In all disputes concerning property, the subsequent legal act is stronger;
however, in the case of a mortgage, a gift, or a purchase, the prior act is more powerful.

That which is performed is an action (*kriyā*), meaning an effect (*kārya*). Among all disputes concerning matters such as debts and the like, the subsequent answer (*uttara*) is stronger. For example: one person establishes the taking of a debt, saying, "I borrowed a hundred [coins] from him," while another establishes its repayment, saying, "I returned it. Since the subsequent answer—namely, the repayment—is stronger, the proponent of that answer becomes the winner because he has established his point. Even though the prior matter was established, the proponent of that prior claim is defeated. Regarding fields and other such property: if one makes a single field a pledge (*ādhi*) for one person and then again makes it a pledge for another, it belongs to the former alone, not to the latter.
When witnesses exist on both sides, the witnesses belong to the plaintiff;
when the initial claim has been refuted, they belong to the defendant.

In that case, one person says, "This field was obtained by me through a formal gift from a certain man," and another says the same. Although witnesses exist for both sides, the witnesses belong to the plaintiff (*pūrvavādin*). In that situation, if the plaintiff's position is refuted and he says, "It is true this was given to him first, but the King took it from his very hand by purchase and gave it to me," then the witnesses of the defendant (*uttaravādin*) also become relevant. Now, the characteristics of litigants who are considered corrupt are stated. Regarding this, Nārada says:
Through physical forms, gestures, gait, movements, and speech,
as well as through changes in the eyes and face, the internal mind is perceived.
Trembling, perspiration, and change of complexion; touching the lips and drying them; scratching the ground, leaving one's place, and looking askance or upwards.
And a change in voice—these the wise declare to be the signs of a corrupt person.
Yājñavalkya: He moves from one place to another, licks his lips repeatedly,
his forehead perspires, and his face turns pale.
With parched mouth and faltering speech, he speaks much that is contradictory;
he does not honor his words or his eyes, and likewise distorts his lips.
He who undergoes a change from his natural state through actions of mind, speech,
or body during a legal proceeding or when giving testimony is declared to be a wicked person.
The intention is that these signs occur by force in one whose mind is already set on defeat. Nārada says:
"Making excuses while wasting time, speaking falsely in the assembly, or speaking after having already said something—these are the marks of one who is losing."

Manu says: He who points out what should not be pointed out, he who denies after having pointed it out, and he who does not understand the matters that are either inferior or superior; [these are liable to punishment].
Furthermore, he who, having stated what was to be stated, subsequently evades it;
and who, when questioned, does not accept a matter that has been correctly formulated.
If, when told "Speak," he does not speak, or if he fails to clarify what has been said,
or if he cannot discern the consistency between what precedes and what follows, he is defeated on that account.
Having said, "There are those who know," if one who has been asked to point them out does not do so,
the judge, by these reasons, shall declare even that person to be defeated.
If the plaintiff does not speak within three fortnights, he shall be punished with a fine and, according to the law,
shall be defeated in his suit regarding the matter of justice.
Bṛhaspati:
But he who, having pointed out witnesses,
does not produce them within thirty nights or three fortnights, incurs defeat.
Kātyāyana says: Having set aside the essential word, one may pursue many non-essential ones in a legal proceeding; however, one should abandon that which is devoid of essence.
Nārada says: Once a legal dispute has been decided, the evidence— whether documentary or testimonial— is rendered useless,
provided it was not previously presented.
Just as the qualities of the rainy season are fruitless when the grains have already ripened,
so too is evidence useless for those whose legal case has already been decided.
[Thus ends the section on the characteristics of defects for the proponent and the opponent.
Now follows the section on the performance of the legal action;
regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
Action is said to be of two kinds: human and likewise divine;
each of these is divided into many varieties by the seers who know the truth.
Oral testimony, documentary evidence, and inference are recorded as the threefold human means of proof;
while the ordeal by balance, ending with the ordeal born of dharma, constitutes the ninefold divine procedure.
Witnesses are of twelve kinds, written evidence is recorded as tenfold,
inference is of two types, and divine proof is ninefold.

The phrase "inference, however, is of two kinds" refers to the inclusion of both presumption (*arthāpatti*) and inference (*anumāna*). To explain: possession (*bhukti*) qualified by certain specific attributes is a cause for ownership; it, moreover, leads to the inference—due to its non-deviation—from such things as purchase, witnesses, or documentary evidence. Or, being otherwise unaccountable, it leads to a postulation; thus, it is said that inference is of two kinds, referring specifically to possession. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states: "They know the threefold means of proof to be witnesses, documents, and possession. As for the indication of a sign (*liṅga*), there are two methods, such as fire, poison, and so forth."
For a debt, documentary evidence, witnesses, or even fragments of reasoning,
as well as divine means of proof, have been declared for the benefit of subjects.

The phrase "or divine" (*daivikī vā*) does not constitute an option of equal weight with the preceding [means of proof]; rather, it applies only when there is an absence of the aforementioned means of proof. Thus says Yājñavalkya: "Written documents, possession, and witnesses are declared to be the means of proof. In the absence of any one of these, one of the ordeals (*divya*) is prescribed."
And so say Nārada and Bṛhaspati:
"When a legal proceeding has been conducted during the day in villages or cities,
and witnesses are available, an ordeal is not to be employed."
On this point, Kātyāyana states:
"When witnesses are available, an ordeal is not prescribed;
nor, when there is a written document, should there be either an ordeal or witnesses in legal disputes."
And so Vyāsa says:
"When witnesses are available, a wise man should avoid divine means of proof;
for one who employs divine means when witnesses are available certainly suffers defeat."
Regarding this, Kātyāyana states the distinction:
"If one party should propose human evidence and the other should propose divine evidence,
the king should accept the human evidence in that case, but not the divine procedure."

When two litigants, plaintiff and defendant, have come before the judges of law, and one relies upon human proof (*mānuṣī kriyā*) while the other relies upon divine proof (*daivī*), it is ruled that the human proof alone is to be accepted. Likewise:
"If even a partial human proof exists, that is to be accepted; but not even a complete divine proof for men who speak [in court]."

Even where the entire matter arises from fate (*daiva*) and only a portion arises from human agency (*mānuṣa*), even then one should not resort to ordeal (*divya*). For example: suppose a defendant denies a lawsuit by claiming that although he received a hundred *rūpakas* from the plaintiff on interest, he does not owe it when demanded; in this case, there are witnesses for the receipt itself, but not for the amount, nor for the specific rate of interest. There, the determination of the interest or the amount cannot be established by ordeal. Furthermore, the defendant cannot be subjected to ordeal for the whole matter under the principle of "proving a part" (*ekadeśavibhāvitanyāya*), because once the nature of the debt is proven by witnesses, the specific amount and rate of interest are established as a matter of course; thus, there is no room for ordeal. As for that which [is stated]: [The text continues with the citation: "But when..."
But for those who commit secret acts of violence, examination by means of ordeals is appropriate,
as well as [examination] through subtle reasoning, gestures, facial expressions, speech, the eyes, and the physical movements of men.

Thus, even that [rule] is intended as a restriction for cases where human means are unavailable. Therefore, in all instances where human means are unavailable, the decision is made by divine proof (*divya*).
The following statements are set forth to establish the application of documents, witnesses, possession, divine proofs, and so forth. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"In cases of verbal abuse and regarding land, one should avoid divine proof."
In connection with the giving and taking of goods in sale, they desire wealth after having purchased.
In matters of gambling, duels, and when a dispute has arisen, witnesses are declared the means of proof; neither divine ordeals nor written documents are required.
Regarding the status that has been proclaimed for guilds, trade associations, corporations, and the like, their proof is documentary evidence; neither ordeal nor witnesses are required.
Likewise, in matters such as gates, paths, works, enjoyment, and the flow of water, possession alone shall be weighty; neither a written document nor witnesses [are required].
On this point Vyāsa says: "An act is said to be of two kinds: done in secret and done openly. An open act must be established by witnesses; a secret act is established by divine means."
In another Smṛti: "In cases of verbal abuse, disputes over land, and even in all four types of violent acts (sāhasa), divine proof (daivikī kriyā) is forbidden; it must be diligently avoided."
The fourfold acts of violence (*sāhasa*) are: killing a human being, theft, adultery, and verbal or physical cruelty.
Killing a human being, theft, violating another's wife, and both forms of cruelty—verbal and physical—constitute the fourfold *sāhasa*.
Thus, according to the statement of Kātyāyana: "Likewise,
when no witness is found for men disputing,
then one should examine them by means of ordeals and various kinds of oaths."
In cases involving the violation of women's virtue, as well as in theft and acts of violence, such a rule is seen to apply; and likewise in all instances of denial of one's own property.
But for those who commit secret acts of violence, examination by means of ordeals is appropriate,
as well as [examination] through subtle reasoning, gestures, facial expressions, speech, the eyes, and physical movements of men.
Likewise, it is stated elsewhere:
"One who fakes gems, pearls, and corals; one who misappropriates deposits; a violent person; and one who consorts with another's wife—these must always be examined by means of oaths."
In cases involving charges of great crimes, as well as the misappropriation of deposits,
the king should examine the matter by means of ordeals, even when witnesses are present.
Where there is equality among witnesses, one should purify [the matter] by means of ordeals;
even when witnesses are available in disputes where the penalty involves the loss of life.
The litigant resorts to divine proof; in that case, he should not question witnesses.
When a doubt arises regarding a written document or the testimony of witnesses, [he may resort to divine proof].

"And when inference is confused, one should not then employ divine means," according to the statement of Bṛhaspati. When a written document has become unreliable and witnesses have been defeated [in their testimony], [one may resort to ordeals].
And when there is an absence of logical reasoning, divine means [of proof] should be employed, provided that the three causes are present.

This is because of the statement of Kātyāyana: "In the absence of any one of these [means of proof], one of the ordeals (*divya*) is prescribed. And because of the statement of Yājñavalkya: "When documentary evidence, possession, witnesses, and written records are non-existent, the ordeal must be administered; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a baseless argument," so say Dhāreśvara, Udyotana, Kṛṣṇa, and others, on the grounds that in private disputes there would otherwise be the possibility of no ordeal being available. For instance:
There may be an act such as writing a document, or an oath, or even an ordeal;
indeed, in all disputes, one should employ an ordeal.

This is because it contradicts the statement of Prajāpati, and because it also contradicts the statement of Yājñavalkya: "In the absence of any one of these [human means of proof], one of the ordeals (divya) is prescribed. Therefore, in all types of legal disputes, even when witnesses and other means are available, if a decision cannot be reached through them, or if they are unavailable, the use of an ordeal is indeed appropriate. Now, one might ask: how can there be an application of ordeals in every case?
"In disputes concerning immovable property, one should avoid ordeals";
likewise,
"in cases of verbal abuse and disputes over land, divine means of proof are forbidden."
Thus,
in the case of gambling, betting, and when a dispute has arisen,
witnesses are declared the sole means of proof; neither divine ordeal nor written documents are required.
Thus, regarding the status that has been proclaimed for guilds, trade associations, corporations, and the like,
the proof thereof is documentary evidence; neither divine ordeal nor witnesses are required.

Because of such statements as these, there is a restriction of specific means of proof (*pramāṇa*) in specific types of disputes. It is said in reply: statements such as these are intended to establish the superior force of specific means of proof like documentary evidence (*lekhyādi*) in specific disputes, but they do not intend to exclude other means of proof such as ordeals (*divyādi*). If that were the case, there would be a contradiction everywhere with the scriptural injunctions that mandate the use of various means of proof. Therefore, when another means of proof is possible, there is no ordeal in a dispute over land. Likewise, in gambling and betting, if witnesses are available, there is neither ordeal nor documentary evidence. Similarly, in disputes concerning debts and the like, if documentary evidence is available, there is the rule: "neither ordeal nor witnesses. In other types of disputes, it is appropriate to resort to other means of proof after stipulating a penalty, such as doubling the fine for the defeated party. However, in disputes over land and the like, even by the imposition of doubling the fine for the defeated party, there is no provision for ordeals and the like; thus, there is no contradiction.

Thus ends the fourth section, the Section on Human Means of Proof (*mānuṣapramāṇakāṇḍa*), within the Section on the Framework of Legal Procedure (*vyavahāramātṛkākāṇḍa*) in the *Vyavahāranirṇaya* composed by the illustrious Varadarāja.
Now, the means of proof are being stated:
among them, human proof is threefold, consisting of documents, possession, and witnesses;
and human proof is traditionally held to be threefold: witnesses, documents, and inference.
Thus, according to the statement of Bṛhaspati: "Furthermore,
since confusion may arise even at the six-month interval,
[the document] should previously have been written on a leaf with clearly legible letters."
A document is said to be that which includes the local customs, the year, month, fortnight, and day, as well as the increase [of interest],
and is marked with the hand-signatures of the debtor, the witnesses, and the scribe.

In this regard, *lekhya* (written evidence): since it makes the meaning of a statement known through words inferred from the handwriting, syllables, and signatures of the author, the scribe, and the witnesses, it is verbal testimony (*śābda-pramāṇa*). Among these, for a document written by another's hand, there is a requirement for multiple witnesses, a requirement for a scribe, and a requirement for an author; these requirements for the totality of written materials are established by the rules of the *śāstra*. For a document written in one's own hand, the lack of requirement for a scribe or witnesses is also established by the rules of the *śāstra*. Furthermore, witnesses, through words rooted in their own direct perception and other means of knowledge, make the meaning known according to the rules declared in the *śāstra*; thus, it is indeed verbal testimony. And the rule in the *śāstra* that "at least three [witnesses] must be virtuous," and so forth, is intended to demonstrate the manner of cognition.

Now, possession (*bhukti*) is discussed—it is distinguished by five specific characteristics. Alternatively, it is a means of inference (*anumāna*) that does not require a logical mark (*liṅga*) such as purchase, which serves as the cause for establishing ownership; therefore, the intention is that possession is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), whether as inference or as presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), like a fragment of reasoning (*yuktileśa*). Regarding this, Nārada states the distinction:
"A written document is always powerful, and witnesses are indeed powerful while they live;
but possession prevails through the lapse of time—this is the certainty in the scriptures."

A document that is free from defects is always authoritative. Witnesses are authoritative only during the period when they are living. After a long time has passed, possession is authoritative. Regarding this, Prajāpati says:

"Written documents are remembered to be of two kinds: royal and local. A royal document refers to edicts and the like granted by the king; a local document refers to promissory notes for debts and the like."
A document executed when granted by a king is called a royal edict (rājaśāsana).
In disputes concerning debts and the like, a document issued by a local official is called a *cīraka*. Regarding that, he states the characteristics of a royal edict (*rājaśāsana*):
"That which is written by the scribes of peace and war with the king’s own hand-signature, marked with the king’s name, and sealed with the royal seal."
It is marked by the years, months, half-months, and days, along with the signs of birth and so forth;
it is endowed with the sequence of clear phonemes, with its order and syllables unimpaired.
This royal edict is the most excellent of all written documents.
Regarding this, Vyāsa says:
"The scribe of peace and war, however, must be personally appointed by the king."
One should engrave the royal edict either upon a copper plate or on a cloth.
A document known as a *cīraka* is written by eminent city scribes, containing the names of the plaintiff, the defendant, and the witnesses, along with the year, month, and other details.

A royal document (*rājalekhya*) is defined as one executed by scribes and others appointed in the royal court, marked with the hand-signature of its presiding official, and sealed with the king’s own seal. A local document (*sthānalekhya*), however, is one executed by scribes authorized in villages, districts, and so forth, marked with the hand-signature of their presiding official, and is called *cīrita*. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states the distinction: "A royal document, a local document, and likewise one written in one's own hand—document is said to be of three kinds; furthermore, that [royal document] is divided into ten types."
A deed of gift, a deed of partition, and likewise a deed concerning boundaries;
a deed of purchase, a deed concerning slaves, and thereafter a deed of mortgage.
A document of agreement, a deed of victory,
and likewise a treaty— these are of many kinds according to the diversity of legal transactions.
But having given land, whatever document one should have made for as long as the moon and sun shall endure;
Thus ends the summary.
Now, the definition:
A document of gift is traditionally defined as that which is neither subject to seizure nor susceptible to removal.
This document of partition constitutes the final determination of the shares.
When a boundary dispute has been settled, it is known as a "boundary document" (sīmāpatra);
likewise, after purchasing a house, field, or the like, one should possess a document containing identical terms and letters [as the original sale deed].
That document which one causes to be made is called a *krayalekhya* (purchase deed);
a mortgage deed is for the purpose of a pledge (*ādhi*), and a slave-deed is for the purpose of a slave.
For the sake of accomplishing their desired objectives, the village, guilds, corporations, and so forth,
have executed this deed of agreement for the purpose of dharma, in accordance with the scriptures.
Having received money for the sake of interest, one should either do the work oneself or cause it to be done;
this is called an *uddāmapatra* (open bond), a document of debt, by the wise.
Kātyāyana states the characteristics of a decree (*jayapatra*):
"It shall be connected with the matter to be proven as it was presented, accompanied by the subsequent legal proceedings,
containing a definitive conclusion, and sealed with the royal seal."

A document of victory (jayapatra) is required to bear the seal of the court assembly, to include the names of both the plaintiff and the defendant, and to be marked with the hand-signatures of the presiding judge and others.
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha states the characteristics of the written record of the proceedings: "The statements of the plaintiff and the defendant, the plaint, the testimony of witnesses,
as well as the decision and how it was determined by himself."
This should be written exactly according to the syllables as it was previously entered;
in all four types of legal disputes, a document of victory is issued for the winner.

When a decision has been reached by means of witnesses and other such evidence, yet there is no document of victory (*jayapatra*), a "document of decision" (*nirṇayapatra*)—that is to say, a "granted document" (*prattapatra*)—must be executed in that case. Thus says Kātyāyana:

"A document that is not contrary to local custom, which clearly possesses the characteristics of the parties involved, and whose sequence and letters are not effaced—that is recognized as valid evidence."
And those members of the assembly present there who are learned in the treatises on law (smṛti), as well as those skilled in the art of writing,
should likewise cause their own signatures to be affixed there.
The plaintiff shall first set down the statements of those who are accused;
thereafter, he shall record the statements of the members of the court, the presiding judge, and the witnesses.
One should cause the definitive opinion of the treatises on law (smṛti-śāstra) to be recorded therein;
when a treaty has been concluded, the document produced for that purpose is called a "treaty-deed" (saṃdhilekhya).
Now, regarding the document of hand-delivery (*karalekhya*),
Kātyāyana states:
"The document of hand-delivery and others are recorded as being accompanied by the established customs of the region."
Furthermore, that measure would be deficient by one year, month, and so forth.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states a specific rule:
"Whatever matter has been settled by mutual agreement through their own consent,
a document should be executed for it, provided with witnesses, preceded by the name of the creditor."

[The name] should be accompanied by the year, month, and half-month; [it should indicate] the caste, one's own lineage (gotra), the name of a fellow student (sabrahmacārin), and the names of one's father and so forth as identifying marks.
When the matter is concluded, the debtor shall record his own name by his own hand:
"What is written above is approved by me, the son of so-and-so."
"Requested by both parties, this has been written by me, the son of so-and-so, named so-and-so"; thus the scribe should write at the end.
Even without witnesses, a document written in one's own hand is declared to be valid evidence in its entirety, except when it was produced through force or fraud.
A debt recorded in writing must be paid by three generations of persons;
likewise,
witnesses [should sign] with their own hands, preceded by the names of their fathers and so forth.
"In this matter, I, so-and-so, shall write as a witness"—thus they should write, being equal [in status].
One who is illiterate or a debtor should have his own opinion recorded;
or a witness, by means of another witness, in the presence of all the witnesses.

When the document is completed, the debtor shall write his own name with his own hand; after him, the scribe, and after him, the witnesses. For those who are illiterate, their own opinion must be recorded by another. In that case, a document written in one's own hand is valid evidence even without witnesses. A document written by another person for one who is illiterate is valid only if it possesses witnesses. Regarding immovable property, in the case of a mortgage, partition, inheritance, gift, or purchase, a transaction is not established without a document.

Thus, this statement of Kātyāyana is intended to emphasize the importance of the document (*lekhya*), and not to exclude other means of proof; for were it so, it would contradict other scriptural injunctions. This is the meaning here: among the aforementioned qualifications of a document, that which serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) in a given case should be adopted there, and not the others, lest they result in having no visible purpose. Furthermore, regarding the document in this context, Yājñavalkya says:
If a document is located in another country, difficult to read, lost, erased,
stolen, torn, burnt, or likewise cut, one should have another document prepared.
The meaning is that when a previously executed document is incapable of being used in legal proceedings, one should cause another document to be made. Vyāsa says:
"A document written by oneself, accompanied by witnesses and signatures, and marked with one's own hand-signature, is superior to one written by another, even if the latter is not publicly known."

Kātyāyana states: A document is established as valid in all cases— provided it was presented at the proper time, read aloud, and likewise reminded [of its contents]— even when the witnesses have died.
Bṛhaspati: A written document is never superseded by witnesses or by an oath;
one suffers loss through neglect due to failure to produce it or failure to hear it [read].
A document that is more than thirty years old, or one that has not been seen or heard by [the parties],
does not attain validity, even though witnesses may still be present.

Vyāsa states the reasons why a document fails to establish its validity: "A document that has not been read, one whose meaning has not been seen, or one brought forward during a legal proceeding, does not attain validity even if the witnesses are still living."
Elsewhere also:
"If the depositor has disappeared, become invisible, or died,
that document is [considered valid] even if the property was not taken back or was returned."
Vyāsa says:
Therefore, a royal edict issued by the king's own hand is held to be more authoritative than one issued by a provincial official when it has come before the court for legal proceedings.
Likewise, elsewhere it is said:
"Where a document concerning the countryside has been executed by a provincial governor or similar official,
whether at the same time as or after [the original], that document concerning the countryside is authoritative."
Bṛhaspati states that when the scribe and witnesses have passed away, one may resolve any doubt by means of other characters written by them:
"If the scribe, along with the witnesses, has met his death,
there shall be no doubt that [the document] is validated by their own handwriting and the like."
When a doubt arises regarding a document, it should be resolved by means of the witnesses, the scribe, and the author;
and when these are found to be corrupt, by means of previous letters written in their own hands and other such evidence.
The king should cause a decision to be made by means of those [means] as they happen to be available.
Nārada says:
A document that has not been heard of, one whose contents have not been witnessed, or one produced for the purpose of litigation,
does not attain validity even if witnesses are still living.
In cases where there is doubt regarding the hand of a debtor— whether he is living or dead—
the determination of that document is made by other documents written in his own hand.
Yājñavalkya: The purification of a doubtful document may be established by means of a signature written in one's own hand and so forth,
as well as by reasoning, acquisition, performance, marks, connection, and evidence of provenance.

When a document is doubtful, its validity is established by other documents written by those same hands; from the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it follows that validity arises from corroboration with other writings in the hand of the witnesses or the scribe. "Attainment through reasoning" (*yuktiprāpti*) means the attainment of a logical connection between the place, time, and person with the object. "Attainment through reasoning" is when it is logically consistent that this specific object could belong to this person at this time and in this place. "Action" (*kriyā*) refers to the production of evidence or the presentation of witnesses. A "mark" (*cihna*) is an uncommon sign of personal ownership. "Connection" (*saṃbandha*) is a prior relationship between the plaintiff and the defendant based on mutual trust, such as lending and receiving. "Source" (*āgama*) is the probable means of acquisition for such an amount of wealth. These are the grounds [for proof]; by these, the validity of the document is established. Kātyāyana states the examination of the document: * **By other documents:** When a document is suspected of being forged, its purity is determined by other documents written by the same hand. * **By handwriting:** Validity comes from the correspondence with other writings in the hand of the witnesses or the scribe. * **By reasoning:** This is the attainment of a logical possibility, such as the connection of place, time, and person with the property. For example: "In this place, at this time, it is reasonable that this person possesses this property. * **By action:** This refers to the performance of the act or the adducing of witnesses. * **By a mark:** This refers to a unique sign of possession. * **By connection:** This is a prior relationship between the claimant and the defendant involving trust, such as transactions of giving and taking. * **By source:** This is the plausible means by which such an amount of wealth was acquired. These are the causes [of proof]. Through these, the validity of the document is established. Kātyāyana thus describes the examination of the document.
If the debtor, upon seeing the document, does not explicitly state a manifest defect,
then the document shall remain valid after the lapse of twenty years.
If a person enjoys property through a document in the presence of one who has the power [to object],
for a period of twenty years, that document is free from defect.

One's own kinsmen deceive women, children, the afflicted, and those ignorant of writing by having them sign documents marked with their own names; such matters are to be understood through reasoning, tradition, and other means.
Vyāsa says:
Where a document executed by one person is seen in the hand of another,
the production of that document must necessarily be obtained from him.
Prajāpati: If a document should happen to have identical names and lineages [to those of the parties],
and the debt has not been admitted, a decision must be reached there by means of an ordeal.
Nārada said: Just as a reflection situated in a mirror appears to be real though it is unreal,
so too do skilled men create images for painting.
Those who are false appear like the truth when written down in the form of documents, and witnesses appear truthful even when they are false; yet those who are true may appear to see what is untrue.
Various states of affairs are observed; therefore, investigation is appropriate. Bṛhaspati says:
There are men who, out of greed, might declare a matter otherwise than it truly is.
Furthermore, there are other evil-minded men who forge documents;
therefore, the king must especially examine both of these matters with care.
Vyāsa says:
Some skilled men write on paper as if they were painting a picture;
therefore, it is held that success is not invariably achieved through the power of writing alone.
[Kātyāyana states: "By means of those who are dull-witted, mute, blind, children, women, groups, the elderly, the afflicted, or the timid;
or due to a defect in the witness, the document becomes invalid, as does [a document] written by the scribe himself."
Whether due to the fault of a fraudulent test by the creditor or likewise by the debtor.
A document executed by one who is dull-witted, mute, blind, a child, ignorant, angry, diseased, distressed, fearful, dependent,
or corrupted by fraud is not valid.
A composition is flawed if it lacks symmetry, measure, and so forth; if it contradicts local custom; if its sequence or syllables are omitted; or if it is devoid of aesthetic flavor (śṛṅgāra).
Bṛhaspati: Where a single witness who is tainted or censured is produced, they declare that document to be a forged one; the same applies if the scribe is of such a character.
Where the letters are displaced from their positions, blurred, indistinct, or deviate from their proper forms—
even if they appear well-placed— such a document shall be considered defective.
A document that is bright but old, or soiled and of recent date,
or one containing erased or corrected syllables, shall be considered forged.
There should be only one document for the accomplishment of a single purpose;
however, if there were many documents, it might even give rise to legal defects.
That which is contrary to local custom, that which is ambiguous, that which lacks proper sequence,
that which is executed by one who is not the owner, and that which is devoid of a valid claim— all such [deeds] are defective.

Kātyāyana says: Just as the witnesses, the scribe, and the author of the document incur guilt for its falsity, so too are the faults attributed to the user; moreover, a fraudulent document is itself rendered defective.
A document executed by the wicked shall be deemed wicked; one executed by the pure, one should declare as pure.
That document [is invalidated] by witnesses, the scribe, and the author who are corrupted by fraud.

Bṛhaspati: A document executed by one who is about to die, an infant, one who is frightened, one who is afflicted, a woman, one intoxicated, one under the influence of vice, or one who is coerced at night, or by means of fraud or force, is not valid.
Vyāsa:
"That which is done by slaves, those who are not independent, children, or women, is not valid; thus those learned in the scriptures know that such a document has no legal authority."
Manu:
In whatever legal disputes false testimony has been given, each such case shall be reversed; even what has been done shall be as if undone.
Whatever is mortgaged, sold, given, or received through fraud,
and whatever is seen to involve deceit— that the king shall annul in every case.
Manu has declared that all matters effected by force— whether given by force, enjoyed by force, or even recorded by force— are as if not done at all.

Yājñavalkya: One should set aside legal proceedings brought about by force or fraud, as well as those concerning women, those conducted at night, those held inside a private chamber, and those instigated by enemies from outside.
Nārada: A legal transaction entered into with women, at night, outside of a village, within a house, or during non-night hours— even if completed, it shall be subject to being performed again.

Kātyāyana states: Whatever defects of a written document there may be, or whatever [defects] are attributed to witnesses, these must be stated at the time of the trial; one should avoid raising them later.
Prajāpati [says]: When a document written by a forger might be identical in name and lineage [to the original],
and the debt has not been recovered, a decision must be made there by means of an ordeal.
And so says Prajāpati:
"When a document has been proven to be forged, or when it is doubtful in the determination of a legal matter,
that document shall be set aside as invalid, and the decision regarding the matter shall be made by means of an ordeal."
Kātyāyana says: "This document was not made by me; it was forged by him.
Setting that document aside, the decision regarding the matter shall be reached through an ordeal."
"A document executed by a non-corrupt scribe and accompanied by witnesses is the ultimate proof of a matter; any other is not proof.
Thus ends the section on documents; now, concerning witnesses.
Regarding this, Manu says: "But one who has been questioned and is undergoing the ordeal, having established his position while seeking wealth,
must be proven by at least three witnesses in the presence of the king and Brāhmaṇas."

"Denying [the debt], disputing; having made his position, having taken his stand—meaning that the king has acted in such a way that he cannot prevail. Likewise: "I shall fully declare what kind of witnesses should be employed by creditors in legal proceedings, and how they must speak the truth."

Householders who have sons, who are native-born, and who belong to the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes, are worthy of being called upon for testimony when summoned by the plaintiff; but no others whatsoever are so worthy, except in times of emergency.

Those who are native-born, of noble lineage, village elders, or leading men; those who are trustworthy among all castes regarding what ought and ought not to be done—such persons, knowing all duties and free from greed, shall be witnesses; one should avoid those who are the opposite.
Nārada says: In matters that are doubtful, when two parties are in dispute,
the ascertainment of the truth is obtained from witnesses, because they have seen, heard, or experienced [the facts].
A witness is to be understood as one who has direct perception through both hearing and sight;

that is, one whose mental activity operates together with both the eye and the ear. This is because of Pāṇini’s rule: "The term *sākṣin* is used in the sense of a direct observer. Thus, a direct observer is a witness. On this point, Yājñavalkya says:
"Those who are ascetic, charitable by nature, of noble birth, and speakers of truth..."
Devoted to righteousness, upright, possessing sons, and endowed with wealth.
Witnesses should be known as at least three in number, devoted to the performance of Vedic and Smārta rites;
they are prescribed as being either according to their respective caste and class, or all may serve for all purposes.
Elsewhere, Nārada states:
"Those who are of noble birth, upright, pure by birth, by conduct, and by wealth—
three or more such persons, being honest and of sound intellect, are to be known as witnesses."

Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, as well as those who are blameless— whether they belong to each respective caste or all of them together— are traditionally prescribed for all [of these rites].
In guilds, guildsmen; among their own castes, those of the same caste;
among outsiders, outsiders; and women shall be witnesses for women.
Again, Nārada says:
"Eleven kinds of witnesses are seen in the treatises by the wise;
among them, five are said to be appointed (kṛta) and six are said to be unappointed (akṛta)."
The written witness, the reminded witness, the incidental witness,
the secret witness, and the subsequent witness— thus the witness is declared to be of five kinds.
Nārada states that there are those who are not [formally] appointed;
furthermore, others are declared to be witnesses when they are not specifically designated—
namely, the village headman, the presiding judge, and the king for the litigants.
Those who are insiders even in the legal matter, those who have been dispatched by the plaintiff, and kinsmen in disputes between families— these also may be witnesses.
Bṛhaspati says: The written, the caused to be written, the secret, the reminded, the kulya, the messenger, the incidental,
the subsequent, and likewise the one found amidst other business.
The king, the official, as well as the village headman, and the witness—these are recorded as the twelve kinds [of witnesses].
By means of this document, the determination of the witnesses' testimony is established.
Then, for the sake of the judge's reputation, he should honor the mediators.
I shall explain their classification correctly and in due order,
by which one's own lineage and that of one's ancestors are recorded through the names of their birth.
He should be known as a resident witness, designated as a "written" witness,
having executed a formal agreement regarding debts and other matters through various transactions.
That which is written down is called "direct" (pratyakṣa), while that which is made to be written is called "caused to be written" (lekhita).
But that which is overheard from behind a wall as the debtor speaks his claim is [known as] "overheard" (śruta).
One who conceals [the truth] as it actually is is declared to be a secret witness.
Vyāsa says:
For the sake of achieving their own purpose, litigants [conceal] the clear statement of the defendant.
He who is made to hear [the testimony] while remaining hidden is called a secret witness.
Bṛhaspati says: One who has been summoned and made a witness in matters such as the transference of a debt,
and is repeatedly reminded of the case, is designated as a *smārita* (one reminded).
In matters of partitioning inheritance or in trade, where a kinsman is designated who is common to both parties and is knowledgeable in dharma, he is proclaimed to be a *kulya*.
He who is sent to hear the statements of both the plaintiff and the defendant,
being approved by both and being virtuous, is declared to be a witness (*dūtaka*).
But when a duty is being performed, whoever happens to come of his own accord and says, "I am a witness for you," he is called an incidental witness.
Where a witness, while departing for another direction or when about to die,
causes another person to hear what was heard [from him], one should know that person to be a subsequent witness (uttara-sākṣin).
He whose trust has been placed by both parties and who has also been informed of the case—
such a person is to be known as a secret witness, as well as one who is present in the midst of the proceedings.
Whatever statement is heard by the king himself from the plaintiff and the defendant,
that alone shall be the witness in that case, even in the event of a disagreement between the two.

If it is objected: "Since it is stated that 'the king is not to be made a witness,' because of this prohibition against the king acting as a witness, how can he possess witness-status? It is replied: His status as a witness here is spoken of with respect to matters understood at the time of observing the legal proceeding; the prohibition, however, refers to other occasions. Thus Vyāsa says: "When the king, seated upon the seat of justice, desires the truth, no one else shall be a witness there except the Lord King himself."
Bṛhaspati: But when a legal case has been decided and a retrial should take place, the presiding officer, together with the members of the court, shall act as witnesses there; it cannot be otherwise.
The determination of peace is considered to be of two kinds: rooted in the king and rooted in the treaty;
in the former, ten factors are described, and in the latter, according to the rule.
Kātyāyana states: When the king is observing the case, the scribe, the judge, and the members of the court in their proper order are declared to be witnesses.
In the event of the loss of a deed of victory, this is the rule: when it exists, that alone is the proof. Bṛhaspati says:
"Where property has been stolen or destroyed on all sides up to the boundary, the village shall be the witness there even in the absence of a document; of this there is no doubt."
Manu:
Where one may see or even hear anything unrecorded,
there, when questioned, one should speak once, exactly as it was seen and exactly as it was heard.
Kātyāyana states: Where the opponent is unable to produce documentary evidence from a foreign land,
one should cause a document sent by those learned in the three Vedas to be presented as witness.
And if witnesses are unable to appear in person, one should establish their testimony through a document executed by them in the presence of learned men. Thus [it is said].
Now, regarding the number of witnesses, Bṛhaspati says:
Nine, seven, five, four, or even three, or both [of two] who are learned in the Vedas (śrotriya) should be consulted; one should never consult only a single person.
Two witnesses who are written down and likewise secret, those written as three, four, or five,
those who have been reminded by chance, kinsmen, and likewise secondary witnesses (uttara-sākṣins).
A messenger, a receiver of a sealed document, one who is involved in the midst of the matter,
as well as the king himself and his superintendent— each of these alone shall be authoritative.
The *dhaṭikāgrāhī* is the calculator (*gaṇaka*). The *adhyakṣa* is the presiding judge (*prāḍvivāka*) and others. Yājñavalkya states:
"Even a single person who knows the Dharma may serve as a witness if he is approved by both parties, except in other cases."
In the case of a deposit, however, even a single witness may be declared [as valid];
here, the testimony of a witness who has been reminded is effective until the eighth year.
Likewise, success is achieved for one who approaches by chance within five years;
and likewise, success is achieved for a secret witness within three years.
Success through a secondary witness occurs likewise within a year;
or rather, no fixed time limit has been observed regarding witnesses.
For those learned in the scriptures say that witnesshood depends upon memory;
he whose intellect, sight, and hearing are never impaired deserves to be a witness even after a very long period of time.
Kātyāyana states: "For slaves, Cāraṇas, and Mallas; for those who live by elephants, horses, and chariots;
and for guilds, corporations, assemblies, and the like—testimony is prescribed among their own members."
The time for witnesses to be summoned is when there is a need for a thorough investigation of the facts;
however, where the testimony is beyond doubt, a decision must be rendered immediately.
Where the testimony is doubtful, however, the decision shall be made by means of divine proof (*divya*).
In all cases, ownership over one's own kin is said to be acquired by oneself. Manu says:
"Whoever, being an eyewitness, should give testimony for litigants..."
Whether inside a house or in a forest, or even when the body itself is in peril.

In the absence of all [other witnesses], it is indeed proper for anyone to serve as a witness in every case. Bṛhaspati states: "Even a single witness who is approved by both parties, provided he is as described [above], may give testimony; there is no restriction regarding time in that case, nor is any other procedure required."
"Within fifty years, no restriction of time is prescribed;
but beyond that, there must certainly be a restriction of time—so Manu has declared."
Now, regarding those who are not witnesses,
Nārada says here:
"Indeed, even those who are non-witnesses are seen in the treatises to be of five kinds by the wise."
He states its fivefold nature:
"From the statement, from the fault, from the division, from what was stated by himself, and from another scripture."
Therein, he explains the phrase "because of their statement":
"Vedic scholars, ascetics, the elderly, and those men who have renounced the world—they are not witnesses because of their statements; no further reason for this has been cited."

He explains the word "due to fault" (*doṣataḥ*): "Thieves, violent assailants, the fierce, gamblers, and likewise executioners—these are not witnesses because of their wickedness; truth is not found in them."
When witnesses have been accepted by the king for the determination of a single matter,
if their testimony should diverge, they shall be considered non-witnesses due to that discrepancy.
He explains the phrase "by his own statements" as follows: "He who, having been summoned by himself, comes and speaks;
he is designated as a 'needle' in the treatises, and he is not fit to be a witness."

In the treatises, it is said that "sūcī" means "sūcaka" (an informer). He explains the phrase "mṛtāntara": "If the matter that ought to be heard is absent, and there is no claimant, where could he exercise witnesshood? Thus, one who is 'between the dead' (mṛtāntara) is not a witness."

"The matter that ought to have been made known" refers to that which might have been stated by the plaintiff or the defendant; "in the absence of that matter" means it was not reported. And when the claimant is no longer present because he has died, regarding what matter or of what nature would one speak as a witness? He is one who has not been designated as a witness. This is what is meant: when the creditor has died and the legal dispute has not been formally reported, if someone, being unsummoned, comes of his own accord and points to the deceased's son, saying, "This person owes such-and-such a debt; I am the witness," he is a non-witness whose name was unknown to the deceased. However, if that matter had been made known to the son by the dying man, saying, "He is the witness," then he indeed becomes a witness to the son regarding that matter. On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
Even virtuous persons would not be valid witnesses after the death of the debtor; however,
those who were informed by the debtor himself when he was near death do indeed become witnesses, even though they are separated by his death.
Regarding this, Manu says:
"Those who have a financial interest in the case, nor friends, nor associates, nor enemies;
those whose faults are known, nor those afflicted by disease, nor those who are corrupt—these must not be appointed [as witnesses]."
A king shall not be made a witness, nor artisans or actors;
nor a Vedic scholar, nor one dwelling in a religious order, nor one who has renounced all worldly attachments.
One who is not dependent on another, nor one who is censurable, nor a thief, nor one who performs forbidden acts;
nor one who is aged, nor a child, nor one alone, nor an outcaste, nor one with impaired faculties.
Yājñavalkya: Women, children, the elderly, gamblers, those intoxicated, the insane, the accused, stage performers, heretics, forgers, and those with impaired senses;
An outcast, a relative, one who has a personal interest in the matter, a friend, an enemy, a thief, one who commits violence,
one whose fault has been observed, and one who has been expelled— these are not competent witnesses.
Prajāpati says: Those who act as slaves, those who are deceitful, Śūdras, atheists, village priests,
long-distance travelers, sea-merchants, and those who administer poison or set fire [to property].

Messengers who act in pairs or alone, those with missing limbs, those who behave like herons, those who have abandoned their wives or the sacred fires, and those who officiate at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice;
Those possessed by spirits, those hostile to kings, those who predict rain or the positions of the stars,
one who uses a single cooking pot, an enemy of companions, and kinsmen, relatives, and friends.

One who lives by poison, one who lives by medicine, one who is a servant to others, one who is appointed [to a task], one who is dependent on another for wealth, one whose property has been relinquished, and one who procreates children with a Śūdra woman— [these are excluded from inheritance].
One who has broken his conduct and then returned to it, one who initiates great sacrifices,
one who is exhausted and weary, one who proclaims his own sins, one with black teeth, and likewise one with deformed nails.
Those who sell themselves, betrayers of friends, rogues, liquor-sellers, those who perform rites for prosperity, magicians, the greedy, the fierce, and those who oppose guilds and corporations;

An oil-presser, a painter, a water-bird, a rogue, a royal servant, one who goes about naked, one who has fallen from his religious order, and those who follow the "cat-vow" or are motivated by mere sophistry— these are [excluded].
Fishermen, cranes, those distressed by their livelihoods, Lokāyatikas, and Buddhists;
likewise, astrologers and bird-omen readers who have fallen away from Dharma.
Manu says:
A Brāhmaṇa who sells human beings, animals, meat, bones, animal milk, water, or clarified butter, as well as a twice-born man who is a usurer; |||
One who quarrels with his father, a family feud-maker, a slanderer,
as well as one who abandons the duties prescribed by Śruti and Smṛti or performs other [forbidden] acts;
What is the use of saying more here? No testimony exists from them [the aforementioned].
Manu states an exception even regarding those who are prohibited, in the event that the prescribed witnesses are unavailable:
"In the absence [of others], the task may be performed even by a woman, a child, or an elderly person."
Whether by a disciple, a kinsman, a servant, or even a hired laborer.
Regarding this, Nārada states the specific rule: "Those who have been designated as non-witnesses— such as slaves, dishonest persons, and the like—
may also become witnesses when the gravity of the matter requires it."
Even among them, a child, one who is alone, a woman, a fraudulent person,
a kinsman, or an enemy shall not give testimony otherwise than the truth.
A fool may lie out of ignorance; a woman, out of falsehood; a forger, from the habit of sin;
kinsmen, out of affection; and an enemy, for the sake of revenge.
A single greedy person shall not be a witness, nor shall women, even if they are many and pure;
this is because the intellect of women is unstable, and also because others who are tainted by faults [are likewise excluded].
The meaning is that others also who are enveloped by faults—that is, those possessed of defects—are not witnesses. On this point, Yājñavalkya says:
"In cases of adultery, theft, verbal abuse, and violence, everyone is a witness. On this point, Uśanas says:
A slave, a blind man, a deaf man, a leper, women, children, the elderly, and so forth—
even these are considered competent witnesses in cases of violence, provided they are not otherwise disqualified.

In all cases where witnesses are free from the fault of partiality, there is no reversal of the rule; however, this does not apply to women and others, nor to thieves and the like, because of their habitual practice of sin and their lack of truthfulness. Furthermore, where witnesses are indeed corrupt and not virtuous, one should set them aside and conduct an examination by means of divine ordeals.
And in all cases of violence, theft, adultery, and in cases of verbal and physical assault, one should not examine witnesses.
Thus, regarding this statement of Nārada, as well as: "In cases of theft, violence, verbal or physical assault, sexual intercourse with a woman,
and the administration of poison and the like, no fault is recorded in witnesses."

Thus, the statement of Vyāghrapāda is intended for the purpose of excluding those who are merely superficially qualified, and not for the purpose of excluding those guilty of faults such as theft. Regarding whether or not an examination of witnesses must be performed, Kātyāyana maintains that it must certainly be done:
"In matters such as debts and in stable transactions, one should examine the witnesses; in cases of violence and heinous crimes, however, examination is prescribed only in certain instances."
Now, regarding the examination of witnesses, Kātyāyana states here:
"The king himself should examine the witnesses who have presented themselves."
Now, all these virtuous persons are worthy of serving as witnesses.
Vṛddhakātyāyana says:
The plaintiff may refute the witnesses designated by him when defects actually exist;
however, a plaintiff who refutes those who are without defect deserves a fine equal to the value of the suit.

Whether it be well-known among the members of the assembly or even established by common worldly consensus, the disqualification of witnesses should be accepted; no other [disqualification] is held to be admissible when it cannot be proven.

When a defendant has raised an objection against the witnesses in court, the witnesses must be questioned as follows: "Is the defect alleged against you true or not? If they admit the defect, then they are no longer valid witnesses. If, however, they do not accept it, then the burden of proof falls upon the objector to substantiate that defect. If he is unable to substantiate it, then the objector shall be punished accordingly. If he does succeed in substantiating it, then those individuals are not witnesses. Furthermore, when all the named witnesses are found to be corrupt, the plaintiff suffers defeat because the contrary is established with certainty. Alternatively, even if the witnesses are defective, if there remains doubt among the members of the court (*sabhyas*) regarding the matter to be proven, then the remainder of the trial must proceed by means of other evidence. Whether such subsequent evidence was previously indicated or not, the trial concludes at that point, according to the rule: "If it was not previously declared. This is not a separate legal proceeding distinct from the one at hand, since it consists merely of stating proofs and objections within that very same lawsuit; all of this has been stated by Kātyāyana.
The defendant must state in court all the defects of the witnesses that were recorded in writing; thereafter, the reply [of the plaintiff] should be given.
They can never serve as witnesses regarding the performance [of the act];
therefore, they must be treated otherwise by the defendant through his legal action.
If the defendant fails to prove his case, he must be made to pay;
all witnesses who have been clearly proven [to be false] are excluded from the status of witnesses by the law of testimony.
Whether it be the defendant or the plaintiff, when proving a defect in the witnesses,
there shall be no separate legal proceeding, provided it is relevant to the matter at hand.

If the plaintiff remains steadfast in his witnesses and has no further desire for debate, he who has been defeated shall be compelled to pay the fine according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures.

"Free from doubt" means independent of any other means of proof; "firmly established before the witnesses" means that at that time, having been defeated, he is to be punished. Kātyāyana states that no delay should be made in a dispute concerning witnesses: "The king must not cause delay in the testimony of the witnesses;
through delay, a great fault arises characterized by the subversion of dharma."
Now, Manu states that the hearing of the testimony of witnesses must be conducted as follows:
"In the presence of the gods and Brāhmaṇas, he should question the twice-born regarding the truth,
while they are facing north or east, in the forenoon, being self-restrained and pure."

In this regard, Nārada says: The plaintiff shall cause the witnesses— who are all present together, of known conduct, and who have understood the matter— to hear [the charges] individually in the presence of the defendant.
