In this regard, Manu says:
"The presiding judge, soothing them, shall appoint all the witnesses within the court in the presence of both the plaintiff and the defendant, according to this procedure."
Whatever you two know of each other’s conduct regarding this matter, speak all of that with truth, for you two possess the status of witnesses here.
Kātyāyana says: In the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant, and in the presence of the matter to be proved, one should cause the witness to give testimony directly; never indirectly.
In some cases, one may act even against those two for the sake of a higher purpose;
this law applies to four-footed creatures, to bipeds, and to stationary beings.
For one may indeed act as a witness at all times during legal proceedings even in the absence of scales, weights, or measures; but not otherwise than this.
On this point, Śaṅkha states:
"The judge or even the king shall cause those assembled [to hear] individually," the remainder being that "preceded by an oath. On this point, Pitāmaha says:
In the presence of Caṇḍikā and near the two disputants,
he should question those whose limbs are smeared with red sandalwood, preceded by an oath.

On this point, Gautama states: “Some say that truth may be established by an oath; this should take place in the presence of the king of the gods (Indra) and Brāhmaṇas for those who are not Brāhmaṇas. Witnesses who perceive no injustice [in taking the oath] do so after two weeks have passed from the time of the ordeal. On this point, Manu says: “If, within seven days of the testimony being given, disease, fire, or the death of a kinsman should befall a witness, he shall be made to pay the debt and a fine.”
On this point, Kaṇva states: "If,
within seven days, there occurs the death of a kinsman, relative, or friend, or if there is loss of wealth or illness, he shall be made to pay the value of the object and a fine."
If a witness, being summoned and free from illness, does not appear within fourteen days for the sake of the teacher's business, there shall be a finding of non-benefit [for him].
After three fortnights have passed, he shall be made to pay both the debt and the fine.
Regarding this, Kātyāyana describes the manner of speaking preceded by an oath:
"Having removed his shoes and turban, he should raise his right hand."
Having touched gold, a cow, seeds, and darbha grass, one should state one's intention.

On this point, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “One should cause the witnesses to swear an oath by means of gold, silver, gems, cows, grain, the sun, fire, the shoulder of an elephant, a horse, a chariot, a weapon, and so forth, as well as by their sons and grandsons, according to the specific nature of the property and the respective caste, in the presence of gods, Brahmins, and the owner. Kātyāyana says: “Witnesses must deliver their testimony while standing within the court, and not elsewhere;
this rule applies to all types of testimony, except in cases concerning immovable property.”
One should cause the testimony of living beings to be recited in the presence of Śiva;
in his absence, however, one should have it given by a Brahmin, and not otherwise.

Likewise, there is no restriction even for witnesses who speak [of their own accord], because of the traditional teaching of Gautama: "Those who are not present [as witnesses] or have not been questioned shall not speak. Regarding this, Manu says: "One should ask a Brāhmaṇa, 'Speak'; a Kṣatriya, 'Speak the truth'; a Vaiśya, by means of [threatening him with the loss of] cattle, grain, and gold; and a Śūdra, by means of these [grave] sins."
The meaning is: "by these sins which are about to be mentioned. Nārada states them as follows:

"Whatever worlds belong to the slayer of a Brahmin, and those belonging to the killer of women and children, and those belonging to the betrayer of friends and the slayer of a cow—those shall be the lot of one who speaks falsely."
O Bhadra, whatever merit you have accumulated since birth—
all of that would go to a dog if you were to speak otherwise.
"O virtuous one, you think of yourself, 'I am alone';
yet this Sage, who observes merit and demerit, dwells eternally within your heart."
King Yama Vaivasvata is he who dwells within your heart;
if you have no dispute with him, then do not go to the Gaṅgā, nor to the land of the Kurus.
Naked, shaven-headed, hungry and thirsty,
and blind, he who gives false testimony shall go to the house of his enemy begging for alms with a skull in his hand.
The sinner who,
when questioned regarding a legal determination, speaks falsely in response, shall go to the blind darkness of hell.
That man who, having arrived at a gathering, speaks what is inconsistent with the facts and not based on direct perception, eats fish along with their bones like a blind man.
Regarding the rule "one should question [them]," he states an exception in certain cases:
"One should treat Brahmins who are cattle-herders, merchants, artisans, actors, servants, or usurers just like Śūdras."
On this point, Manu and Nārada state:
"Listen, O gentle one, to the number of kinsmen he slays by speaking falsely in testimony regarding a particular case, according to the sequence of their enumeration."
One kills five by lying about cattle, one kills ten by lying about cows;
one kills a hundred by lying about horses, and one kills a thousand by lying about men.
One who speaks falsehood for the sake of gold destroys both those born and those unborn;
one destroys everything by speaking falsehood regarding land. Do not, therefore, speak falsehood concerning land.
They say that [the law regarding] women applies to their enjoyment and sexual intercourse, as well as to things produced in water,
all kinds of gems, and those made of horse-hair.
As with cattle, so it is with honey and ghee; as with vehicles, so it is with horses;
as with cows, so it is indeed with silver, garments, grain, and Brahmins.
Having considered all these faults in speaking untruth,
speak the truth directly, exactly as it was heard and exactly as it was seen.

Kātyāyana states: Witnesses who have arrived at the place of dispute must, with great effort, speak the truth regarding the testimony when questioned by those who have brought the suit, or even without being questioned.
The testimony of those witnesses should be accepted as it was spontaneously spoken, provided it is free from defects; once the witnesses have spoken, they should not be questioned again by the king.

If doubt should arise regarding the testimony already given by the witnesses, then they should be questioned again and again; however, when there is no doubt, that which was stated spontaneously must be accepted, and they should not be questioned further—this is the rule for re-examination known to apply to those seated as assessors (*sabhyas*) during the testimony, according to the statement: "Thus says Yājñavalkya."
He whose witnesses declare his claim to be true shall be victorious;
he whose witnesses speak otherwise will certainly suffer defeat.

And so Bṛhaspati says: "If that which has been declared is not deficient in terms of place, time, age, substance, caste, number, and measure, one should indicate that the matter to be accomplished is established."
If a witness, when questioned regarding the matters specified in the explanatory statements,
does not speak in accordance with the facts, that testimony shall not be considered properly delivered.

The meaning is that if the testimony of the witnesses does not accord with the statement made by the plaintiff, then there is no establishment of the matter to be proven. Furthermore, even in cases where there may be disagreement regarding place, time, age, substance, quantity, form, or caste, the testimony must not be otherwise [i.e., it must be consistent].
If witnesses should state a matter that is either deficient or excessive, that too shall be considered as unstated; this is the rule for witnesses as recorded in the legal tradition.

In this regard, Yājñavalkya states that when a matter has been established by witnesses possessing the previously mentioned characteristics as described by the plaintiff, yet the defendant asserts the opposite of the promised fact, if other witnesses should testify in accordance with the plaintiff's claim—provided they are superior in quality or greater in number—then the former witnesses are considered false. As he says: "Even when testimony has been given by witnesses, if others who are more virtuous, or twice their number, should declare otherwise, the former witnesses shall be deemed false."
Regarding this, he himself stated the specific rule:
"In a case where there is the execution of those belonging to the [first three] castes, a witness may speak untruth;
to purify that act, the twice-born should offer a *caru* oblation to Sarasvatī."
And so Manu says:

"In cases where the death of a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya, or a Brāhmaṇa would otherwise be mandated by what has been stated, a falsehood must be spoken; for that [falsehood] is considered superior in such a case."
And they should worship Sarasvatī with oblations of cooked rice (caru) dedicated to the Goddess of Speech,
thereby effecting the supreme atonement for that sin of falsehood.
Or one should offer clarified butter into the fire according to the prescribed rule with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras,
or with the verse beginning "ud," which is addressed to Varuṇa, or with the three verses whose deity is the Waters.
Now, regarding the punishments for false witnesses:
Manu declares the death penalty for those who give false testimony out of greed,
delusion, fear, friendship, lust, or likewise anger.
If testimony is given falsely due to ignorance or childishness, [it is not considered perjury].
I shall now declare, in due order, the specific punishments for anyone who gives false testimony in any one of these cases.
For an offense committed out of greed, the fine is one thousand; for one out of delusion, it is the first *sāhasa*;
for one out of fear, two middle *sāhasas*; and for one out of friendship, four times the first *sāhasa*.
From desire, it is ten times greater than the former; from anger, it is three times that further;
from ignorance, it is two full hundreds; and from childishness, it is exactly one hundred.
The wise have declared these punishments for those who give false testimony,
for the purpose of ensuring that justice does not fail and for the restraint of unrighteousness.
A righteous king, having punished them, shall banish the three castes who practice fraud or deceit; however, he shall only exile a Brāhmaṇa.
Yājñavalkya:
The forger and the witnesses likewise shall each be punished separately;
the fine shall be double the amount of the dispute, and a Brāhmaṇa is ordained to be banished.
He who, having been made to hear the testimony from others, conceals it, being shrouded in darkness, shall be made to pay a fine eightfold; but a Brāhmaṇa, however, one should banish.
For if men do not testify regarding a debt secured by a pledge,
the king shall cause the entire amount, including the pledge, to be paid by them on the fortieth day.
"For that lowest of men who does not give testimony even though he knows [the facts],
he is indeed equal to false witnesses in both his sin and his punishment.
— Kātyāyana.

"Having seized all the property of one by whose greed false witnesses were directed [to lie], he should then banish him from the realm. The meaning is that the forfeiture of all possessions must be carried out against the false witness.
Now, regarding the relative strength and weakness of witnesses,
Manu and Viṣṇu state here:
"In a conflict between witnesses, the king should accept the majority."
But among equals, those superior in virtue; and in a conflict between virtuous men, the best of the twice-born.
Bṛhaspati: In the case of a conflict between witnesses, the majority should be accepted; if they are equal in number, those endowed with superior qualities;
if there is a conflict between those of superior qualities, those who possess documentary evidence; and if those are equal, those who are more discerning.
Wherever there may be a deficiency or an excess in the testimony, one should reject that testimony;
in such a case, the witness should not be punished, for it is the one who fails to speak [the truth] who deserves punishment.
When the portion of the matter to be proven has been declared by the witnesses, it shall be considered complete;
however, in cases involving sexual intercourse, violence, or theft, that which is to be proven must be fully established.
Otherwise: "If one among the witnesses— whether they have been recorded in writing or designated by the plaintiff— should state otherwise, then all of them are not valid witnesses."
On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
"In disputes concerning houses and fields, the decision is reached through the neighbors,
or through the leaders of the city or village, or those who are considered the most senior."
Those who know the title deed, the means of proof, the possession, the time, the name,
and the characteristics of the specific plot of land— they too are witnesses.
In a case that occurred long ago and for which there are no witnesses, one should question secondary witnesses,
or employ oaths, or even apply some subtle artifice of reasoning.
Regarding this, Nārada says: "But when there is a contradiction with the injunction, one should investigate it by means of fragments of reasoning,
through considerations of place, time, purpose, relationship, quantity, price, and so forth."
One with a firebrand in hand is to be known as an arsonist; one with a weapon or a living creature is a killer;
and one seized by the hair is an adulterer caught in the act.
One with a spade in hand should be known as a destroyer of embankments on rivers and the like;
likewise, one with an axe in hand is proclaimed to be a cutter of trees.
In this regard, Prajāpati says:

"Whatever may be the indicator of something through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), that is the logical reasoning (yukti) for it; by means of that, one should purify everything."

Even documents and the like must be accepted as valid means of proof provided they do not deviate from the characteristics previously described. Kātyāyana states: "Where there is equality among witnesses, one should clear the matter by means of ordeals, even when witnesses are available in disputes involving the loss of life."
In a case where divine proof is employed, one should not question witnesses;
however, when a case is decided by means of purified witnesses, satisfaction is not yet reached until the verdict is finalized.
Divine ordeals and the like are seen to be employed against the plaintiff, while they are used against the defendant.
If the plaintiff should again approach with a matter of legal dispute,
the entire case against the defendant shall be decided by means of witnesses alone.
Now, enjoyment (bhukti) is discussed; regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"This rule has been declared for witnesses and for documentary evidence."
Now, the rule regarding the enjoyment [of property] when immovable property has been acquired is stated.

When the sevenfold enjoyment has been obtained— whether through paternal inheritance, legal action, a mortgage, inheritance, valor, or a formal declaration— one attains success through a valid title of acquisition.
Likewise:
"That possession which has come down by succession, that which pertains to a religious endowment, and that which has come through purchase, mortgage, or inheritance—
such possession indeed attains validity."
Likewise:
"Immovable property acquired through partition, purchased, or obtained from a father or the king attains validity through possession; it is lost through neglect."
If one has begun possession by occupying a property and enjoyed it for thirty years without interruption, one shall not displace him from that possession.
"Twenty years" is an alternative reading for "up to twenty years.

Whatever property has been enjoyed by the father according to custom and in accordance with dharma, even when he has died, that [property] is acquired by him through such enjoyment; it belongs to him by virtue of that possession.
But when land has been enjoyed by three persons in due order according to rule,
in the absence of documentary evidence, a fourth person may acquire it there.
The meaning is that for the fourth [type of possession], there is only enjoyment (*bhukti*), and no dependence on title (*āgama*). And so says Nārada:
"In the beginning, however, the cause is the gift; in the middle, possession accompanied by title;
at the end, possession alone is sufficient, provided it is continuous and long-standing."

In the first case, during the first twenty-year period known as the enjoyment of the first person; in the middle, during the second and third periods of twenty years each, there is possession with title (*sāgamabhukti*). Thereafter, in the fourth period, uninterrupted possession for sixty years is itself the sole ground [of ownership]. On this point, Kātyāyana says: "In the treatises, possession that is continuous and long-standing is powerful;
however, it should be understood that even if it is interrupted, it is valid if it was previously established."
There is no fault in a break [in possession] after sixty years of enjoyment. Kātyāyana states:
"In the period governed by the Smṛti, possession of land is accepted as being accompanied by title;
in the period beyond the Smṛti, because there is an absence of traceable evidence, it is established through succession across three generations."

The period of memory (*smārtakāla*) is a time suitable for recollection, known as sixty years or ninety years; it is the period during which the occurrence of memory remains most distinct for a single individual. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states:
"Possession inherited from a grandfather and that from a father are both considered valid;
when maintained by those endowed with age, uninterrupted, and stable, such possession is deemed to extend for sixty years."
The period may be ninety years, or even three generations;
beyond that, possession alone shall be the proof, even in the absence of a title.

The term "ninety years" refers either to a period with few interruptions or to possession by one of low caste. Vyāsa states: "Possession of land that has been enjoyed for twenty years by the owner without interruption is termed 'pauruṣī'; that which is twice as long is 'dvipauruṣī'."
And when it has been tripled for three generations, no further scriptural authority need be sought.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati and Kātyāyana state a specific distinction:
"That which [is established] by agnates, kinsmen, and likewise by one's own people..."
Success will not be achieved through enjoyment of that; one should direct enjoyment toward others.
Elsewhere, Bṛhaspati states:
"Possession for three generations becomes established for others; there is no doubt in this matter.
However, as long as the sapinda relationship has not ceased, it is not established for those belonging to the same lineage (skulya)."
In another Smṛti: "But that which has been enjoyed by one who is not the owner— such as a house, field, or shop—
with the friendly disposition of a kinsman, is not lost through such enjoyment."

The meaning is that the former owner does not suffer a loss [of ownership]. Therefore, possession is established [as a means of proof] in the case of those other than sapinda, samānodaka, or close relatives. Regarding this, Vyāsa states the specific requirements: "Legal title, length of time, continuity, the absence of others' knowledge, and the presence of the defendant—possession is held to consist of these five factors."

One's own knowledge (*svajñāna*), the lack of knowledge by others (*aparavijñāna*), the absence of abuse (*ākrośābhāva*), [the presence of] Bṛhaspati, [title] with possession (*sāgama*), long duration (*dīrghakāla*), non-interruption (*aviccheda*), being unopposed by others (*aparavojñita*), the presence of the defendant (*pratyarthisaṃnidhāna*), and enjoyment (*paribhoga*): possession is thus fivefold.
If, in a single title deed, villages, fields, and gardens are recorded,
then even when only one part is enjoyed, all of them are considered to have been enjoyed.
An eyewitness is superior to inference; a written document is more authoritative than eyewitnesses;
and possession by three successive generations, being unopposed, is weightier than these.
Inference is always a witness until death;
however, a document and possession that remain uncontradicted are authoritative for three generations.
Vyāsa says: If one's father, grandfather, and great-grandfather are all living,
the enjoyment [of the property] by those three living persons should be understood as belonging to a single person.
That which was enjoyed by the grandfather [is lost] without that son;
without those two and his son, his enjoyment extends through three generations.
Likewise, from another source:
"But when land has been enjoyed by three persons in due order, even in the absence of a written document, a fourth person may acquire it there. Agnimitra.
Kātyāyana says: Just as milk becomes curd when influenced by the passage of time, so too, through the lapse of time,
even property inherited from three generations becomes a cause for enjoyment.
Yājñavalkya: Title of ownership is superior to possession, except in the case of that which has come down through a prior succession;
for even where there is title, possession has no strength at all if it is not even slight.

Title-deed (*āgama*) is the cause of ownership arising from purchase and other such means; it is evidenced by documents and witnesses. That title is superior to possession and is more powerful. It is more powerful than any other proof even without possession that has been transmitted through three prior generations. Even with a title-deed, there is no strength if there is a lack of even slight possession. Thus says Nārada:
"Even when a document exists and witnesses are living, that which—especially in the case of immovable property—is not possessed is not secure."
The meaning is that he is weak.
"When one, out of delusion, neglects his own wealth while it is being enjoyed by others,
even though he is present and alive, that very enjoyment brings those [assets] under the control of [the usurper]."
Vyāsa says: Just as a cow neglected by its keeper perishes with the passage of time,
so too land that is enjoyed by others while one looks on is lost through time.

The meaning is that [the title] is diminished by sixty years of time through the enjoyment of the five constituent elements (*pañcāṅga*). Now, one might object: even in the *Āgama*, the authority of title is stated to depend upon possession according to the words of Yājñavalkya: "Where there is no possession, however slight, there is no strength whatsoever in the title."
Possession acquired through pure title attains the status of valid proof;
possession with impure title never attains validity.

Thus, by virtue of this tradition (*āgama*), the validity of possession (*bhukti*) would result in a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*). It is not so; there is no contradiction because that [tradition] refers to a different person. In the first twenty-year period, the tradition is more powerful due to the deficiency of possession. In the second, there is equality between possession and tradition. In the third, possession is more powerful. In the fourth person, possession alone, provided it possesses five characteristics, is the authority; it does not depend on tradition—this is established. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says in the *Pañcādhyāyī*: "If land is enjoyed for three years by someone in the presence of [the owner], without being contested..."
That mark of forbearance should not be taken away from him, unless he should speak against it.
"Quadrupeds, wealth, grain, and so forth, shall suffer loss after a year. Thus it is said.

This statement is to be explained as being for the purpose of showing respect toward the act of enjoyment (*bhukti*), and not as having the literal meaning [of ownership], because it is subject to many counter-arguments. On this point, Gautama states: "Excessive enjoyment of cattle, land, and women is not [permitted]. Thus, excessive enjoyment of these three—cattle and so forth—is not overlooked. Ownership arises even through slight enjoyment provided it is free from verbal abuse (*ākrośa*). Why else would one neglect a cow yielding abundant milk while it is being milked by another, or a fruit-bearing mango tree and the like, or a beautiful female slave being enjoyed by another? As for this statement of Prajāpati: [The text continues with the citation: "Even if a woman is enjoyed by another, she remains his own; likewise, even if land is enjoyed by another, it remains his own. This is also to be understood as intended to show respect for the act of enjoyment, and not as having the literal meaning, because it contradicts other Smṛti texts. For example, Manu says: "One who enjoys a deposit, a pledge, a boundary, a king's property, or a woman belonging to another, shall be punished with the highest fine. And Yājñavalkya says: "He who enjoys a deposit or a pledge without authorization, or enjoys a boundary, a king's property, or a woman belonging to another, shall be punished with the highest amercement. Therefore, the statement regarding the enjoyment of cattle and so forth is merely a figurative expression of respect for the act of enjoyment, and not a literal definition of ownership. Furthermore, the statement of Prajāpati is also not to be taken literally, because it is contradicted by other Smṛtis. For instance, Manu says: "If a man enjoys a deposit or a pledge without authorization, he shall be liable to the punishment for theft. And Yājñavalkya says: "He who enjoys a deposit or a pledge without authorization, or enjoys a boundary, a king's property, or a woman belonging to another, shall be punished with the highest amercement. Consequently, the statement of Prajāpati is also merely a figurative expression of respect for the act of enjoyment, and not a literal definition of ownership.
