For one whose enjoyment, beginning from the time of taking possession,
is uninterrupted for a period of twenty years, one shall not displace them from that [possession].
As for this statement of Nārada:
"Through actual enjoyment, the property of an owner [is lost] after twenty years;
even mortgages and the like may be extinguished, except in the case of the property of a woman or a king."

As for this statement of Yājñavalkya: "If one sees land being enjoyed by another and does not speak out, there is loss of ownership after twenty years; in the case of property [other than land], the loss occurs after ten years."

Thus, other statements as well—which aim at the cessation of ownership based solely on twenty years of possession of the five-fold characteristics—must be understood according to their literal meaning. This is because other texts establish that possession during the period prescribed by the Smṛti, namely sixty or ninety years, is indeed the cause of ownership. Likewise: "He who asserts possession alone, without any title whatsoever, should be known as a thief under the pretext of fraudulent possession."
Thus, from the words of Vyāsa:
"But he who enjoys property without title, even for many hundreds of years,
the lord of the earth should punish that sinner with the punishment due to a thief."

And this is also because of the statement of Nārada: "From the understanding that ownership ceases through mere enjoyment devoid of a title (*āgama*), it is established that enjoyment for sixty years or more, when accompanied by a title, is a cause of ownership.
Now, [an objection is raised]:
"Even that which has been enjoyed through injustice by three ancestors, including the father..."
That which has been handed down through three generations cannot be set aside.
Thus, from the words of Nārada:
"That possession which has been enjoyed for an exceedingly long time by three preceding ancestors,
having come down through the succession of three generations, cannot be overturned even without a title-deed."
From this statement of Vyāsa, it is understood that possession—even without a title (anāgama)—and even for three generations, serves as a cause for ownership.

This is not so; for we observe numerous statements establishing that only possession accompanied by a title (*sāgama*) is the cause of ownership. These two statements are not to be taken according to their literal sense. Rather, they should be explained as referring to the stability [of ownership] after sixty years in the case of property enjoyed by another through improper means. Kātyāyana states: "If land has been enjoyed by others here for twenty years..."
While the king is present, the success of that capable man does not achieve fulfillment here.

Based on such statements as these, Dhāreśvara, Asahāya, Śrīkara, and others maintain that since [the owner] neglected [the property] for so long while being otherwise intent upon his own wealth—even to the point of sacrificing his life—and yet remained indifferent when another was enjoying what was his own, his ownership ceased through the sign of prolonged neglect, which is like a sale or similar transaction; thus, the acquisition of ownership by the other party is inferred.

Likewise, through indifference toward neglect (*virakāla-upekṣā*), the loss of the [property's] essential nature might be suspected in some cases; therefore, it is merely taught that one should not remain silent. Viśvarūpa, Bhaṭṭa Kumāra, Brahmavid-pravara, and others maintain that possession for twenty years causes the loss of enjoyment (*bhoga-hāni*), but not the loss of the essential nature (*svarūpa-hāni*), because otherwise there would be a contradiction with all the scriptural statements.
Similarly, Yājñavalkya states an exception even to the loss of enjoyment in certain cases:
"Excepting property consisting of a pledge, boundary marks, a deposit, and the wealth of the mentally disabled or minors..."
Likewise, [one should not take] the wealth of those who have made a formal pledge, of kings, women, or Vedic scholars.
On this point Manu also says:
"Both a pledge (ādhi) and a deposit (upanidhi) do not suffer from the lapse of time;
even if they remain for a long duration, both must be returned."
Even after a long period of time, ownership does not arise for those two through mere enjoyment; such is the established rule.
Regarding this, Uśanas states a specific rule:
"After ten years, possession becomes the property of the possessor, except for land.
Nārada says:
Whatever property an owner observes being enjoyed by others for ten years while remaining silent and present, he does not deserve to recover it.
If, while he remains silent and maintains equanimity,
the previously mentioned time elapses, the legal proceeding is not established.
If [the owner] is not an idiot and not a minor, and his property is enjoyed [by another], that [enjoyment] is subverted by legal action; the enjoyer deserves that wealth.
The meaning is that the enjoyer deserves it by virtue of the legal proceeding, and not on the basis of prior possession. Thus says Bṛhaspati.
The one who brings forward [the claim] shall establish possession and the title in court;
his son may establish possession alone; but his grandson and those following him have no claim at all.
Kātyāyana says:
The plaintiff, even if possessed of possession, must clear himself of defects in the document;
his son, however, must clear himself of defects in possession, but shall not incur defects in the document.

This is the meaning: when possession has been held for eighty years, sixty years, or ninety years by one’s father alone, by both one’s father and grandfather, or by one’s father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—provided that there is no proof of contrary title—the validity of that possession is established. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states:
"One's own property being given away, its owner shall not obstruct it;
whether given by the heirs or by others, it remains his [the original owner's] only through that [act of giving]."
In another Smṛti:
"If property is given openly by heirs or others to one person,
yet it is later enjoyed by another, the former does not deserve to obtain it."
Kātyāyana says:
He who, seeing another giving away land, does not prevent it,
is not entitled to receive that land, even though he be the owner and possess witnesses.
On this point, Bṛhaspati says: Non-enjoyment of land, failure to produce a document at the proper time,
and the failure to recall witnesses indeed cause the loss of one's own right.
Therefore, one must diligently maintain the authority of the means of valid cognition;
by that, all matters, both stationary and moving, are accomplished.
Vyāsa states: "A legal decision is recorded as being of eight kinds: by means of evidence, reasons, conduct, an oath, the king's command, or the mutual agreement of the litigants."
Written documents, witnesses, and possession are known as the threefold means of proof;
the wise understand inference to consist of logical reason and dialectical argument.
The established customs of the land and traditional conduct have been proclaimed;
oaths corresponding to the nature of the matter are recorded as the ordeal by truth, the balance, and so forth.
In their absence, the wise know that the king’s command is the final decision.

Because there are three types of means of proof (*pramāṇa*), there is an eightfold nature [of evidence]. Bṛhaspati says: "That determination of the means of proof is called legal procedure (*vyavahāra*)."
That which is determined by inference is called conduct (caritra).
A determination of the meaning should not be made by relying on the scriptures alone;
for if one engages in an investigation devoid of reasoning, the loss of dharma arises.
The determination of a disputed matter is declared to be of four kinds: by means of dharma, by means of legal procedure, by means of conduct, and by means of the king’s command.

In all disputes, when there is an absence of the means of proof declared in the Dharmaśāstras—such as written documents, witnesses, and so forth—a decision must be made in accordance with Dharma. When those [means], such as written documents and the like, exist, the decision must be made by them alone. In the event of a conflict between local custom (*deśacāritra*) and judicial procedure (*vyavahāra*), the judicial procedure is to be followed. In the event of a conflict with the royal command, both local custom and judicial procedure are to be set aside. Thus ends the section on human means of proof within the *Vyavahāramātṛkā* of the *Vyavahāranirṇaya* composed by the illustrious Varadarāja.
5. The Section on the Determination of Divine Ordeals.
Now, the divine ordeals are described herein by Pitāmaha:
The balance, fire, water, poison, and the fifth is the sacred libation;
the sixth is said to be rice, and the seventh is the heated gold bean.
The eighth is said to be the blade, and the ninth is that which arises from the Dharma;
one should employ all these divine [weapons] for weighty tasks.
Because they were employed by the high-souled gods for the sake of the lotus (Puṣkara),
and for the sake of mutual purification, they are therefore called "divine" by name.
Fines should be imposed in accordance with the offense, with the intention of distinguishing between the virtuous and the non-virtuous,
and according to place, time, the nature of the matter, and the number [of offenders], and not otherwise.
In matters such as debts and the like, when there is a mutual dispute,
the witnesses should be provided with a specific amount of wealth according to their status.

Regarding this, Śaṅkha states: "In that regard, one should cause [the defendant] to undergo what is called 'divine' ordeal—namely, holding the balance, consuming poison, entering water, holding red-hot iron, the offering of sacrifices and charitable works, the surrender of one's offspring, and other oaths. On this point, Viṣṇu says:

Now, the procedure for the ordeal (*samayakriyā*). In cases of treason against the king or mortal sins, it may be administered at will. In cases of embezzlement of deposits, theft of gold, or acts of violence, one should determine the value in gold according to the amount of the object in all types of monetary disputes. In that regard, for a debt of one *kṛṣṇala*, one should cause a Śūdra to swear by holding *dūrvā* grass; for two *kṛṣṇalas*, by holding sesame seeds; for three *kṛṣṇalas*, by holding silver; for four *kṛṣṇalas*, by holding gold; and for five *kṛṣṇalas*, by holding earth dug up by a plough. For a debt of half a *suvarṇa*, the ordeal of the sacred water-pot (*kośa*) must be given to a Śūdra. Beyond that, punishments are applied as appropriate. For a Brāhmaṇa, any one of the ordeals—the balance, fire, water, or poison—except the sacred water-pot, may be used even for a small amount. In future transactions involving the execution of a formal agreement, the sacred water-pot is required. When the amount is double, the ordeal is as previously described for a Vaiśya; when triple, for a Kṣatriya; and when quadruple, for a Brāhmaṇa. A Brāhmaṇa who has been previously seen to commit offenses should be made to undergo one of the ordeals even for a small amount; however, one whose virtuous conduct is well-known need not do so even in a large amount.
Now, regarding the proper time:
Prajāpati has declared that the balance (dhaṭa) is suitable for all seasons, yet one should avoid using it when the wind is blowing.
The seasons of winter and autumn, as well as the rainy season, are proclaimed to belong to Agni.
Water is said to be wholesome in summer, but it is poison in late autumn and early winter;
one should avoid water that has breached its natural boundaries during the rainy season, for it is then like poison.
Caitra, Mārgaśīrṣa, and likewise Vaiśākha—
these months are common and not in conflict with the celestial [reckoning].
Regarding this, the Grandfather (Brahmā) states the specific rule:
"The test by fire should take place in the forenoon, and the balance should be used in the forenoon;
however, the water ordeal should be administered at midday by one who desires to ascertain the true nature of Dharma."
The ordeal by the sacred water-jar is prescribed for the forenoon of the day;
however, poison should be administered with great care during the final watch of the night.
For divine ordeals for which no specific time has been mentioned, the time is indeed the forenoon;
for it is stated in the words of Nārada: "The administration of all divine ordeals is proclaimed to take place in the forenoon."
Now, regarding the restriction of the performers: the balance is prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa, fire for the Kṣatriya;
water is prescribed for the Vaiśya, and poison is ordained for the Śūdra.
Water, fire, and poison should be administered to strong men;
however, children, the elderly, and women should be examined by means of the balance.
One should avoid fire for those suffering from skin diseases, water for those with asthma and cough,
and one should always strictly avoid poison for those with disorders of bile and phlegm.
On this point, Yājñavalkya says:
"The balance, fire, water, poison, and the sacred libation (kośa) are the ordeals for the purpose of purification here;
these are employed in cases of serious accusation when the accuser has placed his head [as a stake]."
The Grandfather [Manu] says:
One should prescribe the ordeal by balance and the others for those accused on the basis of physical evidence;
however, in cases of suspicion, the ordeal by rice and the ordeal by sacred libation (kośa) are to be used—of this there is no doubt.
And in that case, regarding suspicion of theft, there is the ordeal of the heated gold coin (*taptamāṣa*).
For those accused on suspicion of theft, the *taptamāṣa* is prescribed,
according to the statement "one should designate [the ordeal]."
One should avoid divine ordeals that lack the first stage, such as those beginning with the balance and ending with poison; however, the *kośa* (sacred libation) is considered to be without the head.
For those suspected by kings, for those pointed out by bandits,
and for those intent on proving their own purity, the ordeal should be administered with the exception of the oath upon the head.
The king should cause even divine ordeals to be administered to his servants.
On this point, Nārada says:
"When the person who has taken the oath remains at the head [of the assembly], and the accuser remains present..."
The granting of divine gifts is appropriate except by the command of the king.
Regarding this, the Grandfather (Brahmā) said:
"To one who has stayed for three days according to the rule, or even for a single night,
who is pure and wears wet clothes, the divine [mantras] must always be given."
The state of having stayed for three nights refers to the intention of an extremely defiled person. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"Having summoned one who has fasted and bathed with his clothes on at sunrise, the king shall cause all ordeals to be performed in the presence of Brāhmaṇas."

"If this statement [regarding ordeals] were not applicable to women, provided that justice is being considered"— this is the view of Āṅgirasa regarding its applicability to men, but not to women. For this very reason, Pitāmaha [states]:
"One should examine children, the elderly, and women by means of the balance (dhaṭa).
Likewise, Nārada, after describing the ordeals, says:
"In cases involving an accusation against women regarding their character, as well as in cases of theft and violence..."
"Such a procedure is seen in all cases where the truth is being denied. Thus says Yājñavalkya:
"The balance [is prescribed] for women, children, the elderly, the blind, the lame, Brāhmaṇas, and the sick."
For a Śūdra, fire or water [is the ordeal], or for [one accused of a grave crime], seven barley grains of poison.
On this point, Hārīta says:
"One should administer the fire ordeal to a Kṣatriya, the balance to a Brāhmaṇa, and water to a Vaiśya;
or one may employ any of these ordeals for all castes, except for the poison ordeal, in the case of the most excellent twice-born."
One should not administer poison to a Brāhmaṇa; poison is prescribed for other castes.
However, the ordeals of the sacred water-vessel (kośa), rice-grains (taṇḍula), and the balance (dharmas), as well as that which arises from Dharma itself, [may be used for all].
One should employ oaths concerning one's sons, wife, and so forth at all times;
however, for those who are afflicted by illness, purification by water is not appropriate, nor is poison for those suffering from bilious diseases.
Agnikarma (cauterization) is not prescribed for those suffering from vitiligo, blindness, deformed nails, and the like. Pitāmaha states:
"Women, children, the elderly, those afflicted by disease, the despondent, and the weak [are exempt]."
They should not bathe in waters, for they are considered to have their vital breaths sleeping.
One should never administer fire to those who wear iron armor, water to those who subsist on water,
nor poison to those who are experts in the application of mantras and yoga.
Bṛhaspati says:
One should always avoid divine ordeals for men who are afflicted by poisons;
one should not employ rice-grains as an ordeal for those observing vows or those suffering from diseases of the mouth.

One should avoid the ordeal of drinking from the sacred vessel (kośapāna) in cases of a great accusation, in matters lacking righteousness, against the ungrateful, the impotent, the contemptible, the atheist, and those whose guilt has already been proven.
The grandfather says: For those who have killed their mother, father, a twice-born, a guru, a child, a woman, or a king;
for those burdened with mortal sins (mahāpātaka); and especially for atheists—
Of those wearing sectarian marks such as the Kṣapaṇakas and others who are experts in the rituals of mantra and tantra,
who are born of mixed castes, and who persist in the practice of sin.
A king devoted to righteousness should never administer an ordeal in these very charges, nor in other contemptible ones.

In cases of suspicion regarding a mortal sin (mahāpātaka), the ordeal of the heated axe and the heated gold coin (taptamāṣaka) are prescribed; [the latter applies] when the value is ten niṣkas, half of that, or half of that again.
"In five niṣkas, or half of that, or half of that again, there is a *taptamāṣaka* [as a fine]. This is an alternative reading. Regarding this, Hārīta says:
"In cases of trust, in matters of reconciliation, in disputes, and likewise among heirs..."
One should cause the treasury itself to be delivered to the officiating priests for the collection of ritual fees.
When both parties have agreed, everything divine should be administered with care.
Pitāmaha says:
For those who are tainted by public scandal, the ordeal should be administered except for the [ordeal of] the head.
For those men who are great sinners and have been cursed, in the abode of Indra;
One should cause those who have committed acts of treason against the king to undergo [the ordeal] at the royal gate;
for those born of forbidden unions (prātilomya), the divine ordeal should be administered at a crossroads.
Therefore, in other matters as well, one should employ the ordeal in the midst of the assembly;
the ordeal should be administered according to the prescribed rule by those expert in the methods of ordeals.
But that which is employed contrary to what was prescribed is not true in regard to the means of achieving the goal;
likewise, gifts given at an improper place or time, or those performed outside the sacrificial altar, are ineffective.
They undoubtedly cause a miscarriage of justice here at all times;
[thus ends the determination of the differences regarding time, place, person, and agent for divine ordeals].
Now, the procedure for the balance ordeal is described.
In this matter, Prajāpati has declared:
"The judge shall cause all legal proceedings among divine beings to be carried out,
just as the Adhvaryu priest does in sacrifices, while remaining fasting by the king's command."

Having cut down a tree suitable for sacrifice, like a sacrificial post (yūpa), according to the prescribed mantras, and having paid homage to the world-protectors (lokapālas), the wise should construct the balance scale.
The balance-beam should be made straight, fashioned from *khadira* or *tinduka* wood;
one should have it made of *khadira* wood there, free from blemishes and devoid of white [sap].
In the absence of that, one should use *śiṃśapā* wood, or else *sāla* wood provided it is free of hollows;
such types of wood should be prepared for the balance.
A gentle mantra belonging to the Vanaspati class is to be recited during the cutting;
the balance-beam should be made square, and its two feet likewise.
Immediately thereafter, the two hands should be exactly one and a half [units] in length;
likewise, the two arches (toraṇas) should be made on both sides as well.
The two hanging [ornaments] should always be ten finger-breadths higher than the pillar,
and they should be made to hang downward from the two archways.
The balance-beam, made of clay and bound with cords,
should always be placed facing east and kept motionless on a clean spot, so that its ends touch the top of the scale-pan.
In the hall of Indra, in an assembly hall, at the king’s gate, or at a crossroads,
having suspended two balances on both sides;
It is the settled rule that one should place darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward upon the two scales;
on one side one should weigh the persons who perform the rite, and on the other, auspicious earth.
Examiners who are experts in the measurement of weights and capacity should be appointed [to inspect] the balance, ensuring it is free from bricks, ashes, stones, potsherds, and bones.
Merchants, goldsmiths, and likewise bell-metal workers must always have the balance beam tested by examiners so that it remains perfectly level.
The wise should pour water upon the balance;
that balance upon which the water does not float is to be known as even.
One should always cause a balance-beam to be made, adorned with banners and flags;
having first weighed a man against it, one should then lower him [from the scale].
Having prepared the scale according to the procedure thus described, Pitāmaha stated that the judge should act as follows:
"Then, with palms joined in reverence and facing the east, the judge shall say:
'Come, come, O Blessed Dharma; enter into this divine ordeal.'"
Having invoked Dharma into the balance along with the world-protectors, the Vasus, Ādityas, and the hosts of Maruts,
one should subsequently assign the limbs and other parts [to the various weights].
One should place Indra in the eastern quarter, likewise Yama, the Lord of the Dead, in the south;
Varuṇa in the western quarter, and likewise Kubera in the north.
One should place the world-protectors, beginning with Agni, in the corner regions:
Indra is yellow, Yama is dark, and Varuṇa has the luster of crystal.
Kubera has the luster of gold, and Agni likewise has the luster of gold;
similarly, Nirṛti is dark-complexioned, and Vāyu is praised as being smoke-colored.
Īśāna, however, should be red; thus one should meditate upon these in sequence.
A wise person should worship the Vasus on the right side of Indra.
Bṛhaspati said: Dhruva, Soma, the waters, wind, and fire—these are situated between Deveśa and Īśāna; from there proceeds the course of the Ādityas.
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, Bhaga,
Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, and Parjanya is recorded as the tenth.
Then Tvaṣṭṛ, then Viṣṇu, the youngest who is not the least;
thus these twelve Ādityas have been proclaimed by their names.
To the western part of Agni, they know the abode of the Rudras to be;
there are Vīrabhadra, Sāmbhu, and the highly illustrious Girīśa.
Ajeṣkapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pinākin, and Aparājita; Bhavanātheśvara, Bhuvanādhīśvara, Kapālī, and Viśāmpati.
Sthāṇu, Bhaga, and the eleven illustrious Rudras are recorded;
one should designate the station of the Mothers between Preteśa and Rakṣas.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
as well as Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and Cāmuṇḍā accompanied by her hosts.
They know that the abode of Gaṇeśa is in the northern part of Nirṛti;
the station of the Maruts is said to be in the northern part of Varuṇa.
Śvasana, Sparśana, Vāyu, Anila,
Māruta, Prāṇa, Prāṇeśa, and Jīva— these eight are proclaimed as the Maruts.
In another Smṛti: "Āvaha, Vivaha, Udvaha, Saṃvaha,
Nyāvaha, Nivaha, Pravaha, and likewise Jīvaha."
That differentiation of the Maruts is declared to be by means of the distinction of their names;
on the northern side of the balance, the wise man should invoke Durgā.

The wise know that the worship of these deities is performed by their own names, ending with incense; having offered [these] up to Dharma, one should then present the arghya and other offerings in due order.
After the balance, one should arrange the limbs [of the deity] ending with the ornaments.
Furthermore, in the worship of the balance, red substances such as perfumes, flowers, and so forth should be used, according to the words of Nārada:
"With red perfumes and flowers, with curd, cakes, unbroken rice, and other such offerings..."
"One should first worship the balance (dhaṭa), and thereafter worship the remaining [deities].
Thus [it is said]. The worship of Indra and the others may be performed with red flowers or others. And Prajāpati states that the presiding judge (prāḍvivāka) should perform all of this:
"Then the presiding judge shall be a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas."
Endowed with learning and virtuous conduct, his mind is peaceful and free from envy.
True to his word, pure, skillful, and devoted to the welfare of all living beings,
he should have fasted, be dressed in clean garments, and have cleansed his teeth.
One should perform the worship of all the deities according to the prescribed rules;
likewise, the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed in the four directions by those who have mastered the Vedas.
One should offer oblations with clarified butter, sacrificial grain, and fuel-sticks as the means for the fire-sacrifice,
using the Sāvitrī mantra together with the Praṇava and ending with "svāhā."
One should be intent upon the purpose of the Dharma by writing it down on a strip of cloth or a leaf;
that task, accompanied by this mantra, should indeed be borne upon the head.
This is the mantra:
"The sun and the moon, the wind and the fire, heaven, earth, water, the heart, and Yama;
day and night, both twilights, and Dharma—these witness the conduct of a man. Thus it is said.

Having written the matter under investigation together with this mantra upon a leaf, that leaf should be borne upon the head. And this procedure, beginning with the invocation of Dharma and ending with the placing of the leaf on the head, is declared to be common to all ordeals and is known as the *divyamātṛkā* (the manual of ordeals). Thus says Prajāpati: "One should apply this entire ritual of mantras to all ordeals;
likewise, one should perform the invocation of the deities."
Immediately thereafter, the judge shall address the balance:
"O Balance, you were created by Brahmā for the purpose of examining the wicked;
from the letter *dha* you are the embodiment of Dharma, and from the letter *ṭa* you are [the tester of] the crooked man."
Because you uphold and cause [beings] to cultivate [virtue], you are therefore called Dhaṭa.
With this mantra, one should consecrate the scale. Yājñavalkya says:
"The accused, having been weighed by experts skilled in the balancing of scales, and having been made equal to the counterweight, is lowered after a mark has been made."
O Tula, you were created by the gods of old as the abode of truth;
therefore, speak that truth, O auspicious one, and release me from my doubt.
"O Mother, if I am a doer of evil, then lead me downward;
if I am pure, lead me upward, O Balance"—thus one should consecrate it with this mantra.
In this regard, Nārada says:
Having secured two scales firmly upon the hooks of the balance-beam,
one should weigh a man on one scale and a stone on the other.
One should place a human figure on the northern side and a stone on the southern;
upon that, one should have a pedestal constructed using bricks, earth, and clods of clay.

There is an option between clay and stone for the image. Thus, having placed the leaf inscribed with the name of the defeated party upon his head, he subsequently causes him to mount the balance. Once mounted, one should keep him in that very position for five *vināḍīs*, according to the Smṛti:
"Five *vināḍīs* are to be known and observed by those skilled in time. A *prāṇa* is the duration of the pronunciation of ten long syllables; six *prāṇas* constitute a *vināḍī*.
"Ten long syllables constitute one breath (*prāṇa*); six breaths shall be one *vināḍikā*;
sixty of those make a *ghaṭikā*, and sixty of those are recorded as a day.
Thus Prajāpati stated the cause for determining purity and impurity.
If, when weighed, he increases in weight, he is pure; of this there is no doubt.
But if he remains equal or decreases in weight, that man would not be pure.
Likewise, it is stated elsewhere:
"In the case of the snapping of the enclosure, the breaking of the balance-beam, as well as that of the *dhaṭa* and the *karkaṭa*,
and likewise upon the breaking of the string or the failure of the axle, one should declare [the person] impure."
But when their breaking occurs while the cause is visible, and not due to the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), then one should repair it and perform the weighing again;

for there is a statement in another Smṛti: "In the case of the snapping or breaking of the sling-ropes and so forth, one should weigh the man again. Furthermore, Bṛhaspati says: "In the case of [damage] that is equal [to the weight], there is a repetition of the performance."
If one weighed against a balance is found deficient when placed therein, he shall suffer loss;
but if he is equal, he should be weighed again, and if he increases in weight, he shall be the victor.
Or, in the event of the breaking of the sling or the snapping of the axle, the king shall again grant purification.
In this matter, Prajāpati [declared]:
"The best witnesses are Brāhmaṇas who speak of matters exactly as they have seen them;
wise, pure, and free from greed, they should indeed be appointed by the king."
The determination of purity and impurity is to be understood from their words;
one should satisfy the officiating priests, the domestic chaplain, and the teachers with sacrificial fees.
Then let all the Brahmins declare the purity or impurity regarding the king;
surrounded by the virtuous, the king, having summoned one who is pure, should honor him.
One should issue a document marked with one's own seal for the purpose of clarifying purity, the description of the object, and the grounds [of the claim];
but having punished one who is impure, one should banish him from one's own kingdom.
A king who causes this to be done, having enjoyed the pleasures desired by his mind and attained great fame, is fit for becoming one with Brahman.
Thus concludes the procedure for the balance; now follows the procedure for fire;
then Prajāpati.
I shall proclaim the ritual procedure for the fire as it is enjoined in the scriptures;
one should cause eight mandalas to be made, and likewise a ninth in front.
The first mandala is that of Agni; the second is remembered as belonging to Varuṇa;
the third has Vāyu as its deity; and the fourth has Yama as its deity.
The fifth mandala is said by the wise to have Indra as its deity;
the sixth is called Kaubera, and the seventh has Soma as its deity.
The eighth is indeed that of the Sun, and the ninth belongs to all the deities;
those who know the scriptures recognize these as the eight mandalas.
It is taught that there are two hundred and twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgula) in eight circles; such is the conceptual measurement of the ground.
This mandala is known to be sixteen finger-breadths (aṅguli) in extent;
and the measure of a finger-breadth is eight horizontal barley-corns or three vertical grains of rice.
The measure of a finger has been stated; twelve fingers make a span (vitasti).
"A staff (daṇḍa) is two vitastis or four hastas;
two thousand of those is a krośa, and four of those is a yojana. Thus [it is stated] in another Smṛti.
They say the mandala is thirty-two finger-breadths, with an interval of the same measure;
thus, with eight such mandalas, there are two hundred finger-breadths.
The measurement of the ground is calculated as fifty-six [units] more;
the mandala should be made equal in size to the steps of the performer according to the prescribed proportions.

"Equal steps" (*padaḥ samaṃ*) is another alternative method. In that case, excluding the space measured by nine *maṇḍala*s (circles), there are eight *maṇḍala*s and eight intervals, each measuring sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅguli*). Thus, the total for the finger-breadths amounts to two hundred and fifty-six. Even in that case, only seven *maṇḍala*s are actually traversed, because one stands on the first and casts [the balance] onto the ninth. When the common rules stated in the *Divyamātṛkā*—beginning with "having summoned [the defendant] after he has bathed with his clothes on"—have been performed, and the procedure described in the *Tulāvidhāna* has been completed from the invocation of the deities (*dharmāvāhana*) up to the placing of the leaf upon the head, Prajāpati states a specific rule regarding the fire ordeal (*agnividhi*).
Standing in the western mandala, facing east, with palms joined in reverence and purified,
the qualified persons should examine their hands for scars and other such marks.

Having observed the hands of the person who has crushed rice with both hands, and having marked them at the locations of moles, freckles, moles, calluses, and so forth, with lac juice and other substances— as Nārada says: "Upon all hand-wounds, one should indeed make the marks of a swan"— thereafter, one should place seven leaves of the *aśvattha* tree into the cupped palms of the hands.

"Having filled his cupped hands with seven equal leaves of the *aśvattha* tree"—so it is remembered in the tradition. And one should wrap those [leaves], together with the hands, with thread; the meaning is that one should wrap them around as many times as there are *aśvattha* leaves, namely seven times. Furthermore, the threads should be seven white ones:
"One should wrap the two hands with seven white threads of thread."

Thus, according to the words of Nārada: likewise, one should place seven *śamī* leaves, seven *dūrvā* blades, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) mixed with curd upon the leaves of the *aśvattha* tree; [and] one should place seven *pippala* leaves, *śamī* leaves, and then unbroken rice grains, as well as seven *dūrvā* blades and unbroken rice grains mixed with curd.
According to this traditional injunction, one should likewise place flowers; specifically,
one should deposit seven *pippala* leaves, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), jasmine (*sumanas*), and curd into the hands, and likewise perform the winding with thread there.

Thus, from the statement of Pitāmaha: "Sumanas" refers to flowers. Furthermore, there is this traditional teaching: "But one who, having his hands covered with seven *arka* leaves, takes away heated iron, is pure if he is unburned by the time he reaches the seventh step."

Thus, in the absence of *aśvattha* leaves, it should be understood that this refers to *arka* leaves. On this point, Yājñavalkya says: "Having marked the two hands with crushed grains, one should then place seven *aśvattha* leaves upon them and wrap them with a thread."

Having observed the hands of one by whom grains have been husked—having taken note of the hands and calculated the black scars, moles, calluses, and so forth upon them—one should thereafter place seven *aśvattha* leaves within the cupped palms. Those *aśvattha* leaves should be wrapped seven times with white threads;
one should wrap the hands with seven white thread-strands.

Thus, according to the words of Nārada: one should place seven *śamī* leaves and seven *dūrvā* blades upon the *aśvattha* leaves, along with unbroken grains (*akṣata*) mixed with curd. And so Pitāmaha says: "Seven *pippala* leaves, then *śamī* leaves, unbroken grains, seven *dūrvā* blades, and likewise unbroken grains mixed with curd."
The word "should place" (vinyaset) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Likewise, one should place flowers and so forth.
"Seven leaves of the *pippala* tree, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), flowers, and curd—one should deposit these in the two hands and likewise wind them with a thread," so it is said.
As for this recollection:
"But heated iron, with seven *arka* leaves held in both hands—
if it is pure, with dust removed, it remains unburned at the seventh step."

Thus it is said; this should be understood as applying when *aśvattha* leaves are unavailable. Regarding this, Prajāpati states: "Having made a smooth iron ball eight finger-breadths in size, one should cause it to be placed in the fire; it is traditionally recorded as weighing fifty palas."
Regarding this, Vyāsa says:
"Then, wearing wet clothes and being pure, he should stand facing east with his fingers and limbs extended, having placed a leaf upon his head."
If a blacksmith who is skilled in the work of fire and has seen its application elsewhere should cause [the metal] to be heated in the fire;
The pure twice-born man, having further caused a mass of fire-colored iron, together with sparks and well-protected, weighing fifty *phalikas*, to be fashioned;
To one who is undergoing the third heating, he should say, placing truth before him:
"Hear this law of Manu, presided over by the world-protectors."
O Agni, you are the supreme purifier and the mouth of all the gods;
O Agni, residing in the hearts of all beings, you know their every action.
Having understood both truth and falsehood from you, this is accepted by the Vedas and other scriptures; you ought not to act otherwise.
This man is making you do this by means of this truth;
O Consumer of Oblations, become cool toward him who speaks the word of truth.
Burn the hands of this deceitful man for his sinful falsehood,
and [burn] the meaning of this document according to the facts as it pertains to the accused.
Having announced [the name] upon his very head, according to the sequence for whom it is to be given—
having said this, he should place the funeral ball (piṇḍa) into his two hands.
Having firmly grasped with tongs a piece of red-hot iron that was curved, emitting sparks and flames, and blazing with a radiance equal to a flash of lightning.
Having taken it up with both hands as impelled by the judge,
he should then stand on one [foot] and walk seven steps without turning his tongue.
Unperturbed and free from anger toward the fire, he should proceed slowly;
he must not drop that [fuel] before reaching the ground for which it was intended.
One should not step over the mandala, nor should one place a foot within it;
having gone around the mandala eight times, the person should then release the fire.
But if one causes [the fire] to fall in between and it is not perceived as burnt, one should cause that fire to be brought back; this rule has been firmly established.
Yājñavalkya first states the consecration of the fire for the performer standing within the maṇḍala:
"O Agni, Purifier, you move within all beings;
like a witness, O Sage, declare the truth to me regarding my merits and sins."

"Speak the truth; show [it]," is the meaning. In that regard, first, having cast the well-heated ball into water for the purpose of testing the purity of the iron, and having heated it again and cast it into water a second time, he should take it with tongs during the third heating and, when it has been brought before him, the performer should recite the consecration mantra: "O Agni, you are among all beings... At this juncture, the judge, having established a common fire in the southern region of the mandalas, should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the formula: "To Agni Pāvaka, Svāhā!"

"One should offer clarified butter into the fire one hundred and eight times for the sake of pacification," because this is seen in another Smṛti text. Having stood in the eighth maṇḍala, once the ninth [maṇḍala] has been abandoned to the fire, Yājñavalkya says that one should act in this manner:
"Having released the fire and rubbed his grains, he who is unburnt shall attain purification."
On this point, Kātyāyana states:
"If the accused stumbles or is burned elsewhere than the designated spot, the gods know him to be innocent; one should cause him to undergo the ordeal again."
"Other than the place" means with the two hands at another location. Regarding this, Prajāpati says:
"If the rice-ball falls in between, or if there is doubt, one should take it up again.
Once it has been taken, one should then crush either rice grains or barley."

If the lump falls before reaching the eighth intermediate circle while the person is walking, or if, even after the crushing of rice, barley, and so forth has been performed, there remains doubt as to whether it was burnt or not burnt, then one should take it up again. Even if there is doubt during the second trial, there is indeed a loss [of the case], because there is no statement that one should take it up repeatedly. In that case, a certificate of purity (*śuddhipatra*) should be granted by the king to the pure one; for the impure one, there is only forfeiture, preceded by the imposition of punishment as before.
[Thus ends the procedure for fire.
Now, the procedure for water is stated.
In this regard, Prajāpati [says]:
"I shall now proclaim the ancient, righteous rule concerning water,
which was itself declared by Brahmā for the purpose of examining the auspicious and the inauspicious."
One should worship the arrows with devotion, as well as the bamboo bow;
one should honor them with flowers and lamps, and then commence the ritual act.
In this regard, Kātyāyana states:
"For the sake of purification, one should have arrows made with tips that are not of iron;
they may even be made of bamboo stalks, and the shooter should discharge them with great firmness."
On this point, Nārada says:
"A cruel bow is known to be seven hundred [inches], a medium one six hundred, and a mild one five hundred; this is to be understood as the rule for bows."
Having discharged three arrows with a bow that is not too powerful,
one should immerse oneself in water whenever suspicion arises.
A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya, free from passion and hatred,
standing in water reaching to the navel, may a powerful man paralyze another person.
One who is under a curse should submerge himself while grasping his thighs.
Regarding this, Prajāpati says:
"Three arrows made of bamboo, and also a bow made of bamboo."

In this matter, the measure of the best bow is four cubits increased by eleven finger-breadths; that of the middling is increased by ten finger-breadths; and that of the lowest is increased by nine finger-breadths. The arrows, moreover, should be made of bamboo with tips not made of iron. Regarding this, Prajāpati says: "The thrower should be a Kṣatriya, or else a Brāhmaṇa following that same profession;
being of gentle heart and tranquil, and having fasted, he shall discharge the arrows."
But with a medium bow,
the wise man, having set a target at one hundred and fifty cubits, should discharge three arrows.
For among the arrows within that range impelled by weapons, the wise man should take the middle one and avoid its gliding flight.
Moving, moving, may the arrow go far, even further than far, outside.

Regarding this, the commentators have stated as follows: because of the injunction "one should aim at the target" and the injunction "it should fall," if the arrow falls short of the target, one should take up the arrow, go to that target, and return with speed; if it falls beyond the target, one should take up the arrow, stand at the place where it fell, and from there return with speed—this being for the purpose of both seeing the target and seeing the point of fall. A wise man should not discharge arrows when the wind is blowing excessively, nor on uneven ground, nor where it is crowded with trees and stumps.
One should not perform purification with water from divine lakes;
one should avoid using water that has been drawn up, as well as water from rivers that flow very swiftly.
One should draw water from jars and other vessels and immerse it in still water that is endowed with fragrance, color,
and taste, and which is free from grass and moss, and devoid of leeches and fish.
One should immerse oneself up to the navel, neither in water that is too deep nor in too shallow,
but one should always enter for bathing in water free from waves and mud.
The king should first place a man in the water like a pillar,
depending upon whom men desiring purification may immerse themselves.
In this matter, there is a specific detail from another Smṛti:
"Standing in water facing the east, he should grasp the pillar of Dharma.
The meaning is that, standing in water reaching up to his navel, he should stand facing the east while supporting himself upon a pillar of Dharma made from a tree suitable for sacrifice.
When the third [caste] has been cast off by the agent, the man, through a cause perceived in the dharma, their movement and immersion are equal.
Having caused the performer to face eastward while standing in the midst of the water,
he should then invoke the deities and consecrate the water with mantras.

In another Smṛti: "The arch (toraṇa) should also be erected on level ground near the place of immersion, raised to the height of the person to be tested. When three arrows have been discharged, one man, having gone with speed to the spot where the middle arrow landed, takes it and stands right there. Another man also stands with speed at the base of the arch, at the spot where the arrows were released. Nārada says that these two men must likewise possess such characteristics [of skill]. Of fifty runners, those two who are superior in speed should be employed for the purpose of retrieving the arrows."
In that regard, first the worship of Varuṇa must be performed, according to the words of Nārada:
"With fragrant perfumes and garlands, and with honey, milk, ghee, and so forth,
one should perform the worship to Varuṇa at the outset, being composed in mind."

Having thus first performed the worship of Varuṇa, and having completed the invocation of Dharma (*dharmāvāhana*) and all other worship and fire-offerings (*homa*) accompanied by mantras, as well as the placing of the leaf upon the head and so forth, the judge (*prāḍvivāka*) must perform the consecration of the water with mantras; so says Yājñavalkya:
"O Water, you are the life-breath of living beings, created at the very beginning of creation. You are declared to be the pure cause of all substances and likewise of embodied beings."
Therefore, reveal yourself for the examination of the auspicious and the inauspicious. Regarding this, Viṣṇu says:
"O Water, you move within all beings like a witness."
You alone know the waters, those which human beings do not know.
This man, accused in a legal dispute, is sinking into you;
therefore, you ought to rescue him from this peril according to the Dharma.
When the judge has thus performed the touching of the water, Yājñavalkya states that the person undergoing purification should act as follows: "Having sworn by the water,
saying, 'O Varuṇa, protect me by means of truth,' he should stand in water reaching up to his navel and,
having grasped the thighs, enter the water."

Having consecrated and empowered the water with mantras—thus, while the two stand at the fall of the arrows at the base of the archway—at the sound of the third clap of the hands, the one to be tested plunges into the water. At that very same moment, the person standing at the base of the archway proceeds to a much more distant spot, the middle point of the arrow's fall. When the other arrow-retriever has reached that spot and, having arrived back at the base of the archway, sees that the one who had gone into the water has not emerged, then he is declared pure. This very point has been clarified by Pitāmaha (Yājñavalkya).
A swift man should go from the foot of the archway to the place of the target;
when he has gone there, a second man also, taking up an arrow, should follow with speed.
He went to the base of the archway where that man had gone;
however, when the arrow-retriever arrived, he did not see him there in the water.
When [the deity] has correctly entered within the water, then one should declare purification;
otherwise, he would not be pure if even a single limb is seen.

"Whether from its place or by going elsewhere, [one becomes impure] in that place where it was previously deposited. Thus, impurity is to be understood even when it moves from the place where it was previously deposited to another location. Regarding the phrase "even upon seeing a single limb," this refers to the ears and so forth;
for instance, only the head might be seen, but neither the ears nor the nostrils.
One should also declare him pure who enters into the waters.
Thus, because of this specific statement:
"If a man is seen by a living being while submerged and not swimming, he should dive there again, as indicated by the ten signs."
In this case, a certificate of purification must be granted by the king to one who is pure; conversely, having punished the opposite, he should banish them. [Thus ends the procedure for water.
Now, the procedure for poison is stated.
In that regard, Prajāpati said:
"Now I shall proclaim the procedure for the consumption of poison as it is enjoined;
it should be given to the accused, and it is administered in a dose the size of a barley grain."
Seven or six barley-corns' measure of the poison from Śṛṅgin, Vatsanābha, or Haimaja should be administered.
One should avoid all poisons that are aquatic, as well as those that are decayed, artificial, or derived from the earth.
The lord of the earth should examine medicinal herbs, gems, and those residing in the body of the practitioner, which remove poison through the application of mantras.
In the forenoon, at a cool place, the poison soaked in clarified butter (ghṛta) should be administered. Nārada says:
"In the rainy season, the dose is six barley-corns; in the summer, it is recorded as five barley-corns."
In the winter season, [the measure] is seven barley grains; in the autumn, it is even less than that.
For one who has observed a fast, he should indeed give [the gift] in the presence of the gods and Brahmins,
after having worshipped Maheśvara with incense, offerings, and mantras.
While standing facing south in the presence of the twice-born,
the Brahmin, composed in mind, should give while facing either north or east.

There, the judge, having fasted and worshipped Mahādeva, places before him poison produced from a mountain peak; having performed the worship of Dharma and the other deities, and having placed a leaf upon the head of the person to be purified, he consecrates the poison with this mantra:
"O Poison, you were created by Brahmā for the purpose of testing the wicked;
reveal yourself to the sinful, but be nectar to those who are pure."
O Poison, you are indeed the embodiment of death, created by Brahmā;
protect this man from sin, and if you are truly immortal, become so for him.

Having consecrated [the poison] in this manner, one who is composed, facing north while the person to be tested faces south, should administer the poison. Yājñavalkya says that the person to be tested, having been thus consecrated, should consume it: "O Poison, son of Brahmā, established in truth and righteousness, protect me from this curse; by truth, become nectar for me."
Having spoken thus, one should consume the Śārṅga poison produced from the snowy mountains;
if it is digested without its characteristic effects, one should declare that person to be purified.

The "poisonous impulse" (*viṣavega*) is the transition of one constituent (*dhātu*) into another constituent; for Bṛhaspati states: "The poisonous impulse is the transition of one constituent into another constituent. The constituents and their sub-constituents are sevenfold: skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen, and so forth. Thus, there are seven poisonous impulses. He whose ingested [substance] is digested without these [impulses] is pure. As it has been said:
"But when, immediately after the ingestion, he is free from fainting and vomiting, and remains without any adverse reaction at the end of the day, one should designate him as pure."
In this manner, a certificate of purity should be granted by the king to one who is pure; however, for the other, punishment and so forth must be administered. [Thus ends the procedure for poison.
Now, the procedure for the ordeal by sacred libation (kośa) is described.
In this regard, Prajāpati said:
"I shall now proclaim the ancient, righteous rule concerning the ordeal by sacred libation (kośa).
Listen to those causes for which it must be administered."
In matters of confidence, in all forms of suspicion, and likewise in the business of treaties,
the treasury must always be surrendered for the sake of one's own purification.
One should avoid the ordeal of drinking from the sacred vessel (kośapāna) for those addicted to liquor and women, gamblers, atheists, and the foremost among the twice-born who are heretical.
And likewise Nārada says:
"In cases of great offense, lack of dharma, ingratitude, impotence, or contemptibility;
and regarding atheists, vrātyas, and slaves—one should avoid the ordeal of drinking from the vessel."
In the forenoon, for one who has fasted, bathed, and wears wet clothes,
who is a believer and free from vices, the drinking of the ordeal-water is prescribed.

For one who desires [the fruit] and has faith, in the presence of the gods and Brahmins, whatever deity he is devoted to, that deity should be made the object of his application; indeed, one should cause him to drink from that deity.
Regarding this, the Grandfather (Brahmā) said:
"One should have the devotee drink the water belonging to whichever deity he is devoted to; but if there is no such preference among the deities, one should have him drink the water of Āditya."
One should cause thieves and those who live by the sword to drink [the water] of Durgā;
thereafter, one may give that of another deity to others, but one must not cause Brāhmaṇas to drink it.
One should bathe the trident of Durgā and the orb of the Sun;
as for the other deities, one should bathe their weapons.
Having made the performer face the east, one should have him drink three handfuls [of water].

Regarding this, Viṣṇu states: "Having worshipped the fierce deities and having brought their bathing-water and so forth, he should drink three handfuls while facing the deity, declaring: 'This was not done by me. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
"In the case of a minor offense, however, having bathed the weapons of the gods..."
If it is a derivative form, it is impure and must be regulated; otherwise, it is pure.
On this point, Nārada says:
"If a deformity is observed within seven days, or again within fourteen days, that indeed constitutes the proof of his [guilt]."
If one should experience illness, fire, the death of a kinsman, loss of property, or the depletion of wealth,
one should know that his [previous] purification has not been accomplished.
If a very great abnormality should occur more than two fortnights after [conception],
he should not be pursued by the wise, because the appointed time has passed.
Yājñavalkya:
If, within fourteen days, no terrible calamity caused by the king or by fate befalls anyone, he shall be considered pure; of this there is no doubt.

It has been stated that there is great fear regarding even a small amount [of gold] because it cannot be avoided by embodied beings. This pertains to the scope of "great charges," since it was declared after introducing the rule: "In cases of great charges, these [ordeals are used]. Other time limits for ordeals mentioned by Pitāmaha concern small amounts of wealth, according to the statement: "One should cause the ordeal of the balance to be administered even in a small case. If an abnormality (*vaikṛta*) is observed after three nights, seven nights, twelve days, or fourteen days, he is declared to be the evildoer.

Thus, having divided the substance mentioned in the *mahābhiyoga* into three parts, a period of three nights and so forth should be established for each of the three options. In that regard, after all the rites have been performed—beginning with the invocation of Dharma (*dharmāvāhana*), the worship of all the deities, the offering of oblations (*homa*), the recitation of mantras, and ending with the placement of the document of the oath upon the head—Yājñavalkya says:
"Having worshipped the fierce deities, one should take the water used for their ablutions.
Having made [the defendant] hear [the charge], one should cause him to drink three handfuls (*prasṛti*) of that water."

The presiding judge, having consecrated the water for the *udagra* deity-ablution with the mantra, "O Water, you are the breath of living beings," by means of the water-attestation, should thereafter cause the person to be purified to drink three handfuls of water consecrated by the person being purified with the mantra, "Protect me, O Varuṇa, through truth. The term "having caused to hear" refers to the consecration of both [the judge and the person]. Śātātapa states:
"If, within seven days, or even within fourteen days, there occurs illness, fire, the death of a kinsman, or likewise royal or divine calamity..."
A fierce affliction arises, along with the destruction of livestock, grain, and wealth;
one should designate that person as impure who experiences such misfortunes as these.
In another Smṛti: "Within three fortnights, or on the third day, or even within seven days,
there may be illness, fire, the death of a kinsman, or the loss of livestock, grain, and wealth."
The king should punish that wicked man for whom such terrible omens are seen on all sides, according to the gravity of his offense.

In the case of a minor offense, the period is seven days; for a middling offense, two weeks; and for a major offense, three weeks or twenty-one days—this is the alternative. When this has been performed and no physical change occurs during the aforementioned periods, he becomes pure; a certificate of purity should be granted to him. For the other, punishment and so forth must be carried out.
[Thus ends the procedure for the ordeal by sacred libation.
Now, the procedure for the ordeal by rice is described.
The Grandfather said:
I shall proclaim the procedure for the consumption of rice as enjoined;
it is a settled rule that rice should be administered in cases of theft, and nowhere else.
One who is pure should have white *śāli* rice prepared by anyone at all,
place it in an earthen vessel, and set it before the Sun.
Having sprinkled it with bathing water, one should let it remain in that very place during the night;
at dawn, it should be given to the performer while he is facing the sun.
Having fasted while facing east, bathed, and placed leaves upon his head,
he should then eat rice grains and spit them out into a vessel.
On the leaf of a *bhūrja* tree, or if that is unavailable, on a *pippala* leaf, one should observe for blood; likewise, if his jaw and cheek sink down.
One whose limb trembles should be declared impure.
On this point, Kātyāyana says:
"In the case of bathing the deity, drinking water, or eating unhusked rice that has been moistened..."
One becomes pure by spitting out impurities; otherwise, one remains impure.
Bṛhaspati says:
One who is pure should fast and eat rice grains on a Sunday;
he becomes purified if the spittle is pure, but incurs fault if it is mixed with blood.

In this case as well, having performed the rites common to all ordeals—beginning with the invocation of the deities and ending with the placing of the leaf upon the head—the following is prescribed: when one who has fasted and is wearing wet clothes consumes rice grains and then spits them out, he shall be deemed pure if the spittle is white. A certificate of purity (*śuddhipatra*) must be granted to him; for the other, there shall be punishment and so forth.
[Thus ends the procedure for rice grains.
Now, the procedure for the heated gold coin (*taptamāṣa*) is described.
Regarding this, the Grandfather (Brahmā) said:
"I shall declare the auspicious procedure for the extraction of the heated gold-piece (taptamāṣa).
One should have a vessel made of iron or copper sixteen finger-breadths in size."
One should fill with ghee and oil a circular pit made of clay, four finger-breadths deep, measuring twenty palas.
One should cast a *māṣaka* of gold into that [liquid] when it is well-heated;
then, using the thumb and finger together, one should extract the heated *māṣaka*.
If one shakes the tip of the hand and no blister arises,
he becomes pure according to the Dharma, just as the word of the Grandfather [Brahmā] declares.
Because of the statement "one should lift it up," one should merely lift [the vessel] from the bowl; throwing it outside is not to be observed. He states another alternative:
"Having taken cow's ghee in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, iron, or even clay, one who is pure should heat it over the fire."
One should cast into it a well-purified ring made of gold, silver, copper, or iron,
having washed it once with water.
One should test the ghee— abounding with ripples and waves, and within the range of the sensation of heat— with a moist leaf, listening for the sound of "carut."
Then, one should consecrate that [ghee] once with this mantra:
"O ghee, you are the supreme purifier, the nectar in the sacrificial rite."
O Purifier, you who are cool as snow, become hot;
[I have come] having fasted, bathed once, and arrived wearing wet clothes.
They should cause that signet ring, likewise placed within clarified butter, to be taken up;
then the examiners should examine it for its length of one span.
He upon whom no eruption appears is pure; otherwise, he is impure.

"O Agni, you who are among all beings"—this is the mantra for the consecration of the person to be purified. Here too, everything beginning with the invocation of Dharma (dharmāvāhana) must be performed. A certificate of purity (śuddhipatra) should be given to the one who is pure. Now, for the one who is not pure, punishment and so forth must be carried out. [Thus ends the procedure for the heated gold coin.]
Now the procedure for the plowshare is stated by Bṛhaspati:
A plowshare made of iron weighing twelve palas is prescribed.
It should be eight finger-breadths in length and four finger-breadths in width.
The thief shall lick that [metal] heated to the color of fire with his tongue once;
if he is not burned, he attains purification, otherwise he is defeated.

In the case of stealing from a Brāhmaṇa, rice alone is prescribed; for one of another caste, a plowshare [is prescribed]. Here too, everything such as the invocation of Dharma (dharmāvāhana) must be performed.
[Thus ends the section on the rules for the lunar month in Varadarāja’s *Smṛtisaṃgraha* on the determination of legal proceedings.
Now, the rules regarding dharma are stated; herein Bṛhaspati says:
On two pieces of cloth, Dharma and Adharma should be drawn, white and black respectively,
with mantras such as those for the gift of life and with Sāman chants beginning with the Gāyatrī.
Having addressed [the deity], one should worship with perfumes and white and black flowers;
then, having sprinkled [them] with the five products of the cow, they are enclosed within lumps of clay.
Having made them equal, they should be placed in a new jar, remaining unobserved.
Having performed the invocation of the Dharma and other rites, the accused person recites the consecration mantra: "If I am averse to evil, may the Dharma come into my hand."
Then, without delay, one should take a single ball from the pitcher;
if it is drawn according to the prescribed rule, that person shall be pure and honored by the examiners.
But when unrighteousness is established, the offender should be punished or even banished.

Thus, among the nine ordeals mentioned, the four ordeals of the balance (*tulā*), the heated axe (*paraśu*), water (*udaka*), and poison (*viṣa*) pertain to cases of great accusation (*mahābhiyoga*); the four known as rice (*taṇḍula*), boiling water (*aptamāṣa*), the ploughshare (*phāla*), and the sacred law (*dharma*) pertain to cases of minor accusation (*alpābhiyoga*). The ordeal of the holy water (*kośa*), however, pertains to both. On this point, Yājñavalkya says:
"The balance, fire, water, poison, and the holy water—these are the ordeals here for the sake of purification."
In cases of great charges, these [oaths] are to be administered when the accuser stands at the head [of the assembly].

"These [ordeals], beginning with the balance, [are used] when the plaintiff has placed the wager (śīrṣaka) at risk. "Śīrṣaka" means the head; it refers to the fourth stage of the legal proceeding, characterized by victory or defeat. One who stands upon that is "śīrṣakastha," meaning one who has incurred the penalty associated with it, namely, the portion of the tenfold fine. Alternatively, either party may act according to their own preference, while the other shall place the wager. Even without a wager, one may perform [the ordeal] in cases of treason against the king or in the case of a mortal sin (pātaka).

In this matter, there is no fixed rule that the divine ordeal applies only to those who assert existence and not to those who assert non-existence, as is the case with human means of proof. Regarding the statement, "Or one may perform [the ordeal] according to preference," it means that in cases of suspicion of treason against the king, suspicion of a mortal sin such as the killing of a Brahmin, or suspicion of grand theft, one may perform the ordeal even without the head-piece (śīrṣaka). And it has been stated by Pitāmaha:
"If a man undertakes a divine ordeal for the sake of his own purification, there the ordeal should be administered without the head-piece; such is the settled conclusion of the scriptures."
"Divine ordeals should be administered—except for the *śiras* ordeal—to those suspected by kings, to those pointed out by bandits, and to those intent on proving their own purity.

Because of the statement, "One should cause [the accused] to undergo the *kośa* ordeal even in a minor case," the *kośa* ordeal is to be administered even in a charge of small value. Furthermore, the *taṇḍula* ordeal is prescribed only when there is suspicion of theft.
"However, rice is to be given in cases of theft, and not elsewhere; this is the settled rule," according to the statement of Pitāmaha. Regarding the heated gold coin (*taptamāṣa*) as well:
"The heated gold coin is prescribed for those accused on suspicion of theft."

Because of this statement, some hold that [ordeals] apply only in cases of charges involving suspicion of theft; others hold that they apply elsewhere as well. Still others, however, maintain that other oaths concern matters of small value, and we shall describe those later. Although oaths are also denoted by the term *divya* (divine ordeal), nevertheless, because they determine a verdict at a subsequent time, they are designated separately from the balance (*dhaṭa*) and other ordeals which determine a verdict immediately—this should be understood according to the maxim of the "Brahmin and the Wanderer" (*brāhmaṇaparivrājaka*). Regarding this, Hārīta states a specific rule: "The rules for the *kośa*, the *taṇḍula*, and the *dharmasambhava*..."
One should employ oaths concerning one's sons, wife, and so forth at all times.
Regarding this, Prajāpati states the specific rule:
"On Tuesdays and Sundays, in the presence of Caṇḍikā and Rudra,
the administration of all ordeals is proclaimed for the forenoon."
As for what Pitāmaha said:
"In disputes concerning immovable property, one should avoid ordeals."

This should be explained as follows: even in that case, one should avoid ordeals (*divya*) when documentary evidence, witnesses, and the like are available. Now, one might object: "In other types of disputes as well, there would be no occasion for ordeals if documentary evidence, witnesses, and so forth exist. True. However, in disputes concerning debts and the like, even if the plaintiff has presented witnesses possessing the aforementioned characteristics, if the defendant—accepting punishment and relying on his own steadfastness—insists upon an ordeal, then an ordeal may indeed be employed; this is because defects may arise in the disposition of witnesses, whereas an ordeal is free from such defects. Furthermore, regarding disputes over immovable property, the meaning of Pitāmaha’s statement—that an ordeal should not be accepted when documentary evidence, witnesses, and other forms of visible proof are available, even if the defendant insists on an ordeal by relying on punishment—is not intended as an absolute prohibition of ordeals. For if that were the case, there would follow the undesirable consequence of no decision being reached even in disputes over immovable property in the absence of documents or witnesses.
[Thus are the divine matters], as Nārada has said:
"In that regard, dharma is established in truth, whereas legal procedure (vyavahāra) depends upon witnesses."
"In a matter to be accomplished by fate, one should not employ human effort or a written document. Thus [it is said].

In disputes concerning immovable property, even if the defendant, relying on the threat of punishment, insists on an ordeal (*divya*) despite the existence of evidence witnessed by neighbors and others, an ordeal must not be accepted; this is the purpose of Pitāmaha’s statement beginning with "in disputes concerning immovable property," which is intended to exclude such an option rather than to absolutely prohibit the ordeal. For if written documents, neighbors, and other evidence were absent, there would be the undesirable consequence of no decision being reached in disputes over immovable property. Now, since an ordeal or other means may be employed according to the smallness or greatness of the object at stake, an investigation is conducted for its determination.
