I shall explain in their entirety those designations for copper, silver, and gold which are well-known on earth for the purpose of worldly transactions.
That subtle particle of dust which is seen when the sun shines through a lattice opening is declared to be the first among all measures of length, known as a *trasareṇu*.
Eight dust particles (reṇu) should be known as one nit (likṣā) in measure;
three of those [nits] are a black mustard seed (rājasarṣapa), and three of those are a white mustard seed (gaurasarṣapa).
Six mustard seeds make one middle-sized barley grain; three of those make one *kṛṣṇala*.
Five *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*, and sixteen of those make one *suvarṇa*.
Four *suvarṇas* make one *pala*, and ten *palas* make one *dharaṇa*.
Two *kṛṣṇalas* of equal weight [of silver] should be known as one *rūpyamāṣaka*.
Sixteen of those silver *dharaṇas* constitute one *purāṇa*. A copper coin weighing one *karṣa* is to be known as a *kārṣāpaṇa*, which is also called a *paṇa*.
"Ten *dharaṇas* should be known as one *śatamāna* of silver;
a *niṣka* is to be understood by measure as being equal to four *suvarṇas*. Thus says Yājñavalkya.
A mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam through a lattice is known as a *trasareṇu*;
eight of those are a *likṣā*, and three of those are called a *rājasarṣapa*.
Three of those *gaura* are one *yava*; three of those *yava* are one middle *māṣa*; five *māṣa* are one *kṛṣṇala*; and sixteen of those *kṛṣṇala* are one *suvarṇa*.

Four or five *suvarṇas* are proclaimed to be one *pala*. From six *aṇus*, a *trasareṇu* becomes perceptible to the eye. Eight *trasareṇus* constitute a *likṣā*. Three of those *likṣās* have the designation "royal mustard seed" (*rājasarṣapa*). Three of those royal mustard seeds make one "white mustard seed" (*gaurasarṣapa*). Six white mustard seeds make one medium-sized barley grain (*madhyayava*). Three of those make one *kṛṣṇala*. Five of those *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*. Sixteen of those *māṣas* make one *suvarṇa*. Four of those *suvarṇas* make one *pala*, according to the opinion of Yājñavalkya.

According to the systems of Nārada and others, five *suvarṇas* constitute a *pala*. In that context, four units of worldly measure are called a *kṛṣṇala*. It is well known in the world that one unit of measure is the size of a grain of rice (*vrīhi*). According to the tradition of the scriptures, one unit of measure is the size of a single grain of rice, as stated in the traditional authority (*āgama*): "A *paṇa* of ten measures is said to be the size of a measured grain," and this is also seen in the *Vaikhānasa* and *Ātreya* Saṃhitās.

In this regard, according to both Manu and Yājñavalkya, seven *mānas* less two *kākaṇis* is called a *kṛṣṇala*. Since there are thus three types of *kṛṣṇalas*, it is appropriate to rely upon the *kṛṣṇala* specified in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra for the context of oaths involving *dūrvā* grass and the like; therefore, here the *kṛṣṇala* consisting of six *mānas* less three *kākaṇis* is naturally adopted. However, the *kṛṣṇala* of Manu is adopted based on the qualifications of the performer and other factors. In that case, starting from the amount of stolen property for which there is a need, until the completion of the [first] *kṛṣṇala*, a Śūdra—having fasted, bathed, and wearing wet clothes—should perform the oath with *dūrvā* grass in his hand in the presence of gods and Brāhmaṇas. Being in such a state, starting from the second *kṛṣṇala* up to the third, he should perform the oath as before with sesame seeds (*tila*) in his hand. Starting from the third *kṛṣṇala* up to the fourth, he should likewise perform the oath with silver in his hand. Starting from the fourth *kṛṣṇala* up to the fifth, he should perform the oath with gold in his hand. Starting from the fifth *kṛṣṇala* up to the sixth, the Śūdra should perform the oath holding earth dug up by a plough. Starting from the sixth *kṛṣṇala* up to the tenth, within that range of ten, if the Śūdra possesses no *kṛṣṇalas*, he should perform the oath through his son or his wife. A virtuous Śūdra, in that same matter, should perform the oath by invoking all sins, according to the statement of Manu: "But a Śūdra [should swear] by all sins. Even though here...
... [he should touch] a Śūdra with all the sins;
or else, he should separately touch him on the head with the head of his son or wife.

Thus, although a specific quantity of the substance has not been stated, nevertheless, by way of propriety, these two [ordeals] ought to occur starting from the completion of five *kṛṣṇalas* up to ten *mānas* of copper coins (*paṇas*). If it is asked how so, it is said: In that regard, since the general rule for an ordeal by water (*kośa*) applies—based on the Vaiṣṇava statement, "An ordeal by water shall be administered to a Śūdra"—when the amount stolen is half a *suvarṇa*, it is stated:
"Three hundred grains of rice shall be given, and an ordeal by water when the amount is half of that;
when a hundred is stolen or denied, the ordeal of purification by sacred law (*dharmaśodhana*) must be administered."

Thus, in this statement of Bṛhaspati, since the numbers beginning with "hundred" are to be counted, the measure [of the fine] shall be one *taṇḍula* [of gold]; ten such measures are recorded as one *paṇa*.

According to this statement, only gold measured by the weight of a *taṇḍula* (rice grain) is to be accepted. Regarding the rule that "drinking from the *kośa* [vessel] is for half of that," since drinking from the *kośa* is prescribed for a measure of one hundred and fifty *mānas*, and since one hundred and fifty consists of fifteen *paṇas*, the *kośa* mentioned in the statement of Viṣṇu is restricted to cases exceeding that amount; thus, purification through the *dharma* [oath] should occur above fifteen *paṇas*. Below fifteen *paṇas* and above five *kṛṣṇalas*, there is a requirement for a means of proof (*pratyaya*). Likewise, in this context, the phrase "a Śūdra for all sins" also requires a specific quantity of property; therefore, these two requirements are connected through mutual expectancy. Furthermore, [the following applies]:
One should cause a Brahmin to swear by truth; a Kṣatriya, by his vehicle and weapons; a Vaiśya, by his cattle, grain, and gold; and a Śūdra, by all the heinous sins.
Thus it is recorded that the subject matter of oaths was stated by Manu. After enumerating the ordeals beginning with poison and ending with the *dharmaja*, Bṛhaspati said:
"Truth, vehicles, weapons, cattle, seed-corn, gold, the feet of gods and Brahmins, and the heads of one's sons and wife."
"These oaths have been declared as always easy to perform in matters of small value.

Here, because it is understood that the oaths of Dharmaja pertain to matters of small value, while for Siroddhṛtamahī they pertain to matters of great value—as indicated by the very nature of the examination of *dharma*—it should be known that the Mānavas and Bārhaspatyas prescribe oaths from ten *paṇas* downward for the case of Dharmaja, and from five *kṛṣṇalas* upward for the case of Siroddhṛtamahī.
"One should make a Śūdra carry fire, and likewise cause him to immerse himself in water."

Thus, it should be understood that because the son of Dharma (Yama) provides immediate visible proof as a result, there is no mention of oaths whose results manifest at a later time. For a *śūdra*, the proof of righteousness (*dharmapratyaya*) consists of ten *paṇas* starting from a group of ten up to fifteen. In that same matter, for those who live by the plough—namely, farmers—the plough must be licked. Bṛhaspati states:
"When a hundred [coins] have been taken and denied, the purification by means of Dharma must be administered;
the members of the court must diligently provide the plough for one who grazes [cattle]."

When a hundred units of measure have been taken and denied, the purification of the Śūdra’s guilt occurs as follows: since a hundred measures consist of ten *paṇas*, the meaning is that from fifteen *paṇas* up to fifteen *paṇas* less one (i.e., fourteen), the ordeal by sacred law (*dharmapratyaya*) applies; for that same purpose, it is said that a ploughshare must be given to a Śūdra who is a cultivator. From fifteen *paṇas* up to thirty *paṇas*, the Śūdra shall undergo the ordeal of drinking from the vessel (*kośapāna*). From thirty *paṇas* up to forty *paṇas*, the Śūdra’s ordeal is eating rice (*taṇḍulabhakṣaṇa*). From forty *paṇas* up to fifty *paṇas*, the Śūdra’s ordeal is the heated gold ball (*taptamāṣa*). And so says Bṛhaspati:
In a lawsuit involving four hundred [paṇas], the heated māṣaka ordeal must be administered;
for thirty, rice grains should be given, and for half of that amount, the ordeal by sacred libation (kośa).

In a charge involving four hundred [paṇas], that is, in a charge concerning gold weighing four hundred mānas, the ordeal of the heated *māṣa* (taptamāṣa) must be administered; this is because those [four hundred] consist of forty paṇas, meaning that for a Śūdra charged with forty paṇas, the ordeal of the heated *māṣa* is to be given. The statement "in thirty [paṇas] rice is to be given" also establishes that for a Śūdra charged with three hundred mānas of gold—which consists of thirty paṇas—rice is to be given. From fifty paṇas up to sixty-seven paṇas, the Śūdra’s ordeal is by means of the balance (*tulā*). From sixty-seven paṇas up to seventy-five paṇas, the Śūdra’s ordeal is by means of water (*jala*). From seventy-five paṇas up to one hundred paṇas, the Śūdra’s ordeal is by means of the axe (*paraśu*). From one hundred paṇas upwards, for a Śūdra, there is only the swallowing of poison (*viṣa*) in all cases. And so says Bṛhaspati:
When a hundred [paṇas] have been taken and denied, the ordeal by sacred libation (dharmaśodhana) shall be administered;
when a thousand have not been taken, the ordeal by poison; and when three-quarters [of a thousand] have been taken, the ordeal by fire.
When one-third of the [total] has been traversed, water should be given; when half is reached, the balance (tulā) should always be applied.

In the case of a gold weighing one thousand *mānas* consisting of one hundred *paṇas*, the ordeal for a Śūdra is the consumption of poison. When the amount is reduced by a fourth part of a thousand *mānas*—that is, when it consists of one hundred and fifty-seven *paṇas*—the ordeal for a Śūdra is the carrying of the heated axe. Likewise, when the gold weighing one thousand *mānas* is reduced by a third part—that is, at seventy-seven *paṇas*—the ordeal for a Śūdra is drowning in water. When the amount is half of a thousand *mānas* consisting of fifty *paṇas*, the ordeal for a Śūdra is mounting the balance; such is the meaning. Now, one might ask: in this section on ordeals (*divya-prakaraṇa*), since numbers such as "one thousand" and so forth function as the objects to be numbered, how is it determined that only gold weighed in *mānas* and measured in *tulās* (balances) is intended? It is said in reply: Kātyāyana states as follows:
Having ascertained the measure of all the materials, one should fashion the gold;
then, endowed with the proper measure of gold, one should employ that divine [image].
If the fine is one hundred [paṇas], poison is administered; if it is three-quarters of a hundred, fire is given there;
if it is reduced by one-third, water is used; and for fifty, the balance ordeal is prescribed.
"Drinking from the sacred vessel (kośapāna) [is prescribed] for that [highest amount], or half of it, or ten, five, or seven [paṇas];
for half of that, rice grains (taṇḍula) should be administered; for half of that, the heated gold bean (taptamāṣaka). Thus says Kātyāyana.
Having determined the quantity of gold, poison is prescribed for a loss of one hundred;
however, for a loss of eighty, fire is prescribed as the means of proof.
Fire is for debts of one hundred;
water should be known as applicable for sixty; for forty, the ordeal by balance is prescribed;
or for the destruction of thirty or ten [units], the drinking of holy water (kośapāna) is ordained.
Thus says Bṛhaspati:
"Or, in the case of its loss, [the fine is] half of that, and for the loss of half of that, [the fine is] rice-grains."

Thus says Vṛddha-Manu. In these two statements by Kātyāyana and Vṛddha-Manu, poison is prescribed for the loss of a hundred. However, in the statement of Bṛhaspati, "poison [is used] when a thousand has been stolen," poison is prescribed for the loss of a thousand; thus, it is understood that there is a great contradiction between them. True. When these [texts] must be reconciled, one should apply the statement of Bṛhaspati according to the principle of the majority, following the two [other] statements. This being so, since in the Dharmaśāstras, when a mere number is specified in the prescription of punishments and the like, *paṇas* are generally taken as the things to be numbered because they are established as the unit of currency for legal proceedings (*vyavahāra*), [the term refers to *paṇas*]. In that regard, since the usage of the term *paṇa* is seen in common practice even for four *kākaṇikas*, and because it is well-known among grammarians that "a *kākaṇika* is a fourth part of a *paṇa*," the quantity measured by a *taṇḍula* (grain-measure) consisting of four *kākaṇikas* is taken here as the thing to be numbered in the thousands and so forth. But in the statement of Kātyāyana...
"One *māna* shall consist of a measure of rice; ten *mānas* are recorded as one *paṇa*.

Thus, there is no contradiction in taking the *paṇa* mentioned in this definition of ten *mānas* as the object to be numbered by counts such as a hundred and so forth. Here too, in the case of the numbers "hundred" and so on found in the statements of Kātyāyana and Vṛddhamanu, the *paṇas* themselves are taken as the objects to be numbered. This being the case, in the statement of Bṛhaspati, the numbers "thousand" and so forth are taken as the objects to be numbered, referring to gold weighed against rice.
[As it is said: "One *māna* shall consist of a measure of rice; ten *mānas* are recorded as one *paṇa*."
Because of such statements, there is no contradiction even between the [cases involving] one hundred and one thousand. As for this statement of Yājñavalkya:

"One should not administer the ploughshare ordeal, nor the balance, nor poison, for less than one thousand," here the word *sahasra* (thousand) is intended as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for both nine hundred and five hundred; thus, there is no contradiction. In this context, the word *phāla* refers to the axe (*paraśu*), since it has been shown that the primary meaning of *phāla* pertains to a lesser amount. As for what was stated here by Vṛddhamanu:
When destruction occurs at eighty [years], fire is recorded as the cause;
when at sixty, water is to be known as the cause; and at forty, the balance (dhaṭa) is the cause.
Thus it is said; and as Kātyāyana has stated:
"Poison is administered for [a fine of] one hundred [paṇas], while the fire ordeal is given for seventy-five;
the water ordeal for seventy-five, and the balance ordeal is prescribed for fifty."

From these two very statements, it is understood as follows: starting from seventy-five and up to eighty, fire and water are obtained; likewise, starting from sixty and up to sixty-seven locations, the water-pot and the heated coin are obtained. It should be observed that this is the established rule: for a superior person, the cognition is light, whereas for an inferior person, the cognition is heavy—this being seen from the Vaiṣṇava statement beginning with "the fault previously seen.
Half of that [distance] rice should be given, and half of that is the heated māṣaka.

Thus, even the rule regarding the heated gold coin (*taptamāṣaka*) applies to cases involving small amounts when there is suspicion of theft and the like; therefore, since it is applicable even for small property, there is no contradiction. Where the denial of what was given is the matter at hand, that [test] is prescribed: "In cases of theft and violence, one should cause the ordeal to be administered even for a very small amount."

This is because of the observation of Kātyāyana’s statement. Regarding the phrase "for a Brāhmaṇa, at a future time," the meaning is that even for a Brāhmaṇa, the ordeal by *kośa* (water) is applicable in matters concerning future actions. The previously mentioned measures of wealth apply to the case of a Śūdra. In all the previously mentioned cases, it should be understood that for a Vaiśya the amount is double; for a Rājanya, triple; and for a Brāhmaṇa, quadruple. As for this statement of Bṛhaspati:
"This number [of panas] is prescribed for the low-born; for those of middle rank, it is remembered as double."
However, those possessing the four supreme qualities should be appointed by the examiners.

In this context, the statement “for those of middle rank, it is remembered as being double” should be interpreted as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) that includes even the triple [rank]. For those who are lower than Śūdras, the ordeals are exactly like those for Śūdras; for it is stated in the words of Manu: “All those born of degraded unions (*apadhvaṃsaja*) are declared to have the same legal status as Śūdras. Thus, even for some Brāhmaṇas, the ordeal must be administered just as for Śūdras. And so says Kātyāyana:
One should treat cowherds, merchants, artisans, performers,
servants, usurers, and even Brahmins as one would Śūdras.

In place of an oath involving one's sons, wife, and so forth for a Śūdra, there is an oath with cattle, seed-corn, and gold for a Vaiśya; for a Kṣatriya, with vehicles and weapons; and for a Brāhmaṇa, the oath is by means of a truthful statement.
"One should cause a Brāhmaṇa to swear by truth, a Kṣatriya by vehicles and weapons, a Vaiśya by cattle, seed-corn, and gold, and a Śūdra by all [the aforementioned] sins."
"Or he should touch the heads of his son and wife separately," according to the statement of Manu. Regarding this, there is a specific detail in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"Whether it be an immovable or a movable object that is the subject of the legal claim..."
But at the time of the performance of the ritual, whatever price it rightfully deserves;
"Having made that very [coin] into gold, one should employ it there as a divine ordeal (*divya*).

Regarding this, some hold that although the *paṇas* are to be counted in divine ordeals, since the term "paṇa" is used in common parlance for four *kākaṇis*, and because of the established usage among grammarians that "a *kākaṇika* is a fourth part of a *paṇa*," they believe that gold consisting of four *kākaṇis* itself is what is numbered by counts such as a thousand or a hundred. Others, however, maintain that the count in all divine ordeals refers to copper *kārṣikas*. Still others say: "The measure (*māna*) shall be the size of a grain of rice; ten measures are recorded as a *paṇa*."
Based on this scriptural statement, some maintain that the *paṇa* consists of exactly ten [māṣas]. Others, however, state:
"A *māṣa* should be known as the twentieth part of a *kārṣāpaṇa*;
a *kākaṇī*, moreover, is proclaimed to be a fourth part of a *māṣa*."
From such statements of Auśanasa; likewise:
"The wise say that four *kākaṇīs* make one *māṣaka*;
twenty of those again constitute what is called the principal *paṇa*."
Thus, because of the observation of another Smṛti text, and likewise because of the Smṛti statement,

"A māṣa is declared to be the twentieth part of a paṇa," they consider that the number used in ordeals refers to a paṇa consisting of twenty māṣas. In this way, among the four types of paṇas, the last one is not taken as constituting the status of a paṇa.

"A *paṇa* consists of twenty *māṣas*, but this is declared [to apply] except in the case of divine ordeals (*divya*)," because of the traditional rule (*smaraṇa*) prohibiting twenty *māṣas* in divine ordeals. Likewise: "Having ascertained the quantity of gold," and "Having ascertained the measure of all substances, one should determine the gold."

Likewise, because statements such as "one should calculate gold as the value for all types of objects" lead to the understanding that only gold is to be counted, and because there is no statement establishing that copper *kārṣāpaṇas* are to be counted in ordeals (*divya*), it is logical that only gold *paṇas* are to be counted in ordeals. Regarding the numbers to be counted, such as one thousand and so forth, the *paṇa*—weighing four *kākaṇis* and equal to a measure of rice—is to be counted; in cases such as "loss of a hundred," the *paṇa* is to be counted as consisting of ten measures. Now, is it not the case that eight *kākaṇis* are denoted by the word "rice"? That same thing is also denoted by the word "māya. In that context, within the section on punishments...
"However, a buffalo that causes the destruction of standing crops shall pay eight māṣas," according to this statement;
one should cause [the owner] to pay one-quarter of a paṇa for a cow, and likewise two quarters for a buffalo.
According to these words of Nārada: "Where a fine is prescribed as a māṣa, a pāda, or two pādas,
one should understand that an unspecified [māṣa] refers to a gold māṣaka."

And from the statement of Kātyāyana: "Since the words *paṇapāda*, *dvaya*, and *aṣṭamāṣa* are understood to have the same meaning, it is known that a *paṇa* consists of six *aṣṭamānas*. Likewise, there is the statement of some:
"That which has arisen from the heat of the sun is called a *trasareṇu*;
three groups of eight *trasareṇus* are proclaimed to be a *likṣā*."
Three of those are declared to be a mustard seed (sarṣapa), and that [mustard seed] is weighed as equal to a kākāṇī;
eight kākāṇīs are proclaimed to be a grain of rice (taṇḍula).
Two grains of rice are declared to be one *māṣaka*;
two of those are called a *kṛṣṇala*, and two *kṛṣṇalas* are an *andhikā*.
"The terms *andhikā* and *paṇa* are proclaimed as synonyms.

Here too, they consider the *paṇa* to consist of sixteen *mānas*. Likewise, it is stated in the *Vaikhānasa-Ātreya-saṃhitā*: "The measure [of a *māna*] should be the size of a grain of rice; ten *mānas* are recorded as a *paṇa*."

In this context as well, "eight" alone is denoted by the word *māna* (measure) and the word *taṇḍula* (grain). Therefore, since a *paṇa* consists of sixteen such measures, it follows that it is also to be counted [as a unit] in ordeals (*divya*). True; this is accepted. Since both are established by the scriptures, both are accepted. Consequently, whether consisting of sixteen measures or ten measures, the *paṇa* is taken as a countable unit. In that regard, the rule is: if the person undergoing purification (*śodhya*) possesses merit, a *paṇa* consisting of sixteen measures is taken; if the person undergoing purification lacks merit, a *paṇa* consisting of ten measures is to be counted. Among these, drinking poison (*viṣapāna*) is forbidden in the Kali age, except during the period of the water-vessel ordeal (*ghaṭikāvasthā*). The ancient teachers establish the following rule here: for those born in the natural order (*anuloma*), the ordeal is equal to the caste of the mother; for those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), it is equal to the caste of the father. On this point, there are summary verses (*saṃgrahaśloka*) recited by them:
Poison is prescribed for one hundred [palas], fire for ninety-five, water for sixty;
and the balance and the heated metal ball are declared for forty.
The procedure for consuming heated rice applies to thefts involving four and a half [paṇas];
for the theft of an object of the highest value, the consumption of rice is prescribed.
They say that the treasury of the fifteenth [chapter] is faith in the existence of the future, provided it is held by men;
and among the six [factors], when there is slight apprehension, the source of Dharma is one who possesses aversion [to evil].
In the case of a transgression by a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, the fine shall be ten paṇas;
thereafter, in the case of a Vaiśya, the procedure of oath prescribed in the Smṛtis applies.
For the sake of a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya, or a Brāhmaṇa, that [fine] from a Śūdra shall be two, three, or four times [the amount].
Thus it is said: "In the case of the fourfold qualities of Brahmins, all [ordeals] are considered optional;

Thus it is said: "For a [debt] of one *niṣka*, there shall be an oath of truth; for two *niṣkas*, touching the feet;

And this is the alternative for the fatalist (daiṣṭika), according to the previously stated arrangement.
Now, regarding oaths:
where the ordeals beginning with the balance and ending with the *dharmaja* have not been mentioned by the great-souled ones,
there the person under accusation shall be purified by means of oaths.
Regarding this matter of oaths, Hārīta states a specific rule:
"When wealth has been stolen by numerous thieves and the owner is himself unable to recover it,
he shall establish its quantity and its specific form solely by means of an oath."

When someone’s wealth has been stolen by thieves or denied [by them], the owner—disregarding whether the amount stolen or claimed is large or small—should establish the nature and quantity of that wealth solely through an oath administered to the guardians. As stated in another Smṛti: "The quantity of what was stolen should be verified by his own kin so as not to be deceived; even when the wealth is substantial, he should swear an oath before the guardians."
"Except in other cases,
a creditor who has not had the debt secured by his own kinsmen, sons, servants, and so forth,
shall establish even a large amount of the claim by means of an oath alone."
He himself has said: "When property has been stolen by thieves, the owner, even if the amount is large, should not take an oath;
he should clear himself by means of witnesses alone."

In cases where property has been carried off by thieves or stolen, disregarding whether the loss is small or great, and setting aside both the specific nature and the quantity of the goods, the owner himself may establish his claim through an ordeal (*adṛṣṭa-śapatha*) alone, even when the amount involved is large, such as in the case of elephants and the like. He must not, however, employ a witnessed oath (*dṛṣṭa-śapatha*). Regarding the determination of victory or defeat by means of ordeals, Kātyāyana has shown the specific fines: "He who is cleared [by the ordeal] shall be made to pay half a *śata*; he who is not cleared shall be subject to punishment. And he [Kātyāyana] has stated the same regarding the punishment: *Śatārdhaṃ dāpayec chuddham aśuddho daṇḍabhāg bhavet |* *Daṇḍaṃ ca sa evāha |* [The text continues with the specific fines for various weights of gold. ...and so forth. Thus, the determination of victory or defeat through ordeals is established. Therefore, it is concluded that the ordeal of the balance (*tulā-śapatha*) is indeed applicable in this context. Furthermore, the *Smṛticandrikā* states: "In the case of a theft of gold exceeding one *niṣka*, the ordeal of the balance is prescribed; for lesser amounts, other ordeals are employed. This is also consistent with the view of the *Smṛtiviveka*. Thus, the application of the ordeal of the balance is established. Alternatively, one may interpret the term "balance" (*tulā*) here as referring to the ordeal of the sacred libation (*kośa*), based on the following statement from the *Smṛti*: "The ordeal of the balance is prescribed for those accused of crimes involving the death penalty, whereas for those accused of minor offenses, the ordeal of the sacred libation is ordained. Since the term "balance" is used there as a synonym for the "sacred libation," it is logical to apply the procedure of the sacred libation in this instance as well. This is because the sacred libation is specifically prescribed for cases involving the theft of gold exceeding one *niṣka*. Therefore, the application of the sacred libation is established. Consequently, they hold that the ordeal of the balance is the correct application in this case. One should prescribe punishment in due order for poison, water, fire, the balance, the holy water-vessel, rice, and the ordeal of the heated gold coin.
One should assign one thousand, six hundred, five hundred,
four, three, two, one, and one less [respectively] among those who are inferior.
Yājñavalkya:
He for whom no terrible calamity, whether caused by the king or by fate, occurs within fourteen days [of the ordeal], shall be considered pure; of this there is no doubt.
The defects and non-defects of oaths, as well as the specific times for their examination, are now described. Regarding this, Kaṇva states:
"Within three fortnights, or within twenty-one days, or even within seven days, [the following consequences occur]:
illness, fire, the death of a kinsman, or the loss of cattle, grain, and wealth."
“The king shall punish that sinner for his terrible offense, in whose case such dreadful [signs] as these are seen in every respect. This is the rule:
for a minor offense, seven days; for a middling offense, fourteen days; for a major offense, twenty-one days or three fortnights. Viṣṇu says:
If one should see [these signs] within two weeks or even three weeks,
there will be illness, fire, the death of a kinsman, or perhaps a royal calamity.
"One should know that to be impure, and pure in the opposite case. Thus says Śātātapa:
"If [the impurity] occurs within seven days, or even within fourteen days..."
Or even within three weeks, there may be illness, fire, or the death of a kinsman.
One should predict misfortune for that person who experiences such calamities as danger from kings or fate, and the loss of livestock, grain, and wealth.
Kātyāyana states: In cases of crossing a boundary, [theft from] a treasury, and likewise touching a footprint,
the loss due to fate or the king is held to occur after three fortnights, one fortnight, and seven days, respectively.
Bṛhaspati says:
Within seven days, or even within fourteen days, no calamity arising from the king or from fate shall occur;
one becomes pure through oaths regarding kinsmen, sapinda-relatives, and wealth.

The teachers maintain that misfortune extends up to five generations on the mother’s side and up to seven generations on the father’s side. They say that when one experiences distress regarding the calamity of a kinsman or a relative as if it were one's own, such a calamity is to be understood [as occurring within this range]. Nārada states:
"Within seven days, or even within fourteen days, there may occur illness, fire, the death of a relative, or the loss of livestock, grain, and wealth."
One should not consider him pure whose individual [symptoms] persist,
or for whom a very great abnormality occurs after two weeks have passed.
"He should not be subjected to a formal charge by a wise man because he has allowed the lapse of time.

It has been stated that even a small matter becomes a source of great fear for embodied beings when it is contemplated. This refers to the subject of a major accusation (*mahābhiyoga*), as it is stated after introducing [the topic] with the words, "In cases of major accusations, these [rules apply]. Manu says:
"If, within fourteen days, there is no calamity caused by the king or by fate for one..."
"A terrible calamity arises; he should be known as pure by means of oaths. Thus it is said.

Shorter intervals for oaths were stated by the Grandfather (Bṛhaspati) regarding matters involving small amounts of wealth, based on the statement: "One should cause [the defendant] to take the ordeal even in a small matter.
These intervals range from three nights, seven nights, twelve days, or fourteen days.
"He in whom a physical transformation is observed is declared a wrongdoer.
Thus, having divided the substance into three parts—each less than the amount prescribed for the *mahābhiyoga* (grave accusation)—the three periods of three nights and so forth should be established.
This is from the *Vyavahāranirṇaya* by Varadarāja.
The section on the determination of the two means of valid cognition is completed. 6. Summary of the Means of Valid Cognition: Now follows the summary of the means of valid cognition.
In some cases of doubt, there may even be an absence of proof through human means;
here, in the absence of witnesses and the like, and in certain instances where divine ordeals are unavailable.
In the divine ordeal, however, one should fashion the golden image with its head and staff weighing one and a half [pala];
beginning from there, a Śūdra, holding dūrvā grass in his hand, shall swear an oath starting at half a kākaṇī.

From six mānas minus three kākāṇīs, a *kṛṣṇala* is formed; from twice that amount, a handful of sesame seeds (*tilahastaka*); and from thrice that amount, one holds a handful of silver, while from thrice that [silver] amount, one holds gold.
Having taken earth dug up by a plough four times the weight of his hand,
a low-caste man is freed from sins other than those concerning his children and wife when he has taken it five times the weight of his hand.
When ten living beings are being slaughtered, the purification of the dharma occurs through each group of ten;
in that very matter, one who lives by the plow should lick the plowshare.
Fifteen *kośas* make one *taṇḍula*; thirty *taṇḍulas* are traditionally recorded as making one *taptamāṣa*, and forty of those [make one *karṣa*].
Fifty *tulās* should be known [as the limit]; at sixty-seven, there will be water;
from seventy-five, fire; and from one hundred, the consumption of poison.
These [fines] are prescribed for a Śūdra; for a Vaiśya, they are recorded as double that amount.
Forty *dhānyamāṣas* make one *yava*; two of those make one *kṛṣṇala*.
Two *kṛṣṇalas* are said to be one *aṇvikā*, and that [measure] is also called a *paṇa*.
Three *aṇvikās* and one *kṛṣṇala* are declared to be a *hemamāṣa*.
Four *aṇvikās* are one *śāṇa*; fourteen [of those] are called a *dīnāra*.
Twenty *aṇvikās* are a *niṣka*; that *śāṇa* consists of eight *aṇvikās*.
Two *niṣkas* plus eight *aṇvikās* constitute a *citraka*;
two *niṣkas* plus sixteen *aṇvikās* is called a *karṣaka*.
"Ten *paṇas* make one *niṣka*, or ten *catuṣpaṇas* [make one], or twelve *niṣkas* [make one]; such is the worldly summary of measures."
Half of a *rājasarṣapa* is a worldly *kākaṇi*;
three *kākaṇis* make a *gaura*, which is a *māṣa* consisting of half a grain of rice.
Two *kākaṇis* and two measures (*māna*) constitute a medium-sized barley grain (*yava*);
two *kākaṇis* less than a *sapta-māṣa* is a *kṛṣṇala*.
Eight mānas make one kārṣāpaṇa, and ten mānas make one paṇa;
four onvikās make one śāṇa, and it is exactly the same in common worldly usage as well.
One *māṣa* consists of six *kākaṇis*, another consists of four *aṇvis*;
another is the *kārṣāpaṇa*, and the *niṣkas*—these are the coins that circulate in the eastern region.
A *suvarṇa* joined with eight *aṇvikās* is here called two *niṣkas*;
the *suvarṇa* itself is also termed a *dīnāra* and a *citraka*.
Half an *akṣa* consists of two *niṣkas* and is joined with half-measures starting from the *dvyaṇuka*.
Now, the rule for the measurement of silver:
by the measure of silver, there shall be one *māṣa* consisting of fourteen and a half measures.
Seven *aṇvikās* more than a *niṣka* is the measure of a *purāṇa*, and that is the standard of Manu.
A *śatamāna* and a *pala* shall consist of fourteen and a half *niṣkas*;
with those very [weights], a silver *niṣka* is established, and then the *tāntrika* [measure] is declared.
The measure of the *niṣka* according to the *Pāñcarātra* and *Vaikhānasa* traditions is now stated:
four *aṇvikās* shall constitute one *triniṣka*; a *karṣaka* and a *paṇa* [are the same];
and sixteen of these [triniṣkas] shall be a full *niṣka*, or fifteen and a half, or fourteen and three-quarters.
The lowest [fine] is two niṣkas; the middle should be double that; and the highest should be fourfold.
Alternatively, it may be one and a half niṣkas, or two niṣkas and sixteen [paṇas].
The first is double that [in size], the middle is double the middle, and the highest is double the middle;
[the weights] are the yava, the kṛṣṇala, the māṣa, the suvarṇa, and the silver niṣka.
For those who follow the Vaiṣṇava path, there is indeed no one-sixth share [of the merit] as there is for those who speak according to the teachings of Manu.
Thus ends the *Mānasaṃgraha* by Varadarāja.
7. The Section on the Recovery of Debts (*Ṛṇādāna*). Now, among the eighteen titles of law, the first to be encountered, the recovery of debts, is discussed. On this point, Nārada says:

That which is to be given and that which is not to be given, by whom, where, and in what manner, as well as the law regarding the giving and receiving [of gifts]— this is known as the legal title of "Recovery of Debts" (ṛṇādāna).

"Such a debt is to be paid; such a debt is not to be paid; such a debt is to be paid by this specific creditor; it is to be paid at this time; and it is to be paid in this manner"—thus there are five types regarding the debtor (*adharmarṇa*). Regarding the creditor (*uttamarṇa*), there are two types: the procedure for giving and the procedure for taking—thus [altogether] there are seven types. Since the other [procedures] are preceded by the payment of the debt, Yājñavalkya first states the method for that payment:
"The interest shall be one-eightieth part every month when there is a pledge;
otherwise, according to the order of the castes, it shall be two, three, four, or five percent per hundred."

That which is pledged by a debtor to a creditor for the sake of confidence is called *ādhi*; here, it is termed a "mortgage" (*bandhaka*). In a transaction involving such a mortgage, an eightieth part of the principal lent each month constitutes lawful interest. Thus, on twenty-five *paṇas*, the interest is one-quarter of a *paṇa*. And so says Manu:
"Hear now the interest declared by the words of Vasiṣṭha regarding usury:
five *māṣas* on twenty [*paṇas*] is the lawful interest; it does not fall away from righteousness."

And so says Gautama: “Interest on a loan is lawful at the rate of five *māṣas* per twenty [of principal] per month. When ten *māṣas* constitute a *paṇa*, a *māṣa* is one-twentieth of a *paṇa*, which is half a *taṇḍula*. When twenty *māṣas* constitute a *paṇa*, it is equal to one *taṇḍula*. When sixteen *māṣas* constitute a *paṇa*, the calculation should be adjusted accordingly. Thus, in a transaction with collateral (*sabandhaka*), interest at the rate of one-eightieth part is lawful. Otherwise, in a transaction without collateral (*abandhaka*), for the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, the lawful rate is respectively two, three, four, and five percent per month. For a Brāhmaṇa debtor, the interest is two percent; for a Kṣatriya debtor, three percent; for a Vaiśya debtor, four percent; and for a Śūdra debtor, five percent per month. It is called "two, three, four, or five percent" because an interest of two, three, four, or five [units] is given on this hundred. [The suffix -ka is applied] according to Pāṇini 5.1.47: "That in which interest, profit, toll, tax, and so forth is received. For a Kṣatriya, the interest is two percent on a Kṣatriya debtor, three percent on a Vaiśya debtor, and four percent on a Śūdra debtor. Likewise, for a Vaiśya, it is two percent on a Vaiśya debtor and three percent on a Śūdra debtor. For a Śūdra, it is two percent on a Śūdra debtor. Therefore, in all cases among those of the same caste, two percent is lawful; for the next lower caste, three percent; for the one below that, four percent; and for the one two degrees lower, five percent is the lawful rate. And so says Manu: [Manu 8.140–142] "One percent per month is the lawful interest on gold; two percent on grain; three percent on wool, thread, and cotton; and four percent on liquids, perfumes, and honey. On salt, skins, meat, silk, linen, and wool, the interest shall not exceed more than five times the principal. On liquids, perfumes, honey, clarified butter, molasses, jaggery, lac, wax, silk, linen, conch-shells, shells, wax, tin, lead, and iron, the interest is set at five percent. One may take interest of two percent, three percent, four percent, five percent,
and ten percent per month from the social classes in their respective order.

Regarding this, Nārada says that interest is of four kinds: "Interest is declared to be corporeal (kāyikā), periodical (kālikā), stipulated (kāritā), and likewise compound interest (cakravṛddhi); such is the fourfold interest taught in the scriptures."
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states the distinction:
"Interest is said to be of four kinds, proclaimed by others as fivefold, and declared by others as sixfold; understand it according to its true nature."
Nārada says: There is bodily interest, periodical interest, and furthermore compound interest; there is stipulated interest, crest-interest, as well as enjoyment-interest and profit-interest.
Interest that is bodily is connected with manual labor; that which is to be taken monthly is periodical interest;
compound interest is the interest upon interest; and stipulated interest is that which is agreed upon by the debtor.
That interest which is collected daily is known as "crest-interest" (śikhāvṛddhi);
it increases constantly like a crest, but ceases upon the cutting off of the head.
From a planet, the gain is declared to be praise; from a field, the gain is enjoyment.
Regarding this, Vyāsa says:
"That which is connected with the acts of milking or carrying is declared to be bodily (gain)."
That which is not contrary to the body, such as the constant payment of a fee for the feet and so forth, is bodily [action].
Thus, the interest at the rate of one-eighth is corporeal. Nārada says:
"The interest that flows month by month is known as *kālikā*;
that interest which is personally stipulated by the creditor is called *kāritā*."
Interest upon interest is declared to be *cakravṛddhi* (compound interest). Interest on grain that is collected every day is called *śikhāvṛddhi* (stake-interest). Vyāsa states:
"But that which is enjoyed through the use of a house is designated as *stoma* (rent)."
Grain and the like produced on the land is called *śada*. Kātyāyana states:
"The wealth lent by a creditor shall always be recoverable as double;
however, if it has not reached double, one should calculate the interest according to the original rate."
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states the specific rule:
"Those traveling through forests should pay ten percent; those traveling by sea, twenty percent;
or they may all pay their own stipulated interest on all types of transactions among all castes."

Those who go to the wilderness are *kāntāragāḥ*; those who go to the sea are *samudragāḥ*. For them, ten percent, twenty percent, and one hundred percent are lawful. The phrase "month by month" is also to be supplied here. Regarding interest that has been stipulated (*kāritā*), all [castes] beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, by virtue of the transaction, shall pay the interest they themselves have made or agreed upon, whether there be a pledge or no pledge, among all castes. Now, the specific limit of interest according to the specific nature of the object is stated. On this point, Kātyāyana says:
In the case of gems, pearls, coral, gold, and silver, the interest may increase threefold, twofold, and twofold respectively; the same applies to fruit, firewood, and water.
Manu:
Interest on a loan, when collected at one time, shall not exceed double the principal;
in the case of grain, wool, or beasts of burden, it shall not exceed five times the original amount.

*Śada* refers to the produce of the field, such as flowers and the like; *lava* refers to wool, yak-tail hair, and so forth; and *vāhya* refers to draft animals, such as oxen and horses, and the like. Bṛhaspati says: "Interest on gold is twofold; on cloth and silver, it is threefold; on grain, it is declared to be fourfold; and the same applies to *śada*, draft animals, and *lava*."
Nārada says:
The interest on gold, grain, and cloth is two, three, or four times the principal;
for liquids, it is declared to be eightfold; and for women and cattle, it is the offspring.
Bṛhaspati says: An increase of fivefold is prescribed for vegetables and likewise fourfold for seeds;
an eightfold increase is considered appropriate for salt, oils, and liquors.
It is said that when molasses and honey are administered, their effects manifest after a long time.
Kātyāyana states: "The increase for all types of oils, as well as for liquors, clarified butter,
molasses, and salt, should be known to be eightfold."
Bṛhaspati says: In the case of grass, wood, bricks, thread, stakes, leather, bones, and eyelashes, as well as weapons,
flowers, and fruits, interest does not cease.

In this context, the meaning is that due to the association with wood and other such items, one does not turn back before reaching eightfold [interest]. Viṣṇu states: "For fermenting agents, cotton, thread, leather, armor, weapons, bricks, and charcoal, the interest is non-decreasing; for those not mentioned, it is twofold. Bharadvāja says:
"The increase on gold, grain, and clothing is twofold, threefold, and fourfold respectively;
the increase on ghee is eightfold, and on copper and other metals, it is fourfold."
The interest on oils shall be sixfold; for women and cattle, it is their offspring;
for precious metals and gems, it shall be fivefold; and for cotton, fourfold.
The increase of woods such as sandalwood and the like becomes eightfold;
thus the method of increase has been declared, and there is no increase beyond this.
"There is no interest upon interest," such is the teaching of the Maker of Dharma;
nor should interest ever be taken on unagreed interest, nor on excessive interest.

By the word "copper" (*tāmra*), the inclusion of tin, lead, and so forth—excluding gold and silver—is intended. "Treasures" (*kośa*) means treasures consisting of grain. By the mention of "cotton," the inclusion of cloth and similar items is intended. The mention of "sandalwood" is stated by Asahāya to be an illustration for fragrant substances. Regarding this, Viṣṇu says: "In the case of theft involving the property of a Brāhmaṇa, and likewise in the theft of gold, one must subsequently give back [the stolen object] along with eleven times its value."

In the case of stealing property other than gold belonging to a Brāhmaṇa, as well as in the case of stealing gold belonging to a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, the fine shall be twelvefold immediately. Thus says Pitāmaha:
"For the theft of gems and gold, a twelvefold fine is ordained immediately;
for silver and other such property belonging to a Brāhmaṇa, it is elevenfold immediately."
Silver is considered to have fivefold interest, and land likewise eightfold.
Because of the statement "immediately," there is an absence of compound interest (*vṛddhi*). On this point, Nārada says:
"There shall be no interest on gifts made out of affection, provided they are not explicitly requested."
Even if not formally requested, [the debt] increases after half a year has passed.
Kātyāyana says: If one who has set aside a portion of the debt departs for another region after being requested to pay,
that debt shall begin to accrue interest after three months have passed.
If one who has taken merchandise should depart for another region without paying the price,
or if one who remains in his own country does not pay when asked more than once;
There, he shall pay back the interest that has accrued even if he does not wish to do so,
as well as any debt incurred for the sake of the community, whether it was acquired through his efforts or preserved by him.
After three seasons, one may obtain wealth along with interest.
In such cases as these, an eightieth part [of the principal] is intended as the rate of interest. Kātyāyana states:
"Whatever has been given out of affection does not increase if it was not requested."
If what was requested is not given, the debt increases by five percent per month.

The meaning is that five percent increases every month. Interest shall never accrue on hides, grain, liquor, gambling stakes, the cost of merchandise, the bride-price for a wife, and on amounts received as collateral security.
If it were both self-made and caused to be made, one would incur interest; thus says Saṃvarta:
"There is no interest on a woman's property, nor on profit, nor on a deposit, nor likewise with a debtor."
In cases of doubt and regarding suretyship, it is not valid unless it was made by the person themselves.

On this point, Yājñavalkya states: "If one does not accept their own wealth when it is being offered back after having been lent, that [debt] shall be deposited with a neutral third party; beyond that point, it no longer accrues interest."
On this point, Viṣṇu and Gautama state: "A pledge that has been used does not increase [in value] for one who wishes to give it back, nor for one who is obstructed. Vyāsa says:

"For one who wishes to give back a surety, a pledged object that has been used, or a loan that was not taken, the interest does not increase; likewise, the fine for one who has surrendered, and a white (pure) gift promised."
Now, the procedure for debt is described.

Among these, that which is called "the giving of a debt" (*ṛṇapradāna*) consists of one's own repayment to another, conditioned by the act of returning what was received. It is of several kinds: with collateral and with interest, and without collateral and without interest. Of these, the application of lending with collateral and with interest is now stated. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says: "Collateral (*ādhi*) is defined as a pledge (*bandha*); it is said to be of four kinds."
Both movable and immovable property, as well as that which is merely for protection and that which is for enjoyment.

Hārīta says: A pledge is declared to be of four kinds: the one to be kept (gopya), the one to be used (bhogya), the one serving as proof of debt (arthapratyayahetu), and the fourth, which is made by command (ājñākṛta).
He states their essential nature:
"A pledge for use previously described is called the best;
but a pledge for custody is that which, having given one's own property to others, is kept hidden in the house."
That which is the cause for the understanding of the meaning is called *pratyayādhi*;
that which is established by the command of a king or an assembly is known as *ājñādhi*.
The proclamation is made in the assembly of the Śrāvaṇas. Vyāsa says:
"The seizure of property and its sale, as well as cruel punishment, are prescribed;
both of these shall not exist otherwise—this is the certainty of Dharma."
A pledge (ādhi) is declared to be of two kinds: immovable and movable;
the fulfillment of both occurs through possession, and not otherwise.
If a debtor causes an obstruction to the entry of a pledge,
he shall be compelled to pay an excessive amount for its use and be fined six times the value of that pledge.
This concerns the subject of usufructuary pledges (*bhogyādhi*). Yājñavalkya says regarding the pledge for custody (*gopyādhi*) and others:
"There is no interest on the usufructuary pledge when it is used, nor when it is improved, nor when it is lost;
and it must be restored even if destroyed, except in cases caused by fate or the king."
The cultivation of the property with its appurtenances is the cause of its fitness for use. Nārada says:

"If there should be a loss of the principal of a pledge due to some act of fate or the king, the debtors must pay the value of the pledge; however, if they are unable to do so, it shall remain a usufructuary pledge."
Bṛhaspati:
A pledge for custody [becomes forfeited] after it has doubled in value; likewise, one with a fixed term [is forfeited] upon the expiration of that period.
Once the debtor has been notified at the proper time, the pledge may be used immediately thereafter.
Kātyāyana says:
But where the depositor is not present, the owner shall announce the pledge to the king; thereafter, it is the settled rule that it may be sold publicly.
Vyāsa states: If a pledge consisting of gold or other valuables should be lost due to the fault of the receiver,
the creditor, having cleared off the debt along with its interest, shall cause the borrower to pay the principal value thereof.
If a debtor has placed a pledge at the time of the initial entry into the transaction,
he shall be made to pay one and a half times the value of its use as compensation, and a fine six times that amount.
Kātyāyana states: "If a debtor conceals his pledge, or sells it and so forth by force,
he shall pay a fine three times the value and become liable for the pledge once again."
And so Manu says:
"The unwise man who enjoys a pledge without the permission of the owner must forfeit his interest; that enjoyment shall be the compensation for it."
On this point, Kātyāyana states:
"If one should cause labor to be performed on a pledge without its owner's consent or against his will,
he shall be made to pay the value of the enjoyment and the labor, or he shall not receive the interest."
Nārada says: A pledge must not be used by force; one who uses it shall forfeit the interest. He should satisfy the owner with its value; otherwise, the pledge [is lost] to him.
This refers to the domain of pledges consisting of bipeds, quadrupeds, and other moving creatures. Regarding this, Bhāradvāja says:
At the time of entering into a pledge, if the creditor does not desire the use [of the object], then the enjoyment [of it] perishes;
therefore, after that point, he shall not cause that wealth to increase.
Kātyāyana states: "But whatever has been pledged as a deposit (ādhi) and is destroyed through an act of God or by the king,
the debtor shall be made to pay that debt to the creditors along with interest."
One should not disturb the increase of enjoyment nor the decrease of the object to be enjoyed;
rather, one must simply enjoy as much as is written in the document.
On this point, Nārada says:
Even when being protected, if a pledge should become worthless over time,
another pledge must be provided, or the wealth of the creditor must be paid back.

This [rule] also concerns movable property; for even though immovable property such as land may become worthless, there is no prohibition against others taking possession of it. Alternatively, it refers to cases where the object deposited becomes worthless over time and not due to any other cause. For example, it concerns the case where one says, "I shall return [the animal] when it has reached a state capable of bearing loads," and then, by the force of time alone, buffaloes, horses, oxen, and so forth become worthless through their incapacity for drawing loads and the like; or likewise, when sandalwood, saffron, ghee, jaggery, and so forth become worthless through the force of time alone by losing their fragrance or becoming foul-smelling. This has been clearly stated by Kātyāyana:
If, however, [the debtor] should die or flee due to the fault of the creditor, another pledge must be provided;
the debtor shall be released from the debt.
Because of the statement regarding movable property that "it may be lost or die," he states a specific rule for immovable property:
"If the field is carried away by a flood or confiscated by the king,
another pledge must be provided, or the debt must be paid to the creditor."
Yājñavalkya: When the debtor has presented himself, the pledge must be released by the creditor; otherwise, it shall become forfeited.
If the debtor is not present, the creditor may obtain the value from the family or from another for the sake of the pledge.
Or it may remain there at its value as fixed at that time, without interest;
or, with the consent of the debtor, he may sell it in the presence of witnesses.
But when the debt has become doubled,
then indeed the pledge must be released once the money produced from it has entered [the creditor's possession] and reached the amount of double the principal.
This concerns the subject of a pledge that is to be enjoyed with interest:
"If the pledge is not released when the debt has doubled, it shall be forfeited;
however, a pledge for a fixed term is forfeited at the end of that time, whereas a pledge to be enjoyed for its produce is never forfeited."

The forfeiture of a pledge (*ādhipraṇāśa*) means that, having relinquished its connection with the debtor, it comes under the ownership of the creditor. This refers to pledges consisting of gold and the like; the same applies even to those used for a fixed period. A pledge to be enjoyed for its produce (*phalabhogya*), such as a field or a grove, never perishes. He states an exception to the forfeiture of a pledge: "He shall cause the debt secured by a pledge of good character to be paid with interest;
he shall deliver the substance pledged as a token of truth (*satyaṃkāra*) when it has doubled."

By means of good character and pure intention, a debtor may pledge an object of great value and appropriate for himself only a small amount of wealth. Such wealth does not perish even when it has doubled; rather, having received the double, the debtor must repay it. This refers to the doubling [of the debt] through the arrangement of a pledge (*bandhaka*). Even when the debt has doubled, the double amount must be paid; there is no loss of the pledge. The meaning of the term *satyaṃkāra* (earnest money) is as follows: Merchants, desiring to acquire goods of high value such as betel nuts and other fruits, give two or three unweighed coins into the hand of the seller, settle the terms of the transaction for purchase and sale, and then take possession of the merchandise. In that case, if the one employing the funds should violate the agreement, he incurs a loss of the price. If the buyer violates it, he must pay back exactly double the value of the goods he took. Regarding the matter of the pledge for the creditor once the loan has doubled, [the text] says: *caritreṇa dhaninaḥ svacchāśayatvena bahumūlyam ādhīkṛtyādhamarṇena svalpam eva dravyam ātmasāt kṛtam | evaṃbhūtaṃ dravyaṃ dviguṇībhūte ‘pi na naśyati | kiṃ tu dviguṇaṃ gṛhītvā dātavyam iti | bandhakakalpanayā dviguṇībhūtā | dviguṇībhūte ‘pi dviguṇaṃ dātavyam | nādhināśa iti | satyaṃkārety asyāyam arthaḥ | vaṇijo hi bahumūlyaṃ kramukādiphalaṃ svīcikīrṣantaḥ vikretur haste dvitrāṇi nistulāni datvā krayavikrayavyavahāravyavasthāṃ ca niścitya paṇyaṃ svīkurvanti | tatra yadi dravyaprayoktā saṃvidam atilaṅghayet, mūlyahātim avāpnuyāt | gṛhītrā tadvilaṅghane tadgṛhītadravyaṃ dviguṇam eva deyam | prayukte dviguṇībhūte uttamarṇasya bandhakaviṣayam āha ||* [This concludes the passage.]
Even by means of a formal pledge (*satyaṅkāra*), double the amount must indeed be paid. Bṛhaspati says:
When the term has expired and the profit has ceased, the owner of the pledge becomes the owner of the wealth.
But before ten days have passed, the debtor is entitled to enjoy [the property].
That which does not flow away [as interest] should be the principal share for the creditor;
even beyond the doubling [of the principal], there is the time-bound interest (*kālikā*) for those who have a fixed rate.
Then the king should decide the case with those who know the principles of legal procedure. Vyāsa says:
If the interest accrued is double the principal before the time for repayment has arrived.
But the root alone, or less by one-quarter, or half of that, or even just a quarter.
"Due to the doubling [of the debt], the creditor shall not recover the wealth at all," so says Bṛhaspati.
"When gold has doubled, if the debtor has died or disappeared..."
Having taken that deficient substance, sell it in the presence of witnesses.
Alternatively, he may keep the pledged item for ten days in the presence of the public after its value has been paid;
thereafter, having received a small sum commensurate with the debt, he should continue to use it.
Having stabilized the practice through men skilled in calculation,
one who adopts that which is known as its "bandhu-jāti" shall not commit an error.
On this point Vyāsa says:
"When the value of the property has doubled and the stipulated time has expired,
the creditor becomes the owner of the pledge, provided he has waited for two weeks."
Then, having paid the interest in the interim, the debtor shall undergo imprisonment;
he shall pay the principal amount together with the produce, once the full time has elapsed.

Even when the full period has elapsed, a field or other property that is to be enjoyed as a fruit never perishes; having paid the principal debt established by agreement along with interest, one shall recover the field. In this regard, the pledge for enjoyment (*bhogyādhi*) is of two kinds: the pledge for enjoyment with conditions (*sapratyaya-bhogyādhi*) and the pledge for enjoyment without conditions (*apratyaya-bhogyādhi*). One is for the purpose of clearing the principal together with the interest; that is called the pledge for enjoyment with conditions. The other is for the purpose of clearing the interest alone; that is called the pledge for enjoyment without conditions. Regarding the pledge for enjoyment with conditions, Vyāsa says:
Having agreed upon some rate of interest and having taken the principal according to reality,
enjoy that field for the sake of interest, even if it means the loss of the principal.
Thus, there may be a pledge with a condition (*pratyayādhi*); through a deficiency [in its maintenance], its loss would occur.

A pledge for use (*bhogyādhi*) is for the purpose of clearing a debt along with interest; this is the meaning of the term "pledge for use with a condition" (*sapratyayabhogyādhi*). Kātyāyana describes the pledge for use without a condition (*apratyayabhogyādhi*):
"If, having received goods for the sake of interest, one gives property suitable for use..."
Whether it be movable or immovable property, that is called a pledge for enjoyment (bhogyādhi).
Having paid the entire principal, one shall recover one’s own field and other property.

In the case of a pledge for use (*bhogyādhi*), when the debtor seeks to redeem the mere principal, he shall recover his own field and other property by paying the principal amount received from the creditor. This is the intended meaning of the statement: "This is a pledge for use without [fixed] trust. Bharadvāja states:
In the case of a pledge with trust (*pratyayādhi*), at the stated time, in the absence of interest, the creditor himself [shall restore it].
Having entered into the pledge, he should at that time enjoy the property as recorded in the written agreement.
But when there is a dispute regarding the conditions, the interest that was previously recorded must be paid;
it is the firm conclusion of the scriptures that only that much should be enjoyed.
Whatever additional amount is to be paid there for interest, that the debtor shall pay again;
indeed, the debtor shall fulfill it to the extent of that interest.

The intended meaning of the statement, "In the case of a pledge for enjoyment with interest, at the time of redemption, one should pay the full value including interest if the principal is insufficient, and one should not take anything in excess," is as follows: Bharadvāja states, "If the redemption of a pledge for enjoyment that was [taken] on the full moon of Vaiśākha occurs on the full moon of Āṣāḍha, that [deficit] is the fault of the creditor; therefore, this [deficit] must be made good."
Interest on a low rate increases by way of compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*).
There is no legal release from debt through the enjoyment of all the debtor's property while he remains blind (incapable).
If one enjoys [the property] by force when the time for repayment has arrived, the fine shall be double.
Bharadvāja says:
If one who has not been authorized by his master pledges a pledge, he shall be deprived of his own property; however, if he does so in times of distress, it is as in the previous case.
Kātyāyana says: Those who are mostly pitiable, fraudulent, and base are ruined by the seizure of a pledge;
others of such a nature likewise become destroyers of the pledge itself.
Vyāsa has declared the punishment for two people who pledge the same security:
"If one should provide a single pledge to two parties, what should the procedure be?
Of those two, the earlier claimant shall take it; the pledgor shall be liable for the punishment of a thief."
"Between a mortgage, a gift, and a purchase, the earlier one is indeed more powerful"—from this statement, that which is earlier must be accepted. Bṛhaspati says:
"When a single field is given as a pledge by two parties at the same time..."
That which was previously eaten by one of those two, its efficacy shall be attained by that person.
When two [articles] are presented at the same time, the price should be equal for both;
this rule is fully proclaimed regarding both giving and selling.
Regarding the non-payment of debts, Bharadvāja states a specific sequence:
"Where both the object of a pledge and the principal sum are seen with a creditor, the principal alone shall first be paid; afterwards follows the redemption of the pledge."

The meaning is that between a debt with collateral and one without collateral, the one without collateral should be paid first, and the one with collateral afterwards. If the creditor should possess the property of the debtor at that time, then that debt is extinguished according to that sequence.
The meaning is that, according to that sequence, the debt is reduced by half of that [payment]. Regarding the method for taking a portion of the debt, Yājñavalkya says:
"Having paid the money, the debtor shall write on the back of the document;
or the creditor shall provide a receipt marked with his own hand."
Nārada says: A creditor who has received a pledge should return it to the debtor upon demand;
if he does not return it when asked, he shall suffer the loss of the remainder [of the debt].
Regarding the case of receiving the payment in full, Yājñavalkya says:
"Having paid the debt, one should tear up the document; for the sake of purification, however, one should have another document executed.
Indeed, whatever document was executed with witnesses must be returned along with those witnesses."
Nārada: But regarding what is to be given to a Brāhmaṇa, if he has no descendants, one should offer it to his *sakulyas*; in their absence, to his *bandhus*.
"But when there are no agnates (sakulyas), nor relatives or kinsmen (saṃbandhibāndhavas), then one should give [the debt] to the twice-born; if they too are absent, one should cast it into the water.
Now follows the method of repayment according to the value of the pledge.
Kātyāyana says:
If there is a deficiency due to the lapse of time from the value at the time the price was received, the debtor shall pay only the principal;
he is not required to pay interest.
If the price doubles, the value [of the debt] shall likewise double;
he from whom no interest flows shall remain a creditor only of the principal.
When there is a dispute among litigants regarding the increase in the price of commodities even beyond double its value,
the king should then settle the case with those who know the principles of justice.
Vyāsa states: If a time-bound debt becomes double before the time for its repayment,
then the payment should be either the principal alone, or half of that, or even a quarter.
"The creditor receives back double the debt, yet it is devoid of interest. Thus [ends the section]. Now, the rule regarding the surety (pratibhū) is stated;
herein, Bṛhaspati says:
In the treatises, the wise have observed four types of surety: for appearance, for trust, for payment, and likewise for the delivery of a pledged object.
One said, "I shall show it," while another spoke: "I am the giver; I shall hand over this wealth. Another said: "I shall deliver it."

But first, those two who are proven false shall be made to pay the wealth that was reported at that time; however, in the case of a contradiction regarding subsequent claims, it is the same for those two, or their sons, in their absence.

Now, those who are prohibited from acting as sureties are stated. Viṣṇu says: "The master, an enemy, one under restraint, an official, one punished, one under suspicion, an heir, a friend, a permanent resident, one engaged in royal service, one devoid of passion, an ascetic, a pauper, a child, an elderly person, a woman, and one afflicted by disease are not [eligible] sureties. In the case of an heir and a friend, they may be permitted in certain instances when others are unavailable. Kātyāyana says: "Neither a master, nor an enemy, nor one appointed by a master, nor likewise one under restraint, nor one punished, nor one under suspicion is eligible for this purpose at any time."
Neither an heir, nor a friend, nor those who reside permanently [with him],
nor those appointed to royal service, nor men who have gone forth as renunciants [are liable for debts].
One who is unable to pay the debt to the creditor and an equivalent fine to the king should not be accepted as a surety for the performance of the obligation without being fully examined.
One who is under suspicion is one accused of a crime. "Those who dwell for life" refers to perpetual religious students (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārins*). On this point, Yājñavalkya states:
"Suretyship, debt, and witness testimony between brothers, husband and wife, or father and son are indeed not recorded as valid when they have not yet divided their inheritance."

Some authorities state that there are three types of sureties (*pratibhū*): 1. The *darśana-pratibhū* (surety for appearance), who says, "I shall produce him at the time or place required by you. 2. The *pratyaya-pratibhū* (surety for confidence), who, when asked what kind of person he is, provides a word of assurance, saying, "He is a virtuous man. Both of these are liable to pay [the debt] in the event of his failure to appear or his failure to inspire confidence. 3. The *dāna-pratibhū* (surety for payment), who says, "I myself will give this wealth. In that regard, if the first two die, their sons need not pay. However, the distinction is that if the *dāna-pratibhū* dies, the debt must be paid even by the sons. Thus it has been stated by Yājñavalkya:
Where a guarantor for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*) or a guarantor for trust (*prātyayika*) has died,
their sons shall not pay the debt, except for one who stood as a guarantor specifically for payment.
Prajāpati has declared:

"In times of famine, during a siege of the kingdom, for the sake of religious duties, or likewise in times of distress, only the principal debt is to be paid, not the interest; this is the settled rule."
Kātyāyana says: He who, being pressured by creditors and others, gives a loan on the basis of a surety,
shall be entitled to receive double that amount after three fortnights have passed.

The phrase "twofold" is an illustration of the maximum interest applicable to all liquid assets. Because the term "suffering" (pīḍā) is used here, it is understood that if the debt was given out of greed for doubling the principal and so forth, it shall not increase further; rather, it must be paid according to its actual growth. Yājñavalkya states: "Where a surety has been made to pay the creditors' wealth publicly, that wealth must be repaid twofold by the debtor."
Viṣṇu:
Whatever wealth a surety may pay when pressured by the creditor,
that money must be paid back double to him by the debtors.

Regarding this, Prajāpati states the specific rule: "If the depositor is destitute of wealth and the pledge-holder is wealthy, the value of that [pledge] must be paid by you; he is not entitled to receive interest."

The debtor (*adhamarṇa*) is the one who consumes [the debt]; the *lagnaka* is the surety (*pratibhū*). A debtor who lacks wealth shall pay exactly what has been paid by the surety. This is because, if the payment were made immediately upon being given, there would be no possibility for the surety to be released. Furthermore, since it has been stated that in times of distress—such as famine or national upheaval—one may merely deliver the value [of the debt], this case follows the same principle. Bṛhaspati says: "The creditor shall grant time to the surety for the search of what is lost;
according to the circumstances of the place, for a fortnight, a month, or even a year."
Now, the rules for the recovery of wealth that has been lent are stated. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"One who is recovering a debt that has been acknowledged shall not be censured by the king;
but if he goes to the king while the debt is being recovered [by the debtor], he shall be fined and made to pay that wealth."

A creditor recovering what is owed by a debtor who has admitted the debt while being pursued for it must not be censured by the king. However, if the debtor, while being pursued, goes to the king and, having approached the monarch, continues to press his case against the creditor, he shall be fined one-fourth [of the debt] and made to pay that money to the creditor. This is the counter-example to the rule "by one who deviates from the Smṛti and established custom," because such an act is unjust. And so says Manu:
"He who, while being pursued, reports the creditor to the king according to his own will..."
He shall be made to pay a fourth part of that to the king, and that wealth shall belong to him [the king].

"One should recover the debt through *dharma*, through *vyavahāra*, through *chala*, through *ācarita*, and fifthly, through *bala*. Here, *dharma* means by means of truth; *vyavahāra* means by means of witnesses, documents, and so forth; *chala* means by means of what was stated through negligence; *ācarita* means by means of fasting and other such methods; and *bala* means by means of imprisonment with fetters and so forth—one should thus recover it. Regarding that, Yājñavalkya states the sequence to be followed when several creditors arrive simultaneously:
A debtor shall be made to pay the creditors according to the order in which they were approached;
however, having paid the Brāhmaṇas first, he shall pay the king immediately thereafter.

Among those of the same caste, a debt must be paid back in the exact order in which it was contracted; among those of different castes, one should pay according to the order of the superiority of their caste. Regarding one who is unable to recover the debt themselves, Yājñavalkya says:
"The king shall cause the debtor to pay ten percent upon the amount recovered;
and the creditor, having obtained his wealth, shall be made to pay five percent."

The debtor shall be made to pay a tenth part of the amount recovered as a fine, and the creditor shall be made to pay a twentieth part as wages. Regarding a debtor who is destitute of wealth, [the author] says:
One should compel a man of low caste who is impoverished to perform labor for the sake of the debt;
but a Brāhmaṇa who is impoverished should be made to pay gradually, according to his income.

A debtor who is other than a Brāhmaṇa should be made to perform labor, taking into account his caste, lineage, and capacity. A Brāhmaṇa who lacks wealth should be made to pay as far as possible. Here, the mention of the "inferior" (hīna) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the "equal" as well, by way of demonstrating the absence of superiority. Likewise, the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is for the purpose of indicating the "superior"; thus it was stated by Brahmavitpravara. As Manu says: "The debtor should discharge the debt to the creditor even through labor; one of equal or inferior caste should do so, and one of superior caste should do so gradually."

Thus, one should cause a person other than a Brāhmaṇa to perform labor until his debt is exhausted; however, a Brāhmaṇa shall pay according to his means. On this point, Bharadvāja says: "In the absence of wealth, the debtor's property should be given [in lieu of payment], and for others, it should be given according to that sequence:
grain, gold, base metals, as well as cattle such as cows and buffaloes."
Clothing, land, a group of servants, vehicles, and so forth— in this sequence,
they should be understood as belonging to the creditor, and they must be returned in that same order.
In the absence of a field, there is likewise a grove; in its absence, the purchase of a house;
and in the absence of the acceptance [of gifts] by the twice-born, the passing of time is prescribed.
Now, the transformation through the extinction of debt is described.

Manu states that for one unable to pay the debt, having given something and having made the interest due on the appointed day part of the principal, another transaction for the sake of interest may be arranged:
"He who is unable to pay the debt and wishes to enter into a new transaction..."
Having paid the interest that has accrued, he may change the instrument of debt.
If he should return the loan without having shown that very gold,
he ought to pay as much interest as may have accrued.

"Then" means at that time; "conquered" means obtained as a debt. "Execution" (*karaṇa*) refers to the formal acceptance of the debt. "Exchange" (*parivṛtti*) is a renewed transaction; it does not necessarily mean that gold must be shown. The meaning is that an exchange should be made by mere agreement. Regarding this, Prajāpati states a specific rule: "Having given interest, or a portion of the interest, or even a part of the principal, according to his ability, he should effect the exchange of the execution."
Regarding this, Kātyāyana states a specific rule:
"Even when [the father] is present, or when he is afflicted by disease, or likewise when he has gone abroad from his own country,
the debt incurred by the father must be paid by the sons after twenty years."

Regarding a debt contracted by a father while he was still alive, it must be paid by his sons if he lacks the means to do so; thus says another Smṛti: "Sons shall be made to pay such a debt even while their fathers are living, in the case of those who are diseased, insane, aged, or likewise long absent on travel."
Bṛhaspati: Even while the father is present, the debt must be paid by the sons once it has been proven,
provided the father is blind from birth, an outcast, insane, or afflicted with consumption, leprosy, or similar diseases.

By these statements, while the father is alive, the debt must be paid by the sons alone and not by the grandsons; however, in the absence of sons, it must be paid even by the grandsons. On this point, Kātyāyana says:
"That which must always be paid by the fathers, in their absence, must be paid from their wealth;
or that wealth must then be paid to the owner of it by the sons or grandsons."

The meaning is that if the father’s wealth exists, the debt must be paid from that very wealth; if that wealth is absent, it must be paid from the property of the son and the grandson. "First the grandfather's debt should be paid, then the father's, and thereafter one's own; in this manner should the debts be paid by the sons."
The meaning is "by sons and grandsons. Nārada says:
"A debt incurred by a father, when proven, must be paid by the sons as if it were their own;
a debt of a grandfather must be paid equally [by the grandson], but it is not to be paid by his son (the great-grandson)."

That which has been manifested and established as being like one's own property must be paid by the sons along with interest; by the grandsons, it should be paid without interest.
