In the presence of the grandfather’s wealth, only that [debt] along with interest should be paid. By the great-grandsons and others, even the principal need not be paid from their own wealth; however, if that wealth exists, only the amount along with interest should be paid. That which was acquired in succession and obtained, but was not extracted by the sons—the great-grandsons shall pay that debt of the grandfather, and it ceases with the fourth generation.
Yājñavalkya:
When the father has gone abroad, is deceased, or is overwhelmed by calamity, the debt must be paid by the sons or grandsons; if it is denied, it is established by witnesses.

When [the debtor] has gone abroad or is overwhelmed by calamity, the debt must be paid by the sons alone; when he is dead, it must be paid even by the grandsons. Kātyāyana says: "But when there is a lawsuit involving multiple claims, the creditor shall recover only as much wealth as he proves his own through witnesses; he receives only that much wealth which has been proven."

The principle of "the part revealed" (*vibhāvitaikadeśanyāya*) does not apply here, because there is no concealment of what was done by the father due to ignorance. Now, Bṛhaspati states that the non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*) is included within the same category [as other titles of law]:
Among those who have entered into a single household, he who is seen there shall be made to pay;
but for one who is away on a journey, the son shall receive everything, and for one who is dead, the daughter shall receive her share.

When a guarantee (*prātibhāvya*) has been given for the sake of a village debt by many persons, they are indeed those who have entered into a single liability (*ekachāyāpraviṣṭāḥ*). Therefore, if among them only one is seen, he alone shall pay the whole. If the son of one who is away is found, he shall pay the whole; but if the father is dead, the son shall pay only his own share. On this point, Manu says:
"Even if he is the only one living, he should be made to pay the debt contracted by his sons;
but when [the fathers] are dead, their son is not required to pay that debt of others."
Bṛhaspati says:
A son shall pay all debts contracted under a single title while his father is away;
but when the father is dead, he shall pay the father’s share, and never the debt contracted by another.
Regarding this, the Grandfather (Bṛhaspati) states a specific rule:
"Undivided kinsmen shall pay a debt incurred by a father or a mother;
in their absence, even those who are divided [shall pay], but not what was promised to them."
In the absence of property belonging to the parents or their relatives, that which was promised by them need not be paid; however, if such property exists, it must certainly be paid. Vyāsa states:

"Grandsons shall pay the debt of the grandfather, and sons shall pay for what was undertaken as a surety; they shall pay equally, but it is settled that the grandsons of those two [the son and grandson] are not liable to be made to pay."
A grandson need not pay interest on a debt; nor shall a son who acts as a surety pay interest. Neither of their sons, nor the sons of those two, are liable to be made to pay. Thus says Yājñavalkya:
"If a debt has been contracted for the sake of the family by undivided members, the heirs shall pay it upon the death or departure of the head of the household."
Manu:
"If [the property] taken [as a loan] is lost, and expenses were incurred for the family,
it is ordained that it must be paid by the kinsmen, even if they are undivided."

Nārada says: Whatever debt has been contracted by an uncle with whom one has not divided property, or by a brother, or even by a mother for the sake of the family, the heirs shall pay that entire amount.
But when the father has died, the inheritance should never be given at any time to those who have not attained the capacity for worldly affairs;
it should be given at the proper time according to the rule, otherwise they would fall into hell.
Bṛhaspati: What has been borrowed for the sake of the family by a paternal uncle, a brother’s son, a wife, a slave, a pupil, or a dependent, that the householder ought to repay.

But he who, having been appointed by his master, manages the investment, expenditure, and protection of wealth— whether in money-lending, agriculture, or trade— is known as one to whom the matter has been entrusted (nisṛṣṭārtha).
Whatever has been done by him is authoritative—whether it concerns gain or loss, expenditure or income, whether in his own country or in another; the master must not contradict it.
Kātyāyana says: Whatever has been done for the marriage of a daughter or even for funeral rites,
all of that performed by the family must be paid to the master.
Uśanas says: A fine,
or the remainder of a fine, a toll, or its residue,
as well as that which is not subject to legal dispute, must not be paid by a son.
It should not be paid from one's own wealth; it should be paid when the father’s wealth exists—so says Yājñavalkya:

"A father shall not pay a debt contracted by his wife or son, nor a son for one contracted by his father, except for the sake of the family; likewise, a husband shall not pay what was contracted by his wife."
The husband shall pay the debt of a cowherd’s wife, a liquor-seller’s wife, an actress’s wife, a washerwoman’s wife, or a hunter’s wife,
because their livelihood depends upon him.
This same rule applies to others as well because of the mention of the "cause" (hetu). Nārada says:
"A childless widow, authorized by her husband who is about to die, shall give [the debt];
she may take up to the amount of the inheritance, for where there is inheritance, there is likewise debt."
Yājñavalkya: A debt that was acknowledged by a woman, or contracted jointly with her husband, or one contracted by herself—such a debt she must pay; she is not liable for any other.

For she who, out of affection for her husband, at the time of his death, having been entreated by him, agrees saying "I myself shall give from my own wealth," she should pay even what was incurred by her husband; this refers to a debt contracted by herself as well—this is for the sake of illustration. Kātyāyana says: "If a woman has been urged by her husband or someone else with the intent that he might marry again, 'This debt must be paid by you,' she should be made to pay it even if she did not consent, provided that wealth has been received by the woman."
Viṣṇu: "Whether he has sons or is sonless, the heir to the estate shall pay the debt; for one who is destitute of wealth, the husband of his wife shall pay. Nārada:
"Of the last of the *svairiṇīs* (women of loose conduct) and the first of the *punarbhūs* (widows remarried), he who enjoys their property shall pay the debt contracted by their husbands."
All women who have had previous husbands are said to be of seven types in their proper order;
among them, the *punarbhū* (a remarried woman) is of three kinds, while the *svairiṇī* (an unchaste woman) is of four kinds.

A maiden who has not lost her virginity but has been defiled by the taking of the hand in marriage is declared the first type of *punarbhū* (a remarried woman), due to the performance of the rite of re-consecration.
When a woman is given by her elders out of regard for local customs,
she is known as the second [type of wife], who acts with boldness toward him once she has been obtained.
When there are no brothers-in-law present, a woman who is given by her kinsmen to a sapinda of the same caste is proclaimed as the third [form of marriage].
Furthermore, it is said that the status of being a *punarbhū* (a remarried woman) arises from the sacramental rite of taking the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*) for a third time.
"Whether she has borne children or not, if a woman, while her husband is alive and well,
out of lust resorts to another man, she is first of all a *svairiṇī* (an unchaste woman)."
She who, having transgressed her husband from her youth, resorts to another man and then returns to her husband's house, is proclaimed as the second [type].
When her husband has died, that woman who, setting aside her brother-in-law and others,
approaches another out of desire is proclaimed as the third [type].
But she who, having been purchased with wealth from the man she has obtained, approaches him saying "I am yours," though afflicted by hunger and thirst, is proclaimed as the fourth [type].

Thus, of the four types of *svairiṇī* women, she who is the last; and of the three types of *punarbhū* women, she who is the first—of these two, he who lives with them shall pay the debt contracted by their husbands. For it is declared in the *Smṛti*: "When a man approaches the wife of one who has died without wealth and without sons, he incurs the burden of that man's debt; she is indeed considered his property."
He himself stated elsewhere:
"Among those who take the wealth, the wife, or the son, he who takes the wealth shall bear the debt;
[the son bears it] in the absence of both the wife and the owner of the wealth; and the taker of the wife [bears it] in the absence of both the owner of the wealth and the son."
Because of this statement.

Is it not contradictory to say that "if there is no one who has taken the woman (*yoṣidgrāha*), the son shall pay; and if there is no son, the one who took the woman shall pay," since [the rule] states that "when both are present, nothing need be paid"? There is no contradiction, because [the former rule applies] when there is an absence of both the last-mentioned *svairiṇī*-taker and the first-mentioned *punarbhū*-taker, such that the son must pay; whereas [the latter rule applies] when there is no son, meaning that neither the destitute nor the childless woman-taker shall be made to pay. Alternatively, in the statement beginning with "the one who takes the wealth and the wife" (*dhanastrīhārī*), the middle term "son" (*putra*) refers to a secondary son (*gauṇaputra*), while the final term "son" refers to the primary son (*mukhyaputra*); thus, there is no contradiction. For when both are present, or when neither the son nor the woman-taker is available, the debt must be paid by either one, as stated in the rule regarding the non-payment of debt by one in the absence of the other: "The son [pays] in the absence of the wife and the owner of the wealth" (*putro 'sato strīdhaninoḥ*).

It is understood that when there is no one who takes the wife (*strīhārī*), the debt must be paid by the son; likewise, from the statement "the wife-taker [is liable] before the creditor and the son," it follows that in the absence of a son, the debt must be paid by the wife-taker. When both are present, the debt may be paid by either one. Regarding the phrase "in the absence of the wife-taker and the creditor" (*asato strīdhanino*), if the word "wife" (*strī*) therein refers to the last of the unchaste women (*svairiṇī*)—namely, the remarried woman (*punarbhū*)—then in the phrase "the wife-taker before the creditor and the son," the word "wife" (*strī*) refers to the last of the unchaste women, whether excluding or including the remarried woman; thus, there is no contradiction. For this very reason, Nārada speaks in praise of the primary son.
For fathers desire a son for the sake of their own interest, thinking:
"This son will liberate me from my creditors."
Therefore, once a son is born, he should strive with effort to liberate his father from debt, renouncing his own self-interest, so that the father does not go to hell.
If an ascetic who maintains the sacred fires dies while still burdened by debt,
both his austerity and his fire-sacrifice— all that becomes the wealth of the creditors.

The highest debt is the *uttamarṇa* (debt to the superior), pertaining to the gods, sages, and ancestors, consisting of sacrifice and the vow of celibacy; the lowest debt is the *adhamarṇa* (debt to the inferior), pertaining to human beings. Bṛhaspati says:
"He who, having taken a loan from one who is free from bonds, does not repay it to the owner, shall be born as his slave, servant, wife, or animal in that man's house."
Therefore, the repayment of the debt must necessarily be carried out by the son, grandson, wife, and others.
[Thus ends the section on the Recovery of Debts in Varadarāja’s *Vyavahāranirṇaya*. 8. The Section on Deposits (*Nikṣepakāṇḍa*).
Now the title of dispute known as "Deposits" (nikṣepa) is discussed. Regarding this, Nārada says:
"When one deposits one's own property with another out of trust and without hesitation, that is called 'Deposit' by the wise; it is a title of legal dispute."
That which is deposited in another's house, being separated from other objects and not concealed, is known as *aupanidhika*.
Yājñavalkya: When an object contained in a vessel is handed over by being placed in one's hand without prior notice,
that property is termed *aupanidhika* (a sealed deposit), and it must be returned in exactly the same manner.

A *upanidhi* is indeed a specific variety of deposit (*nikṣepa*). A sealed object placed in a casket or similar container, without disclosing its form or quantity, is an *upanidhi*. It must be returned exactly in that same state. A deposit (*nikṣepa*), however, is that which is handed over after disclosing its form and quantity. Bṛhaspati states:
"That which is given unannounced, concealed, uncounted, not shown, and marked with a seal, is known as *aupanidhika* (a sealed deposit)."
Kātyāyana says: That which is sprinkled and deposited, that which is handed over for delivery, and that which is returned to another— that object is known as *upanidhi* (an open deposit).
Manu says:
A wise man should deposit a trust with one who is of noble birth, endowed with good conduct, knowledgeable in dharma, truthful, possessed of a large following, wealthy, and honorable.
Bṛhaspati said: Having examined knowledge, the household, the householder, its fruit which is prosperity, virtues, truth, purity, and kinsmen, one should establish one's treasure therein.
Manu: Whatever object a person deposits in the hand of another in whatever manner, that must be received back in exactly that same manner; as the delivery was, so shall be the recovery.
But he who himself should deliver [the deposit] upon the death of [the depositor],
he must not be prosecuted by the king, nor by the kinsmen of the depositor.
If a gift was made by someone privately, or received privately, it must be returned privately; as the giving was, so must be the taking.
What was deposited without witnesses should be returned without witnesses; what was deposited with witnesses should be returned with witnesses.
In the absence of witnesses, [the judge] should, by means of spies endowed with appropriate age and appearance, truly entrust gold to him under various pretexts.
"He should be sued"—this is the ellipsis. Yājñavalkya says:

"But that which has been stolen by the king, by fate, or by thieves need not be made to be paid. If, however, it is not returned when sought, he must be made to pay [the value] and a fine equal to that."

If there is loss due to the king, fate, or thieves, he should not be made to pay. In the absence of such loss, if the owner demands and requests [the object] and he does not give it back, then he should be made to pay an equivalent fine for that and the object itself; so says Kātyāyana: "In the event of the destruction of a deposit through negligence or hostility, it must be restored to the depositor; however, this is not the case if it is due to fate or the king."
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"One should protect property entrusted by another with as much care as one's own;
Yama has declared that if it is lost through fate or by the king, it need not be repaid."
He says with respect to the consumer:
"If he uses [the property] at his own will while living, he is to be punished and made to pay that [value] along with interest;
this same rule applies to borrowed goods, items held in trust, deposits, and so forth. Thus it is said.
Kātyāyana has stated the nature of borrowed goods and those deposited for safekeeping: "Whatever is taken after having requested it,
in whatever manner, for the purpose of accomplishing one's own business, and which is to be returned exactly as it was—
that is called 'borrowed' (yācitaka)."
That which is given by me on the basis of another's word for a task to be performed along the path,
saying "it must be given by you," is called *anvāhita*.
Bṛhaspati states the nature of *nyāsa*:
"When property is deposited in another's house due to fear of kings, thieves, and the like, or for the sake of deceiving heirs, it is designated as *nyāsa*."

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera," there is the inclusion of gold deposited in the hands of a goldsmith for the purpose of fashioning ornaments such as bracelets, as well as that which has been returned by the goldsmith for the sake of inspiring confidence in a wealthy person. And so says Nārada:
"In the case of the misappropriation of a deposit, one should protect it with great effort; [the king] shall inflict punishment [for its loss]."
This same rule is seen to apply to articles borrowed or pledged,
as well as to craftsmen, deposits, bailments, and counter-deposits.
The same procedure for the return of a deposit is to be understood as applying to borrowed items and the like. Regarding these matters, Kātyāyana states the measure of interest:
"If one does not return a deposit, the remainder of interest, or the proceeds from a purchase or sale when asked for, the debt increases by five percent per month."

The rule regarding punishment—that one who consumes [the goods] at will shall be fined—is addressed to the wealthy, not to the indigent; for the latter, there is only the obligation to pay with interest. And so says Kātyāyana:
"He who has consumed [the goods] shall be made to pay with interest; he who neglected them shall be made to pay the same amount;
he who destroyed the goods through negligence shall be made to pay a small portion less."
If the loss occurs through negligence, he shall be made to pay the full amount; if the loss occurs through ignorance, it is reduced by one-fourth—so says Brahmavitpravara. Bṛhaspati states:
If the goods should be destroyed due to an act of God or the king, there is no fault in that case, provided the deposited items are returned along with them.
Kātyāyana says: Whatever has been deposited with someone, that he should protect with great care;
if it is lost through the act of God or the King, the depositary deserves to be made to pay what was received.
Manu says: "If [the property] has been stolen by thieves, lost in water, or burnt by fire,
one need not give it back, provided that he does not take anything from that [person]."
Bṛhaspati: If the depositary, through negligence or indifference, should cause the deposit to be lost,
or if he does not return it when requested, he shall be made to pay it back along with interest.
If one should accomplish any business of one's own by means of property deposited with another,
he shall be punished by the king and shall also be made to pay that property along with interest.
Kātyāyana states:
If a deposit is being refined by an artisan over the number of days specified, the artisan shall set it aside after that period; even if it is destroyed by fate, he must restore it.
Regarding the share of the depositary for protecting a deposit and the like, Nārada says:
"When a calamity caused by gods, thieves, the king, or fire has occurred,
whatever he protects by his own effort, a tenth part of that is declared as his share."
Kātyāyana states: "If one should personally recover property from a thief, from water, or from fire, a tenth part of it shall be given to him; this rule applies to all types of goods."
Bṛhaspati says:
Whatever merit may accrue from giving gold, silver, garments, and so forth,
that same merit belongs to another who protects one who has sought refuge, and likewise [the merit of protecting] one who has come for shelter.
Just as there is guilt for a woman in betraying her husband, or for a man in killing his son or friend,
so too is there guilt for men in consuming or neglecting a deposit entrusted to them.
Manu:
Whatever man may seize the property of another by means of fraudulent pretexts, he should be executed publicly with various forms of capital punishment along with his accomplices.

This concerns a low subject. Viṣṇu states: "The king shall cause the one who misappropriates a deposit to pay back the wealth along with the interest. And Kātyāyana says that the fine shall be equal to that amount: "He who, having taken a borrowed item, does not return it when asked for it, should be seized by force and compelled to give it; he who does not give it shall be fined."
He himself has stated the manner of interest:
"In the case of the price of goods, for the sake of taxes, and likewise upon the denial of a deposit,
the interest shall increase by way of compound interest (cakravṛddhi) until it becomes fivefold."
After three fortnights, there may be interest; after three months, it shall become tripled.
Beyond that, it shall increase according to the rule of compound interest (cakravṛddhi).
Bṛhaspati says: Where a dispute arises concerning a secret deposit,
it is ordained that an ordeal shall serve as the means of proof for both parties.
Thus ends the ninth section, the Chapter on Deposits (*nikṣepakāṇḍa*), in the work of the illustrious Varadarāja. Now begins the Chapter on Sale by One Who Is Not the Owner (*asvāmivikrayakāṇḍa*).
Regarding sale by one who is not the owner, Nārada says:
When property belonging to another— whether deposited, lost, found, or stolen—
is sold in the absence of the owner, that is to be known as "sale by one who is not the owner" (asvāmivikraya).
Manu:
"A purchase or sale that is made by one who is not the owner is to be known as invalid; such is the established rule in legal proceedings."
Yājñavalkya:

Purity [from the charge of theft] comes from the production of the seller; the owner recovers the property, the king receives a fine, and the buyer recovers the price from whoever was the seller of that [stolen] item.
Kātyāyana: One should rescind a sale by one who is not the owner, as well as a gift and a pledge. Manu: [same].
One who sells another's property while not being its owner and without the consent of the owner— one who is a thief yet considers himself no thief— should not be admitted as a witness.
Having recovered property sold by one who is not its owner, the true owner shall take it back;
the buyer’s innocence is established by an open purchase, whereas theft results from a secret purchase.
Yājñavalkya:
One may reclaim property sold by another once the defect has been made manifest;
[otherwise], in the case of a fraudulent sale, a low price, or an improper time, he is a thief.
In another Smṛti:
"One may either make the purchase public or pay the price;
the time for bringing the price shall be granted there according to the amount of the object."
Kātyāyana states:
However, one whose title is not subject to challenge must prove the purchase itself;
once the purchase has been proven, the king should say to him, "He owes you nothing."
And one should conduct the purchase openly with trustworthy ministers of one's own;
no other procedure is prescribed there, whether divine or human.
Bṛhaspati: When a sale occurs within a house or outside a village, in secret, or from a distance of a hundred *yojanas*,
or when it is for a low price or purchased under duress, it should be recognized as a sale by one who is not the owner.
Bṛhaspati:
When something has been purchased from one whose identity is unknown, or who has fled or died,
the owner shall take half the price as compensation, while the purchaser retains his own wealth.
Marīci:
When the specific qualities are unknown and no price can be ascertained,
an equal loss shall be assigned to both the buyer and the owner of the lost property.
In another Smṛti:
"If he does not produce the pledge, or if he fails to reimburse the purchase price,
he shall be made to pay the debt to the creditor according to the claim, as well as a fine."
Yājñavalkya:
He who recovers from the hand of another property that has been stolen or lost,
without having reported it to the king, shall be fined ninety-six *paṇas*.
Manu says:
"He who steals this [scripture] shall be deprived of his wealth along with his lineage for six hundred births;
one who has no lineage shall incur the guilt of a thief upon being caught stealing it."

One who commits the sale of what belongs to another according to this rule is praiseworthy if it was done through ignorance; however, if done intentionally, he deserves punishment like that of a thief.
Nārada says: Having recovered property sold by one who is not the owner, the true owner shall take it back;
provided it was obtained from a slave, from one with no ownership right, or from a dishonest person, and in secret.
One who purchases an item of low value at an improper time shall incur the blame for that defect.
Bṛhaspati states: But he who, having sold land, does not enable the buyer to enjoy it as is appropriate [shall be held liable].
He shall give that wealth to him; otherwise, he incurs the punishment for a thief.
Kātyāyana states: "In the case of those designated as 'given' or 'purchased,' however, in the event of a dispute, there shall be a redemption;
one should give a field similar to that [original one], but if unable to do so, one should bring about satisfaction."
Śaṅkha says:
But one who sells what does not belong to him, such as a house, a field, or the like,
shall give that property back to its owner, or pay its value according to the wish of the purchaser.

In the case of intentional action, one should pay a fine equal to that [damage] or provide land or other property of equal value; in the case of unintentional action, no fine is required, but one should instead pay the market value of the goods at that time or something similar. However, in the *Kṛṣṇīya*, there is this distinction regarding purchase and exchange: in the case of purchase, one should pay the price or provide land of equal value; but in the case of exchange, it is stated that one may take back one's own property.
The section on Sale by One Who Is Not the Owner (Section 9) is concluded. 10. The Section on the Ten Topics beginning with Partnership (Section 10).
Next, the title of litigation known as "partnership" (saṃbhūyasamutthāna) is discussed. Regarding this, Nārada states:
"Where merchants and others perform an undertaking collectively..."
That is known as the legal head of title concerning partnerships.

For those who, through skillful means, perform actions together for the sake of the fruit, there is a "throwing-in" (prakṣepa) which serves as the support and the supported; by that, they may arise from their respective parts.

When those performing an enterprise in combination for the sake of a profit exceeding the individual efforts and purposes of each person deposit capital, that deposit serves as both the foundation and the means. In that case, the meaning is that whoever has contributed whatever amount of capital should perform labor proportionate to it, and likewise receive a share of the profit accordingly.
Whichever share belongs to whom—whether equal, greater, or less—in that case, his loss, expenditure, and increase shall be of that same kind.
The meaning is that for a small portion there is a small [fee], and for a large portion there is a large one. Bṛhaspati says:
"Trade and these other activities should be performed by wise men who are incapable, lazy, afflicted by disease, unfortunate, or without support."

One should carry out affairs together with those who are of noble birth, skillful yet not indolent, wise, experienced in detecting flaws, knowledgeable regarding income and expenditure, pure, and brave.
Yājñavalkya: When merchants perform work for the sake of profit through a partnership,
the gain and loss shall be according to their respective capital, or as determined by their agreement.
Kātyāyana says: Whatever artisans or even merchants may be assembled together,
the fruit obtained there by those performing work according to their respective shares is equal.
Those very same persons are declared to be examiners and witnesses for one another in a disputed matter or in a case of fraud, provided they are not possessed by hatred.
If anyone among them is known to be a cheat in buying or selling, he must be cleared by means of oaths; this is the rule for all disputes.
When a loss of the purchase price occurs there due to acts of God or the king,
it is declared that this [loss] shall be apportioned among all [the partners] according to their respective shares.
But if one who has not been specifically designated should, through negligence, cause the property to be lost while it is being withheld,
they shall give him a tenth part as compensation and take the remaining shares for themselves.
Nārada says:
If one person should incur a debt, his heir shall pay it;
or, in the absence of an heir, all those who are capable [of paying] shall do so.
Bṛhaspati: A king should take a sixth, a ninth, or likewise a twelfth part from those born of the Śūdra, Vaiśya, and Kṣatriya castes; however, he should take a twentieth part from a Brāhmaṇa.

If, after the lapse of the [stipulated] period, he does not return by any means whatsoever, then the king shall take that property; however, in the case of a Brahmin's property, he should seek out a Brahmin [to whom it may be given].
Manu:
The king shall cause property whose owner has disappeared to be kept for three years;
within three years the owner may recover it, but after that time the king shall take it.
Nārada says:
Property that has no owner and no heir, having remained for ten years, the king may then take for himself; in this way, dharma is not violated.
Yājñavalkya: Upon the casting of half [the metal into the crucible], the king shall take a twentieth part as a toll (*śulka*).
That which is obstructed, that which is fit for the king, and that which has been sold, all go to the king.
When a deceased person has gone to another country, his kinsmen or relatives may take his property; if they do not come, the king shall take it upon their absence.
One should abandon what is dishonest or unprofitable; if unable to do it oneself, one should have it done by another.
By this, the rule for officiating priests, cultivators, and laborers has been declared.
Nārada said: "The officiating priest (ṛtvij) is seen to be of three kinds by the ancients:
one appointed by the ancestors, one chosen by oneself, and one who performs the priestly office out of affection and of his own accord."
Manu:
If an officiating priest (ṛtvij), once chosen for a sacrifice, should abandon his own duty,
a share proportional to that work must be given to him by the co-performers.

If one performs half the work, half the share should be given; if one performs a quarter of the work, a quarter share should be given, and so forth. By men here who perform their respective tasks together, the allotment of shares for the workers must be determined according to this sequential method.
In whatever rite specific fees for individual components have been prescribed,
he alone who performed that component shall receive them, or alternatively, all the priests may share them together.
Manu says: "The Adhvaryu shall take the chariot, and at the establishment of the sacred fires, the Brahman shall take a horse;
the Hotṛ shall also take a horse, and the Udgātṛ shall take the cart at the purchase [of the Soma]."
At the *ādhāna* (the laying of the fires) and at the *kraya* (the purchase of the Soma). Now he states the distribution of the common sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*):
"Of all [the priests], the principal ones are the *ardhin*s; the others are *ardhin*s by half of that [share].
Those who receive a third part are the *tṛtīyin*s, and those who receive a fourth part are the *pādin*s."

This is the meaning: there are sixteen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), beginning with the *hotṛ*. Among them, the four principal ones—the *hotṛ*, *adhvaryu*, *brahmā*, and *udgātṛ*—are entitled to half of a hundred cows; by virtue of the requirement that the shares of all others be fulfilled, they receive a half-share consisting of forty-eight [cows]. The other four—the *maitrāvaruṇa*, *pratiprasthātṛ*, *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*, and *prastotṛ*—are entitled to half of that, namely a quarter-share consisting of twenty-four [cows]. Those who receive a third share—the *acchāvāka*, *neṣṭṛ*, *agnīdhra*, and *pratihartṛ*—receive a third share consisting of sixteen parts of the principal portion. Finally, those who receive a fourth share—the *grāvastut*, *unnetṛ*, *subrahmaṇya*, and *potr̥*—receive a fourth share consisting of twelve cows, which is the fourth part of the principal share. In sacrifices such as the *Vājapeya* where the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are equal for all, Manu says: [Manu 8.213] "In a sacrifice where the sacrificial fees are equal, the distribution of shares is determined by the order of their appointment. [Manu 8.214] "The *hotṛ* takes one-twentieth of the fee; the *adhvaryu*, the *brahmā*, and the *udgātṛ* take one-fifth each; the remaining eight priests take one-tenth each. [Manu 8.215] "Or, according to some, the *hotṛ* takes one-third; the *adhvaryu*, the *brahmā*, and the *udgātṛ* take one-fourth each; and the remaining eight priests take one-eighth each. [Manu 8.216] "Alternatively, the *hotṛ* takes one-half; the *adhvaryu*, the *brahmā*, and the *udgātṛ* take one-third each; and the remaining eight priests take one-sixth each. [Manu 8.217] "Or, the *hotṛ* takes one-half; the *adhvaryu* takes one-third; the *brahmā* and the *udgātṛ* take one-sixth each; and the remaining eight priests take one-twelfth each. [Manu 8.218] "Or, the *hotṛ* takes one-half; the *adhvaryu* takes one-fourth; the *brahmā* and the *udgātṛ* take one-eighth each; and the remaining eight priests take one-sixteenth each. [Manu 8.219] "Or, the *hotṛ* takes one-half; the *adhvaryu* takes one-eighth; the *brahmā* and the *udgātṛ* take one-sixteenth each; and the remaining eight priests take one-thirty-second each. [Manu 8.220] "Or, the *hotṛ* takes one-half; the *adhvaryu* takes one-sixteenth; the *brahmā* and the *udgātṛ* take one-thirty-second each; and the remaining eight priests take one-sixty-fourth each. [Manu 8.221] "Or, the *hotṛ* takes one-half; the *adhvaryu* takes one-thirty-second; the *brahmā* and the *udgātṛ* take one-sixty-fourth each; and the remaining eight priests take one-hundred-and-twelfthth each. [Manu 8.222] "Or, the *hotṛ* takes one-half; the *adhvaryu* takes one-sixty-fourth; the *brahmā* and the *udgātṛ* take one-hundred-and-twelfthth each; and the remaining eight priests take one-two-hundred-and-fortythth each. [Manu 8.223] "Or, the *hotṛ* takes one-half; the *adhvaryu* takes one-hundred-and-twelfthth; the *brahmā* and the *udgātṛ* take one-two-hundred-and-fortythth each; and the remaining eight priests take one-four-hundred-and-ninety-sixthth each. [Manu 8.224] "Or, the *hotṛ* takes one-half; the *adhvaryu* takes one-two-hundred-and-fortythth; the *brahmā* and the *udgātṛ* take one-four-hundred-and-ninety-sixthth each; and the remaining eight priests take one-nine-hundred-and-seventy-secondth each. [Manu 8.225] "Or, the *hotṛ* takes one-half; the *adhvaryu* takes one-four-hundred-and-ninety-sixthth; the *brahmā* and the *udgātṛ* take one-nine-hundred-and-seventy-secondth each; and the remaining eight priests take one-one-thousand-nine-hundred-and-fourty-fourthth each. [Manu 8.226] "Or, the *hotṛ* takes one-half; the *adhvaryu* takes one-nine-hundred-and-seventy-secondth; the *brahmā* and the *udgātṛ* take one-one-thousand-nine-hundred-and-fourty-fourthth each; and the remaining eight priests take one-three-thousand-eight-hundred-and-sixty-eighthth each. [Manu 8.227] "Or, the *hotṛ* takes one-half; the *adhvaryu* takes one-one-thousand-nine-hundred-and-fourty-fourthth; the *brahmā* and the *udgātṛ* take one-three-thousand-eight-hundred-and-sixty-eighthth each; and the remaining eight priests take one-seven-thousand-seven-hundred-and-thirty-sixthth each. [Manu 8.228] "Or, the *hotṛ* takes one-half; the *adhvaryu* takes one-three-thousand-eight-hundred-and-sixty-eighthth; the *brahmā* and the *udgātṛ* take one-seven-thousand-seven-hundred-and-thirty-sixthth each; and the remaining eight priests take one-fifteen-thousand-five-hundred-and-twenty-fourthth each. [Manu 8.229] "Or, the *hotṛ* takes one-half; the *adhvaryu* takes one-seven-thousand-seven-hundred-and-thirty-sixthth; the *brahmā* and the *udgātṛ* take one-fifteen-thousand-five-hundred-and-twenty-fourthth each; and the remaining eight priests take one-thirty-one-thousand-one-hundred-and-forty-eighthth each. [Manu 8.230] "Or, the *hotṛ* takes one-half; the *adhvaryu* takes one-fifteen-thousand-five-hundred-and-twenty-fourthth; the *brahmā* and the *udgātṛ* take one-thirty-one-thousand-one-hundred-and-forty-eighthth each; and the remaining eight priests take one-sixty-two-thousand-two-hundred-and-ninety-sixthth each. [Manu 8.231] "Or, the *hotṛ* takes one-half; the *adhvaryu* takes one-thirty-one-thousand-one-hundred-and-forty-eighthth; the *brahmā* and the *udgātṛ* take one-sixty-two-thousand-two-hundred-and-ninety-sixthth each; and the remaining eight priests take one-one-hundred-and-twenty-four-thousand-four-hundred-and-ninety-twelfthth each. [Manu 8.232] "Or, the *hotṛ* takes one-half; the *adhvaryu* takes one-sixty-two-thousand-two-hundred-and-ninety-sixthth; the *brahmā* and the *udgātṛ* take one-one-hundred-and-twenty-four-thousand-four-hundred-and-ninety-twelfthth each; and the remaining eight priests take one-two-hundred-and-forty-eight-thousand-eight-hundred-and-eighty-fourthth each. [Manu 8.233] "Or, the *hotṛ* takes one-half; the *adhvaryu* takes one-one-hundred-and-twenty-four-thousand-four-hundred-and-ninety-twelfthth; the *brahmā*
If a sacrificer should abandon an officiating priest, or if an officiating priest should abandon a sacrificer—
provided both are capable of the rite and free from fault— their punishment shall be one hundred [paṇas] each.
Nārada said:
Regarding these [officiants], when they have come through hereditary succession, the duty lies with them personally; likewise with those who are appointed for a specific rite.
In the case of those engaged by chance, once they have been dismissed after performing the sacrifice, there is no sin whatsoever against the lineage.

Regarding this, Kauṭilya states the specific rule: "In sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma, if the officiating priest fails after the *dīkṣaṇīyā* ceremony, he receives a fifth share; after the purchase of the *soma*, a fourth; after the middle *upasads* and the removal of the *pravargya* vessel, a third; after the *agniṣomīya* animal sacrifice, a second; after the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*), three-quarters; after the midday libation (*mādhyandina*), the whole amount; and [the full fee is due] when the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇās*) have been led forward.
Thus says Bṛhaspati. Now, let the procedure for farmers and others be heard; it is stated as follows."
By means of external factors such as farmers, seeds, and so forth, as well as the equipment for the field.
A wise man should carry out agricultural work together with those who are capable,
in the forest, near the city, and likewise along the royal highway.

One should diligently avoid a field that is saline and overgrown with thorns; however, one should select a field that is provided with pits for irrigation, well-watered, and surrounded on all sides by other fields.
When a field has been well-plowed and sown at the proper time, one reaps the fruit;
likewise, [one avoids] those who are emaciated, the very aged, the enraged, the diseased, and the fugitive.
A wise farmer should not take as a draft animal one that is one-eyed or lame;
for by using such a beast for sowing seed, damage to the field will arise.
It is declared that this [right] belongs to him to whom it pertains, and not to others; such is the certainty.
Loss of the field and loss of enjoyment—this is proclaimed as the ancient law of usurers.
One who refines gold, silver, threads, wood, stone, and leather,
and is skilled in those crafts, is called an artisan (śilpī) by the wise.
Where goldsmiths and others perform their craft collectively,
they shall receive wages according to their respective shares in accordance with the work performed.
Kātyāyana says: Artisans consist of apprentices, those skilled in the work, and masters;
they shall receive one, two, three, or four shares respectively, in ascending order.
Bṛhaspati says: When people join together to construct a mansion, a temple, a pond, or leather implements and tools, the leader among them is entitled to half of the profit.
This indeed is the rule for dancers proclaimed by the virtuous:
one who knows the rhythm receives one and a half shares, while the singers receive equal shares.
Kātyāyana says: Whatever wealth may have been seized from a foreign kingdom by thieves under the king’s command,
they shall divide it according to the rule after setting aside one-tenth for the king.
But the leader of the thieves shall take four shares from that;
the brave one, three shares; the capable one, two; and the thief, however, only one share each.
If anyone should happen to seize those [objects] as they are being carried away,
an equal act of merit must be performed for him for the sake of his liberation.
Thus ends the third head of dispute, named "Joint Undertaking. Now, "Non-delivery of what has been Given" is discussed. Regarding this, Nārada says:
When one who has given a gift improperly desires to take it back,
that point of dispute is known in law as *dattāpradānika* (the non-delivery of what has been given).
That which is not to be given, that which is to be given, that which has been given, and that which has not been given—
these fourfold paths of giving are to be understood in legal proceedings.

That which is not to be given (*adeya*) is unworthy of being given; that which is to be given (*deya*) is worthy of being given; what is given (*datta*) is stable; and what is not given (*adatta*) is unstable and subject to reversal—thus is the fourfold path of giving.
In this regard, eight things are traditionally held to be not to be given, one thing is to be given, seven kinds of gifts are known as "given," and sixteen types constitute "not given."

Nārada stated that there are eight things that must not be given away: a deposit, a borrowed item, a pledge, that which is held in common, a trust, one’s wife and children, and one’s entire estate when there are descendants.
"For even when a person is beset by the most grievous calamities,
the teachers declare that there are things which must not be given, namely that which has been promised to another.
Regarding this, Dakṣa states a specific exception:
Common property, what has been requested as a deposit, a pledge, one's wife, her wealth,
an object placed in another's charge (*anvāhita*), a sealed deposit (*nikṣepa*), and one's entire estate [cannot be divided] when there is a male descendant.
Even in times of distress, these nine things should not be given away by the wise;
he who gives them is a foolish soul and that man incurs the need for expiation.
Regarding this, Kātyāyana states the specific rule:
"Neither sale nor gift should be made by those who are unwilling;
however, one may apply one's wife, sons, and all property to oneself."
In times of distress, however, giving away or even selling [the sacred object] must be performed;
otherwise, one would not be able to proceed—such is the certainty of the scripture.

The distinction regarding giving and taking [a child] depends on the relative gravity of the offense. On this point, Vasiṣṭha states: "A person is born from the union of semen and blood, having the mother and father as his cause. Regarding the giving, selling, or abandoning of such a person, the mother and father have authority. However, one should not give away or receive in adoption an only son; for he is for the continuation of the lineage of the ancestors. But a woman may not give away or receive a son without the permission of her husband. Kātyāyana says: "Household property and land inherited in succession, whether from a father or a grandfather..."
One should not give [anything] to one who is enriched with sons and grandsons without his permission.
Bṛhaspati says:
"In the case of a marriage [gift] that has come down by tradition, no gift at all is prescribed.
And likewise Manu:
Whether divided or undivided, heirs have equal rights over immovable property;
for no single person has authority over it in matters of gift, mortgage, or sale.
Manu:
If wealth has been given by someone to another who asks for it for the sake of dharma,
but that wealth subsequently does not serve such a purpose, it shall not have been properly given, and it must be returned by him.
Nārada states that there is only one kind of person worthy of receiving gifts:
"Whatever wealth remains after supporting one's family is what should be given; he who gives anything else while withholding that [proper gift] incurs sin."
Regarding this, Kātyāyana states the specific rule:
"One's entire property, with the exception of the house and whatever wealth is required for the maintenance of the family and so forth—that may be given; otherwise, it shall not be given."
One's own [wealth] is that which one has acquired by oneself.
Men have no regard for their sons, wives, or kinsmen;
they are masters over their own property in all matters.
The meaning is that they have mastery over their own wealth acquired by themselves. Now, the specific results arising from the specific nature of the recipient when giving is stated.
Vyāsa says: "A gift given to the blind and others yields a hundredfold merit; a gift to one's daughter yields infinite merit."
A gift given to a father is said to be hundredfold, while that given to a mother is said to be thousandfold.
A hundred thousand [coins] were given by Dakṣa to his uterine sister as an imperishable gift.
[He gave likewise] to his mother and father, to his guru, to a friend, to one who is humble, and to a benefactor.
But that which is given to the poor, the helpless, and the distinguished becomes fruitful.
Bṛhaspati says: A gift given to a Śūdra is said to be equal [in merit]; to a Vaiśya, it is twice that;
to a Kṣatriya, threefold; and to a Brāhmaṇa, it is traditionally held to be sixfold.
For a *śrotriya*, that [fine] is one thousand; for a sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*), it is double that;
for a teacher (*ācārya*), it should be known as triple; and for those who have maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), it is double that.
To one who knows the Self, [the gift] is ten thousandfold; to an Agnihotrin, it is infinite;
to a Soma-sacrificer, it is ten thousandfold; and to a teacher of Brahman, it is infinite.
Bharadvāja said:
They say that giving consists of a single essence, and that it should be preceded by water;
without the offering of water, the gift of Dharma does not exist.

On this point, Āpastamba says: "All gifts that have no visible purpose are preceded by water. Gautama says: "The giving of alms, when preceded by water, is for the sake of invoking blessings, as it is among righteous acts of giving. Bṛhaspati says:

"A woman should give her own property to her female relatives, excluding those who are of the same lineage (tantu). In the absence of female relatives, she should give it to her [male] kinsmen; in their absence, to the twice-born."
Nārada has declared that there are seven kinds of gifts:

the price for merchandise, wages, that given out of satisfaction, that given out of affection, that given in return for a favor, and that given for the sake of a woman's dowry; thus is the gift remembered as being of seven types.

The price of merchandise—that which is given as the value for goods purchased, as wages for work performed, or out of satisfaction to actors and the like; that which is given out of affection to daughters, sons, and others; that which is given to one who has rendered assistance in the form of a return favor; that which is given as a bride-price (*śulka*) to the kinsmen of a maiden for the purpose of marriage; and that which is given for the sake of spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*) or as a gift of grace—all these seven kinds of what has been given must not be reclaimed. Bṛhaspati says: "Wages, [gifts] out of satisfaction, the price of merchandise, the bride-price, and [gifts] to one who has assisted..."
That which is given with faith, favor, and affection is remembered as being of eight kinds.
Manu says: A gift given to one's mother, father, a teacher, a friend, a humble person, or a benefactor, as well as to the poor, the helpless, and those who are distinguished, becomes fruitful.
What is received as a dowry, inherited in due order, or obtained through prowess,
as well as what is given with the permission of the wife, kinsmen, or the owner— such a gift shall be established as valid.

In the case of property received as a dowry (*saudāyika*), it requires the wife’s consent; in the case of property inherited through lineage (*kramāgata*), it requires the consent of the sons and others; and in the case of property acquired through valor (*śauryaprāpta*), it requires the master’s consent. Thus says Kātyāyana:
"For the purpose of protection from fear, for the sake of defense, and likewise for the accomplishment of necessary business..."
One should know that what is obtained by this method has been rendered as a reciprocal service.
"Even if it were said, 'I shall give my entire possessions to whoever rescues me from here when I have fallen into a life-threatening danger,' it would not necessarily come to pass."

Yājñavalkya: The acceptance [of a gift] should be public, especially in the case of immovable property; that which has been promised as a gift must indeed be given, and having given it, one should not take it back again.
Kātyāyana says:
He who, having promised a gift to a Brāhmaṇa of his own accord,
does not give it, shall be made to pay it like a debt and shall incur the first amercement.
On this point, Viṣṇu states: "One who does not give what has been promised shall be compelled to give it and be punished with the first amercement. Hārīta says:
"By failing to give what was promised and by revoking what has been given, one goes to various hells and is born among the animal species."
Gautama: "Even after having given a promise, one should not give to one who is joined with unrighteousness. Bharadvāja:
"That which has been promised by word but not fulfilled through action is a debt connected with wealth, both in this world and in the next."

The meaning is that what has been promised must be given, like a debt. Nārada states that there are sixteen types of what is not [legally] given: "But what is not given by those overcome by fear, anger, grief, or the force of illness; likewise, by means of a bribe, in jest, through a mistake, or by fraud."

That which is done by one who is a child, deluded, lacking independence, afflicted, intoxicated, or insane, and that which is done with the desire for gain, thinking, "This person is my agent" and "This is my deed."
When one says "this is a worthy recipient" regarding an unworthy recipient, or when an act is joined with unrighteousness,
that which is given through ignorance is considered by tradition to be as good as not given.
The words *bhaya* (fear), *krodha* (anger), and *śoka* (sorrow) are each connected with the word *vega* (impulse). Kātyāyana states:

"That which is given by those who are not their own masters due to lust or anger, by the afflicted, the impotent, the insane, or the deluded, as well as that given in exchange or in jest—that one may take back."
Hārīta says:
When, for the sake of countering the insults of those who are destitute of wealth,
a gift is given to the perpetrators out of fear of them, that is called *bhayadāna* (a gift out of fear).

Nārada has described the characteristics of bribery: "From the reporting of theft, violence, outrages, and adultery; from the sight of one who has lost his livelihood; and likewise from the instigation of untruth."
Whatever has been obtained by these [means] is called "obtained through bribery."
Regarding this, Kātyāyana states the specific rule:
"But if one who has been appointed to duties should receive a bribe,
he shall be made to pay that entire sum as well as a fine eleven times its value."
But if one who is not appointed should receive a bribe for the sake of performing a task,
there is no fault in him if it is for the purpose of providing a reciprocal service.
If a bribe has been promised for the sake of accomplishing a particular task,
it must not be given under any circumstances if that task remains unaccomplished.
If it had already been given to him previously, he should be compelled by force to restore it.
He states the specific punishment for those appointed [to office] who subsist on bribes:
"Having publicly proclaimed those mortals who live by bribery from his own realm,
the king shall confiscate all their property and banish them, with the exception of the Brahmins."

"Having done that [fraud], one should subject even others to execution and the like. "Others" refers to those other than Brāhmaṇas. By the word "and the like" (*ādi*), the amputation of limbs and so forth are included. [Gifts made] in jest, in play, by way of exchange, when showing one thing while giving another at the time of delivery; [gifts made] through deception, by means of falsehood, or by one who is a child (under sixteen years of age), or by one who is deluded (through illness, sleep, mental confusion, etc., or being ignorant of worldly and Vedic matters). Those who are not independent have been described by Nārada.
All subjects are not independent; the lord of the earth is independent.
A disciple is not independent of himself, for independence resides in the teacher.
Wives, sons, slaves, and whatever property one possesses are not independent;
however, the master of that which has come down through succession is independent.
A child is to be known as being like one still in the womb until the eighth year;
from the sixteenth year onwards, he is called a youth (bāla), and before that, he is termed a pogaṇḍa.
One who knows legal procedure is independent of others except for his parents;
indeed, even if he is advanced in years, he remains dependent while they are alive.
Of these two as well, the father is superior, because of the observed predominance of the seed;
in the absence of the progenitor, the mother [is superior], and in her absence, the elder brother.

It is given by one who is diseased and afflicted; it is given by one intoxicated by intoxicants such as the drinking of *śīdhu* liquor; it is given by one who is insane due to wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and so forth. And thus it has been stated by Nārada:
"Five types of insanity are fully described as arising from wind, bile, and phlegm."

Even that which has been given in sixteen ways is considered as "not given" because it must be recovered: (1) given with the thought, "This man is my benefactor," and with the desire for a return; (2) given to an unworthy person, such as the husband of a *vṛṣalī* (a woman of low caste), under the impression that he is an ascetic; (3) wealth obtained for the purpose of a sacrifice given to one who squanders it on gambling and the like. The status of being "not given" applies to what was given out of distress (*ārtadatta*) only when it concerns matters other than religious duties (*dharmakārya*), according to the statement of Kātyāyana:

"What has been given by one who is healthy or by one in distress for the sake of a religious duty, having been so declared—if it is not given and the donor dies, the son must be made to give it; there is no doubt in this matter."
Likewise, this statement is a summary of the meaning:
"Whatever is mortgaged or sold through fraud, or received as a gift or given away through fraud,
or wherein one perceives deceit— that the king shall annul it all."

Yoga is a limiting condition (*upādhi*). When purchases, sales, gifts, or acceptances have been made under a specific condition such as yoga, those transactions cease upon the removal of that condition.
Now, certain statements concerning specific types of giving are stated. Regarding this, Bharadvāja says:
"That which is given to worthy recipients only with a specific purpose in view..."
Therefore, they call that the gift of wealth; its fruit, however, is of this world.
When a gift is given out of passion for women, whether for the sake of some perceived purpose or through attachment to those who are unworthy, that is called "the gift of lust."
That which is given to others out of shame in an assembly, having heard [of one's own faults],
is called *vrīḍānāma* by those who perceive the truth.
That which one gives out of joy upon seeing or hearing something dear is called "joy-giving" (harṣadāna); its fruit is seen right here in this very life.
That gift which is bestowed upon loved ones during times of prosperity or adversity is merely worldly; indeed, its purpose is seen only within this present life.
For even that effect which an independent agent might produce when not abiding in its natural state,
those who maintain the reasons for non-independence declare to be as good as unproduced.
Those afflicted by speech driven by desire and anger, by fear and calamity,
and those overwhelmed by passion and hatred, should be known as having returned to their own nature.
Therefore, such things as these are not to be given. Bṛhaspati says:
"That which is given with the words 'after my death' does not bring about ownership;
because it has not been truly given, it shall fall to the heir upon his death."
Nārada:
He who accepts what has been given out of delusion, and he who bestows what ought not to be given—
both of these should be punished by a king who knows the Dharma.
Bṛhaspati: One who consumes what has not been given and likewise one who gives what ought to be given must be punished. Manu:
He who takes what should not be taken and he who gives what should not be given—
both of them are to be punished like thieves and made to pay an equal fine.

Thus ends the fourth head of dispute, titled "Non-delivery of what has been given. Now follows the discussion on "Failure to Serve after Having Agreed," as stated by Bṛhaspati: [The section on] *abhyupetyāśuśrūṣā* (failure to serve after having agreed) is now being explained. Bṛhaspati says:
But when one, having undertaken service, does not perform it,
this is called the legal head of dispute known as "Failure to Perform Service after Undertaking It."
"Having agreed, 'I shall perform service as my duty for you,' he who does not perform that work—this subject of dispute concerning 'having agreed to serve' is now stated in detail. Nārada says:
"In the legal treatises, five types of servants have been observed by the wise;
four types are laborers, and among them, the slaves are fifteen-fold."

Those who undertake service are seen to be of five kinds by scholars in this treatise and in other treatises. Among them, four types—those who have entered into work, those appointed to it, those who are dependent, and those who are independent—are mentioned; then he speaks of both [groups]:

"Disciples, resident pupils, hired servants, and fourthly, those performing extra duties—these are declared to be laborers (*karmakara*); whereas slaves (*dāsa*) are those born in the house and so forth."
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati spoke on the conduct of a disciple:
"The triple Vidyā is declared to be characterized by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas;
for the sake of that, one should perform service to the teacher as enjoined by the scriptures."
It is fourfold by way of knowledge, discernment, desire, and purpose;
furthermore, each of these is divided according to the distinction of its activity.
Crafts are said to be the working of gold, silver, and so forth, as well as dance and the like; training in these, one should perform the work in the teacher's house.
Nārada says:
From the moment of initiation, the disciple should serve his guru with self-restraint;
he should likewise adopt the same conduct toward the guru’s wife and the guru’s son.
This is the instruction for the three who have studied the three Vedas:
having returned home and presented the teacher’s fee to the guru, he should go to his own house; this is declared to be the conduct of a student.
Desiring to acquire his own craft with the permission of his relatives,
he should dwell in the presence of a teacher for a well-determined period of time.
The teacher should instruct him at his own home, providing him with food;
he should not make him perform any other work, and should treat him like a son.
Kātyāyana and Bṛhaspati state:
"He who does not cause [the pupil] to master his craft, but instead makes him perform other tasks, shall incur the first amercement; from that, the pupil withdraws."
If one should abandon a teacher who is teaching him without fault, he ought to be restrained by force; he deserves both death and imprisonment.
Even when he has been trained, the pupil should complete the prescribed period;
whatever work he performs therein belongs to the preceptor alone as its fruit.
Having mastered the craft and performed a circumambulation of the teacher at the proper time,
the pupil departs after having honored him according to his ability.
Nārada says: A hired servant is to be known as being of three kinds—superior, middling, and inferior.
Their wages, based on the work performed, should correspond to their capacity and devotion.
In this regard, the highest type of hired laborer is the soldier, the middling is the farmer, and the lowest is the porter; thus is the hired laborer of three kinds.
Bṛhaspati says: Among them, the best is the soldier; the middle is the plowman;
the lowest is said to be the porter, as well as the domestic servant.
Those who bear the burden [of livelihood] are recorded as being of two kinds: those who live by agriculture and those who live by cattle.
From the grain produced and likewise from the milk, one receives that which has been prescribed.
Nārada says:
He who is authorized over even the property of the family and stands above it should be known as an *adhikarmakara*; he is also remembered as a *kauṭumbika*.
For these four are proclaimed as performers of auspicious deeds;
however, the remaining fifteen servants are partakers of inferior karma.
Bṛhaspati says:
One who has been supported for a day, half a month, six months, three months,
or a year shall perform the work promised and receive what was stipulated.
Nārada said: Action is also declared to be of two kinds—unwholesome and indeed wholesome. Unwholesome action is said to be the service of a slave; the other is declared to be wholesome.
Cleaning the house door, impure places, and the chariot’s refuse; touching private parts, eating while impure, and the taking up and discarding of feces and urine.
Service performed for one's master by means of his own limbs at will, or even ultimately, is to be known as inauspicious action; other than that, it is auspicious.
Kātyāyana says:
The voiding of feces and urine, as well as massaging while naked,
and generally the carrying of corpses and the like— these tasks should be performed by the sons of female slaves.
Nārada says:

One born in the house, one purchased, one obtained, one received as an heir, one supported during a time of distress, and likewise one who has been placed there by the master; these are the [types of slaves].
I was liberated from great bondage; won at stake in battle, I approached you saying, "I am yours," and was made to enter the life of a wandering ascetic.

"The slave by gift (bhaktadāsa), likewise the one supported by a female slave (baḍavābhṛta), and the one who has sold himself—these are recorded in the scripture as the fifteen types of slaves. Thus it is said.

One born of a female slave in one’s own house is "born in the house" (*gṛhaja*). One purchased from another for one’s own wealth is "purchased" (*krīta*). One obtained through acceptance as a gift and so forth is "received" (*labdha*). One who has come down through the lineage of the father and others is "inherited" (*dāyādupāgata*). One supported during a famine with food, clothing, and so forth is "supported in times of distress" (*anākālabhṛta*); he too, like the previous types, is established by the master either by taking property or for the purpose of performing labor for interest. One who is "entrusted" (*āhita*) is one unable to pay his own debt who is liberated from a great debt [by the master]. One obtained by the king in battle; one won in some wager out of rivalry; one who has agreed, saying, "I am your slave"; one who has transgressed after having gone forth [into homelessness] due to some cause; one who has been "made" (*kṛta*) by engaging [with the master], saying, "I will perform labor for such a length of time"; one who has approached [the master] saying, "I am a slave for as long as you give me food," is a "slave for food" (*bhaktadāsa*). A "mare" (*vaḍavā*) is a domestic female slave not [permanently] bound; one who has entered into slavery on account of living with her is "supported by a mare" (*vaḍavābhṛta*). Bṛhaspati says:
He who enjoys another's female slave should be known as a "mare-keeper" (vaḍavābhṛta);
he must perform that work for the master just as any other hired man would.
He who sells himself after taking money—these fifteen are performers of inauspicious deeds.
Among them, the first group of four is not released from slavery except by the favor of their master; for them, servitude is hereditary.
That lowest of men who, being independent, sells his own self is the most contemptible of all these; even he is not released from servitude.

Among these fifteen types, the four—namely those born in the house, purchased, obtained as a gift, and inherited—are not released from slavery even if the master does not wish it; they are released only if the master, being pleased, releases them, otherwise they remain perpetual slaves. Likewise, the last one—the self-sold—is exactly the same. Nārada says:
"Whosoever among these should rescue his master from a life-threatening danger, he shall be released from slavery and shall receive a share equal to that of a son."
One who has been supported by a slave girl for a year is released from that slavery by giving a pair of cows;
however, even if it was consumed during a famine, one is not purified from that act by such a gift alone.

One who dies during a famine is liberated by giving a pair of cattle; the meaning is that whatever was consumed during a famine, which ought to have been protected, is expiated through that specific act. Even if one has been placed [as a slave], if the owner should redeem him by paying the wealth, or if he should cause him to approach [him as a free man], he too ranks immediately after the purchased slave.

The sixth [type of slave] is one who has been pledged; if the master releases him after he has paid the wealth as it was received, then he is freed. And this follows the law of the purchased: the destination of the purchased applies to him as well.
However, by paying the debt along with interest, the debtor is released from slavery.
The seventh is one released from debt; he is freed after paying the principal and the interest.
One who has set a time limit is liberated upon the expiration of that time;
you have come to me saying "I am yours," having entered the fray of battle and been won as a stake.
They shall be released by providing a substitute person (*pratiśīrṣapradāna*) through an act of equal merit.

Having approached [the creditor] after making a time-limit agreement, saying "I am yours," and having been defeated in battle or defeated at the stake, all three are released by giving a human substitute whose actions are equal to one's own.
However, a man who has fallen from the religious life (*pravrajyāvasita*) shall become the slave of the king alone.
For him there is no liberation from vows, nor is there any purification whatsoever.

One who has abandoned the life of a renunciant is declared to be the king’s slave; he is a lifelong slave, eternally impure, and unfit for social intercourse. A slave for food is immediately released by the master’s neglect of his sustenance, and one bound by a mare is released by the mare’s death.
A slave for food is released from slavery by not being given food; one maintained as a "mare-slave" (baḍavābhṛta) is released by the restraint of the mare. Kātyāyana says:
But if a man has intercourse with his own female slave and she subsequently gives birth, then, having considered the seed, she and her offspring shall be made non-slaves.
Nārada said: He who, with a joyful heart, desires to make his own slave a non-slave,
should quickly take a water-pot filled with water from the slave's shoulder and break it.
One should scatter fresh flowers over his head and,
having said "Not a slave" three times, should then release him while facing the east.
From that time forward, he should be addressed as one protected by the favor of his master;
he becomes one whose food may be eaten and from whom gifts may be accepted by virtuous people when he stands before them.
Bṛhaspati says:
Sons born of female slaves shall be slaves, whether they were begotten by their master or by another;
if the progenitor is the owner, the sons are not his slaves.
Kātyāyana says: A woman who was not a slave but was married by a slave shall also attain the status of a slave,
because her husband is her master, and since he is himself under the authority of his own master.
Vyāsa says: A female slave belonging to another may not become the slave of anyone else;
however, if one goes with her after paying a bride-price (śulka), the man who goes does not incur slavery.
A man who pays a fee for approaching a temple servant girl (devadāsī) does not thereby enter into slavery.
However, if no fee is paid for the sake of the seed, that seed belongs to the owner of the field.
Kātyāyana states: "But he who, out of lust, by force makes a woman who has sought refuge his slave, or transfers her elsewhere, shall be punished; and that [act] shall be as if it were not done."
He who, by force, enjoys a nurse or a non-servant woman as if she were a slave,
or the wife of an attendant, shall incur the first amercement.
He who, being capable and not in a state of distress, desires to sell a devoted female slave who is crying out [in protest], shall incur a fine of two hundred [paṇas].
Nārada says: Just as one is not entitled to the offspring of cows, horses, camels, female slaves, buffaloes, goats, sheep, and the like,
so it is also with the wives of others.
When seed is sown in another's field, the owner of the seed does not obtain the fruit;
likewise, the offspring belongs to the progenitor, and those women who have been maintained for a fee [belong to their paymaster].
But when [the seed] is offered without a fee, the fruit belongs to the owner of the field alone;
for that which is sown in the field by the owner's ignorance [belongs to him].
In that case, there is no share for the owner of the seed;
rather, it belongs to the owner of the field alone, since the seed carried by the current or the wind has sprouted in his field.
One who possesses the field but does not sow the seed does not obtain the fruit;
a great bull may produce calves for the owner of the cows among whom he wanders while grazing.
O bull, for you whose cows exist, that virile seed of yours has been sown in vain; for it is held by tradition that when seed is sown in a field with the owner's consent,
the offspring belongs to both the owner of the seed and the owner of the field.
Without a field there would be no crop, nor does it exist without a seed;
therefore, according to the Dharma, offspring are held to belong to both the father and the mother.
Now, those entitled to servitude are described. Kātyāyana states:
"Servitude is to be recognized as applicable to the three [lower] castes, but never for a Brāhmaṇa;
among the castes, servitude occurs in the direct order [of precedence], not in the inverse order."
Indeed, when Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras relinquish their independence,
one should never compel a Brāhmaṇa to enter into servitude, even toward a person of the same caste.
In one who is endowed with virtue and study, no rite should be deficient due to desire;
even in that case, the best of the twice-born should not perform an inauspicious act.
For by the servitude of a Brāhmaṇa, the majesty of the king is destroyed. Nārada says:
Servitude among the castes occurs only in the direct order, not in the inverse order.
For one who abandons their own duty, servitude elsewhere is considered equivalent to being a wife.

A Brahmin who abandons his own duty (*svadharma*) and falls from the state of renunciation (*pravrajyā*) becomes the slave of a Kṣatriya or others; just as taking a wife is permitted only in the direct order of castes (*ānulomya*) and not in the inverse order (*prātilomya*), so too is slavery. Uśanas says:
"Neither a teacher, nor a *sapiṇḍa* relative, nor a Brahmin, nor those of the lowest castes, nor a twice-born man superior in learning, may enter into the state of slavery."

The statement "neither a guru nor a sapinda" refers to persons of other castes distinct from Brāhmaṇas. For a Brāhmaṇa, one born of the lowest caste (*antyayoni*) is not a slave. For one of equal caste, such as a Kṣatriya and so forth, one who is superior in learning is not a slave. Kaṇva states:
"All those of unknown birth are never slaves of the twice-born;
likewise, one who is superior in learning, a kinsman of the same lineage (*sajātīya*), a sapinda, and even gurus [are not slaves]."
Viṣṇu: "He who employs a man of the highest caste in servitude shall be punished with the highest amercement. Kātyāyana:
"But one may employ a Śūdra in servitude, whether he was purchased or not;
for he was created by the Self-existent One himself specifically for servitude."
Nārada said: Wife, son, and slave—these three alone are declared to be without property.
Whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they themselves belong; such is the fruit thereof.
The section on the non-performance of service after having entered into an agreement is completed. Now follows the non-payment of wages. Nārada says:
The procedure for the giving and receiving of wages for servants has been declared;
the non-payment of such wages is recorded as a title of legal dispute.
The master of the work shall give wages to the servant in due order—
at the beginning, middle, and end of the task— as has been determined.
But when the wages are not fixed,
the merchant, the cowherd, and the farmer shall each receive a tenth part of the profit from cattle, seed-corn, and crops respectively.
"Cow-seed" refers to the lineage of cows. The mention of "cows" is an indicative term for all livestock. Thus says Yājñavalkya:
"But he who employs laborers without having fixed their wages shall be made by the king to pay a tenth part [of the profit] from trade, livestock, and crops."
If one should neglect the place and the time, or should effect a gain in an improper manner, then the master’s will prevails; if more work has been performed, more should be given.
Whatever amount of work one performs, that much indeed is his wage;
even if both [tasks] are impossible, he should accomplish what is possible according to the instructions.

Furthermore, he who causes work to be done without having fixed the wages must be made to pay a tenth part to the king. From trade, cattle, and crops, merchants, cowherds, and farmers receive a tenth part of their profit, cattle, seed, and harvest respectively. Regarding the increase of cattle: if one who performs work appropriate to the place and time "should transgress" (atīyāt) the place or time; or if, in that very same place and time, he should perform the work otherwise than according to the acquisition of the cause—that is, he does it poorly—then in that case, regarding the master's desire (chanda) for the payment of wages to that servant, he may give as much as he wishes, but not the full wage. However, when an excess of profit is produced due to knowledge of place, time, and so forth, then even an additional fee should be given. But when a single task with a fixed wage, being performed by two or many people, becomes "unfinishable" because of being overcome by illness or other causes and thus does not reach completion, then [the payment] shall be according to the work actually performed. When the task is accomplished by two or many, however, one should act according to what was heard [previously]; one should give to the two or the many exactly what was agreed upon, but not the whole amount to each individually, nor according to the specific portion of work done. Thus says Bṛhaspati.
The plowman shall take one-third or one-fifth [of the crop];
the laborer hired for food and other provisions shall take a fifth part from the plow.
One who is supported by a commission should take one-third of the harvested crop;
thus says Nārada: "Whatever implements for work have been entrusted to them for the performance of the task..."
It should be protected with a sense of trustworthiness, never by deceit.
Vṛddha-Manu says:
"Those who are skilled in sea-voyages and who perceive the requirements of place, time, and purpose shall determine the wages; this applies if no agreement has been made beforehand."
Bṛhaspati says: A servant must not commit even the slightest act of deception against his master;
he incurs a loss of wages, and from that, a legal dispute arises.
When a hired laborer, having received his wages, does not perform the work if he is capable,
he shall be made to pay a fine equal to double those wages.
The word "shall be made to pay" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Manu says:
"Whether he is afflicted or healthy, if one does not perform that work as agreed, his wages shall not be paid, even if the work is only slightly incomplete."

Nārada says: Having promised to perform work, one who does not do it should be compelled by force to do so; having received wages, one who does not perform the work shall pay double the wages as a fine.
Manu says: "If a hired servant, though not ill, fails through arrogance to perform the work as stipulated,
he shall be fined eight *kṛṣṇalas*, and his wages shall not be paid."
Nārada says:
If he abandons his work before the term is completed, he shall suffer the loss of his wages;
if he departs due to a fault of the master, he shall receive payment for as much work as he has performed.

If he does not cause the goods to be carried, or abandons the merchandise, the vehicle, or the draft animal, he shall be made to pay a quarter of the wages; if he abandons them halfway, he shall pay the full amount.

Viṣṇu: "A hired laborer who abandons his work before the term is completed shall forfeit the entire wage. He shall pay a hundred *paṇas* to the king. If the goods are lost through his own fault, he must restore them to the owner, except in cases of damage caused by fate or the king. If the employer dismisses the laborer before the term is completed, he shall pay him the full wage and a hundred *paṇas* to the king, except when it is due to the laborer's own fault. Yājñavalkya: "The carrier shall be made to pay for goods lost unless the loss was caused by the king or by fate.
