Furthermore, one who causes an obstruction to the departure shall be made to pay double the wages."

If he abandons her on the way after she has set out, he must pay her the seventh part of the fee as wages; if he abandons her halfway, he must pay the entire fee, and the same applies to the one who causes her to be abandoned.

When he abandons [the servant] before setting out on the journey that has already begun, he shall be made to pay a seventh part of the wages along with the wages themselves. If he abandons him just as he has set out, then a fourth part along with the wages; if on the halfway point, the whole amount. Furthermore, when the master abandons the hired servant at these aforementioned places, the same amount previously mentioned must be paid by him to the servant. Vṛddha-Manu says: "If a merchant, having sold that merchandise on the way, should abandon the servant, then half of the wages must be paid to him, and he (the servant) shall receive that half."
Kātyāyana says: If that merchandise should be lost or stolen on the way,
he shall receive wages proportional to the distance traveled.

He who abandons a companion on the road when he is exhausted or afflicted by illness shall first incur the punishment for violence; if he fails to provide protection in a village, he shall be punished after three days.
Regarding courtesans, Nārada said:
Having received the fee, if a courtesan does not wish to comply, she shall pay double;
likewise, if the payer of the fee does not wish to comply, he shall suffer the loss of the fee.
Bṛhaspati says:
One who is ill, exhausted, distracted, or preoccupied with royal business,
and who does not come when invited, is declared to be a "barren mare" (baḍavā) and is beyond reproach.
Nārada says: A man who does not pay the bride-price, or who enjoys a woman [already married] without [her husband's] consent,
or who approaches her in an improper manner by means of blows, teeth, nails, and so forth, [is liable for punishment].
"By 'out of order' is meant by a forbidden path; 'striking' means beating.
He who approaches [the wife] in a non-vaginal way, or discharges [semen] with his arms, shall be made to pay eightfold the nuptial fee (śulka) and an equal amount as a fine."
Those libertines who reside there, with the courtesans as their primary concern—
the decision regarding matters arising from them is declared by them.
Regarding those who dwell having built a house on another’s land, Nārada says: "He who,
having built a house on another's ground and paid the fee, should dwell there,
may take that grass, wood, and so forth and depart."
But having stayed overnight in another's land without a formal invitation,
one who is departing should by no means take grass or wood.
Whatever grass, wood, or bricks have been placed there,
all of that must be reported to the owner of the land as they are being removed.

By the word *stoma*, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) given to them for the purpose of experiencing their houses is meant. Vyāsa states: "He who, out of affection, has lived in a house for a very long time, [the owner] gives him wood as he departs; it is not otherwise when a *stoma* has been given."
Otherwise, it concerns the owner of the field. Kātyāyana states:

"He who, having taken a house, a cow-pen, a shop, or the like, on lease, does not return them to the owner, shall be made to pay [the property] along with the rent for as long as he has withheld them."

If one who has taken elephants, horses, cattle, donkeys, camels, or other such animals on lease does not return them after having completed his purpose, he shall be made to pay the rental along with the value of the animals.
By the word *bhāṭaka*, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is meant. Nārada says:
"One should bring back the vessels that carry the *stoma* [offerings] when the time for their return has arrived;
if they are broken or lost, the liability shall fall upon the receiver, except in the case of an accident."
Manu states the rule for the toll of those traveling by boat:
"A vehicle should be made to pay one paṇa at a ferry; a man, half a paṇa;
an animal and a woman, a quarter; and an empty-handed man, half a quarter."
Vehicles with full containers shall be made to pay a ferry-toll according to their value;
those with empty containers, as well as men without belongings, shall pay whatever little they possess.
Over a long distance, it should be determined according to the location and the time at the crossing;
one should know that this applies to a riverbank, but there is no such defining characteristic for the ocean.
A pregnant woman in her second month or beyond, as well as a renunciant,
a sage, Brāhmaṇas, and those bearing religious marks, shall not be made to pay a ferry-toll at a crossing.
"Whatever of the dyers' goods should be lost through their negligence,
that must be paid by the dyers themselves, having assembled together, each from his own share.
Thus Nārada states the rule for the payment of the value of a garment lost in the hands of a washerman.
One-eighth of the value is lost for a garment washed once;
for one washed twice, one-half [of that]; for three times, one-third; and for four washings, exactly one-half [of the original value].
But beyond the point where half has been exhausted, there is a gradual increase by one-quarter portion until it reaches the state of being worn out;
for that which is worn out, there is no fixed rule regarding its exhaustion.

For a garment purchased for eight *paṇas* that has been washed once and damaged, a compensation of one *paṇa* less one-eighth (*pādona*) shall be paid; for one washed twice, less one-quarter (*pādona*); for one washed thrice, less one-third; for one washed four times, half [of the price] shall be given, namely four *paṇas*. Beyond that, for each subsequent washing, a reduction of one-quarter [of the price] shall be applied. This continues until the garment is worn out; for a garment that is worn out and damaged, the price shall be determined according to the owner's discretion. Yājñavalkya: A washerman who wears another person’s garment shall be made to pay three *paṇas*;
however, for selling, mortgaging, pledging, or borrowing it, he shall pay ten *paṇas*.

A washerman is one who cleans clothes. If he takes the garments entrusted to him for washing and wears them himself, he shall be fined three *paṇas*. However, if he sells them, or pledges them—having made an agreement such as, "I shall give you this garment for your use for such a period, and you must likewise give me this much money"—or if he gives them away to his own friends, or takes them as a pledge, he shall be fined ten *paṇas*.
Thus ends the section on the non-payment of wages; [this concludes] the dispute between the owner and the herdsman.
Now follows the dispute between the owner and the keeper. Regarding this, Manu says:
"I shall duly declare, according to the true principles of dharma, the dispute arising from the transgressions of both owners and keepers in relation to livestock."
A cowherd who is paid with milk may, with the consent of the owner of the cattle, milk another cow for his wages; this shall be the compensation for a herdsman who receives no other pay.
Nārada says: From a hundred cows, a heifer shall be the cowherd’s fee; from two hundred, the milk of one milch-cow.
Or, the milk of all the cows may be given to the cowherd every year on the eighth day.

The cowherd’s wages shall be one two-year-old heifer for every hundred cows; for every two hundred cows, one milch-cow shall be given annually, or else the entire milk produced on the eighth day. He shall bring the cows back to the cowherd every day at the end of the night;
having been grazed and watered, the cowherd shall return them in the evening.

Day after day at dawn, the master leads [the cattle] to the cowherd and entrusts them to him. That cowherd, having tended them in the forest—having grazed, played, and drunk their fill of water—must bring them back in the evening and return them to the master. And so says Yājñavalkya:

"The cowherd shall return the cattle in the evening exactly as they were entrusted; however, having received his wages, he must be made to pay for those that have died or been lost through negligence."
Nārada says:
If a cow meets with misfortune, the cowherd should strive to remedy it to the best of his ability;
if he is unable, he should report the matter to his master for the sake of its recovery.

If a disaster occurs, he should exert himself to the best of his ability with remedies and the like. If he is unable to do so, he should go quickly and inform his master. One who fails to exert himself, fails to raise an alarm, or fails to inform his master, that cowherd deserves to pay the price of the animal and a fine to the king.
Bṛhaspati:
"In the event of destruction due to the fault of the keeper, however, a fine for the keeper is prescribed;
[the penalty] shall be twelve and a half paṇas, or the value of the property itself, to be paid by the owner."
Vyāsa says:
When cattle are seized during a village procession or while resting in the kingdom,
whatever is lost or stolen therein, the herdsman is not at fault.
Nārada says:
But when goats and sheep are hemmed in by wolves and the herdsman does not come to their aid,
if a wolf should forcibly kill one, that fault shall lie with the herdsman.
This has been clearly stated by Nārada:
"By this, the dispute regarding all cattle is fully described;
for the purity [of ownership] among kings may be established by the sight of the calf, the horns, and so forth."
By this dispute concerning cowherds, the disputes regarding the keepers of buffaloes, goats, sheep, and so forth, are explained. Manu says:
"He should give the two ears, the hide, the tail-hairs, the bladder, the sinew, and the gallstone to the owners of the animals, showing these parts when they have died."
Now, regarding the rules for the pasture land for cattle,
Yājñavalkya states a specific point here:
"The pasture for cattle is according to the will of the village and according to the authority of the king."
A twice-born man may take grass, fuel, and flowers from anywhere as if they were his own.
The distance between a village and its fields shall be one hundred bows;
for a market town (kharvaṭa) it shall be two hundred, and for a city, four times that.
Manu:
If cattle should damage grain that is not enclosed there,
the king shall not inflict punishment upon the keepers of the animals.
Yājñavalkya states: "There is no offense regarding a field situated on a path or at the edge of a village pasture (*vivīta*).
A *vivīta* is land intended for growing horse-gram (*kuluttha*), niṣpāva beans, or cotton."
One who acts according to desire without being prompted by another deserves punishment like a thief.
Nārada says: If crops are destroyed by cattle or other animals after they have passed over the enclosure,
the keeper shall be punished therefor, provided he did not prevent it to the best of his ability.
Regarding this, Kātyāyana states a specific rule:
"If a man demands back grain that was destroyed by cattle,
his ancestors do not eat [the offerings], nor do the dwellers of heaven."
This is for the wealthy man:
A fence should be made around the field on the path such that a camel cannot look over it,
nor can an animal leap over it, nor can a camel break through it, nor can dogs and pigs.
Yājñavalkya says:
And one should construct a fence there such that a camel cannot look over it;
and one should block every opening through which the snout of a dog or a pig might pass.
One should provide great protection against all [harm] starting with goats;
for deer that have tasted the savory flavor cannot be turned back by mere suffering.
Grain destroyed by cattle, even if permitted by the neighbors, must be paid back to the owner of the field by the owner of the cattle; such grain is recovered with great effort.
Kātyāyana says: As long as the crop is being destroyed, so much must be paid by the owner of the cattle;
straw should be given to the owner of the cattle, but the grain to the cultivator.
Or, according to Nārada, based on the nature of the damage:
"One should cause a cow to pay a fine of one māṣa, and likewise a buffalo two māṣas; this applies to the owner, the herdsman, and the head of the household."
Likewise, for goats, sheep, and calves, the fine shall be half a māṣaka.

By the word "māṣa," merely the measure [of the fine] is expressed. This, however, refers to the case of eating [the plant] with the intent of causing it to sprout again, which is preceded by ignorance. Kātyāyana states: "A cow should be fined one-quarter of a paṇa, and likewise a buffalo one paṇa; similarly, for goats, sheep, and calves, a quarter-paṇa is proclaimed as the fine."
This refers to absolute destruction. Yājñavalkya says:
"In a pasture, the liability for these [animals] is equal; it is the same as for donkeys, camels, and buffaloes.
As long as the crop is destroyed, for that long the owner of the field shall receive compensation."
If a cow that has strayed due to the fault of its keeper should destroy crops, there shall be no punishment for the owner of the field;
the keeper alone deserves that punishment.
A female buffalo that destroys standing crops shall be fined eight māṣas;
a cow shall be fined half of that, and a goat or sheep half of that again.

This concerns the case of female buffaloes, goats, and sheep. Viṣṇu states: “During the day or at night, for each mouthful [eaten], a cow is fined one *māṣa*; however, a cow that eats only a single mouthful is not to be punished. For all others, a calf is fined one *māṣa*. A female buffalo is fined ten [māṣas], a donkey or camel six, and a goat or sheep four. Nārada says: “For those that are exhausted, the fine is doubled; for those driven by wind, it is quadrupled.
But for those caught in the act of stealing, the wise declare the punishment to be the same as that for a thief.”
Yājñavalkya:
For those who sit down after having eaten [the crops], the fine is double that which has been stated;
it shall extend as far as the crop is destroyed and as far as the fruit belongs to the owner of the field.
But the owner of the cattle who strikes [the cow] deserves the previously mentioned fine;
in that case, there is no fault on the part of the master as long as there is a keeper for the four-footed animals.
"O Apālā, the fault for the destruction of the crops is recorded by the wise as belonging to the owner. Nārada says:
"Whether seized by royal officers or struck by a thunderbolt,"
Or if one is bitten by a snake, or even if one has fallen into a pit;
Even if [the animal] is killed by tigers and the like, or afflicted by diseases,
there is no fault on the part of the herdsman, nor is there any fault on the part of the owners.
For elephants and horses are not to be punished, for they are traditionally held to be the protectors of the subjects.
Uśanas says: Those with one eye,
those with a crooked horn, a bull that has been branded,
a cow that has recently arrived, one that has recently calved, and one suffering from diarrhea are not to be punished.
Cows are not to be punished during festivals or during rites such as the ancestral śrāddha ceremonies.
Manu says:
"A cow that has calved within ten days, a bull, and likewise a sacrificial animal for the gods—
whether they have a keeper or are without a keeper— Manu has declared these to be exempt from punishment."
Nārada says: A cow that has recently calved, a bull, a horse, and an elephant must be kept away [from the funeral site] with great effort for ten days; their owner incurs no fault.

Yājñavalkya says: Bulls that have been set free, sacrificial animals, those who have recently given birth, guests, and others of this kind, as well as those whose property has been seized by divine calamities or royal authorities, are to be released from liability for damage.
Kātyāyana states: "In cases of beating animals— whether they be of low, high, or middle rank—
the owner shall determine the punishment to be inflicted."
If, as cows are leaving the village,
one should go out from their side through negligence and eat the crops, that fault belongs to both the owner and the herdsman.
Thus ends the dispute between owner and herdsman; now follows the non-observance of conventions. Regarding this, Nārada says:
The established rule of heretics, guilds, and other such groups is called *samaya*; the non-fulfillment of that rule is recorded as a ground for legal dispute.

A compact (*saṃvit*) or agreement (*samaya*) is that which is made by many virtuous people for the purpose of protecting the community. Its violation is called the non-fulfillment of the agreement. Bṛhaspati states:
"The convention and the making of an agreement among villages, guilds, and assemblies must be carried out in matters concerning obstacles, as well as in matters of dharma."
Two, three, or five persons who speak for the welfare of the community should be appointed;
their word must be followed by the village, guilds, corporations, and so forth.
The construction of assembly halls, water-stations, temples, ponds, and gardens,
as well as the refinement of the destitute and the poor, and the performance of sacrificial rites.
And we must partially fulfill the cessation of the nest;
that which is written here on this leaf is the righteous formal agreement.
Kātyāyana says: He who destroys what is logically consistent, he who gives no opportunity to the speaker,
and he who speaks what is illogical— such a person shall be punished with the first amercement.
The royal edict has issued in accordance with the Dharma;
therefore, its practice must first be carried out by the command of the king.
That man who does not observe the laws set forth by the king deserves censure;
he who reviles the royal edict deserves punishment and imprisonment.
Bṛhaspati states the punishment for the violation of an agreement:
"But he who, being capable, violates an agreement that ought to be observed by those who are capable,
shall be punished with the confiscation of all his property and banishment from the city."
In that case, whatever man creates a division or shows indifference [toward the community],
a fine of four suvarṇas and six niṣkas is ordained for him.
Yājñavalkya: But he who misappropriates the property of a corporation, or whoever violates an agreement,
the king shall confiscate all his property and banish him from the realm.
In another Smṛti:

"The king should cause a wicked Brāhmaṇa who violates the established rules to go forth with his hair shorn, wearing only a crest-lock, clad in the directions as his garment (naked), and being fanned by human hair."
Bṛhaspati:
But he who destroys common property, or insults those learned in the three Vedas,
or obstructs the process of legal testimony, shall be banished from that city.
One who inflicts wounds, a slanderer, a creator of dissension, as well as one who commits acts of violence,
and one who is an enemy of guilds, corporations, or the king, shall be swiftly banished from there.
The heads of families, guilds, and assemblies, as well as the inhabitants of cities and the countryside,
shall carry out the social boycott of evildoers by withholding speech, censure, and cooperation.

Whatever punishment or favor toward men is carried out by them according to their own duty, that must also be approved by the king; for they are traditionally considered to have been delegated with full authority.
If those who have become possessed by hatred should cause harm to even a single person,
they must be restrained by the king and punished along with their followers.
When a conflict arises between the assemblies and their leaders,
the king should then investigate the matter and establish them upon his own path.
Kātyāyana states: "If one person eats from the same vessel as another, or sits in the same row as someone with whom he ought not to eat,
he shall be punished for that act unless he demonstrates the other's fault."
The Punishment for Misappropriating the Property of a Corporation.

Now, regarding the punishment for misappropriating the property of a corporation (*gaṇadravya*), Bṛhaspati says: "Those who, having come together and reached a unanimous agreement, misappropriate what is due to the king..."
Those merchants who flee shall be made to pay eightfold.
For the sake of accomplishing the collective work or in the presence of kings and other authorities,
whatever one may obtain from that shall be shared equally among all.
Whether it be for six months or even a month, the property should be divided according to their respective shares;
or it should be given away to those who are destitute, the elderly, the distressed, women, children, the sick, and the diseased.
This is the eternal law regarding heirs and others:
whatever has been acquired, preserved, or a debt contracted for the sake of the family,
as well as what was obtained through the favor of the king— all that belongs equally to everyone.
Kātyāyana states: One who has been dispatched on the business of a collective body shall deliver whatever he may obtain;
if he does not deliver it himself, he should be made to pay eleven times its value.
The lord of the earth, having honored those who have come for the business of the assembly with gifts, respect, and hospitality, should dismiss them once their business is accomplished.
Whatever one may obtain from that, it shall be equal for all.

The mention of the "lord of the earth" (mahīpati) is also indicative of ministers and others. Some hold that when one enters a city or similar place formed by a collective body and, upon the dissolution of that collective form, obtains something individually, it is common property—like wealth acquired through undivided means. That is incorrect; even if the collective body has not been dissolved and there is no visible cause for its dissolution, what is obtained belongs exclusively to the individual. [The section on the non-observance of conventions is concluded. Now follows: Non-delivery after sale.

Now, the legal title known as "Non-delivery after Sale" is discussed. Regarding this, Nārada states: "When, having sold a commodity for its price, it is not delivered to the buyer—that is called the legal title of 'Non-delivery after Sale'."
In this world, there are two kinds of substances: the immobile and likewise the mobile;
all of these are called "merchandise" in the context of the laws of buying and selling.
The wise have recorded its method of giving and receiving as being sixfold:
by counting, by weighing, by measuring, by performance, by appearance, and by women.

The merchandise is of six kinds: (1) *gaṇima*, which is to be counted, such as betel nuts; (2) *tulima*, which is to be weighed on a scale, such as gold, sandalwood, and saffron; (3) *meya*, which is to be measured by dry or liquid measures such as *prasthas*, such as rice and the like; (4) that which is acquired through labor such as plowing, such as oxen and the like; (5) that which is valued by its appearance, such as swords and the like; and (6) that which is valued for its luster, such as gems and the like. Thus, the procedure for the giving, receiving, and seizing of such merchandise is sixfold.
If one, having sold merchandise for a price, does not deliver it to the buyer, he shall be made to pay the loss of the immovable property and the profit from the use of the movable property.

If one who has received the price does not deliver the merchandise to the purchaser, he shall be made to pay for whatever deterioration occurs to the purchased cloth or other goods during that period of use. Since it is impossible to restore the actual deterioration, he shall be made to pay an amount corresponding to it. In the case of moving property, such as bipeds or quadrupeds, he shall be made to pay the value of their labor during that time. And regarding that value: "If the price should fall due to a change in market rates, he shall deliver the merchandise with interest. This rule applies to local traders; for those who travel to distant regions, the profit depends on the destination.

If the seller fails to deliver the goods sold, he shall forfeit the value of the goods according to the market price at that time. At the time of delivery, he must pay for the goods at the price prevailing at the time of purchase, plus any subsequent increase in value. If the goods are lost due to the passage of time while being transported across regions, and their value has decreased, he must pay the diminished value along with any profit earned from the journey.
Or, if the goods are destroyed, burnt, or stolen, that loss falls solely upon the buyer, provided the seller did not deliver them after having sold them.
Furthermore:
But he who, having shown an item as faultless, later reveals it to have a defect,
shall be made to pay double the price and an equal amount as a fine.

If a seller, having shown a commodity as flawless at the time of fixing the price, delivers it with a defect, he shall be made to pay the buyer twice that price and be fined an amount equal to that price. Likewise,
one who sells to another person and then delivers it to yet another hand shall also be made to pay twice that amount and be fined the same sum.
If a buyer does not accept merchandise being offered after it has been purchased,
the seller, by selling it elsewhere, incurs no offense.
This rule has been proclaimed regarding merchandise for which the price has been paid;
when the sale is made without the price having been paid, there is no transgression on the part of the seller.
He establishes what was stated previously:
"For the sake of profit, merchants engage in the buying and selling of all commodities;
and that profit, having depended upon the market price, may or may not become great."
Regarding the measure of profit, Yājñavalkya says:
"A merchant who buys and sells immediately shall take five percent on goods from his own country, and ten percent on those from a foreign land."
Therefore, even if another person has engaged in a conversation regarding a purchase, if the price has not been paid, the sale must be completed by this [original] party once a profit is realized.
Nārada says: "Therefore, a merchant should determine the value at that place and at that time."
One should not proceed by crooked means; the merchant's path alone is superior.
The meaning is that since the merchant's path is superior, one should not proceed by a crooked way. Yājñavalkya says:
"Even if it has been sold, it may be resold if the previous buyer does not take it back;
however, if the loss is due to the fault of the buyer, that loss shall belong to the buyer alone."
If a defect arises in a commodity due to an act of God or the king,
the loss belongs solely to the seller who, having been asked, does not deliver it.
Kātyāyana says: He who, having purchased and received an undamaged commodity, does not accept it,
shall obtain his own property by paying one-tenth of the price.
If the object has not been obtained at the time of the transaction, one should certainly not cause it to be delivered once it has been made;
such is the law within ten days, but beyond that, there is no rescission.
Bṛhaspati:
If an unwise man sells merchandise knowing it to be defective,
he shall be made to pay twice that amount, as well as an equal fine as a penalty.
Vyāsa says:
Having given his word of honor to the two of them, he should present the merchandise at the proper time;
if he does not accept it when it is being offered, that merchandise shall be considered as relinquished.
Regarding the specific case of land, Bṛhan-Manu says:

"If the purchase of a field is nullified because a portion of the land's price was not paid, or if it is seized by the king, the seller must pay the remainder of the principal; however, the buyer shall not [be liable]."
Vṛddhayājñavalkya states: "If the price for the purchase has not been paid in full, the delivery of the remainder is prescribed;
or else, there is a rescission of the sale, or the purchase proceeds as far as what has already been paid."
The gift should be made at the time of agreement; thereafter, the purchase is finalized.
In the absence of the seller's wealth, the purchase stands as far as what has been paid.
If the remainder of the purchase price is not paid by the buyer after it has increased,
he may recover the goods sold at the market rate appropriate for that time.
Thus ends the eighth head of dispute, named "Non-delivery after Sale. Now follows "Repentance after Purchase. Regarding this, Nārada says:
When a purchaser, after buying a commodity for a price, does not hold it in high regard,
this is called the legal head of dispute known as "repentance after purchase."
Regarding this, Manu states what items are not to be sold:
"One form mixed with another does not deserve to be sold;
nor that which is defective, nor that which is deficient, nor that which is concealed by distance."
Likewise elsewhere:
"But as for land that is common [to all], a base man should not give it away;
nor should he take it, nor seize it, nor indeed sell it."
In this context, Manu has stated that all items subject to sale without restriction are as follows:
first, a treasure-trove (nidhi) is always mentioned, followed by a deposit (nikṣepa); thereafter, water and stones, as well as those things which do not produce income (akṣiṇyāgāmin).
The *siddhas*, *sādhyas*, and those fit for sale are proclaimed as the eight *bhogas*.

"Bhogas" means that which is enjoyed; the meaning is that they are worthy of enjoyment. It should be understood that these eight have been exemplified. And Bṛhaspati has stated their essential nature:
"A treasure-trove is declared to be a temple of the gods, and a deposit is a vessel of wealth."
Water refers to ponds, lakes, and the like; stones refer to minerals and so forth.
The mountains, rivers, lakes,
houses, gardens, forests, and so forth will remain inexhaustible and shall endure for all time to come.
Those already established and prepared for their own enjoyment by ancestors, grandfathers, and others,
as well as those acquired by oneself, are likewise to be accomplished and diligently brought to fruition through effort.
"Thus, the wise should understand enjoyments in their general nature;
they may be employed in all matters—whether for giving, mortgaging, or selling.
Regarding the cessation of what has been purchased, Nārada says:
If a buyer, having purchased a commodity for a price, considers it a bad purchase,
it must be returned to the seller on that very same day, provided it is still unblemished.
If the buyer gives [the price] on the second day, he should pay a thirtieth part of the value as a fine;
on the third day, that fine is double; after that, it belongs to the buyer alone.
This should be understood as referring to the period following the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) toward material objects. Bṛhaspati states:
"That which has been sold by one who is intoxicated or insane, for a low price, or out of fear;
or that which was sold by one who is not independent or is deluded—this must be relinquished and returned to him."
Vyāsa has stated the time for returning [deposits]:
"The examination of hides, wood, bricks, thread, grain, wine, juice, cloth, silver, and gold must be performed immediately."
"Sadyaḥ" means on that very day. Gold, silver, garments, and liquids are to be examined within a single day; however, the examination of pearls, diamonds, and corals shall take seven days.
For bipeds, however, it is half a month for males, but double that for females;
for all seeds, it is ten days, and for metals and clothes, one day.
Yājñavalkya: The examination of seeds, iron, draft animals, gems, women, milch cattle, and men shall take ten, one, five, seven days, one month, three days, and half a month respectively.
Bṛhaspati: For horses, silver, gold, grain, metals, and garments,
as well as for products made of leather and wood, the period of examination shall be one day.
Kātyāyana says: A merchant who is expert in commodities, knowing the specific loss and profit of each article, should not exercise regret after having purchased it.
One should personally examine the merchandise and show it to others;
having accepted what has been examined and approved by many, one should not reject it again.

Yājñavalkya: A merchant who understands the decline and increase in value of commodities should not exercise regret after having purchased them; if he does so, he shall be liable to a fine of one-sixth.
Nārada says:
But a garment that has been worn, or one that is worn out and soiled—
even if sold while defective— it shall not belong again to the seller.

Therefore, there is no reversal [of the transaction] once one has proceeded after examination and learned of the defects. Regarding the decrease or increase in the value of garments due to their use, Nārada says by way of illustration:
"The value of a garment washed once is reduced by one-eighth;
for one washed twice, by two-fourths (one-half); for three times, by three-fourths; and for four times, by half."

But beyond the point where half [of the lifespan] has been exhausted, there is a gradual reduction by one-quarter [of the remaining duration], until it reaches the state of being worn out with its tenfold parts diminished; regarding the exhaustion of the sixth [element], there is no fixed rule.

In the phrase "twice or thrice," the word *pāda* (quarter) refers to half a quarter (*ardhapāda*). Therefore, if a garment washed once is destroyed, there is a loss of half a quarter; if washed twice, a loss of one quarter; if washed thrice, a loss of half a quarter; and if washed four times, half of the price is lost along with an eighth part in the fifth [washing]. In the sixth [washing], however, the rule is according to one's discretion and not from the scripture. Thus, due to the destruction of parts of the cloth, there is a proportional loss of the value according to the sequence of the cloth's destruction. Regarding commerce in sandalwood, saffron, and so forth originating from other continents, Kātyāyana states:
Having divided one's own wealth into five parts, three parts are called the principal;
the fourth part is the profit, and the fifth is called the falsehood.
Regarding this very subject, Bṛhaspati says:
"Without [the consent of] the heirs, one may not take five parts or three parts of the property appropriate for that [transaction] in succession;
success [is achieved] through three, and the purchase must be made payable; the fourth part is [permissible], but not the fifth."

These two statements concern trade in saffron and other goods brought from foreign islands; for this very reason, the fourth part is called profit and the fifth part is called "untruth. Regarding this, Vyāsa says: "In that regard, others perform the exchange of merchandise through fraudulent means, by mixing it with other dissimilar items of inferior value."
Bṛhaspati: In the case of both types of fields, whether in partition or in exchange,
the accomplishment of the transaction shall depend upon the written record provided by those two.
The valuation of gems, horses, and mules is determined by experts;
that of goods situated in the marketplace is by the king's command; and that of cattle and land is by the mutual agreement of both parties.
Kātyāyana says:
Its value is not determined by neighbors nor by assemblies;
rather, it is that which the buyer shall agree upon with the seller, saying, "This belongs to him."
"This indeed is the price of the field for sale. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states a specific rule:
"Whosoever among them is known to be a deceiver in buying or selling must be cleared by means of oaths; this is the procedure in all such disputes."
He himself has explained the nature of purchase, sale, and barter, as well as the nature of exchange: "Taking one's own property of a different kind from another,
the relinquishment of what arose from a purchase— when the values are equal— is barter."
Vyāsa says: Taking a heterogeneous substance belonging to another from someone else and relinquishing the price— this mutual transaction is the cause of ownership.
An exchange with an object of the same kind is known as *parivṛtti*;
an exchange involving inequality is declared to be a sale (*vikraya*); and when mixed, it is known as a barter (*vinimaya*).

These—purchase, sale, exchange, and barter—are the causes and effects that generate ownership (*svatva*). In this context, that which one wishes to abandon in the world is called "value" (*mūlya*), such as gold and so forth; that which one desires to acquire is called "merchandise" (*paṇya*), such as fields, houses, and so forth. Among these, purchase (*kraya*) is the acquisition of merchandise preceded by the relinquishment of value. Sale (*vikraya*) is the acceptance of value that generates ownership in the value itself, preceded by the relinquishment of merchandise. Exchange (*parivartanā*) is the acceptance of a homogeneous thing preceded by the relinquishment of a homogeneous thing. When there is inequality, exchange itself is designated by the term "hire" (*avakraya*). In an exchange involving heterogeneous and homogeneous things mixed together, if the heterogeneous portion is greater, it becomes hire; if the homogeneous portion is greater, it is exchange. When the homogeneous and heterogeneous portions are equal, it is barter (*vinimaya*). Others maintain that barter is a distinct category consisting of the mutual acceptance of merchandise and value. Now, Kātyāyana states the establishment of purchase and the other transactions: [The verse follows: *Paṇyaṃ gṛhītvā yo mūlyaṃ na dadyāt tatra krayaḥ smṛtaḥ |* *mūlyaṃ gṛhītvā yaḥ paṇyaṃ na dadyāt tatra vikrayaḥ ||* *sajātīyaṃ parityajya vijātīyasya saṃgrahaḥ |* *parivartanā sā proktā vaiṣamye tv avakrayaḥ smṛtaḥ ||* *vijātīyādhike sā syād avakrayaḥ samākhyayā |* *sajātīyādhike tu syāt parivartanā nāmataḥ ||* *sājātyavaijātyayoś ca sāmye vinimayaḥ smṛtaḥ |* *paṇyamūlyayor anyonya-svīkāre vinimayaḥ paraḥ ||* [And further: *Vinimaye 'pi yad dravyaṃ duṣṭaṃ vāsyād aduṣṭavat |* *dātā tad eva gṛhṇīyād dātā cādho 'dhamaṃ vrajet ||* *naṣṭaṃ deyaṃ vinaṣṭaṃ ca rājñā caiva hṛtaṃ tathā |* *agninā ca hṛte naiva dātā taddoṣabhāg bhavet ||* *deśaṃ kālaṃ ca bhogaṃ ca jñātvā caiva vicakṣaṇaḥ |* *kuryād dānaṃ pratigrahaṃ ca nyāyato 'nyathā doṣabhāk ||* [And: *Krayaḥ prakāśaḥ kartavyaḥ svasvatvasya prasiddhaye |* *vikrayādau ca sarvatra pramāṇaṃ krayapatrakam ||* *anyathā naiva sidhyeta dānādhamanavikrayāḥ |* *svatvahetuḥ krayas tatra phalaṃ svatvam udāhṛtam ||* [And: *Vinimayo hi vikrayavad draṣṭavyaḥ sarvakarmasu |* *parivartanā caiva tathaiva hy avakrayaḥ smṛtaḥ ||* *Vinimaye tu ca hṛte naiva dātā taddoṣabhāg bhavet |* *deśakālāv ubhau jñātvā kuryād dānaṃ pratigraham ||* *Vinimaye 'pi yad dravyaṃ duṣṭaṃ vāsyād aduṣṭavat |* *dātā tad eva gṛhṇīyād dātā cādho 'dhamaṃ vrajet ||* gṛhṇīyād dātā cādho 'dhamaṃ vrajet ||* *Naṣṭaṃ deyaṃ vinaṣṭaṃ ca rājñā caiva hṛtaṃ tathā |* *agninā ca hṛte naiva dātā taddoṣabhāg bhavet ||* *Deśaṃ kālaṃ ca bhogaṃ ca jñātvā caiva vicakṣaṇaḥ |* *kuryād dānaṃ pratigrahaṃ ca nyāyato 'nyathā doṣabhāk ||* *Vinimaye 'pi yad dravyaṃ duṣṭaṃ vāsyād aduṣṭavat |* *dātā tad eva gṛhṇīyād dātā cādho 'dhamaṃ vrajet ||* *Naṣṭaṃ deyaṃ vinaṣṭaṃ ca rājñā caiva hṛtaṃ tathā |* *agninā ca hṛte naiva dātā taddoṣabhāg bhavet ||* *Deśaṃ kālaṃ ca bhogaṃ ca jñātvā caiva vicakṣaṇaḥ |* *kuryād d
If the price is more than half [the value], the purchase is valid; the buyer shall pay the deficient amount. The purchase as well as the sale may be rescinded within ten days.

When half the price has been paid or when less than the full amount has been paid, both the purchase and the sale are rescinded. Likewise, a contract for exchange, a contract for barter, and a partition of property that was equal shall be rescinded within ten days; if they were unequal, they may be rescinded within nine years.

In the case of equality, there is a cessation after ten days as generally obtained; it does not extend beyond that. When there is inequality, the cessation occurs after nine years. Vṛddha-Kātyāyana says:
"A boundary, a change [of ownership], or an unequal [division] in three parts, as well as those established by royal decree or by a virtuous person, are declared to be non-revocable."
The aforementioned loss through purchase is also resolved within ten years;
for moving property, the aforementioned loss is traditionally held to last up to twelve years.
An exchange made with an excess of goods is a purchase;
if it is deficient, it is a sale; if the two are equal, they are both alike.
In that case, one should understand there is another alternative, as in the case of a man in the form of a deer.

Regarding the threefold transformation, there is no inclusion of kinsmen and so forth, because the inclusion of kinsmen and others pertains to the subject of pure purchase, and because it is impossible to provide the specific individuals required [for such a transaction]. Bṛhaspati states:
"But in all sales, one should record the well, trees, and so forth."
Whatever else there may be, such as waterways and so forth, Bṛhaspati [has declared].

They say that even when something has been purchased, it still belongs to the seller if it is milk that has turned sour, ripened grain, a tree or fruit fit for consumption, a well, a pond, or a lofty house.
The meaning is that if these [documents] are not written, they do not belong to the purchaser. Kātyāyana states:
"A purchase is established when the price is more than half [of the value]; in the case of the aforementioned [documentary] proof, it is established after ten years;
a lease is established by threefold enjoyment; and a debt-transaction is established immediately."
In this context, the word *avakraya* refers to exchange. A verbal pledge (*vācika-ādhi*) regarding immovable property is established after ten years;
regarding movable property, it is established after twelve years, even if the stated profit has not been realized.
Now, regarding the purchase of permission [to collect revenue],
Yājñavalkya (Kātyāyana) states:
"But when a taxpayer has fled, [the debt shall be recovered] together with the surety for the tax."
The members of the assembly may sell a tax-paying field for the purpose of revenue.
Prajāpati says:
A quarter or half of the price is prescribed for a purchase made under compulsion;
having paid that entire price, one acquires one's own field.
After three enjoyments, it shall attain firmness for the purchaser thereafter.
Nārada says: But if, after a field has been sold by his own consent, the owner of the field should have regret...
Having paid the entire price for it, one may enjoy it until the threefold enjoyment is completed.
The meaning is that one shall not receive [the property] after nine years have passed. Bhāradvāja says:
"The command, the seizure, the purchase, and the tax—these are prescribed as forms of punishment;
those who know the Dharma understand that both [seizure and purchase] would be invalid in any other case."
Katyāyana states regarding the aforementioned method of purchase:
"Having first established the time for repayment along with interest,
that which is previously specified by saying 'this is what must be purchased' [is the price]."
Then that property of the creditor shall belong to you upon the aforementioned gain. Bharadvāja said: "And taking some wealth with me, I will give it to you at some time."
If there is no purchase [of that field] at this price, then what of it? This is the argument regarding the field.
That [possession] is said to be "of stated acquisition" because it was not returned at the stated time;

and because of that stated acquisition, the land is considered "appropriated. Through that stated acquisition, even if it has been enjoyed for twelve years, ownership shall pass [to the acquirer] by the established sequence; this is held to be equal by the virtuous when agreed upon.
A purchase made by command is subject to the aforementioned period of ten years for recovery of profit;
however, a lease or a debt-purchase is settled immediately with a one-third share of the profit.
Regarding this matter of land, Kātyāyana states what constitutes an improper price: "By neighboring residents who are assembled, knowledgeable, and fearful of sin,
[the value] of fields, groves, houses, and so forth, as well as of bipeds and quadrupeds [should be determined]."
They say that the price is "determined" after dividing it into eight parts;
however, if it exceeds one part or falls short of it, it is considered improper.
Even after a hundred years have passed, all of that is revoked.
Vyāsa says: In the matter of buying and selling, whatever price a commodity rightfully deserves...
That [occurs] in the fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, or even the eighth degree.
If the purchase and sale of inferior goods are revoked,
then all that which was performed shall be as if unperformed, even if it involved a low price.
This statement is recited in the *Dharmadroṇa*.
If the price is less by more than one-eighth of what was determined by the neighbors,
because that [price] itself is improper, there is a right of rescission for both parties regarding the purchase.
In a purchase that is slightly less than what was stated, or inferior, there is no fault at all;
in buying and selling, it may fall short by some small portion in terms of value.
Other people who know the law say that even what has been done is as if undone.
Bṛhaspati says: That which exceeds a quarter more than the price or is less than the price is considered improper.
But the accomplishment of the purchase would not occur even in hundreds of years.
If a purchase is made in secret, whether at a price that is too low or too high, the fault lies with that very act;
both those who carry out the transaction shall be punished.
Likewise, in another Smṛti:
"If the price is less by more than one-eighth than that determined by the neighbors, the sale is not valid even after hundreds of years."
In the presence of all four neighbors, the eastern direction is the strongest;
likewise the northern and the western; but in the absence of all others, the southern direction prevails.
Afterwards, those who share the same water; after that, those who are closely connected;
after that, kinsmen; and after that, those who are associated with them.

If that [boundary] is not obstructed by rivers, streams, roads, and the like, it must always be accepted by the neighbors; but in the case of an obstruction by water-courses and such, it must be determined accordingly.
If there is no obstruction by the road or other such things, it should be seized by the immediate neighbors in the order previously mentioned, in the absence of those previously specified.
Bhāradvāja says:
The relatives, neighbors, and creditors shall take possession of the land in that order;
after them, the agnates; and in the absence of all these, those of other castes.
Persons of other castes, kinsmen, Bṛhaspati,
uterine brothers, sapindas, sodakas, and those of the same lineage (gotra),
as well as neighbors, creditors, and villagers— these seven are considered eligible for the purchase of land.
Vyāsa says: For land, the period of rescission for both the buyer and the seller is ten days;
for the *sapiṇḍas*, it is twelve days; beyond this, the transaction is irrevocable.
The neighboring lords of that time, the creditors of that time,
and the sapinda relatives of that time are considered to be those who must be informed regarding a purchase.
In the *Pañcādhyāyī*:
"Relatives, neighbors, and creditors are declared to be witnesses for a relative at that time;
but all those [witnesses] for others, such as a buyer or a seller, must wait ten days or more."
That field which goes to relatives and others due to the seller’s meager price is [considered valid] in other cases; however,
those standing before [the court] are declared fit for purchase, but not for sale.
They do not deserve to revile him, for they have passed away during that very day.

Relatives, neighbors, and creditors may exercise their expectation or indifference only within that same interval; not beyond a day. For both the buyer and the seller, ten days is the period for rescission (*anuśaya*).
A purchase of immovable property is intended to be valid only through the testimony of relatives and others;
otherwise, the sale would be invalid, and both parties would be subject to punishment.
This statement is made in the presence of relatives and others:
"Relatives, neighbors, and creditors who have gone outside the village during the purchase do not deserve to object once three fortnights have passed from the time of the purchase."
Regarding absence, Kātyāyana states:
"In one's own village, it shall be ten nights; in another village, three fortnights;
in another kingdom, six months; but if there is a difference in dialect, it shall be a year."
Prajāpati says: Having obtained the permission of neighboring kinsmen, vassals, and creditors who are nearby,
one should perform the purchase or sale after having caused witnesses to be heard.
Kātyāyana says: It is the settled rule that there is no legal right to buy or sell land without having obtained the consent of one's kinsmen and others who are nearby and blameless.
Prajāpati says: If one sells or purchases goods without having obtained the permission of relatives and others who are nearby and blameless,
both the buyer and the seller deserve a fine equal to the value of the transaction.
"Those standing nearby" refers to those residing in the same village. Bṛhaspati states:
"If they are present, the relatives and others of the purchaser should be questioned;
otherwise, having ascertained that the transaction has been completed, one may then express one's desire [to annul it]."
Or he may obtain it after three fortnights or after three months; thus says Bharadvāja.
The sale of land is not permitted with creditors residing in another village.
In the case of debtors belonging to one's own village, however, both [the principal and the interest] are prescribed in the absence of wealth.
On this point, Manu says:
"If, after having purchased or sold anything here, one should have cause for regret,
he may give back or take back that object within ten days."

The term "that property" (*tad dravyam*) refers to the very same [property] itself. It is understood that in the event of loss caused by fate or the king, even something of the same kind (*sajātīya*) must be returned. While explaining an alternative reading (*pāṭhāntara*) for this verse, the Commentator stated this meaning: when the price being paid is not accepted because it is unfit for receipt, then it must be deposited with a neutral mediator (*madhyastha*). Thus Vyāsa says: "In the case of goods intended to be given for another's sake, and likewise in sales and other transactions, they must be deposited with a mediator; otherwise, the transaction is not finalized."
He shows that the previously mentioned period of ten days applies even in the case of those who are wealthy and so forth. Manu says:
"In whatever matter a person may have cause for regret after it has been performed, he should be restored to the path of dharma by this rule."
And so it is stated in another Smṛti:
"When ten days have elapsed, a pledge becomes established as secured;
likewise, land and other property become purchased through the manifestation of ownership."
Regarding this, Kātyāyana states the specific rule:
"The purchase of immovable property is accepted only when based on the testimony of relatives and others;
it is not accepted by the wise in cases of exchange, cultivation, or gift."
The period of impurity for land is ten days for both the buyer and the seller;
for the sapindas, it is twelve days, after which it cannot be contested.
Bharadvāja says:
At sunrise during the forenoon, at a crossroads in the middle of a village,
a learned man should cause the Brahmins to hear [the proclamation] in the presence of kinsmen and neighbors.
Having received the price as it is, one should indeed show everything at the time of purchase.

In this regard, for a purchase made with [proper] acquisition (*śuddhakraya*), the period for rescission (*anuśaya*) for both the buyer and the seller is ten days. For a purchase made at an improper price (*uktālābhakraya*) or by command (*ājñākraya*), the period for rescission for the buyer is ten days. However, for the owner (*svāminī*), in the case of a purchase of immovable property at an improper price, the period for rescission is ten years; for movable property, it is twelve years. In the case of a purchase by command, the period for rescission for the owner is nine years. In the case of a purchase by command or at an improper price, there is no opportunity or entry for relatives (*jñāti*) and others. Because giving away the price constitutes a prohibition against sale for the sake of avoidance, and because there is no contradiction with the mention of relatives regarding ownership (*svatva*) when the sale takes the form of a gift, the opportunity for relatives and others is unimpeded even in a sale that is effectively a gift. In that context, for a purchase at an improper price, even if the seller lacks immediate activity, the cessation of ownership and the transfer of another's ownership are established through the prior intention alone; thus, the nature of the purchase is not contradicted. The statement, "A purchase is valid if the price is more than half [the value]," does not apply to all purchases, but rather to purchases at an inappropriate price, according to the statement of Kātyāyana.
Even if only a small amount of the price is paid, the sale shall be considered completed;
the remainder must be paid with compound interest, except according to a prior agreement.
If, in the absence of an agreement such as "I shall give it after this much time has passed," one does not give what is requested,
the debt increases by compound interest.

At the time of making the agreement, the remainder of what was previously given should be paid. Even at that time, if it is requested and not given, it increases by way of compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*).
Regarding that as well, Kātyāyana states the rule for interest:
If a deposit, the remainder of interest, or goods purchased or sold are not returned when demanded,
they increase by five percent per month.
In another Smṛti:
"The commodity purchased, the property of another,
and that which has been forcibly seized shall increase by way of compound interest until it becomes fivefold."

The meaning is that a twentieth part of the fixed price increases month by month until it becomes fivefold. By this, even when only a small amount of wealth is paid, the sale is indeed established. And so says another Smṛti:
"Even a mere *māṣa* of wealth, once it has reached the buyer through the seller, pervades the entire earth, just as a tiny amount of poison spreads through the body."

Since it is stated that what is half-given and what is not given at all constitute a non-sale (*avikraya*), how can a sale be established by giving only a small portion? It is replied: even in the case of a rescinded sale (*apakraya*), if the price is paid at the agreed-upon time, the sale is valid; otherwise, it is not.
They call a sale where half is given and half remains unpaid a "rescinded sale" (*apakraya*);
such a rescinded sale is nullified if the payment is not made at the proper time.
According to this statement:
"If land or other property, having been enjoyed as it was used,
has yielded more than expected and its value has increased, then the debtor shall obtain [the ownership of] that pledge."
When a debtor, having been reprimanded, gives a field to a creditor,
is it not the case that by making the half-given portion free of encumbrances and obtaining it through royal favor, he makes it equal for all?
Yājñavalkya: One who has been dispatched on behalf of a corporate body shall deliver whatever he may obtain;
if he does not deliver it himself, he shall be made to pay eleven times the amount.
The lord of the earth, having honored those devoted to the affairs of the assembly who have completed their tasks with gifts, respect, and hospitality, should dismiss them.
Therefore, whatever one might obtain, that should be equal for all.

The mention of "the king" is also an illustration for "ministers. Some hold that when a collective task—such as entering a city—is undertaken and a specific gain is acquired upon the completion of that task, it is common property, like wealth acquired by those who have not divided their assets. That is incorrect; even when the collective body has not been dissolved and even when there is a visible cause for the acquisition, what is obtained belongs specifically to the individual.
It has been determined: "In this matter of obtaining Śāntalā, you must relinquish [your share]."
"When the principal along with the interest has been received, you must pay it back to me."
Thus concludes the section on rescission after purchase; now follows the dispute over boundaries and the determination of boundary disputes. Yājñavalkya says:
In a dispute over boundaries, the neighbors of the field, the elders and others, the herdsmen, those who cultivate the boundary lands, and all those who frequent the nearby forests [shall decide].
They should establish the boundary, marked by landmarks such as mounds of earth, charcoal, husks, trees,
embankments, anthills, depressions, bones, and shrines.
At the time of constructing a village, one should establish boundary markers that are both visible and invisible. Bṛhaspati says:
"Wells, step-wells, tanks, shrines, groves, temples, high ground, low ground, river currents, reeds, thickets, and heaps of stones."
One should always cause these marks of light to be made on the boundary,
as well as others that are buried, so that the earth may not consume them.
Manu says:
One should establish boundary trees— namely the Nyagrodha, Aśvattha, Kiṃśuka, Śālmali,
Sāla, Tāla, and other milky-sap trees.
Stones, bones, cow-hair, husks, ashes, potsherds, dried cow-dung, bricks, charcoal, gravel, and likewise sand;
And whatever objects of this kind the earth would not consume due to their age,
those he should cause to be placed inconspicuously at junctions and boundaries.
Bṛhaspati:
Those substances which are imperishable by their very nature—
having placed these in jars, one should have them deposited at the boundaries of the land.
Thereafter, one should diligently show it to children who have reached the age of puberty;
and likewise, when they are old, they should show it to the dogs.
In this way, when there is knowledge of the succession, no confusion regarding the boundary arises.
Manu:
"If there should be doubt even when characteristic marks are observed,
the determination in a dispute regarding a boundary shall depend solely upon the testimony of witnesses."
Kātyāyana states:
One who is a neighbor on all sides should carry out the determination of a field;
likewise, he should do so for village boundaries and for cities and districts.
Regarding fields, ponds, rice paddies,
and groves, as well as houses, palaces, dwellings, and temples of kings and gods.
When neighboring vassals have become corrupt for the sake of achieving their own interests, one should show great regard for wealth;
however, one must effect their removal through those associated with them—of this there is no doubt.
Those who are attached to, or associated with, those who are corrupt are declared to be "associated with them.
However, a king who understands the Dharma must not treat such people as being utterly corrupt.
Having dismissed wicked vassals, he should, after deliberating with others such as hereditary ministers and the like, have the boundary established; thus do those who know the Dharma understand it.
Nārada says: The boundary is declared to be of five kinds: that marked by a banner, that marked by fish, that established by a deposit, that free from fear, and that determined by the king's command.

It is called *dhvajinī* because trees and other such objects, by virtue of their height, resemble banners. It is called *matsinī* because it possesses water; for the word "fish" (*matsya*) is indicative of the water that serves as the fish's support. It is called *naidhānī* because it contains deposits, husks, and charcoal, which, due to being buried underground, resemble hidden treasures (*nidhāna*). It is "free from fear" when there is mutual agreement between the plaintiff and the defendant. It is "established by royal decree" when, in the absence of marks known to the local people, it is determined by the king's will. Manu says:
"In the absence of neighbors, however, and of hereditary witnesses to the boundary, one should also interrogate these men who dwell in the forest."
Hunters, fowlers, cowherds, fishermen, root-diggers,
snake-catchers, gleaners, and others who dwell in the forest.
On this point, Bṛhaspati says: "Sworn by their respective oaths, they shall declare the determination of the boundary;
they shall show the hidden deposits; that is the authoritative rule."
Nārada says: A single man, even if he is highly trustworthy, shall not determine a boundary;
because of the gravity of this matter, this procedure is established for a plurality of persons.
Yājñavalkya says: Wearing red garlands and garments, the upholders of the earth (the kings) led the way along the boundary,
while he, wearing red garlands and garments, took earth upon his head.
A man who is devoted to truth and has observed a fast should point out the boundary.
Nārada says: "Now, if the neighbors should speak falsely in the determination of the case..."
All of them shall be punished individually by the king with the middle amercement.
The false testimony of witnesses is known by the occurrence of misfortune caused by gods or kings after three fortnights;
likewise in a boundary dispute, in the ordeal of the sacred water-pot, and in the ordeal of touching a cow's hoof:
"In cases involving the gods or kings, [the result] is expected after three fortnights, three fortnights, and seven days respectively."
Thus it is stated. Kātyāyana says:
"A village is declared to be the neighbor of a village; a field is the neighbor of a field;
and a house is specified as the neighbor of a house, encompassing it on all sides."
Those who were formerly neighbors there but later went to another country are proclaimed by the sages as *maula* (original inhabitants), because they are rooted in that very place.

Yājñavalkya states that in the absence of boundary marks and witnesses, the king shall determine the boundary: "In the absence of knowers and boundary marks, the king is the establisher of the boundary. Next, regarding the establishment of a river as a boundary, Bṛhaspati says:
When land has been brought from another village and given to someone else by a great river or by the king, how should the legal decision be made in that case?
Land that has been abandoned by a river or granted by a king belongs to him alone;
otherwise, men would not obtain any property resulting from royal or divine causes.
The decline and rise, as well as the life itself, of human beings depend upon the power of the king and fate;
therefore, in all undertakings, one should not disregard what has been done by them.
If one person causes a pit to be dug in one place on the ground, while another has it situated elsewhere on a riverbank,
one should not disturb that [pit] of his.
When a field with standing crops has been transgressed and the land becomes covered by the flow of a river's current, the owner of the land shall regain it.
Kātyāyana says:
One should not construct water-channels for the discharge of rainwater on the property of another.
Likewise:
"One should construct dwellings with walls of excrement, urine, and water, and provided with fire-places and pits,
leaving a space of two *aratnis* from the wall of another.
Likewise:
That which has been seized by a king through anger or greed, or by fraud or according to law,
but then given away by him out of satisfaction to another, does not attain validity.
If land has been taken from someone while he was enjoying it without proof of ownership,
or if it has been given to one superior in merit, one must not dispossess that person of it.
Bṛhaspati:
From the time of its initial construction, whether it be a house, a water source, a shop, or the like,
one should not displace that which has been used by anyone.
Nārada said:
A dam is seen to be of two kinds: excavated (khāta) and likewise built-up (bandhya).
An excavated dam is for the flow of water; a built-up dam is for its retention.

A boundary embankment is not prohibited in the middle of another's field, provided it possesses great utility and causes little harm; indeed, an increase is desired when there is a loss [to the owner].
Disregarding slight loss, only increase is desired. Yājñavalkya says:
"A dam that causes little harm and brings about prosperity should not be prohibited;
likewise, a well that carries water onto another's land while being situated on one's own field."
If one constructs an irrigation channel on a field without informing the owner, the produce belongs to the owner when it has been harvested; in his absence, it belongs to the king.
Nārada says: He who should construct a bridge without first having asked his master about what has already been undertaken or already built shall not partake in its fruit.
Kātyāyana says: But he who performs a renovation of a house, a garden, or a tank without the consent of the owner does not obtain [the property].
Regarding the cultivation of fallow land, Nārada said:
"If someone should cultivate a field that belongs to an owner who is incapable, deceased, or missing— provided he does so without opposition— he shall enjoy the fruit thereof."
If a field is being drawn for cultivation, the owner may return;
having provided all the necessary treatment for the fallow land, he shall regain possession of the field.
Then, by a reduction of one-eighth part each year, until eight years have been completed;
at the conclusion of the eighth year, he shall obtain the field he has enjoyed.
Kātyāyana states: If, due to incapacity, the cultivator does not pay the expenses incurred for the purpose of reclaiming waste land,
the farmer shall receive the produce minus one-eighth of it.
He may enjoy it for eight years, but after that, it belongs to the owner.
Nārada says: "In one year, half of a fallow field becomes [the tenant's]; in three years, a fallow field [becomes his]."
A field that has reached the end of five years' cultivation is equal to a wilderness.
Yājñavalkya: He who does not cultivate a field that has been tilled by the plow, nor causes it to be cultivated, shall be made to pay the fruit of the cultivation;
another shall cause that field to be cultivated.
Kātyāyana:
Whoever, having taken a field, neither cultivates it nor causes it to be cultivated,
shall be made to pay the crop-rent to the owner and a fine equal to that amount to the king.
The field’s yield is the *śada*.

If it has lain fallow for a long time, one-tenth [of the yield] is assigned when it is being cultivated; likewise, one-eighth if it is well-prepared, and one-sixth according to the established condition.
Bhāradvāja says:
When the rites of purification with ashes, water, and so forth are performed upon a field,
one who enters that field after the grain has been harvested becomes the owner of the wealth of his own cultivation.
If a field has been cultivated prior to the time of entry by the holder of the land,
the owner shall obtain that field along with the produce that arose therefrom, even without payment for it.

On this point Viṣṇu states: "In the case of a dispute regarding the boundary between two villages, the fine is two hundred [paṇas]; in the case of a dispute regarding the boundary of a field, eight hundred; in the case of crossing the boundary, eight thousand; and for taking water from one field to another, or for obstructing it, one shall be fined eight hundred. Śaṅkha says: "Having punished the violator of the boundary with the highest amercement, he should have the boundary re-established. Kātyāyana says: "Regarding trees grown in the middle of the boundary between two fields, their fruit and flowers shall be shown as common property to the owners of both fields."
But if branches produced in one field are situated in another field,
the owner of those [branches] shall be the one whose field they occupy.
Prajāpati [declares]: "But for those born in another's field, if they grow on the main branch elsewhere,
he alone shall be their owner, since they are situated upon his field."
To the seed-owner, however, one should give a third part as his share;
two parts shall belong to the owner of the field, for the share of the owner is highly commended.
If there should be an obstruction caused by that [tree], the owner of the field may climb the trees by means of their roots and cut back the branches;
even the fruit-bearing branches of those trees situated on his own boundary may be cut.

In the case of plants such as plantains, areca palms, and the like, where there is only slight obstruction caused by branches growing from another tree, the owner of that tree alone is entitled to the enjoyment of its produce.
Even if produced in another's field, if it bears fruit in a different field,
then the branch situated there would likewise share in the fruit.
The section on boundary disputes is concluded. Now, the legal title known as "union between man and woman" is discussed. Regarding this, Nārada says:
That legal subject in which the rites of marriage and so forth for women and men are proclaimed is called *strīpuṃsayoga* (the union of woman and man).

Śaṅkha: "Having been authorized by his teacher and permitted by his mother and father, he should take a wife. Nārada: "Among Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, for the purpose of taking a wife, a spouse of the same caste is best; and for a woman, a husband of the same caste is best."
Up to the seventh degree on the father’s side and the fifth degree on the mother’s side,
those who are of the same *gotra* as well as those who share the same *pravara* are ineligible for marriage.

Yājñavalkya: [One should marry] from a great family of Vedic scholars (śrotriya) renowned for ten generations, beyond the fifth on the mother's side and likewise beyond the seventh on the father's side.
Vasiṣṭha says: "The fifth [generation] from the mother's kin, and the seventh from the father's kin. Kaṇva says:
A Kṣatriya [should marry] beyond the third [generation] on the mother's side and the fifth on the father's side.

By the force of this statement of Kaṇva, the statement of Paiṭhīnasi—"the third [generation] from the mother's side and the fifth from the father's side"—should be understood as referring to Kṣatriyas and others. Sumantu says: "Kanyās (unmarried girls) are ineligible for marriage up to the fifth and up to the seventh [generation]. All the wives of one's father are mothers; their brothers are maternal uncles (*mātula*s); their sons are the sons of maternal uncles; their sisters are maternal aunts (*mātṛṣvasṛ*s); their daughters are the daughters of maternal aunts; and their daughters are sisters. Their offspring are sisters' children (*bhāgineya*s). Therefore, there is no mutual marriage among these. Otherwise, they all cause a mixture of castes (*saṃkara*) and become outcasts (*patita*). The same applies to the teacher of those [outcasts]. On this point, Kāśyapa says:
Seven types of girls who are to be reborn [as one's own daughters] are to be avoided as the lowest of their families:
she who has been given by word, she who has been given by thought, she for whom the auspicious marriage-thread ceremony has been performed,
she who has gone around the fire, and she whose hand has been taken in marriage.
And she who has been touched by water, and she who gives birth to a reborn being.
Thus these [women] have been described by Kāśyapa as burning the family like fire;
yet even a tree burnt by fire may sprout again after a long time.

And a family burnt by such a rebirth does not sprout again. Baudhāyana states: "If one should unknowingly marry a woman of the same *gotra*, he should maintain her as if she were his mother. If she has given birth, he should perform a *kṛcchra* penance for one-fourth of a year, and then offer clarified butter with the two verses beginning 'That which [you took] from my self' and 'Agni has given back the sight,' and with the *kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras beginning 'Whatever offense against the gods... Nārada says:
"The formal selection (*varaṇa*) of the bride and groom is prescribed to take place prior to their union."
The taking of the hand by way of choosing [the bride] is a consecration (saṃskāra) characterized by two features.
For those two, the choice [of a wife] is said to be indefinite because of the perception of faults;
however, the status of being a wife is fixed by the taking of the hand and the recitation of the mantras.
Yājñavalkya: "One who has been carefully tested for virility, who is young, intelligent, and beloved by the people. And likewise Nārada:
Having examined a man for his masculinity by the very characteristics of his own limbs,
if he is found to be a man without any doubt, he is worthy to receive a maiden.
He himself stated the characteristics of masculinity:
"One with well-knit collarbones, knees, and bones; with well-knit shoulders and neck;
with thick, firm, and thin skin; and with a gait and voice that are not sluggish."
"The seed and feces float, and the urine is frothy and cold;

by these characteristics one is a male (pumān), but one with the opposite traits is a eunuch (ṣaṇḍaka). Thus [it is said]. "With unhesitating gait and voice" means having a continuous and unhindered gait and voice. "Having frothy urine accompanied by sound"—the same author also states the characteristics of a eunuch:
In the treatise, sixteen types of eunuchs have been observed by the wise;
for them, the method regarding those who are curable and those who are incurable has been stated in due order.
In the medical treatises, those such as Dattātreya have stated who is curable and who is incurable. In the Purāṇa:
"One who is naturally impotent, one who is sterile, and likewise one who is impotent for half the month;
[these are incurable] due to a teacher’s curse, disease, or likewise due to the wrath of the gods."
The envious man, the eunuch, he who emits semen through the wind, the one whose vulva is in the mouth,
the one whose seed is impotent or cast away, the modest man, and likewise the husband of another woman.
These fourteen types of eunuchs should be avoided with great effort.

A *pakṣaṣaṇḍa* is one who is unable to move for half the month; his virility is impaired by the curse of a preceptor, or likewise by disease, or likewise by the offense of a deity. An *īrṣyāṣaṇḍa* is to be known as that man whose virility arises upon seeing a woman being served by another man. [In this case], virility arises for the man being served, not for the woman. A *vātaretas* is one whose semen is discharged due to the wind-disease (*vāta*). Regarding the phrase "the vulva in the mouth" (*mukhe bhaga*), the mention of the "mouth" is for the sake of illustration; it means that the function of the vulva occurs elsewhere than the vulva, for virility does not arise when [intercourse] is performed with the mouth of the vulva—so say some. An *ākṣiptabīja* is one who experiences pleasure from union, but there is no semen at the proper time. A *moghabīja* is one who has semen but no offspring. A *śālīna* is one who, upon seeing a woman, does not become excited due to shame. An *anyāpati* is one whose virility occurs with another woman, but not with his own wife. Such specific types of eunuchs (*ṣaṇḍa*) are to be avoided. Nārada also states the time for the examination of eunuchs:
Among those, the first two are incurable; the one called *pakṣa* should be treated for a month, while the duration for this triad is traditionally held to be a year in successive order.

If he is first found to belong to the prohibited class of eunuchs (*ṣaṇḍa*), one should observe him for a month. Then, having ascertained his condition after that period, if he remains impotent (*apuṃstva*), he is to be abandoned. Regarding the three subsequent types of eunuchs—those caused by a teacher, illness, or a deity—one should wait for a year before abandoning them; there is no penalty in these cases.
As for the other four types of eunuchs mentioned, such as those born of envy (*īrṣyā-ṣaṇḍa*) and so forth, they are to be abandoned like outcasts, as is a woman whose womb has been violated.
How much more so for one whose womb is unviolated, who has merely undergone the rites of betrothal and the grasping of the hand?
When the husband is incapacitated, his seed is fruitless, and he is unable to perform his duties,
another man is ordained as the husband for the woman after she has waited for one year.
Even the penis of a modest man falls when he sees a wanton woman;
one should therefore approach him while he is dressed in humble attire and surrounded by intoxicated women, children, and the like.

Even for a modest man, the sexual organ does not rise in the presence of an arrogant woman; if it does rise, it is suppressed. One should humiliate him with women of inferior dress and lacking splendor so that he feels no shame; likewise, one employs intoxicated, young, or other such women. Once his modesty has been overcome in this way, he will proceed even with his own wife.
"The husband of another—any man who would be a non-human toward his own wife—shall obtain another as his husband; this is the work of Prajāpati."

Women were created for the sake of offspring; the woman is the field, and the man is the possessor of the seed. The field and the seed must be bestowed upon one another; one who has no seed does not deserve the field.
The father himself, or the mother with the father’s consent, may give away the daughter;
likewise may the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, the paternal kinsmen, or other relatives.

But in the absence of a mother, if she [the paternal grandmother] exists in her natural state, they should give their daughters to her while she remains in that natural state; if she is not in her natural state, those of the same lineage should give them.
He states the defects:

"Those afflicted by long-standing or loathsome diseases, those with physical deformities, those who have had sexual intercourse, those who are impudent, and those whose hearts belong to another— these are proclaimed as the defects of a maiden."

Those with chronic diseases are those afflicted by urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, colic, and the like. The distressed are those beset by royal seizure, poverty, and so forth. The deformed are those with impaired limbs. Those who have had sexual intercourse are those with whom [the girl] has previously consorted. The audacious are the shameless who proceed forcibly toward what ought and ought not to be done. Those whose affection is fixed elsewhere are those whose desire is directed toward another—such as, for example, a maiden’s defects; these are shown for illustrative purposes, and other well-known ones should also be understood. He states the defects of the groom:
"The insane, the outcast, the impotent, the unfortunate, one who has abandoned his kin, and the two aforementioned defects of a maiden—this group of defects pertains to the groom."
