Thus, five types of insanity have been fully described: those arising from wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha);
the fourth is caused by the loss of wealth, and the fifth is caused by all of these combined.

Thus, those afflicted by insanity, those who have fallen [from their caste], those who have committed great sins (mahāpātaka) and the like; the impotent, those whose virility is impaired; the unfortunate, those hated by all; those abandoned by their kinsmen; and the two previously mentioned defects of a maiden, as well as those with chronic diseases and loathsome diseases—this collection of defects pertains to the groom. Eight forms of marriage for the castes, known as sacraments (saṃskāra), have been proclaimed;
of these, the Brāhma is the first, and likewise the Prājāpatya.
The Ārṣa, the Daiva, the Gāndharva, and likewise the Āsura;
following that is the Rākṣasa, and the eighth and lowest is the Paiśāca.
Having invited the bride and honored her, one should give her away well-adorned; this is the Brāhma rite.
Having said, "May you both perform your duty together," it is ordained as the Prājāpatya rite.
Having given a garment and a pair of cattle, the marriage is called Ārṣa;
that which takes place within the sacrificial altar for the officiating priest performing the rite is Daiva.
They say that when both parties desire one another, it is the fifth, called the Gāndharva marriage;
while the Āsura marriage is to be known by the practice of giving a bride-price.
The Rākṣasa marriage is said to be that which is performed by force;
likewise, the eighth and lowest is the Paiśāca, resulting from approaching a woman while she is asleep or intoxicated.
Of these, four types of marriage beginning with the Brāhma are declared to be lawful;
the Gāndharva is common to all, and the three beyond that are unlawful.
One should not defile an unblemished maiden, nor should one defile an unblemished groom;
for if no fault exists, there shall be no annulment when the two abandon one another.
If a man, having given a daughter according to the law, does not deliver her to the bridegroom while the groom is himself faultless,
he shall be punished by the king like a thief.
But for him who gives away a maiden who has defects without having declared them,
the king shall inflict the punishment prescribed for the first degree of violence.
If a man should declare a girl to be "not a virgin" when she is indeed one,
he shall incur a fine of one hundred [paṇas] for failing to demonstrate her defect.
But if a man, having accepted a maiden, should depart for another country, he must be compelled—
even against his will— to marry that very same maiden.

Regarding this, Yama states the prohibition against Śūdra women: "A slayer of a Brahmin does not become a slayer of a Brahmin; rather, the husband of a Vṛṣalī is the slayer of a Brahmin. The child who is born therein becomes a slayer of a Brahmin by that very act."

In this context, "vṛṣalī" refers to a Caṇḍālī woman. And so Manu says: "For one who has drunk the saliva of a vṛṣalī, for one who has been defiled by her breath, and for one born of her, no atonement is prescribed."
Nārada says: But if a groom, having accepted a maiden, should depart for another country,
and three seasons have passed, the maiden may choose another groom.
Manu says:
A maiden who has reached puberty should wait for three years;
after this period, however, she may take a husband of equal status.
A maiden choosing her own husband (svayaṃvarā) must not take for herself any jewelry belonging to her father, her mother, or given by her brother; if she should take it, it would constitute theft.
One who takes away a maiden who has reached puberty should not pay a bride-price to her father;
for by obstructing her menses, he would be depriving the father of his rightful ownership.
Nārada said:
If a bridegroom more excellent [than the first] should arrive when the bride-price has already been received for the maiden,
it would be a falsehood to speak words consistent with dharma, artha, and kāma in that situation.
"One may take back even what was previously given for the sake of a better [match]. Likewise, Yājñavalkya states:
"One may take back even a previously given [girl] if a superior suitor arrives.
Having given away a girl, one who takes her back is to be fined and must pay the expenses along with interest."
If the bride has died, one may take what was given [as a gift], after deducting the costs for funeral expenses and debts.
In the absence of a suitable suitor, one who takes her away should be punished. On this point, Vasiṣṭha says:
"If the groom should die after she has been given by water and word..."
And she should not be bestowed by means of a mantra; such a maiden belongs to her father alone.
Manu says: "The mantras recited at the taking of the hand are the definitive mark of wifehood;
their completion, however, should be understood by the learned to occur at the seventh step."
Vasiṣṭha says:
If a maiden has been forcibly abducted but not consecrated with the sacred mantras, she may be given to another according to the prescribed rite; for she remains a maiden just as before.
Yama says: "A girl is not considered betrothed by water alone nor by word alone;
husbandhood arises from the sacrament of taking the hand at the seventh step."
In another Smṛti:
"If she is one whose virginity is intact, or even one who has gone away and returned,
she deserves to undergo the marriage rite again with a husband born of her second marriage."
Vasiṣṭha: If the giver of the bride-price should die after the bride-price has been received for the maiden,
she should be given to the husband's brother, provided the maiden consents.

In the case of a failure to consummate the marriage with a maiden, there is simply a cessation of the rite. Śātātapa says: "But a maiden who has been wedded and has reached her husband yet has not had sexual intercourse, returns to her husband again; she is just like a maiden."

Kātyāyana says: "And if he belongs to another caste, is an outcast, or even a eunuch; or if he is engaged in improper occupations, is a *sagotra* relative, or suffers from a chronic or severe disease."
If the husband is impotent, or otherwise released from his manhood by medical means,
she— even if already married— should be given to another, adorned with all her ornaments.
If a man departs after having given the bride-price as well as the woman’s property (strīdhana) for a maiden,
she should be kept for one year and then given to another according to the prescribed rule.
Now, if news should arrive, one should wait for three years;
beyond that, the maiden may be given to another according to one's wish.
If, after showing one girl, another is given to the bridegroom,
Manu declared that he may marry both for the price of a single dowry.
If, after concealing her own faults, she obtains a maiden,
there shall be a loss of the gift for the groom, and the maiden shall also be returned.
Nārada:
If one gives a defective maiden to an unworthy man without having disclosed her defects,
he shall be made to pay a fine by the king as prescribed for the first degree of violence.
Viṣṇu states: "If one should give away a maiden without disclosing her defects, he shall pay a fine of one kārṣāpaṇa according to the scale of fines and shall maintain her. Manu says:
"To an excellent, suitable, and worthy suitor, one should give that maiden in accordance with the prescribed rite, even if she has not yet reached marriageable age."
He himself states the explanatory passage (arthavāda) for this:
"A maiden, even if she has reached puberty, may remain in her father's house until death;
yet he should never give her in marriage to one who lacks good qualities."
Nārada says: A maiden should not neglect her menses; she should inform her kinsmen.
If they do not give her to a husband, they shall be equal to killers of embryos (bhrūṇahan).
As many seasons as pass for her without a husband,
so many sins of foeticide shall belong to him who does not give her [in marriage].
Manu says:
A father who does not give [his daughter] in marriage at the proper time is censurable; a husband who does not approach his wife is censurable;
but when the husband has died, a son who does not protect his mother must be reproved.
One who is merely censurable is one who deserves punishment:

a father who does not give [his daughter] in marriage at the proper time, a husband who does not approach his wife during her season, and a son who does not provide for his mother; such persons are to be reproached and punished according to the law.
Manu states the causes of women's corruption:
"Drinking, association with wicked people, separation from her husband, wandering about, sleeping [alone], and dwelling in another’s house— these are the six things that corrupt women."
They do not examine form, nor is there any fixed regard for their age; whether he is handsome or ugly, they enjoy him simply because he is a man.
"For women are without sensory power and without sacred mantras; they are falsehood—this is the established rule.
Thus [Manu] states the purpose for which women exist: "The highly fortunate ones are for the sake of procreation; offspring are the lights of the household."
Between women and the goddesses of fortune within homes, there is no distinction whatsoever.
The procreation of offspring, the nurturing of those born,
and the daily conduct of worldly life— all these are visibly dependent upon women.
Offspring, religious duties, service, and supreme pleasure— all these,
as well as heaven for one's ancestors and for oneself, are indeed dependent upon the wife.
Bṛhaspati: A wife should be honored by her husband with garments, ornaments, and beautiful things,
as well as during festivals by her paternal kinsmen, brothers, fathers-in-law, and other relatives.
Where women are honored, there the deities rejoice;
there prosperity, progeny, and purity prevail, and all actions become fruitful.
She who does not transgress against her husband, being restrained in mind, speech, and body,
attains the worlds of her husband and is called "virtuous" by the righteous.
Dakṣa said: She who is joyful-minded, constant, discerning in her place and conduct, and who acts for the pleasure of her husband—she alone is a wife; others are merely women.
"A woman who rises before [her husband], is skillful, occupies a lower seat and bed, and is not harsh in speech but is compliant, indeed becomes so through meritorious deeds. Thus says Nārada.
When her husband has died, the husband's kin are the masters of a woman who has no son;
they are the authority over her disposal and protection, as well as her maintenance.
When the husband’s family is extinct, devoid of men, and without support,
and when his agnates (sapiṇḍas) are no longer present, the father’s side becomes the woman’s authority.
At the conclusion of both [the husband's] periods of absence, the king is declared her master;
he shall provide for her maintenance and restrain her if she deviates from the path.
Vyāsa says: The husband, the son, the father, the brother, the paternal uncle, the maternal uncle,
and likewise the maternal grandfather— these seven are recorded as the authorities over women.
The authority over women is declared to be according to their own will when they have a family of kinsmen;
however, women are traditionally considered to be like the ignorant, the dull-witted, the insane, children, and the elderly.
Regarding the cremation of women, Aṅgiras says: "The woman who, upon the death of her husband, ascends the funeral fire,
being equal in conduct to Arundhatī, is glorified in the heavenly world."
For as many thousands of years as there are hairs on a human being— three and a half crores— one is glorified in the heavenly world.
Just as a snake-catcher forcibly extracts a serpent from its hole,
even so she takes her husband and goes away with him.
She from whom a daughter is given away purifies three lineages—those of her mother, her father, and her husband; she who follows after her husband purifies him.
There, with her husband as her supreme delight, she sported together with him in great joy for as long as the reigns of the fourteen Indras endure.
"Whether he be a slayer of a Brahmin, ungrateful, or even a betrayer of a friend—that man she purifies; so has Aṅgiras declared."
For virtuous women alone,
once their husband has died, no other duty is ever to be known than entering the fire.
As long as a devoted wife does not burn her body in the fire when her husband has died,
so long shall that woman never be released from her female body in any way whatsoever.
For women who have entrusted their husbands to the state of virtuous conduct and who are distressed at the mere thought of separation,
once their husband has passed away, there is indeed no path other than entering the fire.

Śaṅkha, Likhita, Hārīta, Uśanas, Bṛhaspati, and Vyāsa have declared that virtuous women may follow their husbands in death. Regarding this, Viṣṇu states: "Upon the death of her husband, [the wife] shall observe celibacy or ascend after him. As for this statement:
"A woman of the Brāhmaṇa caste who is devoted to her deceased husband must not kill herself by suicide, thinking 'I shall go to heaven'."
This refers to the subject of entering the funeral pyre separately, because of the statement:
"Having ascended the separate pyre, a Brahmin ought not to depart [without her].
Therefore, this rule is common to all from those whose children are no longer infants up to the Cāṇḍālas, provided they are not pregnant; as Manu says, [such women] are to be abandoned.
Even after accepting her according to the prescribed rites, one may abandon a girl who is afflicted by disease, corrupted, or found to be fraudulent, as she is thus censurable.
But for that evil-minded man who gives away a daughter in marriage without disclosing her defects,
that act of giving a maiden becomes futile.
He states what must be done by one who travels abroad:
"A man who has business should travel after providing for his wife's livelihood;
for a woman, even if she is steadfast, may become corrupted when distressed by a lack of livelihood."
A husband receives his wife as a gift from the gods, not by his own will;
doing what is pleasing to the gods, he should always support that virtuous woman.
Women were created for the purpose of procreation, and men for the purpose of continuing the lineage;
therefore, the Veda declares that their religious duty is common to both, performed together with the husband.

Āpastamba states: "No division of property exists between husband and wife. For from the time of taking the hand (marriage), there is joint status in ritual acts, as well as in the fruits of merit and in the possession of wealth. Likewise, while his wife is endowed with virtue and offspring, he should not take another; in the absence of either [virtue or offspring], another may be taken before the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*). For once the *ādhāna* has been performed, she is connected to the rituals through her very existence. Now, Manu declares the duties of a woman whose husband is away on a journey:
"When the husband has gone abroad, she should maintain herself by providing for his livelihood and remaining firm in her observances."
But if he has gone abroad, she may live without any formal arrangement by means of blameless crafts.
Yājñavalkya states: A woman whose husband is away on a journey should renounce play, bodily adornment, attending social gatherings or festivals, laughter, and visiting the houses of others.
Bṛhaspati: One should not engage in personal adornment, nor witness dancing, singing, social assemblies, or festivals, nor indulge in meat or sexual intercourse while the master is away on a journey.
Hārīta says:
"While her husband is away on a journey, she should not adorn herself, nor should she loosen her braid.
Thus, the period for waiting upon one who has gone abroad has been stated.
A man who has gone abroad for the sake of dharma should be waited for eight years;
if for the sake of knowledge or fame, six years; but if for the sake of pleasure, three years.
Kātyāyana says: A woman must not be left without support by her father or husband when the master has been away for six years;
nor when he is lost, or even when he has gone forth as a renunciant. For the third year... [is required].

Gautama states: "If the husband has disappeared, there is a period of waiting for six years; if he is heard from, she may go to him; but if he has entered the religious order (pravrajita), there is a cessation [of the marriage] due to the risk of attachment. For a Brāhmaṇa, the period is twelve years in the case of a separation due to study. A wife may wait for eight years for a Śūdra husband who has gone abroad; for Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, and Brāhmaṇa husbands, she shall wait for twice, thrice, and four times that duration respectively.
Yama says:
A husband who does not take her to himself shall wait for ten years;
for a Brahmin woman, he shall wait for twelve or eight years—so indeed Manu has declared.
A Kṣatriya may marry eight women of his own class, or six daughters of Vaiśyas;
however, no time limit for marriage with a Śūdra woman is prescribed, nor is there any violation of dharma in doing so.
Nārada says: Specifically, in the case of a woman who has not given birth, her status [of being considered "lost"] lasts for one year;
this time is prescribed for women whose husbands have gone abroad when there has been no news of them.
Kātyāyana says: When a husband has died and she has been entrusted by her kinsmen to another man,
and she has borne a child from him, how should it be when he returns?
A husband may rightfully take back that wife, even if she has children;
however, Manu declared that those sons belong only to the owner of the field, not to the owner of the seed.
"One who has fallen from the state of renunciation and takes a wife again shall not be her master there; for he is a despised slave.
Thus Manu speaks regarding even the husband's abandonment of his wife in times of distress.
A husband should wait for one year for a wife who hates him;
after a year has passed, he may take back her property and no longer live with her.
*Ādāya* means [taking] ornaments and so forth. *Saṅghāḥ* refers to co-residence or a mobile group. Regarding those who may be superseded (*adhivettavyā*), Manu says:
"A barren wife may be superseded in the eighth year; one whose children have died, in the tenth;
one who gives birth only to daughters, in the eleventh; but one who speaks unpleasantly, immediately."
A wife who drinks liquor, is of improper conduct,
is hostile, is diseased, is violent, or is always harsh in speech may be superseded [by taking another wife].
Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "One may take as a wife a woman who is not unchaste, who does not hate men, and who is not contrary. Devala says:
"A husband who has no desire for his wife should wait for eight years;
however, he should wait ten years for one whose children have died, and twelve years for one who gives birth only to daughters."
Then, for the sake of a son, he should lawfully obtain a wife according to the prescribed rite;
for those who speak from a state of desirelessness, there is nothing in this world superior to the attainment of a son.
If there is a wife who is a *rohiṇī*— that is, accomplished in her virtuous character—
she should be informed [of the new marriage] and may be superseded by another, but she must never be treated with contempt.
He who, having left one wife for the sake of desire, wishes to obtain another,
being capable of satisfying the previously married woman with wealth, may marry the other.
"One for a Śūdra, two for a Vaiśya, three for a Kṣatriya, and four for a Brāhmaṇa; for a king, there may be as many as he desires. Regarding the superseded wife (*adhivinnā*), Yājñavalkya says:

"One should give an equal amount as *ādhivedanika* (compensation for supersession) to a wife who has been superseded; however, if no woman’s property (*strīdhana*) was given to her, one should provide wealth [to the new wife] according to the circumstances. Thus [it is said]. Nārada states the punishment for one who abandons a wife endowed with qualities such as conformity:
A man who abandons a wife who is compliant, not foul-mouthed, capable, virtuous,
and a mother of children, shall be punished by the king with a heavy fine.

"One may abandon a wife who is afflicted with leprosy, outcast, barren, insane, or devoid of menses, or one who is disliked by her husband; she may be abandoned at a sacred ford, but never by means of a ritual act. Thus says Yama.
If a woman who has bathed after her menses does not approach her husband,
she shall be proclaimed in the midst of the village as a destroyer of the embryo and banished.
But a woman who, while in her husband's residence, passes her fertile season in vain,
he shall proclaim her as a killer of the embryo among her kinsmen and banish her.
Baudhāyana says:
"But a woman who has been superseded by a co-wife, if she should depart from the house corrupted,
she must be immediately confined or abandoned in the presence of the family."

Regarding which wife among many is fit for religious duties (*dharmakārya*), Viṣṇu says: "When there are many wives of the same caste (*savarṇā*), one should perform religious duties together with the eldest alone; when they are of mixed castes, even with the youngest provided she is of the same caste. In the absence of a wife of the same caste, however, with one of the next lower caste; but a twice-born man must never [do so] with a Śūdra woman. Manu prohibits the acceptance of a bride-price (*śulka*) in the giving away of a daughter:
"Even a Śūdra, when giving away his daughter, should not take a bride-price."
For by accepting a bride-price, one effectively commits a concealed sale of one's daughter.
A maiden who has been purchased with wealth is not ordained as a wife;
she is neither for rites to the gods nor for rites to the ancestors—Kāśyapa declared her to be a slave-girl.
Yama says: "A maiden who has been purchased by purchase is not ordained as a wife;
likewise, in rites for the gods and the ancestors, she is a slave-girl designated as a wife."
Now, regarding adultery with women, Bṛhaspati says:
"Understand that adultery, which is the root of all evil, is of three kinds."
Two types are produced by force or inducement, while the third arises from affection.
Furthermore, that [action] is said to be of three kinds: inferior, middling, and superior.
That which is committed by one who is unwilling, or who is intoxicated, insane, or heedless, is the inferior kind.
Even if she protests in private, that act is committed by force;
having brought her to the house by means of a pretext and having given her an intoxicant.
They know that the union which is brought about by her is produced through external conditions (upādhi),
whether by mutual passion of the eyes or by the dispatching of a female messenger.
It should be understood that [the act] performed out of greed for beauty and wealth arises from passion;
likewise, there is the casting of sidelong glances, laughter, and the dispatching of female messengers.
The first act of gathering is considered to be the touching of ornaments and garments;
the sending forth of perfumes, garlands, fruits, food, and new clothes [is the second].
They know that conversation in private constitutes the middling form of seduction;
likewise, sharing a bed or seat, playing, kissing, and embracing do so as well.
This is declared by those who know the scriptures to be the highest form of seduction (*saṃgrahaṇa*).
Nārada says: at the confluence of rivers, at sacred fords (*tīrtha*), and in gardens and forests.
When a woman and a man come together, that is recorded in tradition as *saṃgrahaṇa* (adultery).
Manu says:
"Acts of service, dalliance, touching her ornaments and garments,
and even sitting together on the same bed— all this is declared to be *saṃgrahaṇa* (adultery)."
The showing of teeth, feet, and nails; the bearing of a fetus; and the wearing of another's clothing, ornaments, or weapons.

By these signs, women who are devoted to adultery should always be recognized. Regarding this, Āpastamba states: "A young man, adorned with ornaments, who unintentionally enters another's wife's quarters or addresses a maiden [inappropriately], should be restrained by words; but if he does so intentionally with a wicked intent, he should be punished. On this point, Manu says:
"Beggars, bards, those initiated for sacrifice, and artisans likewise—"
They may engage in conversation with women without being restrained.
One who has been forbidden shall not engage in conversation with women;
however, one who converses despite being forbidden deserves a fine of one suvarṇa.
Yājñavalkya: In the case of forbidding a woman [from going], one should pay a fine of one hundred; but for a man, the fine shall be two hundred.
In the case of both [man and woman] forbidding each other, the punishment is the same as that for adultery (saṃgrahaṇa).
Manu: The king, having branded with terrifying punishments those men who have set out to violate the wives of others, shall banish them.
A non-Brahmin who commits adultery deserves a punishment ending in death;
for the wives of all four castes are declared to be most worthy of protection.
Yājñavalkya: In the case of those of equal caste, the highest fine [is prescribed]; in the case of approaching [a woman] in the direct order of castes (ānulomya), however, the middle fine;
in the case of the reverse order (prātilomya), death for men, and the cutting off of the nose and other [limbs] for women.

Nārada says: One's mother, maternal aunt, mother-in-law, maternal uncle’s wife, father’s sister, the wife of a paternal uncle or a friend, a female disciple, a sister, her friend, and a daughter-in-law; [these are the women with whom sexual intercourse is forbidden].
A daughter, a teacher’s wife, one of the same lineage, one who has sought refuge,
a queen, a female renunciant, a nurse, a virtuous woman, and one of the highest caste.
Having approached any one of these women, he is called a violator of the Guru's bed;
for that offense, no punishment other than the excision of the penis is ordained.
Yājñavalkya: One who approaches his mother’s co-wife, a sister, the daughter of his teacher,
the wife of his teacher, or his own daughter, is a violator of the Guru’s bed.
"Having cut off his organ, that is his execution; likewise for a woman who desires it. Vyāsa says:
But when she has come desiring him, the punishment for the man who approaches her is considered to be half."
Manu:
A Brāhmaṇa who approaches a guarded Brāhmaṇa woman by force shall be fined one thousand [paṇas];
he who has sexual union with a willing woman shall be fined five hundred.
Shaving the head is prescribed as the punishment for a Brāhmaṇa;
however, for the other castes, the punishment shall be one that ends in death.

A Brāhmaṇa who approaches an unguarded Vaiśya woman or a Rājanya woman, or a Śūdra woman, shall be fined five hundred; but if he approaches a woman of the lowest castes (antyajastri), he shall be fined one thousand.
For a wicked man who has been accused for a year, the fine is double;
likewise, it is the same amount for cohabiting with a *vrātyā* or a *caṇḍālī*.

Yājñavalkya: Upon approaching a woman of the lowest caste, one should brand him with the mark of a eunuch and banish him; a Śūdra who does so should likewise become an outcaste. For an Ārya who approaches a woman of the lowest caste, the punishment is death.
Manu has declared the punishment for women:
"But a Brāhmaṇī woman who, deluded by passion, serves a Śūdra,
the king shall cause to be devoured by dogs in a place for the execution of those condemned to death."
If a Brāhmaṇī woman serves either a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya,
her punishment shall be the shaving of her head and her departure on a donkey.
Bṛhaspati:

A woman who, having come to a man's house, entices him with touching and other such acts and seeks to have sexual intercourse with him, shall be punished there; for the man, half the fine is prescribed.
But one whose nose, lips, and ears have been cut off should be made to labor until exhausted and then submerged in water,
or else be devoured by dogs in a place where many people are gathered.
But she who was enjoyed against her will, if she remains chaste, he shall maintain her in his house,
with soiled limbs, sleeping on the ground, and subsisting on a mere morsel of food.
She should perform an expiation consisting of either the Kṛcchra or the Parāka penance as prescribed;
however, if she has been enjoyed by one of a lower caste, she is to be abandoned or even put to death.

Yājñavalkya says: "There is no fault in approaching women of higher castes who are willing; otherwise, there is a fine. Otherwise, if one approaches them in the reverse order [of caste], death is prescribed."
Manu states the punishment for defiling a maiden:
"But that man who, out of arrogance, violates a maiden by force,
his fingers shall be cut off and he deserves a fine of six hundred [paṇas]."
One who defiles a willing woman shall not suffer the same punishment as one who cuts off her finger;
rather, he shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas] in order to prevent the recurrence of such conduct.
(Nārada:
"But when a maiden is willing and he is of the same caste, there is no transgression;
however, having adorned her and honored her, he alone shall marry her."

Once the act of approaching has been committed, he who has performed the penance should marry her—once she has likewise performed her penance and is adorned—according to the prescribed mantras. Vyāsa says: "But that lowest of men who approaches a woman who has already been enjoyed by many, they declare his punishment to be like that for a prostitute, and not like that for another's wife."
A wanton woman who, afflicted by lust, desires someone of her own accord,
shall be banished from the country by the king after being publicly proclaimed in the presence of the people.
Yājñavalkya: A man who has sexual intercourse with female slaves who have been taken into his household, or likewise with female servants,
even though they are women with whom one may lawfully consort, shall be made to pay a fine of fifty paṇas.
For forcibly approaching a prostitute, a fine of ten paṇas is prescribed by tradition;
if she is unwilling and many men do so, each shall pay a fine of twenty-four [paṇas].
For one who approaches a woman in an improper place, or for one who urinates upon a man, the fine is twenty-four [paṇas]; the same applies to approaching a female ascetic.
Nārada says: One who commits adultery with a woman of animal-birth (paśuyoni) shall be fined one hundred and ten [paṇas];
for cows, the fine is the middle amercement; and the same applies for women of the lowest castes (antāvasāyin).

As for the statement that one who has sexual intercourse with a *śūdra* woman or a female artisan (*ardhakī*) shall bathe with their clothes on and offer eight thousand oblations of the *gāyatrī*, that refers to a case of intentional repetition where the person is inclined toward penance; in such a case, there is no punishment. On this point, Manu says:
"Two hundred and fifty *paṇas* are recorded as the first *sāhasa*;
the middle is to be known as five [hundred], and the highest is indeed one thousand."

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Twenty-four [paṇas] and ninety-one are declared the first *sāhasa*; two hundred and five hundred constitute the middle; six hundred and one thousand constitute the highest. Yājñavalkya says:
"A fine of one thousand and eighty *paṇas* is the highest *sāhasa*;
half of that is declared the middle; half of that again is recorded as the lowest."
In all cases, specific numbers should be understood in consideration of the gravity or lightness of the offense. Regarding the protection of women, Manu says:
"No one is capable of protecting women by force;
rather, one should employ them in the accumulation of wealth and in its expenditure."

In purity, in truthfulness, in the cooking of food, and in the preservation of household goods—by "household goods" (pāriṇāhya) is meant furniture such as seats, beds, vehicles, and so forth. Regarding women, Dakṣa says:
"All women are like leeches [in their desire], [to be satisfied] by ornaments, clothing, and food."
For when they are well-conducted yet constantly dissipated, they indeed drag a man down.
That poor leech takes only blood;
but the other [the woman] takes wealth, mind, flesh, virility, strength, and happiness.
Full of apprehension in childhood, but in youth intent upon sensual pleasures,
a woman regards her own husband as mere straw in old age.
While she was engaged in her own desires, she was not restrained out of affection;
yet it would have become harmful later, like a disease that has been neglected.
For whatever kind of man a woman associates with, she gives birth to a son of that same kind;
therefore, for the sake of the purity of offspring, women must be guarded with great effort.
Manu says: Women must be protected especially from even the slightest opportunities for misconduct;
for if they are not guarded, they will bring sorrow upon two families.
For seeing this supreme dharma common to all castes,
husbands strive to protect their wives, even if they are weak.
For by protecting his wife, a man diligently protects his offspring, his conduct, his lineage, himself, and his own dharma.
There shall be mutual fidelity until death;
this, in brief, should be known as the supreme duty of husband and wife.
Thus ends the section on legal titles concerning joint undertakings and the like, in the *Vyavahāranirṇaya* composed by the illustrious Varadarāja.
11. The Section on the Partition of Inheritance.
Now follows the division of inheritance;
on this point, Nārada says:
"Where the division of the paternal estate is being arranged by the sons..."
That which is called "partition of inheritance" is declared by the wise to be a subject of dispute.

Viṣṇu states: "If the father divides the sons, he may do so according to his own will regarding property acquired by himself. Regarding this authority to "divide the sons," Nārada says: "When the mother’s menses have ceased, when the sisters have been given away in marriage, or when sexual intercourse has ceased and the father’s desire has subsided..."
A father who is diseased, enraged, whose mind is attached to sensual objects,
or who acts contrary to the scriptures, is not competent to make a partition.
Bṛhaspati says: "The partition among brothers has been demonstrated for the case of the absence of parents;
it is also commended when the mother's menses have ceased, even while both parents are alive."

On this point, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “While the father is alive, the division of the inheritance shall be made by the eldest alone, provided he is aged, of impaired mind, or long ill. Gautama says: “After the father’s death, the sons shall divide the inheritance; while the mother is still living, they may do so after her menses have ceased, if she desires it. Hārīta states: “Or rather, while still living, having divided [the estate], he may resort to the forest or enter the stage of an elder (vṛddhāśrama). Or, having distributed a small portion and taking the greater part for himself, he may live [there]; even if he should become impoverished, he may take again from them. He should also divide those who are in decline. Now, in this regard, they cite a Vedic text concerning the drawing and offering of the cups: ‘The father is the Āgrayaṇa cup, the other sons are the other cups. If the Āgrayaṇa should fail or spill, one should draw [it] again from the other cups. If the other cups should spill, one should draw [them] from the Āgrayaṇa. It should spill and fail from the other cups. Thus it is explained. Nārada [says]: [omitted].
Or rather, the father himself, having reached old age, may divide the sons.

From such statements as these, it is understood that partition may sometimes be performed by the father and sometimes by the sons. Likewise, the time for partition is also understood to be of several kinds: one occasion is when the father has a desire to divide; likewise, even while the father is still living, if he is indifferent toward property, partition occurs. Even in the absence of the father’s desire, partition takes place by the will of the sons once the mother has ceased her menses. Similarly, even while the mother is still menstruating and the father is unwilling, partition occurs by the will of the sons if the sisters have been given in marriage, or if the father is unrighteous, or afflicted by a chronic illness. Furthermore, there is another time after the father’s death, as Prajāpati has stated that partition should be made for the sake of increasing religious merit (*dharma-vṛddhi*).
Thus they may dwell together or separately out of a desire for Dharma;
Dharma increases through separation, therefore separation is consistent with Dharma.
Thus Bṛhaspati said:
"For those living together under a single cooking fire, the worship of the ancestors, the gods, and the twice-born shall be one;
for those who are divided, that same worship must be performed in every house."
Nārada says: For brothers who have not divided their inheritance, a single religious duty prevails;
once division has occurred, their religious duties shall also become separate for each.
Likewise, Vyāsa says:
"While the parents are living, the brothers are ordained to live together;
in their absence, for those who have divided, their dharma increases."
Yājñavalkya: If the father should effect a partition, he may divide the sons according to his will;
either by granting the eldest a superior share, or all may be equal sharers.

When the father desires to make a partition, he may then divide [the estate] according to his own will, either equally or unequally. Because such will is unrestrained, the author states another rule beginning with "or the eldest":
"The eldest shall have a twentieth part as an extra share, and from among all the property, whatever is the best;
half of that shall belong to the middlemost, and a fourth to the youngest."

In the manner stated by Manu, the division should be made such that the eldest receives the best portion, the youngest the smallest portion, and the middlemost the middle portion. He states the established conclusion: "Or all may have equal shares. In that regard, however, an unequal division by choice applies only to wealth acquired by oneself; but since the ownership over ancestral property inherited from the father is equal among sons and grandsons, an unequal division by choice is not appropriate. On this point, Yājñavalkya says: "Land acquired by the grandfather, or a fixed endowment, or even other property..."
In that case, there would be equal ownership for both the father and the son.
And likewise Viṣṇu states: "In regard to ancestral property, the ownership of the father, son, and grandson is equal. Kātyāyana says:
"Ancestral property shall be common to both the father and the son;
however, regarding what was acquired by the father himself, the son does not possess ownership."
Likewise, Vyāsa says:
"In the case of a house or field inherited through succession, the father and sons have equal shares;
sons are entitled to a partition of paternal property even against the father's will."
Bṛhaspati: Regarding property acquired by the grandfather, whether movable or immovable,
equal ownership is declared for both the father and the son.
Vyāsa states:
"Regarding property acquired by one's own effort without the paternal grandfather or father,
obtained through learning, valor, and so forth, the ownership of the father is traditionally recorded therein."
If he should make a gift out of his own desire, he may do so from that wealth and then effect a division;
but in his absence, those sons are declared to have equal shares.
Bṛhaspati:
"Neither the gift nor the sale of immovable property or bipeds— even if acquired by oneself— is valid without having assembled all the sons."
Vyāsa states this exception:
"Even a single person may perform the giving, mortgaging,
or sale of immovable property in times of distress for the sake of the family, and especially for the sake of dharma."
He is the father and the master of all things, such as gems, pearls, and corals;
but of all that is stationary, he is neither father nor grandfather.

From such statements as these, it is understood that in the property of a grandfather, the ownership of the son and grandson is equal; whereas in property acquired by the father himself, he possesses independence. Furthermore, there are these two statements from Manu:
"The wife, the son, and the slave—these three alone are declared to be without property;
whatever they acquire belongs to him [to whom they belong]."
Likewise:
"After the death of both the father and the mother, the brothers, having assembled together, shall divide the paternal inheritance; for they have no authority while the two are alive."
As for this statement of Devala: "When the father has passed away, the sons shall divide the father's wealth;
for they would have no ownership over it while the faultless father remains."

Thus, such [passages] refer to a lack of independence (*asvātantrya*), not to a lack of ownership (*svatvābhāva*); for the venerable author of the *Bhāṣya* stated in the section [beginning with] "Aitishayana says it belongs to the male" that this is due to the mention of a specific gender. And so says the *Śruti*: "For the wife is the mistress of the household goods (*pārīṇahya*). Likewise, Hārīta states: "While the father lives, sons have no independence regarding the taking, giving away, or pledging of property. Furthermore, on the view that ownership (*svatva*) arises precisely at the time [of birth], the injunction "he should divide" found in all the *Smṛtis* is appropriate. Otherwise, if ownership were absent prior to partition, one would have to say "he should give to the sons. Similarly, on the view that ownership arises from partition, a son who has only one child would have no ownership after his parents' death, because there would be no partition [of the estate]. Therefore, even in the case of ancestral property, a son's ownership exists by virtue of his entry into the family alone. And so says Bṛhaspati:
Those humans who are born, those yet to be born, those dwelling in the womb, and those residing in the world of the ancestors—all of them desire that livelihood; therefore, it must not be cut off.

Those who are about to be born are specified as "those staying in the womb" in the form of sesame, beans, and so forth. Those who have been born are "possessors of latent tendencies" (*anuśayin*); being connected with the person on that side, they are said to be "staying with the father. For instance, having transformed for some time into the form of phlegm and then into the form of semen within the father, they enter the mother through her connection with him; thus they are called "those staying in the womb. In this way, from the point of connection with the father and mother onwards, they possess ownership over their respective wealth. There is partition of what already belongs to one; ownership does not arise from partition. Therefore, in the case of property acquired by oneself, the partition occurs according to the father's wish, because of the preeminence of the acquirer. But in the case of property inherited by succession, the partition occurs according to both the father's wish and the sons' wish. Regarding the partition of self-acquired property, Nārada says:
But for those who have been divided by the father himself with unequal shares of wealth— whether more, less, or equal—
that same rule shall apply to them, for the father is indeed the master of all.
And so says Bṛhaspati:
"The shares, whether equal, deficient, or excessive, which have been assigned by the father to his sons must be maintained exactly as they were; otherwise, those sons should be disciplined."

Yājñavalkya states: "The partition made by the father is declared to be lawful even for those who have received unequal shares. Although an unequal division is indeed seen in the scriptures through such statements as "in this manner," nevertheless, because it is loathed by the world, it should not be practiced.
"One should not practice even a dharma that leads away from heaven and is despised by the world"—because of such a prohibition. And likewise, Prajāpati [states]:
"Just as even the duty of *niyoga* (appointment for procreation) does not apply to a cow to be immolated (*anubandhyā*) and the like."
Likewise, even the division of the inheritance does not take place at present.

Just as the practice of *niyoga* (levirate) is not performed upon the death of a husband because it is loathed by the world, and just as the immolation of a cow (*gavālambha*) is likewise avoided, so too the rule of preferential allotment (*uddhāradharma*) should not be practiced in the Kali age due to its being loathed by the world. Regarding the specific rules for partition during the lifetime [of the father], Nārada says:
"When dividing his own property, the father shall receive two shares.
And likewise, Bṛhaspati says:

In the division of property during the father's lifetime, however, the father shall take two shares for himself. Thus say Śaṅkha and Likhita: "If he has only one son, he should make two shares for himself. Regarding bipeds and quadrupeds, an additional form is the bull, which belongs to the eldest. In that regard, the father’s taking of two shares refers to property acquired through inheritance. On this point, some hold that the wife is without a share; Yājñavalkya states:
"If he should make the shares equal, the wives must be made sharers of equal portions."
To those women for whom no woman’s property (strīdhana) has been given by either the husband or the father-in-law.

When the father, by his own will, makes all his sons equal sharers, then wives of the same caste as their husbands must also be made sharers of portions equal to those of their sons. For those wives to whom separate property (*strīdhana*) has been given by the husband or the father-in-law, the completion of their shares must be made in consideration of that given property, because it has been stated in that regard concerning supersession (*adhivedana*): "He whose wife has been superseded shall give her an equal amount as compensation for supersession (*ādhivedanika*). To her who has not been given separate property, he shall assign half of that [compensation]; but to her who has already been given [property], he shall assign half."

In this context, the word *ardha* refers to a single portion. Therefore, the meaning is that the completion of the share must be made in relation to what was previously given. Having thus stated that mothers are entitled to equal shares in a partition during the father's lifetime, Yājñavalkya states that they likewise become sharers of equal portions even when the father has died: "When sons divide after the death of the father, the mother also shall take an equal share. To the same effect, Nārada says:
The mother shall be an equal sharer with her sons when her husband has died.
On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
"In his absence, however, the mother is an equal sharer of a portion with her sons."
Vyāsa says: "The wives of one's father are declared to receive equal shares;
and all paternal grandmothers are declared to be equal to mothers."

It is also appropriate that the grandmother’s share be determined in the same manner as the mother’s. Viṣṇu states: “Mothers shall receive shares corresponding to the shares of their sons, as well as unmarried daughters. Likewise, Bṛhaspati says: “The mothers shall have equal shares with them, and the unmarried daughters shall have a fourth part. Kātyāyana says:
For unmarried daughters, however, a fourth part is prescribed;
for brothers, three parts are prescribed, but it is recorded that these shares are equal when the wealth is small.
On this point, Manu says:
"The brothers shall give to their sisters from their own shares, each separately, one-fourth part from his own share; those who are unwilling to give shall become outcasts. Thus it is said.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "When [the estate] is being divided, one should give [to the daughters] that which is the daughter's ornament, the wedding gift, and the woman’s property (strīdhana) which the maiden shall receive. Here, "daughter's ornament" refers to jewelry suitable for a maiden. Likewise, Paiṭhīnasi says: "The maiden shall receive the wedding gift and the woman’s property. On this point, Bodhāyana states: "The daughters shall receive their mother’s ornaments, whether they were inherited from her family or otherwise. Regarding this, Vyāsa says:

"Those who have not yet been initiated [into marriage] there, as well as the maidens, should be provided with the sacraments according to the rules by their elder brothers from that paternal wealth itself."
Nārada says:
Even when paternal wealth is not available,
the sacramental rites that must necessarily be performed for brothers by those already consecrated should be carried out by drawing [the funds] from one's own share.
Yājñavalkya: But those who have not been consecrated should be consecrated by their brothers who have already been consecrated;
and the sisters, having been given a fourth part from their own share, [should be consecrated].

Since the rite of *pāṇigrahaṇa* (taking the hand in marriage) for daughters is explicitly mentioned in all the *Smṛtis*, the elders hold that for sons as well, the rites up to marriage must be performed by the elder brothers who have already been consecrated. Regarding this, some maintain that only enough wealth to cover the cost of the rites should be given to the daughters, and nothing else. Others, however, believe that when there is abundant wealth, a fourth part of the son’s share should be given, whereas when the wealth is small, the shares should be equal. Furthermore, Manu speaks of partition after giving something to one who is indolent:
"But among brothers, he who, though capable of supporting himself by his own labor, does not desire wealth..."
He is to be excluded from his own share, having been given something for his subsistence.
Yājñavalkya states:
"For one who is capable but makes no effort [to earn], a separate partition may be made after giving him something.

Āpastamba says: "All those who are endowed with righteousness are entitled to shares; however, even the eldest, if he misappropriates assets through unrighteous means, shall be deprived of his share. Gautama says: "Even the son of a wife of the same caste, if he conducts himself unjustly, shall not receive a share—so say some. In such cases, having gone to the very end [of the matter], a division must be performed by giving at least betel leaves and other such items.
Manu states who are unworthy of inheritance:
"All brothers who persist in improper occupations do not deserve the wealth.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "For one who has been rendered unworthy of the vessel [of ritual], his share of the estate, the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa), and the water offerings are excluded. Bṛhaspati says:
Even one born of a wife of the same caste, if he lacks good qualities, is not entitled to his father’s wealth;
that [wealth] is declared to belong to those Śrotriyas who offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) for him.
A son protects his father from creditors and debtors;
therefore, there is no purpose served by one who acts in the opposite manner.
What is done with that cow which neither gives milk nor is pregnant?
What is the purpose of a son who is born neither learned nor righteous?
A son who is devoid of learning, heroism, and wealth, who is bereft of austerity and knowledge,
and who is lacking in proper conduct, is considered equal to urine and excrement.

Nothing at all should be given to such wicked persons. Now, Manu speaks regarding those who must be maintained: "The impotent and the outcast, those born blind or deaf, as well as the insane, the idiotic, the mute, and whoever else is devoid of [vital] faculties, shall receive no share."
However, it is right for a wise man to give to all of them according to his ability—food, clothing, and oil for anointing; for by failing to give these, he would become an outcast.
If, however, there should somehow be a desire for wives on the part of eunuchs and others,
their offspring, having produced progeny, shall be entitled to the inheritance.

Yājñavalkya: A eunuch, one who has fallen from his caste, one born of such a union, a cripple, one who is insane, one who is mentally dull, a blind person, and one afflicted by an incurable disease— these should be maintained [by the family] but are entitled to no share of the inheritance.
Their sons born of their own wives are faultless and entitled to inherit;
their daughters, moreover, must be maintained until they are given away to husbands.
The childless wives among them who are of virtuous conduct must be maintained;
however, those who are unchaste as well as those who are hostile should be banished.

An outcast (*patita*) is one who has committed the murder of a Brahmin and so forth; "born of such" (*tajja*) means born from an outcast. One who is insane (*unmatta*) is overcome by forms of madness characterized by wind, bile, phlegm, their combination, or possession by spirits. One who is idiotic (*jaḍa*) has impaired faculties and is incapable of discerning between what is beneficial and what is harmful. Prior to the partition of these [properties], they incur disqualification from a share due to their defect; however, this does not apply once the property has already been divided. The sons of these [men], such as the impotent and others—whether legitimate (*aurasa*) or born of the wife (*kṣetraja*)—are entitled to inherit shares provided they are free from defects that would bar them from receiving a portion. A son born of the wife is possible for the impotent man; for the others, even legitimate sons are possible. By mentioning the legitimate and the son born of the wife, other types of sons are excluded. The daughters of these men, such as the impotent and others, must be maintained; they are to be supported until they have been consecrated by the sacrament of marriage. Likewise, the wives of the impotent and others who are of virtuous conduct must be maintained; however, those who are unchaste should be expelled. Thus says Devala.
When the father has died, those who are impotent, afflicted with leprosy, insane, idiotic, blind, outcasted,
the offspring of an outcast, or one who has assumed the marks of a religious order (liṅgin) do not share in the inheritance.
To those who belong to the class of outcasts, a portion of food is given;
their sons, being free from fault, shall receive their father’s inheritance.

One born of an outcast has no connection to inheritance because of his own outcast status. Viṣṇu states: "Those who have entered another stage of life (āśrama), as well as the impotent, the insane, and the outcast, are non-partakers [of inheritance]; however, maintenance must be provided for the impotent and the insane. Gautama says: "The idiot and the impotent must be maintained; the offspring of the idiot is entitled to a share. Regarding the acquisition of property by one who remains undivided among those who have been divided or undivided, Manu declares:
"But one born after partition shall take the paternal wealth alone; or those who may have reunited with him shall share it together with him."
Bṛhaspati:
Those uterine brothers who are divided from their father, or those born of different mothers,
as well as those born later, they are the heirs to the paternal inheritance.
The first-born son has no authority over his share of the paternal estate once he has been divided; so it is stated in another Smṛti:
"Whatever was acquired by the father himself after he had been divided from his sons..."
All that belongs to one born after partition, his ancestors are declared to have no authority over.

Just as with wealth, so it is with debt, and in matters of giving, pledging, and buying; they have no mutual authority over one another, except regarding the performance of purification rites with water.
Yājñavalkya states that even for one born after partition, a share shall be assigned from their own portions in the absence of paternal wealth:
"A son born after partition from a wife of equal caste is entitled to a share;
or his share may be determined by deducting from the visible assets the income and expenses."

Viṣṇu states: "Those divided by the father shall give a share to one born after the partition. Yājñavalkya declares that the grandson has an equal share with his [own] son: "Whether it be land acquired by the grandfather, a fixed endowment, or even other property, the ownership therein shall be equal for both the father and the son."
Bṛhaspati:
He whose debt, document, house, or field is ancestral shall be the recipient of his share therein,
even if he has been absent for a long time.

When the paternal grandfather’s wealth is common to both the father and the son, and if one of them has many sons who—having produced sons of their own—remain or have died, the division of inheritance in that case is stated by Yājñavalkya: "But for those who have multiple fathers, the allotment of shares is according to the fathers; the meaning is that these grandsons share the portions through the medium of their respective fathers. Bṛhaspati says:

But whatever is acquired by those who are united, all of them shall share in equal portions; their sons, whether of unequal or equal status, are declared to be entitled to receive the paternal shares.

Whatever has been acquired by those who are united and undivided through agriculture and other means, even if obtained by one individual alone, belongs equally to all. "Their sons" refers to their [the brothers'] sons; they shall receive shares from the father himself according to the rule of unequal shares. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states a specific rule:
"When a younger brother has died while the family remains undivided, one should provide for his son with a means of subsistence such that he does not receive a share of the grandfather's estate."
He shall receive his paternal share from his uncle or from that uncle’s sons;
for according to law, that very share belongs equally to all brothers.
Or his son may also receive it, after which there shall be cessation [of the claim].

When a son who has not yet divided the inheritance dies, his son—who has not received a livelihood from his grandfather—should be made an heir to the estate. His share of the inheritance is that portion belonging to his own father; since the grandfather is deceased, its acquisition occurs through the division of his own share from the paternal uncle. If the paternal uncle is also deceased, its acquisition occurs through the division of his own share from that uncle’s son. Even upon division from the son of the paternal uncle, that same share shall be the one which would have been his by right among the brothers. This is what is meant: "The sons of brothers, whether equal or unequal, are heirs to their own fathers' shares. Upon the death of the preceding ancestors, even the grandson should receive only the fourth share. From the fifth descendant onwards, there is cessation of the claim due to the absence of *sāpiṇḍya* (lineal kinship). Devala also states this cessation up to the fourth degree.
When undivided kinsmen who have already divided their property live together again, a further distribution of the inheritance shall take place up to the fourth generation; such is the settled rule.
Those who are not sapinda shall be kulyas; beyond that point, there is a division of the funeral cakes (pinda).
They desire an equal distribution of the cakes when dividing the inheritance.
This rule has been declared for kinsmen of the same caste;
in this case, the inheritance of one who is of the same caste is a single whole and is not to be divided.

Even among those who have been divided but later reunited, there shall be a redistribution of inheritance up to the fourth degree among *sakulyas*. *Sakulyas* are those who are not *sapindas*. Beyond this point, there is no division of inheritance, because they are not *sapindas*. Only when *sapinda*-relationship exists is there a division of inheritance; therefore, since the fifth-degree relative lacks *sapinda*-relationship, there is no division of inheritance. The rule stated thus far applies only to those born of wives of the same caste (*savarṇa*). For it is not the case that there is inequality in the distribution of inheritance among brothers born of wives of different castes, since those born of wives of the same caste belong to the same class. Kātyāyana also states the cessation of inheritance beyond the fourth degree.
Having returned the inheritance and given what remains, one should divide the residue;
that [residue] should be taken by the sons of those [deceased heirs] in order, up to the fourth generation.

By the term *pratipradāna* (returning), a debt is expressed. Sapiṇḍa relationship extends up to the fourth person inclusive, as previously stated; however, this should be understood to apply when the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather have died. When they are living, because of the sapiṇḍa relationship of the three preceding ancestors as well, the sapiṇḍa relationship extends up to the seventh person. With this intention, Bṛhaspati says:
"Whether it be the third, the fifth, or even the seventh [ancestor], land should be given by the kinsmen of the lineage to one who has come from that lineage."
Regarding this, Nārada states that the division of inheritance among heirs occurs when distinguished by the settlement of debts:
"Whatever remains from the paternal estate, after paying the father's debts and whatever debt was contracted by the father himself,
that must be divided by the brothers so that the father would not remain a debtor."

By the term *pitṛdāya* (paternal inheritance), the funeral rites for the father and others are meant. Thus says Kātyāyana: "A debt contracted by a brother, a paternal uncle, or a mother for the sake of the family must be paid in its entirety by the heirs at the time of partition."
Therefore, the inheritance is obtained by one who has settled his debts. Prajāpati says: "The house, the field, and the quadrupeds should be divided while they are visible;
in cases of suspicion regarding hidden property, an ordeal is prescribed therein."
Bṛhaspati says:

Household utensils, vehicles, and the like, as well as objects of enjoyment, ornaments, and servants, are divided when they are visible; however, when they are hidden, the ordeal by sacred libation (kośa) is prescribed.
Yājñavalkya: Where property that was mutually misappropriated is discovered after partition, they shall divide it again with equal shares; such is the settled rule.
Manu says: "When all debts and assets have been distributed from here and there,
whatever may subsequently be discovered, all that one should bring to equality."

The rule for the distribution of houses and so forth among the eldest and the others has been stated. Regarding that, a specific detail from another Smṛti is as follows: "In the division of a house, the portion to the south belongs to the eldest; immediately after that, to the next [eldest]; and likewise for the others. Kātyāyana says:
"When the division of fields, gardens, houses, and so forth has occurred, the southern part or the western part shall belong to the eldest."
Regarding this, Devala states the specific rule:
"The Niṣāda who is the only son shall receive two shares from the Brāhmaṇa;
however, a sapiṇḍa or a sakulya who offers the funeral oblation (svadhā) shall take [the remainder]."

The term *niṣāda* refers to one born of a Śūdra woman. The mention of "half" and "one-third" should be understood as applying to a Śūdra who performs excessive service. Regarding this, Manu states a specific rule: "Whether he has sons by wives of equal caste or even no sons at all, one should not, according to the law, give more than a tenth part to the son of a Śūdra woman."
The son of a Śūdra woman by a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya father does not inherit property;
whatever his father may give to him, that alone shall be his wealth.
Bṛhaspati:
A virtuous son born of a Śūdra womb who serves a childless man shall receive a means of subsistence;
the rest of the inheritance, however, the sapinda relatives shall take.

Statements such as "the son of a Śūdra woman does not share in the inheritance," which prohibit inheritance, should be understood as referring to those who do not perform service. Gautama states that even for the sons of those born in the reverse order (*pratiloma*) who are fit for social intercourse and who perform service, the father must provide a livelihood: "But those born in the reverse order are like the son of a Śūdra woman. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states a specific rule:
"Land obtained through gift (*pratigraha-bhū*) must not be given to a son of a Kṣatriya or other [lower caste], even if his father gave it;
upon the father's death, the son of a Brāhmaṇa woman shall take it."
When the father has died, the son of the Brāhmaṇī wife alone shall take [the inheritance]. Regarding this, Vṛddha-Manu states a specific rule concerning the "Brahma-gift" (brahmadāya):
"The sons of the Brāhmaṇī wife shall take the land received as a Brahma-gift;
likewise, all the twice-born [sons] shall take the house, as well as the fields and the homestead."
By the mention of the "twice-born" (dvija), the son of a Śūdra woman is excluded. Bṛhaspati states:
"One born of a Śūdra woman by twice-born men is not entitled to a share of land;
he shall receive everything from his own caste—thus the law is settled."

Regarding this, Manu states the specific rule: "Whether born of a Śūdra’s slave woman or of a female slave belonging to a slave, the son who is born shall, with permission, take a share; such is the established law."
And likewise Yājñavalkya says:
"Even one born of a Śūdra woman by a Śūdra through desire shall be a sharer of the inheritance;
when the father has died, the brothers shall make him a recipient of half a share."

The seizure of property by the son of a female slave (dāsīputra) in all cases should be understood to apply only when there is an absence of sons, grandsons, daughters’ sons, and others who are equal or superior. This is because [Manu] has stated, beginning with "even one born of a Śūdra woman to a slave," up to "if he is without brothers, he shall take everything, except for the son of the daughters.
Manu states the definition of these twelve types of sons in order to explain their inheritance: "But that son whom a man himself procreates on his own consecrated wife..."
One should recognize him as the legitimate son, the first in order of conception.
He who is born on the bed of a man who has died, is impotent, or is diseased,
by means of the husband’s own duty through a wife duly appointed, is known as a *kṣetraja* son.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states the specific rule:
"A son begotten by means of *niyoga* upon the wife of another by one who is childless is,
according to the law, the heir to the property and the giver of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) for both."

His nature consists of two types of sons: the son born of the seed (*bījaja*) belongs to the progenitor (*bījin*), whereas the son born of the field (*kṣetraja*) belongs to the owner of the field (*kṣetrin*). It is logical that his nature comprises these two types of sons through such a division. This [son] is a *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa* (belonging to two lineages); because he arises from a portion of the seed, his superiority over the *kṣetraja* should be understood. On this point, Bṛhaspati says: "Having worshipped Agni and Prajāpati, [the son] is produced as prescribed by Gautama;
others, however, say that for one who has no son, a daughter may be designated as a son (*putrikā*)."
In another Smṛti: "According to some, she becomes a 'putrikā' by mere intention alone. Herein lies the rule for the *putrikā*. Vasiṣṭha says:
"I shall give you this unbrothered maiden, adorned;
whatever son is born of her, he shall be my son."
Manu says: A sonless man may, according to this rule, make a daughter an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), [stipulating]:
"Whatever offspring may be born of her shall be the one who performs my funeral rites."
In former times, Dakṣa Prajāpati himself created his own daughter by this very rite for the sake of the prosperity of his own lineage.

In this case as well, there are two kinds of sons: some say that the appointed daughter (*putrikā*) herself is the son; others say she is the mother of the son. Manu says: "The son whom the mother or the father gives away with water in times of distress—one who is similar [in status] and given with affection—should be known as the 'given' (*datrima*) son."
But he whose adopted son is endowed with all good qualities shall indeed inherit that estate, even though he has come from another lineage.
An adopted son shall not share in the lineage or the inheritance of his biological father.
Nārada: "The funeral cake (piṇḍa) follows the lineage and the inheritance; the ancestral offering (svadhā) ceases for one who gives [the inheritance] away.
This is from the section on witnesses in the Akhaṇḍādarśa. Kātyāyana: [as cited above].
If the son of one who has been given away dies while he himself is still alive,
[the latter], having performed the entire ritual up to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, shall obtain the inheritance.
If one should purchase from his mother and father a son for the sake of offspring,
he is that man’s *krītaka* (bought) son, whether he be similar or dissimilar [to him].
One who is deprived of his mother and father, or abandoned by them without cause,
and who touches himself [as a gift], is known as one "given by himself" (svayamdatta).

The meaning is that one should touch or give [him]. "But he whom one should make similar, who is discerning of virtues and faults, and who is endowed with the qualities of a son— he is to be known as the 'artificial' (kṛtrima) son."
He who is born in a house and whose father is not known belongs to him by whom he was begotten on the bed,
having been secretly conceived in his own home.
A son whom one may adopt after he has been abandoned by both his parents or by either of them is called an *apaviddha* (abandoned) son.
A son whom a maiden bears in secret in her father's house, they know by the name *kānīna*, as he is born from the maiden and not from the husband.

"He is the son of the husband alone, not of the maternal grandfather. Yājñavalkya says: "A maiden-born son (kānīna), born of an unmarried girl, is considered the son of the maternal grandfather. Nārada says:
He who has an unknown father, being the son of an unmarried woman or born in secret from his mother,
shall offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his maternal grandfather and inherit his property.

If there is a man to carry the burden [of the funeral rites], the son of the carrier is the one; if he is not present, then, with the mother's permission, the son of the maternal grandfather is the one. Vasiṣṭha says:
"The daughter who has not been given away in marriage may obtain a son through a man of equal status;
by that son, the maternal grandfather becomes the possessor of a grandson (pautrin); he shall offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) and inherit the wealth."

Manu says: "If a woman who is pregnant is married, whether her condition is known or unknown, the child in her womb belongs to the one who marries her; such a son is called *sahoḍha* (one born with the bride)."
A woman who has been abandoned by her husband, or one who is a widow, may, by her own will, produce offspring again; he is called a *paunarbhava*.
The son whom a Brāhmaṇa may procreate through lust upon a Śūdra woman is a corpse even while still alive; therefore, he is known as a Pāraśava.
Even while living, he is like a corpse.
The wise declare that these eleven types of sons, beginning with the *kṣetraja* as previously described, are substitutes for a son, intended to prevent the failure of religious rites.
Svāyambhuva Manu has declared twelve kinds of sons for men;
among them, six are kinsmen and heirs, while six are kinsmen who are not heirs.

Bodhāyana has stated that the first group of six [sons] possesses the right to inherit the estate (*rikthabhāktva*), while the latter group of six possesses the right to belong to the lineage (*gotrabhāktva*). In this regard, although sons are listed in various orders across all the *smṛtis*, one should disregard the textual order (*pāṭhakrama*) and instead effect the division of the groups according to the logical order (*arthakrama*). For this very reason it has been said:
"In the absence of each more excellent [son], the less excellent one is entitled to the inheritance;
yet, by virtue of his birth, the legitimate son (*aurasaputraka*) is the most excellent and thus the most superior."

The son of the body, the son of an appointed daughter, the son begotten on the wife, the adopted son, the made son, the son born in secret, and the cast-off son— these they declare to be the heirs to the inheritance.

The son born of an unmarried girl (kānīna), the son received with a bride (sahoḍha), the purchased son (krīta), the son of a remarried woman (paunarbhava), the son self-given (svayaṃdatta), and the Niṣāda— these they declare to be sharers of the family name (gotra).
In some places, the superiority of the *aurasa* (legitimate) and *kṣetraja* (son born of the wife) sons is stated:
"The *aurasa* and *kṣetraja* sons are sharers of the father's inheritance;
but ten others, in their respective order, are sharers of the lineage and a portion of the inheritance."
By the word "empty share" (*riktāṃśa*), mere subsistence is intended. He states the rule for the share of the *kṣetraja* son:
"One should give a sixth part of the paternal wealth to the *kṣetraja* son; then the legitimate (*aurasa*) son shall take five parts of the paternal inheritance. (Or: "five parts").
Bṛhaspati: "The legitimate son alone is declared the sole owner of the paternal wealth;
the appointed daughter is said to be equal to him, while all others are recorded as being entitled only to maintenance."
On this point, Manu says: "The son born of an unmarried girl (kānīna), the son received with a bride (sahoḍha), and he who is born of a woman kept in secret (gūḍhaja)—
of these, the one who marries them is to be known as the father, and they are the heirs of that father."

By these statements, there are six heirs to the kinsman’s estate; others are entitled only to food and clothing. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha states a specific rule: “If a son born of the wife (*aurasa*) should be born after he has been adopted, he shall receive a fourth share. This refers to a case of abundant wealth where an *aurasa* son is born after the adoption of a given son (*dattaputra*); in such a case, the adopted son receives a fourth part of the *aurasa*’s share. Kātyāyana says: “When an *aurasa* son has been born, sons of equal caste (*savarṇa*) receive a third share; those of unequal caste (*asavarṇa*), however, are entitled only to food and clothing.”
And so says Bṛhaspati:
"All these sons of a non-aurasa [wife] are traditionally held to be heirs;
however, once an aurasa son is born, their status as the eldest no longer remains."
Those sons of theirs who are of the same caste as their father shall share a third part of the inheritance;
those who are of lower caste shall depend upon him, provided with food and clothing.
What need is there for much?
Only the biological son is the master of the paternal wealth;
however, for the sake of avoiding cruelty toward the others, he should provide them with a livelihood.
Some maintain that this [verse] is intended as a praise of the legitimate son (*aurasa*). As for the statement of Nārada:

"The maiden-born (*kānīna*), the one born of a pregnant bride (*sahoḍha*), and he who is born of a remarried woman (*ūḍhā*)—the husband of these women is to be known as their father, and they are entitled to a share of the father's property."
Thus, this statement that "there are six heirs among kinsmen" is intended to include the *kānīna* and the others within the aforementioned group of six kinsmen who inherit. Bṛhaspati says:
"The thirteen sons have been declared by Manu in their proper order;
among them, the *aurasa* and the appointed daughter (*putrikā*) are the causes for the continuity of the lineage."
Just as oil is remembered by the wise as a substitute for clarified butter when the latter is unavailable,
so too are the eleven types of sons considered substitutes for the daughter-son (putrikā) and the legitimate son of the body (aurasa).

Now, the extension of the status of a son (*putrātideśa*). Regarding this, Manu says: "Among brothers born of the same father, if even one should have a son, Manu has declared that they are all possessed of a son by means of that son."
Hārīta says:
Among many born of one [father], if even one should have a son,
they are all undoubtedly possessed of sons by virtue of that son.
If among many women who share a single husband, one should have a son,
they all obtain the status of mothers of sons through that son.
Manu has declared the existence of a substitute, whereas Hārīta has declared the absence of a substitute, based on the statement: "They attain the state of those who have sons. Bṛhaspati says:
"If there are many uterine brothers born of one father, when a son is born to even one of them, they are all considered to have sons."
This same rule is ordained for many wives who have a single husband;
if among them only one has sons, he alone is the giver of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) for all of them.

The elders maintain that the local scriptural injunctions concerning [the status of] a son and so forth have their purport in this very matter: "By these [rites] alone is the funeral ceremony (*ūrdhvadaihika*) performed. In that regard, when there is an expectation of a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the one who performs the consecration, Dakṣa says: "Now, if the performer of the consecration should be desirous of a fee regarding the deceased, he then obtains a thousand cows, or a hundred, or even five."
"Prajāpati said:
'He who would burn a wealthy teacher or another, or [burn] a hundred or a thousand cows, should accept [the gift]'— so spoke Prajāpati."
Paiṭhīnasi says: Those twice-born who perform the funeral rites and the offering of water for a deceased teacher or other relative go to the world of Brahmā.
Bharadvāja says:
Now, if the preparer of the funeral rites should be desirous of a fee and be a learned man (mṛtavid),
he shall take a tenth part, a fifth, or even the whole.
Kātyāyana says: If someone other than the son, the pupil, or the uterine brother should perform the cremation,
that Brāhmaṇa who performs the funeral rites and offers the water libation shall take the wealth of the deceased from that [estate].
A claimant shall take a tenth part of the property, or a fifth, or even the whole;
for property with many guardians, a tenth part; for property with few guardians, a fifth.

Śaunaka says that for one who has no son but whose father is still living, the entire estate belongs to the father.
