If someone other than a son or a pupil should perform the cremation, he may take from that wealth as his sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) either a thousand cows or a hundred, according to the value of the property.
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says: "One who burns a deceased person—whether a *sapiṇḍa* or a non-*sapiṇḍa*—who was wealthy or a guru [must perform the rites].
He also states that the inheritance should be divided only after the debt has been paid.
Regarding a debt contracted for the sake of the family by brothers, a mother, or paternal uncles,
Manu states that it is not to be divided.
But whatever wealth he has acquired through learning,
as well as that which is friendly, that received at marriage, and that received with the honey-mixture (madhuparka), shall belong to him alone.
On this point, Yājñavalkya says:
"One who recovers property that has come down in succession or property acquired through effort need not give it to the heirs, nor indeed what is obtained through learning."
Kātyāyana says: That which is acquired through valor, that which is obtained through learning, and that which is remembered as "woman's property"—
all this is not to be divided among the heirs at the time of partition.
A physician must never give his medical knowledge to those who lack knowledge;
however, he may impart that knowledge and its wealth to those whose knowledge is equal to or superior to his own.
Nārada says: A physician shall not, against his will, give a share from his own wealth to one who is unlearned in medicine,
unless he has acquired that wealth by relying upon the paternal estate.
Both the property acquired through valor and that obtained from a wife, as well as whatever may be the wealth of learning— these three are indivisible, as is any gift received from a father.
And for one to whom his own wealth has been given by his mother out of affection, this same rule is seen to apply; for the mother is as beloved as the father.
Bṛhaspati:
Having honored with perfumes and garlands whatever belongs to the father— such as clothing, ornaments, beds, and vehicles— one should present them to the recipient of the śrāddha meal.
And regarding women who are united [in marriage],

those who see the truth have said that "field," "pūrtam" (charitable works), "yogam" (acquisition through effort), and "iṣṭam" (sacrificial rites) are indivisible; likewise, beds and seats are declared to be indivisible.
If a man alone recovers land that was previously lost,
others receive their respective shares after he has given them a fourth part as their portion.
Yājñavalkya: Whatever else has been acquired by oneself without detriment to the paternal estate,
as well as what is obtained from a friend or through marriage, shall belong to the heirs.
Likewise,
Bṛhaspati states: "Whatever has been given by both parents to anyone shall belong to that person alone as their property."
What has been given by the grandfather, by the father, and by the mother—that must not be taken away from him; likewise, so too the property acquired through valor and the property of a wife.
Manu and Viṣṇu:
That which one acquires by one's own labor without depleting the paternal estate,
being obtained through one's own exertion, one is not obliged to give away against one's will.
Kātyāyana says: When one has acquired knowledge from another by providing him with food,
that which is thus obtained according to the rule is called "knowledge acquired through [the gift of] knowledge."
But that which is obtained through learning after it has been offered as a stake according to an agreement should be known as "learning-wealth" (vidyādhanam); it is not subject to partition.
That [knowledge] was obtained from a disciple, from officiating as a priest, from questioning, from the resolution of doubtful questions,
from the instruction of realized knowledge, from debate, and from convincing others.
They say that the wealth of knowledge is not to be divided during partition;
for this same rule applies even to arts, as well as whatever may be in excess of the purchase price.
That which is acquired through the sale of knowledge, as well as from officiating at sacrifices or from a pupil—this they call "wealth from learning"; anything other than this is common property.
One should know that wealth acquired through union with a wife is "nuptial";
all such property is to be understood as conducive to spiritual merit (*dharma*).
Manu and Viṣṇu declare that clothing, a vessel, an ornament, prepared food, water, women,
and the management of security and welfare are not to be divided.
He who maintains the family of a brother who is acquiring knowledge shall receive a share from that wealth acquired through learning, even if he himself has not studied.
Manu:
Whatever property the eldest son acquires after the father has died,
the younger brothers have a share in it, provided they have been maintained through their learning.

But if wealth should accrue through the efforts of all the sons, including those born of ignorance, the division therein shall be equal; such is the settled rule regarding what is not ancestral property.
Vasiṣṭha states that one who has himself produced [wealth] from an *ārjaka* (a barren cow) shall take two shares: “He by whom this was produced by himself shall indeed take two shares. Vyāsa says:
Whatever wealth, such as vehicles or weapons, one acquires through valor or other means while relying on common property, the brothers are entitled to shares therein.
Two shares of that [property] shall be given to him, while the remaining [co-heirs] share equally. Now, regarding what is subject to partition, Kātyāyana says:
Whatever was inherited from the grandfather, whatever was inherited from the father, and whatever was acquired by oneself—
all this is to be divided when there is a partition among the heirs.
Having first returned the inherited property, one should divide the remainder;
that [debt] should be paid by the sons in due order, extending even to the fourth generation.
Bṛhaspati:

Household utensils, vehicles, and the like, as well as milch animals, ornaments, and those engaged in labor, are divided while being visible; in the case of hidden property, a treasury (deposit) is prescribed.
Bṛhaspati says:
Wealth acquired by brothers who have been trained in learning within the family, whether from their father or otherwise, must be divided; so says Bṛhaspati.

Therefore, the partition [of the estate] should be made by the sons, grandsons, and others. On this point, he (Yājñavalkya) states the specific rule: "From the wealth that has arisen, one should set aside half for the purpose of those [rites], diligently performing the monthly, six-monthly, and annual *śrāddha* ceremonies separately."

On this point, Viṣṇu states: "He who takes away the wealth [of the deceased] shall offer the *piṇḍa*; he who inherits from someone shall perform the *śrāddha* for that person. If both [the heir and the wealth-taker] are present, one should give for three generations.
Having taken movable and immovable property, gold, silver, grain, liquids, and clothing, one should cause these to be given at the monthly, six-monthly, and annual *śrāddhas*.
Beds, seats, clothing, umbrellas, fans, and finger-rings should also be given at a *śrāddha*. The division of other property that is not [specifically designated] must be made.
In the absence of sons, the inheritance is taken [by others].

On this point, Viṣṇu states: "The wealth of one who has died without offspring goes to his wife. In her absence, it goes to the daughter. In her absence, it goes to the father. In his absence, it goes to the mother. In her absence, it goes to the brother. In his absence, it goes to the brother's son. In his absence, it goes to a *sakulya* (a distant kinsman). In his absence, it goes to a relative (*bandhu*). In his absence, it goes to a fellow student (*sahādhyāyin*). In his absence, with the exception of the property of a Brāhmaṇa, it goes to the King. The property of a Brāhmaṇa, however, Brāhmaṇas alone shall take. Bṛhaspati says: "But when a man has died destitute of wife and sons..."
The mother should be known as the heir to the inheritance, or else the brother with her permission.
On this point, Vriddha-Manu says: "A sonless widow, protecting her husband's bed and remaining steadfast in her vows,
shall offer his funeral cake and receive his entire share."
Prajāpati [declared]: "In the Vedas, in the Smṛti-tantras, and in worldly custom,
the wise have held that a wife is half of one's own body, sharing equally in the fruits of merit and demerit."
For one whose wife has not passed away, half of his body remains alive;
while half the body is living, how could another take possession of his wealth?
Bṛhaspati says: The wife is the heir to the husband's wealth; in her absence, the daughter is declared [the heir];
in her absence, the brother’s son, the kinsmen (sakulyas), and likewise the relatives (bāndhavas).
Kātyāyana says: Now, for one who has no son, the wife born of a family, or even the daughters, are [the heirs];
in their absence, the father, the mother, the brother, and the sons are declared [to be so].
The Grandfather [Brahmā] declared: "When paternal kinsmen— such as the father’s brothers or those related by blood— are present,
the wife of one who has died without a son shall take his share."

Bṛhaspati says: A woman who died previously shall take [her husband’s] fire; one who has ascended the funeral pyre together with him shall take his sin. Her sapindas or kinsmen who stand in her way [shall take it].
The king should punish those who destroy property with the punishment prescribed for thieves. On this point, Yājñavalkya says:
"The wife, the daughters, the parents, and likewise the brothers..."
His son, a member of the same lineage, a kinsman, a pupil, and a fellow student.
In the absence of these, each subsequent one among them becomes the heir to the wealth of the deceased who died without a son; this rule applies to all castes.

When a man has died without a son, having been previously separated from his co-heirs and not reunited with them, his wife who is married, chaste, and devoted to religious rites shall take the entire estate. If there are many wives, whether of the same caste or of different castes, they shall divide the property among themselves according to their respective shares. Regarding this, Vyāsa states a specific rule: "After two [sons], the remaining inheritance should be given to the wife of the deceased;
moreover, whatever wealth was given by her husband, she may enjoy that as she pleases."

Even beyond two thousand [paṇas], she may receive what is given by her husband according to his will. However, if nothing is given, only two thousand paṇas of wealth may be taken by the wife, and no more. In the absence of the wife, the daughter who is unmarried takes it. Thus says Kātyāyana: "The wife who is unfaithful to her husband is the heir to his wealth; in her absence, however, it is the daughter, provided she be unmarried."
And so Devala says:
"The paternal wealth and the marriage-endowment should be given to the daughters;
in the absence of a son, the daughter born according to dharma shall inherit the property as a son would."

The *sāpiṇḍya* relationship belongs to the maiden alone, according to the statement of Manu: “The wealth shall be taken by that *sapiṇḍa* who is the nearest,” and from the statement of Āpastamba: “In the absence of sons, the *sapiṇḍa* who is the closest. From these, it is understood that the inheritance belongs specifically to the nearest *sapiṇḍa*. Even in the absence of an unmarried daughter, the inheritance should be taken by a married daughter who is not a *sapiṇḍa*, because she possesses *sāpiṇḍya*—characterized by connection to the same body—and because of her proximity. On this point, Manu and Nārada say: “As one’s own self, so is a son; by the son, the daughter is equal.”
While she remains alive, how could another take away his wealth?
Nārada says: In the absence of a son, however, the daughter [is the heir], because an equal lineage is observed;
both the son and the daughter are the perpetuators of the father's lineage.
Bṛhaspati says: A wife is the inheritor of her husband's wealth; in her absence, the daughter is so ordained. For men, a daughter arises from every limb, just like a son.
How could another man take her paternal inheritance?
In the absence of a daughter, the daughters' sons (dauhitrāḥ) shall take [the inheritance]. And so says Viṣṇu:
"Those who have neither sons nor grandsons as their progeny, the daughters' sons shall obtain the wealth;
for in the ancestral rites of offering the *svadhā*, grandsons and daughters' sons are considered equal."
In the absence of a grandson, the duties of a grandson must be performed by the daughter's sons alone. Thus says Manu:
"According to the law, there is no difference between the duties of a son's son and a daughter's son;
for both of them were produced from the body of their father and mother."
Likewise:
"In this world, no distinction is found between a son's son and a daughter's son;
for even through a daughter's son, one is delivered to the other world just as by a son's son."
Smṛti:
"As is one's own self, so is a son; a daughter is equal to a son.
In this world, according to the law, there is no distinction between a grandson and a granddaughter."
Manu says:

Whether she be appointed or unappointed, the maternal grandfather becomes the father of a grandson through whatever son she bears who is similar [to himself]; by that grandson, he shall offer the funeral cake and inherit the wealth.
Likewise: "The daughter's son alone shall take the entire estate of one who dies without a son;
in his absence, the mother and father are the heirs. And so says Manu:
The mother shall obtain the inheritance of a son who dies childless;
in her absence, the father; and in the absence of both parents, the brothers are the heirs to the wealth. Among the brothers, the uterine brothers shall first take it. Devala says:
"Then the uterine brothers shall divide the inheritance of one who dies without a son."

The two statements, “the mother shall obtain the inheritance” and “the uterine brothers shall divide [it],” do not concern the sequence [of succession]; rather, they concern merely the entitlement to take the property. Thus, there is no contradiction. In the absence of uterine brothers, their sons are the heirs to the wealth. In the absence of those two, the half-brothers and their sons [succeed]. In the absence of the sons of brothers, their own sons are the heirs to the wealth. Beyond that, due to the absence of *sapiṇḍa* relationship, the *samānodaka* (distant sapindas) [succeed]. In their absence, the *gotraja* (members of the same lineage) are the heirs to the wealth. And so says Baudhāyana: “The great-grandfather, the grandfather, the father, oneself, the uterine brothers, the sons of a woman of the same caste, the son, the grandson, and the great-grandson—these, as long as they are undivided in inheritance, are called *sapiṇḍas*. Even when divided in inheritance, they are called *sakulyas*. The meaning is that the property goes to those born in that lineage. In the absence of *sapiṇḍas*, the *sakulya* [inherits]. Regarding the aforementioned *sapiṇḍa* relationship: while the three ancestors—the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—are living, there is *sapiṇḍa* relationship with all three preceding ones. The *sapiṇḍa* relationship extends up to seven persons. And likewise says Bṛhaspati.
The sapinda relationship ceases with the seventh person;
however, the status of being a samānodaka (distant kinsman) ceases with the fourteenth.
Another alternative has also been stated by that same author:

"Some say that due to the non-remembrance of births, that [person] is called the ultimate lineage-holder (*gotra*). In the absence of *samānodaka* relatives, those of the same *gotra* (*sagotra*) shall inherit the property; in the absence of *sagotra* relatives, kinsmen (*bāndhava*) shall do so.
"There are three kinds of kinsmen," says Baudhāyana:
"The sons of one's father's sister, the sons of one's mother's sister,
and the sons of one's maternal uncle are to be known as one's own (maternal) kinsmen."
The sons of one's father's paternal aunt, the sons of one's father's maternal aunt,
and the sons of one's father's maternal uncle are to be known as paternal relatives (pitṛbāndhava).
The sons of one's mother’s paternal aunt, the sons of one's mother’s brother’s wife,
and the sons of one's mother’s maternal uncle are to be known as maternal kinsmen (mātṛbandhu).

In the absence of all relatives, the disciple [inherits]; in the absence of a disciple, a fellow student (*sabrahmacārī*); in the absence of that, any learned *śrotriya* may take it. As for the property of a Kṣatriya or others, in the absence of those ending with the fellow student, the king shall take it. This same order of succession applies to all castes. However, Udyotana and Asahāya maintain this view: "Neither brothers nor fathers, but sons are the heirs to the father's estate."
The father shall take the inheritance of one who dies without a son, or the brothers themselves.

In this statement of Manu, by the use of the particle *eva* in the phrase "or indeed the brothers themselves," it is understood that in the absence of sons, the brothers alone are entitled to take the property first. For instance, according to the texts of Śaṅkha and Likhita: "The property of one who has died without a son goes to his brothers; in their absence, the mother and father shall take it; and in their absence, the wife, or the eldest [brother]. Thus, the right of the brothers to take the property first is established. Likewise: "Then the uterine brothers, or the daughters, or even the paternal kinsmen, or the father himself, shall divide the inheritance of one who is without a son."
The mother, the brother, and the wife of the same caste [are the heirs] in that order;
in their absence, the kinsmen and those living together shall take [the property].

And from this statement of Devala, it is understood that first the uterine brother (*sodarabhrātṛ*) of one who dies childless shall take the wealth; in the absence of a uterine brother, some say the mother and father shall take it, while others say the reunited coparcener (*saṃsṛṣṭin*). Still others say that in the absence of those mentioned, the *bhāryā* (wife) [takes it]. As for those statements beginning with "The wife and the daughters," which intend the wife to be the first to take the wealth, all of them refer to a wife who has been authorized (*niyuktapatnī*). Furthermore, those statements which establish the inheritance for daughters refer to the case where there is no father. Others, however, maintain that women have no connection to inheritance, based on the Vedic revelation: "Therefore, women are powerless and non-inheritors."
The object to be taken should be seized from the assembly after bathing following the smoke-offering;
as stated in the Purāṇa:
"When the husband has died, having counted out the garments, food, and clothing..."
Thus, from the words of Vyāsa; likewise elsewhere:
"But other than a Brāhmaṇa, the king devoted to dharma shall provide a livelihood for those women; this is remembered as the rule for inheritance."
According to these words of Nārada: "If a widow who has reached the prime of youth becomes harsh [in disposition],
then a livelihood must be provided for the sake of exhausting her lifespan."
Thus, from the statement of Bṛhaspati;
and likewise—from the statement of Manu: "The childless wives of these [deceased men], provided they are of virtuous conduct, must be maintained"; and likewise—
"An *āḍhaka* of food fit for a widow should be given to one who is bereft of her husband," according to the statement of Prajāpati; likewise:
"For the sake of food, [one should give] rice in the first part [of the day], and in the afternoon, [rice] with fuel."

Based on this statement, they maintain that for a childless widow, there is only the maintenance by her kinsmen, and no acquisition of inheritance; rather, the acquisition of the inheritance belongs to the kinsmen alone. All of this is incorrect.
[The rule is: "The father shall take the estate of one who dies without a son, or the brothers themselves."

Thus, even in the statement of Manu, because there is no word indicating a specific order, there is no exclusion of the wife from the first [place]. By the use of the particle *eva*, the brother’s priority is established in relation to the father. Likewise, even in the statement of Manu—"The mother shall obtain the inheritance of a son who dies childless"—because there is no word intended to convey a sequence, there is no exclusion of the wife. Although in the statements of Śaṅkha, Likhita, and Devala, the first acquisition of wealth by uterine brothers is understood, nevertheless...
Because of the statement of Viṣṇu: "The wealth of one who has died childless goes to the wife";
because of the statement of Bṛhaspati: "[The inheritance] of one deprived of wife and son [goes to the daughter]";
and because of the statement of Vṛddha-Manu: "A sonless woman [should occupy] the bed of her husband."
On account of the statement of Prajāpati, "In the sacred tradition (āmnāya) and in the Smṛti-tantra";
on account of the statement of Bṛhaspati, "The wife is the heir to the husband's wealth";
and on account of the statement of Kātyāyana, "Now, for one who has no son, a woman born of a noble family [is the heir]."

On account of the statement of Pitāmaha, "while kinsmen are present," the statement of Bṛhaspati, "of one who has died without a son," and the statement of Yājñavalkya, "the wife and the daughters," [it follows that...].

Since the seizure of the entire estate by a wife of virtuous conduct is understood from many statements as being primary, the interpretation of those two [conflicting] statements must be made in accordance with them. As for the text, "The property of one who has died without a son goes to his brother," the meaning is that it goes to the brother with whom he was reunited (*saṃsṛṣṭa*).

Alternatively, to avoid contradicting the mention of multiple orders in the sequence of recitation, the wife, the daughter, and the mother and father must be inserted in the preceding order. As for the claim that all statements concerning the inheritance of a wife refer only to a wife who has been "appointed" (*niyuktā*), that is incorrect, because there is no introduction to the practice of *niyoga* anywhere [in these contexts]. Similarly, it is also incorrect to say that all sentences concerning the inheritance of a daughter refer only to an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), because the act of making someone an appointed daughter is likewise never introduced anywhere. Furthermore, as for the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating, "Therefore, women are powerless and non-inheritors," its purpose is merely to indicate that there is no share for a wife in the *pātnīvata* cup, since the word "power" (*indriya*) is seen to refer to Soma in the statement, "Power, indeed, is the drinking of Soma. Moreover, the word "power" (*indriya*) here does not refer to virility.
"A male becomes [male] when the semen of the man is in excess, and female when that of the woman is in excess";

thus, since the potency of women is also observed, it cannot be said that women are devoid of *indriya*. Therefore, it is more appropriate that the word *indriya* refers here specifically to *soma*. Regarding the statement "the *dhūmāvasānika* (smoke-ending) portion is to be taken," this means that if the husband dies while possessing little wealth and the inheritance is insufficient for her livelihood, she should take the *dhūmāvasānika* portion sufficient for her subsistence; or else, the rule concerning the *dhūmāvasānika* refers to the case of an undivided husband.

Regarding the statement, “wealth has been produced for the sake of sacrifice” (*yajñārthaṃ dravyam utpannam*), the word “sacrifice” (*yajña*) here is intended as an indication of religious duty (*dharma*) in general; for if it were intended to refer specifically to the ritual sacrifice itself, there would be a contradiction with its being for the purpose of giving and offering (*dāna-homa*). Consequently, since women also have access to *pūrta* (charitable works) and other such duties, there is no contradiction. The phrase “something [is forbidden] except for a Brāhmaṇa” is understood from the context to refer to women who are not under the protection [of a male relative]. The statement, “if she is a widow or in a state of sexual union,” is aimed at prohibiting the seizure of the entire estate by one whose infidelity is suspected. The rule, “their childless wives must be maintained,” is understood from the context to concern the wives of eunuchs and others; since they lack a connection to wealth through their husbands, the text speaks only of their maintenance, and thus there is no contradiction. Furthermore, statements such as “one āḍhaka should be given to a woman deprived of her husband,” and likewise “a prastha of rice for the sake of food,” also refer to women whose infidelity is suspected. As for this statement of Nārada: [The text continues: “If a woman, having been given property by her father, husband, or sons, departs from the household and lives elsewhere, she shall forfeit that property; they may take it back. This refers to a woman who, having received property from her father, husband, or sons, leaves the home and resides elsewhere; in such a case, she loses that property, and they may recover it. And they should provide for her maintenance until the end of her life;
thus it is said:
"But as for the share of those who have reunited, that [share] is ordained for them alone."
Thus, the aforementioned *saṃsṛṣṭi* rule is intended solely for the maintenance of childless women. As for this statement of Kātyāyana:
"When one who was reunited has died, in the absence of sons, the father shall take the property;
or the brother, or the mother, or the paternal grandmother, in that order."

This [rule] should also be understood to apply in the absence of a wife and daughters. While the husband is alive, she is the owner of the entire estate along with him; when he has died, how could she be left without property? Therefore, it is indeed proper that a wife of virtuous conduct should take the entire estate.

However, some maintain that the rules concerning the wife’s inheritance apply to cases of small wealth, whereas in the case of large wealth, the inheritance belongs to the paternal kinsmen (*jñāti*). Regarding the class of remarried women (*punarbhū*), Bhāradvāja says:
If two men, born of the same woman by two different fathers, should dispute over her property,
whichever of them has paternal inheritance shall take that, and not the other.
The meaning is that they should take only the wealth produced by themselves. Now follows the division of women's property; regarding this, Manu says:

"But when the mother has passed away, all the uterine brothers and the uterine sisters shall divide the mother's estate equally. Thus, unlike the paternal estate, neither a preferential share (*uddhāra*) nor an unequal division should be made; rather, he states that this further rule must be followed: that there is an equal division of the mother's property among the uterine brothers and the [uterine] sisters.
To those who may be their daughters, something from the maternal grandmother's wealth should also be given out of affection, according to what is appropriate for them.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states the specific rule:
"The woman's property belongs to her children, and the daughter is entitled to a share of it;
however, if she is unmarried, she receives only a token honorarium."

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “All uterine brothers and unmarried daughters are entitled to an equal share of their mother’s inheritance. Gautama says: “A woman’s property belongs to her daughters who are both unmarried and unsettled (without a husband or family support). Vasiṣṭha states: “The women shall divide the mother’s dowry (*pāriṇāhya*); this follows the recurring phrase “they shall divide” (*vibhajeran*). Yājñavalkya says: “The daughters [inherit] the remainder after the debt from the mother; or, with the consent of those two, the daughter’s son. The meaning is that in the absence of daughters, their lineal descendants—the sons—shall take it. Nārada says: [as follows].
In the absence of the mother, her daughters [inherit];

in the absence of the daughters, their offspring; and in the case that sons are present but daughters are absent, their offspring—the maternal nephews (mātṛdauhitrāḥ)—should take [the inheritance]. This is the meaning. Kātyāyana states:
"But in the absence of daughters, the inheritance shall go to the sons."
Manu states: "That which may be the *yautaka* (separate property) of the mother belongs exclusively to the unmarried daughter (*kumārī*).

*Yautaka* refers to the woman's property obtained from the maternal family; that belongs to the unmarried daughter alone. Regarding woman's property obtained from the husband's family, sons and daughters are equal by virtue of *sāpiṇḍya* (the sapinda relationship). In the absence of an unmarried daughter, even married daughters are equal to sons if they are *pratiṣṭhitāḥ* (established); those who are *apratiṣṭhitāḥ* (unestablished) are those who are childless, based on the Vedic statement in the Brāhmaṇa, "Offspring indeed is the foundation," or those who are destitute. Manu describes the specific distribution of woman's property according to this sequence.

Whatever property may belong to a woman, having been given by her father in any manner whatsoever, that a Brāhmaṇī wife shall take; or it shall belong to her unmarried daughter, or to the offspring of such a daughter.

In a marriage performed according to the prescribed order, if women other than the Brāhmaṇī wife die without issue, their property shall be taken by a daughter born of the Brāhmaṇī wife; or, in her absence, by her son. It is not the husband or others who take it. The phrase "given by the father" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for all types of woman's property (strīdhana). On this point, Pāraskara says: "The woman's property is declared to belong to the unmarried daughter;
however, she does not receive anything from that of a married daughter, whereas the son of a married daughter is entitled to an equal share."

Manu states the definition of a woman’s property (strīdhana): "That which is received at the nuptial fire, that which is given at the bridal procession, that which is given as a token of affection, and that which is obtained from brothers, mothers, or fathers— this is declared to be the sixfold property of a woman."

Regarding this, Nārada states the specific details: "That which was received in the presence of the sacred fire, that which was received in the presence of the *āhavanīya* fire, the inheritance from the husband, as well as what was given by brothers, and what was given by the parents— this is declared to be the sixfold property of a woman."

On this point, Yājñavalkya says: "That which is given by the father, mother, husband, or brother; that which has come to her at the fire (during marriage); and that which is received upon supersession [by another wife], and so forth, is declared to be a woman's property."

On this point, Viṣṇu states: "What is given by the father, mother, son, or brother; what is received at the nuptial fire; what is given upon taking a second wife (adhyavedanika); what is given by relatives; the bride-price (śulka); and what is received for the establishment of the sacred fires—these constitute a woman’s property. Devala says: "Maintenance, ornaments, the bride-price, and gains shall constitute a woman’s property. Kātyāyana [says]:

Whatever wealth has been acquired through crafts, or whatever is accompanied by affection, the husband has ownership over that property; however, the remainder is declared to be the woman's separate property (strīdhana).

The meaning is: that which is obtained out of affection from others than the husband, namely from kinsmen; that which is acquired through one's own crafts; that which is obtained out of affection from kinsmen other than the husband; and the "residue," which refers to wealth characterized as *adhyagni* (given at the wedding fire) and so forth—in these, women possess ownership, which is to say, it is their *strīdhana* (woman’s property). He himself has stated the nature of *adhyagni* and the rest:
"That which is given to women at the time of marriage in the presence of the sacred fire is proclaimed by the virtuous as *adhyagni*-derived woman’s property."
Furthermore, whatever a woman acquires while being led away from her father's house is declared to be the woman’s property known as *adhyāhavanika*.
Whatever is given out of affection by the mother-in-law or the father-in-law,
that which is offered at the salutation of their feet, is called "acquired through beauty."

Whatever is obtained by a woman from her paternal or maternal kinsmen after marriage is declared to be *anvādheya*; likewise, that which is obtained from her kinsmen [before marriage] is also so defined.
Whatever price is obtained for household utensils, vehicles, milch animals, ornaments, or articles for work— that is declared to be *śulka* (toll or duty).
Manu also states that even for a woman who has no son, the heirs vary according to the type of marriage:
"The property given as a dowry, as well as what was given by her husband out of affection—
this wealth shall belong to her offspring when she has passed away while her husband is still living."

Whatever property was acquired in marriages according to the Brahma, Daiva, Arsha, Gandharva, or Prajapatya rites, it is ordained that upon the death of a childless wife, it belongs to the husband alone.

The meaning is that among the five types of marriages mentioned, if a wife dies childless, her property belongs to the husband alone. However, in the case of those marriages such as the Āsura and others, it is ordained that if she dies childless, the wealth given to her shall belong to her mother and father.

In the case of the three marriages—those of the Asuras, Piśācas, and Rākṣasas—if the woman dies childless, that which was given by her parents belongs to the parents alone; this is the meaning. Devala states: "The property of a woman is common to her sons and daughters. If she dies childless, the husband, the mother, the brother, or even the father shall take it."

By the first half [of the verse], it is stated that when the mother has died, among the eight types of marriage, the sons and daughters have an equal share in the woman’s property (*strīdhana*). By the second half, it is stated that in marriages such as the Āsura and others, that property must be returned by the givers themselves: what was given by the husband, the husband shall take; what was given by the mother and others, they alone shall take. Kātyāyana says:
"In the absence of daughters, however, that inheritance shall belong to the sons.
But what was given by kinsmen, in the absence of kinsmen, goes to the husband."
Sisters, together with their kinsmen, shall divide [the inheritance] along with their husbands;
this is the righteous rule established for the division of a woman's property.

The phrase "in the absence of daughters" and so forth refers to the eight types of marriage [beginning with the *brāhma*]. The phrase "given by kinsmen" (*bandhudattam*) refers to the *āsura* and other such marriages. In the absence of sons, that which is given by kinsmen—such as maternal uncles and others—belongs to them alone. In the absence of kinsmen, what is given by them goes to the husband. He states another alternative with the half-verse beginning "the sisters": when kinsmen are present, property given by kinsmen should be shared; thus it is said, "Sisters who have husbands should divide [it] together with their kinsmen. On this point, Kātyāyana says:
"In the case of the *āsura* and other marriages, whatever paternal wealth has been obtained by a woman as her separate property (*strīdhana*)," [it belongs to her].
In their absence, it is ordained that this [property] belongs to the children of those [parents], or to the parents themselves.
Yama says:
Whatever property is given in marriages such as the Āsura and others,
if she dies childless, the father alone shall take that wealth.

Gautama: "The sister's dowry belongs to the uterine brothers after the mother [has passed away]; some say it belongs to them even before. Yājñavalkya: "Likewise, what was given by kinsmen, as well as the dowry and the subsequent gift (anvādheya), when she dies childless, the kinsmen shall obtain that."

In this regard, the *śulka* (bride-price) is of two kinds. One is that which is given to the bridegroom as the price for the sale of the girl; that goes to the mother or to the brothers. The other *śulka* is that which is given as the price for the girl’s ornaments and household utensils; that must not be taken back by the givers. On this point, Bodhāyana says: "But if a daughter appointed to provide offspring (*putrikā*) should somehow die childless, her husband shall take that wealth without hesitation."
Likewise, Devala and Bodhāyana state:
"The uterine brothers shall divide the inheritance of a deceased maiden equally;
in their absence, it shall belong to the mother, and in her absence, to the father—in that order."
Manu says:
"The ornaments which may have been worn by women while their husband was alive, the heirs shall not divide; those who do divide them fall."

Since the property of a maiden (*alaṅkāra*) is not given [as a gift] and is not the property of a woman, it becomes the husband’s property; thus, when the husband has died, the sons would normally be entitled to its division. This [verse] provides an exception to that rule. Kātyāyana states: "Ornaments obtained by women from the husband's family or from the father's family shall not be divided; while she is alive, one should not apply them [to other purposes]."

Āpastamba states: "Some say that ornaments and the wealth of her kinsmen belong to the wife. Regarding the ownership of ornaments given out of affection, Nārada declares an exception concerning immovable property: "Whatever has been given by an affectionate husband to his wife, even after he has died, she may enjoy it as she wishes or give it away, with the exception of immovable property."

“Immovable property given out of affection” means that when the donor has died, it does not become the woman’s own property. Some, however, say that immovable property given out of affection is indeed not her own; they maintain that it is stated to be unfit for gift in the absence of a person with authority to permit it. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states an exception: “In times of famine, for religious duties, during illness, or when there is an obstruction [to livelihood], the husband is not required to return the wife’s property taken by him unless he so desires.”
Kātyāyana says:
Neither the husband, nor the son, nor the father, nor the brothers have authority over the woman’s property,
whether in its acquisition or its disposal.
For if any one among them should consume the woman's property by force,
he shall be made to pay it back with interest and shall also incur a fine.
If he should eat that very same thing after having obtained permission and with a sense of pleasure,
he should be made to pay its price, provided that he is wealthy.
Having learned that [the debtor] is diseased, afflicted by calamity, or oppressed by creditors,
he may, out of affection, give what has been relinquished according to his own will.
Devala states: "The means of subsistence, ornaments, the nuptial fee, and profits shall constitute the woman's property (strīdhana).
Her husband has no right to enjoy this himself unless there is a time of distress."
If she spends it fruitlessly on liberation or pleasure, she should return it with interest;
however, she is entitled to enjoy the woman’s property when it is used to alleviate the distress of her sons.
Kātyāyana says: A woman who is intent on doing harm, shameless, wasteful of wealth,
and devoted to adultery does not deserve to receive a woman’s property.
The brother has promised that the woman's property shall be given by the sons like a debt;
whether she remains in her husband's family or resides in her father's family.
Vṛddha-Manu says:
"The inheritance obtained from her own husband, excluding the *śulka*, she is entitled to;
she shall divide the remainder, for she is indeed a sharer."
Kavaṣa says:
Whatever price for the sale of a daughter, or even the bride-price (*śulka*), has been paid, she shall cause its loss; indeed, she becomes an heir (*aṃśinī*).
Kātyāyana says: That which is obtained by a married woman or even by an unmarried girl from her husband, from her father’s house,
from her brother, or from her parents, is declared to be *saudāyika* (gift of affection).
Upon receiving the wealth given as a dowry, independence is prescribed for women;
since that was given by them for the sake of kindness, it serves as their means of subsistence.
It is proclaimed that women always possess independence over their *saudāyika* (dowry) property;
they may sell or give it away as they wish, even in the case of immovable assets.

The intention is that in times of distress, even in the absence of the consent of the husband, sons, and others, there is no fault in acts such as sale. On this point, Yājñavalkya says: "To a superseded wife, he should give an equal amount as compensation for supersession;
to her to whom no separate property (strīdhana) has been given, he should assign half of that [compensation] if it has already been given."
In this context, the word "half" (ardha) refers to the portion that completes [the whole]. Kātyāyana states:
"Now, if he has two wives and does not favor her again, even if she has relinquished her claim out of affection, he must be compelled by force to restore it to her."
Wherever the deprivation of food, clothing, and shelter is observed,
there a woman may take her own [belongings] during the partition of the estate among the heirs.
This is the law for a woman who has been formally given away: she shall reside in her father's family until she reaches marriageable age;
but when afflicted by illness or during the time of her husband's death, she may likewise go to her husband's family.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states the distinction:
"A mother’s sister, a maternal uncle’s wife, a paternal uncle’s wife,
a father’s sister, a mother-in-law, and a former wife are proclaimed to be equal to a mother."
If these women have no biological son, nor a daughter’s son (dauhitra),
nor the son of that daughter, their wealth shall be inherited by their sister’s sons and the others mentioned in order.

The commentators have stated that this statement does not apply when there are sapinda relatives up to the fourth degree; however, it does apply when there are asapinda relatives beginning from the fifth degree.

Others have established the following arrangement: regarding the six female relatives beginning with the mother’s sister, when their respective male counterparts—the sister’s son (*svasrīya*) and so forth—are eligible [to inherit], in cases concerning the property of a childless woman where the husband would otherwise be entitled, then in his absence, among the three male relatives connected through him, first the husband’s younger brother is entitled to the wealth of the elder brother’s wife by virtue of the closest proximity. In his absence, her own brother’s son is entitled; in his absence, the son-in-law (*jāmātṛ*) is entitled. Since the suffix *apatya* in the term "sister’s son" and so forth conveys the notion of offspring in general, some maintain that the connection to inheritance is appropriate for both women and men.

Others, however, maintain that although the extension [of the rule] applies equally to both women and men, because the cognition arises first in the case of men alone, and because of the observation of the explanatory passage (arthavāda) stating, "Therefore, women are devoid of [legal] capacity," the connection with inheritance belongs to men alone and not to women. Now, regarding the inheritance of those who have reunited: there is the inheritance of those who have reunited. On this point, Manu says:
If those who were divided while living together should divide again, the division in that case shall be equal; there is no right of primogeniture in that instance.
The meaning is that, in the partition among those who have lived together as co-sharers (*saṃsṛṣṭin*), the preferential share (*uddhāra*) due to the eldest must not be made.
Regarding those among whom the eldest or the youngest has fallen away from the distribution of shares,
or if either one dies, his share is not lost.

Based on the statement, "There is no burning of the share for those who are perpetrators of great sins" (*mahāpātakinaḥ*), the share of those men—whether the eldest or the youngest—from whom the [right to] receive a share has ceased due to such acts as killing a Brahmin, or who has been excluded, is not lost. Nor should his co-residents (*saṃsṛṣṭin*) take it. To address the expectation of how it should then be handled, that same author says:
"The uterine brothers, having assembled together, shall divide it equally;
as well as those brothers who were reunited (*saṃsṛṣṭa*), and the uterine sisters."

The uterine brothers (*sodarya*) shall assemble and divide the share of one who has fallen [from caste], died, or become an ascetic. Those brothers who are reunited (*saṃsṛṣṭa*), even if they are not uterine, shall divide it together with the non-reunited uterine brothers. The term "uterine" (*sodarya*) refers to those who share the womb, even in the absence of a connection through property; whereas for those of a different womb, the term refers to those who share property, even in the absence of a connection through the womb. Likewise, the uterine sisters of the deceased shall also divide the inheritance equally with the aforementioned uterine brothers and those reunited with them. Regarding the phrase "those brothers who are reunited," the teacher Viśvarūpa stated that the mention of "brothers" is intended to include wives and others in cases of reunion with someone other than the father or paternal uncle. Now, Yājñavalkya says:
But a reunited coparcener shall give and take the share of one who was reunited, and likewise a uterine brother shall do so for a uterine brother— both for one born and for one deceased.

"Reunited property" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*) refers to divided wealth that has been mixed together again. One who possesses such property is called "reunited" (*saṃsṛṣṭin*). Regarding those who are reunited, Bṛhaspati states the following rule: "One who, having been divided, lives again in one place with his father, a brother, or a paternal uncle out of affection, is said to be 'reunited'."

When a reunited coparcener has died, the reunited coparcener shall give the share to the son born subsequently from a wife whose pregnancy was unknown at the time of partition. In the absence of such a son, the reunited coparcener himself shall take the deceased’s share, and not the wife or other heirs. If a reunited uterine brother dies, his uterine brother who is also a reunited coparcener shall give the share to the son born of that union. In the absence of a son, he himself shall take it. Regarding the question of how the property is to be taken when a reunited coparcener has died without a son, while there exist both a non-reunited uterine brother and a reunited brother from a different womb, [the author] says:
But a uterine brother who is a reunited coparcener shall not take the wealth of one born of a different womb;
even one not reunited may take it, but one who is reunited shall not take the property of one born of a different mother.

A uterine brother born of another mother (an *anyodarya* or *sāpatna* brother) shall not take the entire property of one who was reunited (*saṃsṛṣṭin*), but rather only half; the other half shall be taken by the non-reunited brother. To address the question of who this "non-reunited" brother is, the author says: "the reunited. This means one born from the same womb (*ekodara*), that is, a uterine brother (*sodarya*). Regarding the phrase "not one born of another mother," the explanation must be made by supplying an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of the word "only" (*eva*). [The meaning is: "In the case of a reunited brother, only one born of another mother shall not take the property of the reunited brother; rather, even a non-reunited uterine brother shall take it. Here too, because of the hearing of the word "not" (*na*), the restriction "only one born of another mother" is understood through negation. Therefore, an ellipsis must be supplied. In the case of the reunited brother, once the inheritance of the wife has ceased, their maintenance must be provided from her ornaments.
Likewise, Nārada says with regard to one who has reunited:
"And they should provide maintenance for his women until the end of their lives.
Some maintain that this aforementioned rule regarding the acquisition of property by the reunited partner applies only in the absence of sons, wives, and daughters. Similarly, Bṛhaspati [states]:
If anyone should die or somehow renounce the world, his share is not lost; it is ordained for his uterine brother.
His sister, however, deserves to receive a share from that [inheritance];
this is the law for one who is childless and lacks both a wife and a father.
Indeed,
they should provide for his maintenance until the end of their lives,
provided they preserve the bed of their husband; otherwise, they may forfeit their shares among the other women.

From this statement of Nārada, it is understood that only when a wife exists does a *saṃsṛṣṭin* (one who has reunited after partition) receive the property. True; there is no contradiction, for Nārada’s statement regarding women refers to those [wives] who are unfit for inheritance. The elders maintain that in those Smṛtis where terms such as *yoṣit*, *vidhavā*, *anārī*, *strī*, or *bhāryā* are employed, they refer only to their maintenance; whereas in those Smṛtis where the term *patnī* is used, they refer to the taking of the inheritance. Regarding this distinction, Bṛhaspati says:
"But among those who have reunited, whoever [acquires wealth] through learning, heroism, or other means..."
To him who has attained [the property], two shares must be given; the remaining [sons] shall have equal shares.
Kātyāyana states: "Among those who have reunited, the reunited shall inherit; among those who remain separate, the separate shall inherit.
In the absence [of a male heir], they should be known as the takers of the property, provided they are not without seed and are mutual sharers."

When one among those who are *saṃsṛṣṭa* (united in interest) dies without a son, the property belongs to the *saṃsṛṣṭin* alone. Likewise, when one among those who are not *saṃsṛṣṭa* dies without a son, the property belongs to those who are not *saṃsṛṣṭa*. In their absence, it belongs to others as well. When those who are *saṃsṛṣṭa* die childless and without any remaining kin, those who are not *saṃsṛṣṭa* take that wealth. Similarly, when those who are not *saṃsṛṣṭa* die childless, those who are *saṃsṛṣṭa* take that wealth. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states the specific rule:
"The heirs to the property of forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*), ascetics (*yati*), and students (*brahmacārin*) [are as follows...]"
In due order, they are the preceptor, the good disciple, the spiritual brother, and those who share the same sacred ford.
In this regard, the Blessed Viṣṇu states: “The preceptor or the disciple may take the property of one who has become a forest-dweller.
Thus ends the section on the Partition of Inheritance in the *Vyavahāranirṇaya* composed by Śrī Varadarāja.
12. The Section on Gambling, Betting, and Other Sixfold Matters.
Now, gambling and betting (dyūta-samāhvaya) are being discussed; their definitions are stated by Manu:
"In this world, that which is performed with inanimate objects is called gambling (dyūta)."
That which is performed by means of living beings is to be known as *samāhvaya* (gambling with animate creatures).
Nārada says: Gambling with dice, sticks, and so forth, conducted through verbal debate,
as well as playing for stakes with birds and other creatures— this is the category known as *dyūta-samāhvaya* (gambling and betting).
Let birds, rams, deer, and the like seize one another;
having made a wager, they strike at each other—this they call a challenge.

In this context, *dyūta* (gambling) refers to that game played with non-living objects such as dice and the like, preceded by a wager (*paṇa*). *Samāhvaya* (betting on living creatures) refers to that which is performed with living beings—such as wrestlers, rams, buffaloes, or cocks—preceded by a wager; this is the meaning.
Manu says:
"The king shall prohibit both gambling and betting on living creatures within his kingdom."
These two faults are the destroyers of the kingdom of those who rule the earth.
In a former age, a great and most bitter enmity was seen to arise from gambling;
therefore, a wise man should not indulge in gambling, even for the sake of amusement.
The meaning is that a great enmity is to be seen in the gambling match of the Son of Dharma.
"The king shall cause to be executed all those who engage in gambling or betting, or who cause them to be done, as well as Śūdras who assume the marks of the twice-born."
Kātyāyana says: Since strife inevitably arises from gambling, just as poison from the mouth of a serpent,
therefore the king should desist from it, for that is indeed a vice of the senses.
If it is to remain visible, one should have that gateway constructed with its archway closed,
so as not to cause confusion among the noble ones, and providing a handhold for them.
Bṛhaspati says:

Gambling was forbidden by Manu because it destroys truth, purity, and wealth; however, when it is conducted by others [under supervision], it may be permitted provided it includes a share for the king.
For that which is presided over by a *sabhika* is indeed a means of identifying thieves.
A *sabhā* is an assembly hall equipped with all the implements for play, such as dice and so forth; he who owns such a place is the *sabhika*. Yājñavalkya states:
"In the case of a stake involving a hundredfold interest, the *sabhika* shall take five percent."
Scoundrels, gamblers, and thieves might seize ten for every hundred.

A stake (glaha) is defined as a wager devised by gamblers through mutual agreement. In that context, a "hundredfold interest" (*śatikavṛddhi*) refers to an interest—whether amounting to one hundred or more—that is based upon that stake. Therefore, from a rogue gambler, the keeper of the gaming hall (*sabhika*) shall take five percent (*pañcakaṃ śatam*) for his own profit; this means he should take the twentieth part of the winnings. From the other type of gambler, who charges a full hundredfold interest, the master of the hall shall take ten percent (*daśakaṃ śatam*), which is the tenth part of the won property.
Gambling should be conducted with a single stake for the purpose of ascertaining the skill of the players;
this same rule is to be understood as applying to betting on animal fights and challenges.

One should make it single-faced, having a single principal [side], says Kātyāyana. The master of the gaming house (sabhika) shall conduct the gambling; he shall pay the king the amount due, and he shall take a ten percent increase on the stake from the defeated player.
The winner shall give his own wealth, and the winnings must be taken back within three fortnights, or immediately by the keeper of the gambling house from the gambler; of this there is no doubt.
Nārada says:
The master of the gambling house shall conduct the game;
he shall pay one hundred to the king as a fee, and his profit from conducting the gambling shall be ten percent of that hundred.
Alternatively, a gambler who, having given the king the share as prescribed, engages in open gambling,
incurs no fault.
When the dice fall twice in favor of the stake for a gambler, they say that victory belongs to his opponent; such is the defeat of the gambler.
Kātyāyana says: Whether it be a single form or a double form, victory is seen for that gambler whose dice fall favorably.
Bṛhaspati:
Whatever loss anyone may incur in a duel,
the stipulated wager for that must be paid by his master.
Nārada said: But if a man engages in gambling without being authorized by the king,
he shall not obtain his desired object, and he deserves punishment.
One should remove wicked counterfeit gamblers from the gambling circle;
it is prescribed that all such persons be disciplined by having a rosary tied around their necks.
Yājñavalkya:
Those who play with fraudulent dice or by means of deception should be banished by the king, marked with a brand.
Viṣṇu: "In gambling, the hands of those who play with fraudulent dice shall be cut off; the fingers of those who play by deception shall be cut off at the joints."
Gamblers should stand as witnesses for gamblers in matters of doubt;
those who were present there shall indeed be their witnesses.
This same rule is to be understood as applicable to gambling with living creatures and to challenging duels. The section on gambling and challenging duels is concluded. Now follows verbal abuse.
Now, the title of dispute known as verbal abuse is being discussed. Nārada says:
"Speech that consists of insults directed at a person's country, caste, family, or physical condition, and which has a contrary meaning, is called verbal abuse."
The notion of "defamation" (*nyaṅgasaṃjñā*) refers to speech involving the mention of the cutting off of limbs such as the head or hands. And so Kātyāyana says:
"To mimic or to utter that which is censured in the world, such as the sounds 'huṃ' or 'you' (*tvaṃ*), is called verbal abuse (*vākpāruṣya*)."
Because of its harshness, vulgarity, and intensity, that [abuse] is also recorded as being threefold;
and according to the sequence of their gravity, the punishment for each here is likewise progressively more severe.
Nārada says:

That which is contemptuous and harsh should be known as *aślīla*, while that which is designated as a physical blemish (*nyaṅga*) is called *tīvra* by the wise when it consists of reproaches involving acts leading to loss of caste (*patanīya*).
Kātyāyana says: When one, by means of limbs designated as non-existent— or whether they be unreal or real— somewhat reviles another, that is recorded as harsh speech (*niṣṭhurā vāk*).
When one, out of anger, uses speech to revile or mock others by means of the conduct,
country, or family [of those being addressed], that is considered by the wise to be *aślīlā* (obscene or vulgar speech).
That speech which is joined with great sins, which causes hatred toward the world, and which brings about the loss of caste— that is known as intense (tīvra) speech.
Bṛhaspati:
The reviling of [others] based on their country, caste, family, and so forth, by associating them with sin,
without the use of physical force— that is called the first form of verbal abuse (*vākpāruṣya*).
Speaking of a sister, a mother, or their relatives, as well as proclaiming a minor offense (upapātaka),
is declared by those who know the scriptures to be middling verbal harshness.
The discourse on forbidden foods and drinks, the proclamation of a mortal sin, and harshness are declared to be the highest [forms of verbal abuse]; the wise call them intense.
Kātyāyana says: "Those who proclaim the faults of one who is actually faultless for the sake of provoking anger,
and those who speak under false pretexts— they know such a man to be 'corrupt in speech' (vāgduṣṭa)."
Manu:
One who slanders his mother, father, wife, brother, son,
or teachers shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas], as shall one who does not yield the path to his teacher.
Kātyāyana says: "He who says, 'I spoke this out of delusion, confusion, rivalry, or affection,' and adds,
'I shall not speak it again,' for him one should prescribe half the fine."
On this point, Bṛhaspati states: "In cases of verbal abuse between equals, the punishment is equal; for an inferior, it is recorded as double;
and for a superior, the punishment is half."
On this point Viṣṇu states: "Even one who speaks the truth regarding those who are one-eyed, lame, and so forth, shall be fined two kārṣāpaṇas. Yājñavalkya says:
"If one insults those with deficient limbs or senses by means of true, false, or distorted praises, he shall be fined twelve and a half paṇas."
If a man swears, "I shall violate your sister or your mother," the king shall cause him to pay a fine of twenty-five [paṇas].
For verbal injury involving the destruction of the arms, neck, eyes, or thighs, the fine is one hundred [paṇas];
for those involving the feet, nose, ears, hands, and so forth, it is half of that.
But one who is unable [to provide security] and speaks thus should be fined ten paṇas;
likewise, one who is able should be made to provide surety for his safety.
One who insults his sister-in-law or similar relatives shall be fined fifty paṇas;
[this is the view of] Manu and Nārada.
A Kṣatriya who reviles a Brāhmaṇa deserves a fine of one hundred [paṇas].
A Vaiśya shall pay one hundred and fifty, while a Śūdra deserves corporal punishment.
Five hundred brahmins shall be fined for slandering a kṣatriya;
for a vaiśya, the fine shall be twenty-five; and for a śūdra, the punishment is twelve.
Bṛhaspati says: This disciplinary rule has been prescribed for a virtuous Śūdra who is without fault;
however, a Brāhmaṇa should not incur guilt by using harsh words against one who is devoid of merit.
Likewise: "A Vaiśya, however, should be fined one hundred [paṇas] for insulting a Kṣatriya;
a Kṣatriya, when reviling a Vaiśya, deserves half of that as a disciplinary fine."
For insulting a Śūdra, a fine of twenty-five [paṇas] is prescribed for a Kṣatriya;
for a Vaiśya, it is declared by those learned in the scriptures to be double that amount.
A Śūdra who defames a Vaiśya shall be made to pay the first amercement; likewise,
one who defames a Kṣatriya shall pay the middle amercement, and one who defames a Brāhmaṇa shall pay the highest amercement.
On this point, Manu and Nārada state:
"One born of a single caste who insults those of twice-born status with harsh speech shall suffer the cutting off of his tongue, for he is of inferior origin."
But for one who pronounces their name or caste with malice,
an iron spike ten fingers long, glowing with fire, shall be thrust into his mouth.
Regarding a Śūdra, Bṛhaspati says:
"If he should out of pride give instruction in dharma to the twice-born,
the king shall cause hot oil to be poured into his mouth and his ears."

With the term *śūdra* understood as the subject, Gautama states: "Now, if he should overhear the Veda, his ears are to be filled with molten tin and lac; if he recites it, his tongue is to be cut off; if he retains it, his body is to be torn apart. Regarding this, Yama says:
"If he should recite even a single *ṛc*, one should have his tongue cut into pieces. Manu [says]:
Those who speak of minor or secondary sins, or who proclaim great crimes,
shall be made to pay fines of the first, middle, or highest degree respectively.

On this point, Yājñavalkya states: "The insult of those learned in the three Vedas, of the king, or of a deity is punished with the highest amercement; that of caste-groups (jātipūga) with the middle amercement; and that of a village or a district with the first amercement."
Nārada says:
Having reviled a king who is established on his own path,
purification occurs either by the cutting off of the tongue or by the confiscation of all one's property.

For a Brahmin, the confiscation of all property; for one of another caste, the cutting off of the tongue. Yājñavalkya: Having cut out the tongue of one who speaks what is undesirable to the king, as well as one who reviles him or breaks his counsel, the king shall banish him.
Nārada said:
In this world, two are proclaimed to be beyond reproach and exempt from punishment—the Brāhmaṇa and the king; for these two sustain this entire universe.
Having called one who has fallen [from virtue] "fallen," or having called a thief "thief" again, one incurs a fault equal to that of the speech; if it is false, one becomes twice as guilty.
Even a Brāhmaṇa, by engaging in verbal abuse toward one of his own caste under the pretext of debts and the like, becomes guilty of a minor offense (upapātakin).
Now, the legal head of dispute known as *daṇḍapāruṣya* (assault) is discussed. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"With hands, stones, clubs, ashes, mud, or dust..."
And the striking with weapons is called verbal and physical violence.
Nārada said: For that [homicide] as well, a threefold classification is observed according to the sequence of mild, middling, and superior:
by means of threatening with a weapon, causing it to fall without hesitation, and the manifestation of a wound.
Because of the removal of the three types of thorns— those that are inferior, middling, and superior— they say there are exactly three kinds of fines in that matter of purifying the realm.
Yājñavalkya:
For touching [another] with ashes, mud, or dust, a fine of ten paṇas is prescribed;
for touching [another] with impure matter, the heel, or spittle, double that is prescribed.
In the case of similar women who are the wives of others, the punishment is likewise; however, it is double for those of higher status.
For those of lower status, the punishment is half; there is no punishment when [the act] occurs through delusion, intoxication, and the like.
Kātyāyana states: For discharging vomit, urine, feces, and the like below the navel, the fine is fourfold;
for such acts in the middle of the body, it is sixfold; but at the head, the punishment is eightfold.
For raising the hand [to strike], a fine of twelve [paṇas] shall be imposed;
for actually striking those of the same caste, that same fine is declared to be double.
Bṛhaspati: When a stone or a piece of wood is raised [to strike], the first fine shall be imposed;
likewise, for mutual assault with hands or feet, the fines shall be ten and twenty [paṇas] respectively.
For striking with bricks, clods of earth, or wood, the fine shall be two māṣakas;
for drawing blood, the punishment prescribed by the wise should be double that amount.
Yājñavalkya: A man who causes pain with wood or other implements without shedding blood shall be made to pay thirty-two paṇas; if blood is seen, the fine is double.
Manu:
"One who pierces the skin shall be fined one hundred [paṇas], as shall one who causes blood to flow;
one who cuts the flesh shall be fined six niṣkas, but one who breaks a bone shall be banished."
Bṛhaspati states: For piercing the skin, the first amercement is the punishment; for piercing the flesh, however, the middle amercement;
for piercing a bone, the highest amercement; but for causing death, the penalty is execution.
In the case of cutting off the ears, nose, or hands, or in breaking the teeth or limbs, the middle amercement shall be imposed; it shall be double if the limb is severed.
Kātyāyana states:
"According to Bhṛgu, for the cutting off of the ears, lips, nose, feet, eyes, tongue, penis, or hand, the highest fine shall be imposed; for the piercing [or severing] of these, the middle fine."
Manu:
When an assault is committed against humans or animals,
one should impose a punishment in proportion to the extent of the suffering caused.
Yājñavalkya:
A limb that causes pain to a Brahmin shall be cut off from a non-Brahmin;
however, if he merely raises [his weapon] to strike, the first amercement is the punishment, and for actual contact, half of that.
Nārada:
By whatever limb a lower caste person should offend against a Brāhmaṇa, that very limb of his must be cut off; in this way he may attain purification.
Bṛhaspati:
When two persons strike each other, the punishment shall be equal; it is traditionally held that it should be the same for both.
However, the initiator and the one who persists in the assault shall be made to pay a higher fine.
Nārada says:
He who first brings a false accusation shall certainly be the one who bears the guilt;
he who does so afterwards is also a wrongdoer, but the punishment for the former is more severe.
Bṛhaspati: A man who reviles in return when reviled, or strikes back when struck,
or even kills an assailant, shall not be considered guilty.

Now Vṛddhakātyāyana says: "If one who has been addressed with harsh words gives up his life after being so addressed, or if one who has been struck gives up his life after being struck, he for whose sake that person dies shall incur no guilt."
Manu and Nārada state:
A person of lower birth who seeks to share a seat with one of superior birth shall be branded on the hip and banished, or his buttock shall be cut off.
The king shall cause the two lips of one who spits out of pride to be cut off;
he shall cause the penis of one who urinates [upon him] to be cut off, and the anus of one who passes wind [upon him].
One who seizes him by the hair should have both hands cut off without hesitation;
the same applies to seizing him by the feet, the nose, the neck, or the testicles.
Manu says: "One must strike below [the navel], and never at the head;
but one who acts otherwise deserves the punishment as previously stated."
Kātyāyana states: Just as the punishments have been prescribed for verbal abuse according to the inverse and direct order of castes,
so too shall the punishments be inflicted in the same sequence for physical assault.
Manu:
Furthermore, he who causes injury to another’s limbs, or to his wounds or blood,
shall be made to pay the expenses of recovery, or else the full penalty.
Bṛhaspati: In cases of pressing a limb, as well as piercing or cutting it,
the offender shall be made to pay the expenses for its recovery, as well as whatever was seized during the quarrel.
Nārada says: A father is not liable for punishment on account of his son's offense, nor is a horse for that of a dog;
nor is the owner of a monkey liable for its actions, provided it was not sent by him.
Yājñavalkya: Even if capable of preventing it, an owner who does not restrain fanged or horned animals shall pay the first amercement; if they have already caused injury, he shall pay double.
In a case where a person has been killed without witnesses, the legal proceeding must be investigated by means of physical marks, logical reasoning, and scriptural tradition,
out of fear of false evidence being fabricated.
Bṛhaspati says: When the victim is seen slain but the killer is not seen,
he must be identified by the king through inference based on prior enmity.
His neighbors, both immediate and distant, as well as his friends and kinsmen,
should be questioned by the king's officers using conciliatory and other such means.
He is to be identified by men through his association with the accused, or by means of a *cihnahoḍha* (a stolen article as evidence).
Kātyāyana says: "Where many people, filled with rage, strike at a counterfeit object..."
But he who strikes a vital spot is declared to be the slayer.
And he who strikes their vital points shall be made to pay the fine as prescribed;
likewise, the instigator and his accomplices are sharers in the guilt for that purpose.
The basis, the giver of weapons, the provider of sustenance for actions,
the instructor of proper methods, and the one who demonstrates their destruction.
One who is engaged in the work of indifference, one who rejoices in what is flawed,
and one who is capable of failing to prevent [wrongdoing]— all such persons are perpetrators of the act.
A Brahmin shall never receive corporal punishment;
rather, having bound him in secret confinement, the king should cause him to be provided with food.
But the Brahmins should also cause [the offender] to perform penances according to the nature of the offense.
Kātyāyana states:
If one does not perceive the grounds for an assault through the [testimony of] witnesses and so forth,
and that case has not been established by witnesses, then one should employ divine proof (divya) in that matter or on the path.
On this point, Yājñavalkya says: "But he who causes suffering [to another] shall pay the expenses incurred in recovering that person. Kātyāyana says:
He shall also pay for the expenses of treatment until the wound is healed.
Manu says: "The wife, the son, the slave, the female slave, and the servant as the fifth—"
Those who have committed an offense should be beaten with a rope or a split bamboo cane.
Yājñavalkya: In cases of causing pain, drawing blood, or cutting off a limb or member,
the fine for small animals shall be two paṇas and upwards, in successive order.
In the case of cutting off the male organ or causing death, the middle amercement shall be the fine;
for these same acts involving large animals, the punishment is double.
In the context of the rule "he shall be fined one hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*," Viṣṇu states:

"One who destroys the virility of animals, as well as one who kills an elephant, a horse, a camel, or a cow, shall have one foot amputated. A seller of meat and one who kills domestic animals shall be fined one hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*, and he must also pay the value of those animals to their owner. One who kills wild animals shall be fined fifty *kārṣāpaṇas*. A bird-killer and a fish-killer shall be fined ten *kārṣāpaṇas*. One who kills for sport shall be fined one *kārṣāpaṇa*."
Kātyāyana states: For the killing of wild animals and birds, the fine is three paṇas; for the killing of snakes, cats, mongooses, dogs, and pigs, it is twelve paṇas for men.
Manu says:
"For driving a cow, a heifer, a sacrificial animal, a bull, or a draft ox, one shall incur the first amercement; for killing them, the highest."
Kātyāyana says: A man shall not drive exhausted, hungry, or thirsty animals—such as donkeys, cows, buffaloes, camels, and the like—at an improper time; he shall incur the first amercement.
In the case of killing a human being, one quickly incurs guilt equal to that of a thief;
for large living creatures such as cows, goats, camels, and oxen, the guilt is half.
For the killing of small animals, the fine is ten *dama*;
for auspicious wild beasts and birds, the punishment shall be fifty *paṇas*.
For donkeys, goats, and sheep, the fine shall be five māṣakas;
for the killing of a dog or a pig, the fine shall be one māṣaka.
Kātyāyana says:
"In the case of killing living beings, one should cause restitution to be made in kind;
or, Manu has declared that a price equivalent to the animal should be paid."
On this point, Manu says:
"Svāyambhuva Manu has declared ten places for the application of punishment; in these three castes [the king] may proceed, but a Brāhmaṇa should depart unhurt."
The generative organ, the belly, the tongue, the hands, and the feet as the fifth;
the eyes, the nose, the ears, wealth, and likewise the body.
Bṛhaspati says: The hand, the penis, the eyes, the tongue, the ears, and the nose;
the neck, the feet, the *sandaṃśa*, the forehead, the lips, the anus, and the hips.

These fourteen grounds for punishment have been specified; this refers to cases involving grave offenses. For a Brahmin, the forehead or the ears [are the marks of punishment], and no other punishment is ordained.
Yama said: "One might destroy this entire world, yet nothing is equal to [the offense against] a Brāhmaṇa;
therefore, a king should not even contemplate his killing in his mind."
They say that Brāhmaṇas are not to be slain, even if they are established in every kind of sin;
whatever is beneficial for Brāhmaṇas, that the king should practice.
One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is established in every kind of sin;
one should banish him from the kingdom, leaving him with all his wealth and unharmed.
If a twice-born man persists in an act deserving of death while possessing complete wealth,
the king shall banish him after proclaiming his guilt in an assembly.

Baudhāyana states: "In the cases of a Brāhmaṇa's murder of a Brāhmaṇa, sexual intercourse with the Guru’s wife, theft of gold, or drinking liquor, he should be branded on the forehead with red-hot iron with the marks of a headless torso (*kabandha*), a vulva (*bhaga*), a dog's paw (*śvāpada*), or a liquor-sign (*surādhvaja*), and then banished to another district. Manu says: "For violating the Guru’s bed, the mark of a vulva should be made; for drinking liquor, the sign of a liquor-flag; for theft, the mark of a dog’s paw should be made; and for killing a Brāhmaṇa, the mark of a headless man."
Indeed, those who are unfit to eat with, unfit to sacrifice for, and unfit to study with— those who engage in disputes and are excluded from all righteous duties— shall wander the earth in misery.
But these, having been branded with the mark, must be abandoned by their kinsmen and relatives;
they shall be without compassion and without salutation—this is the ordinance of Manu.
But those of the higher castes who perform penance as prescribed shall not have a mark branded on their foreheads by the king; rather, they should be made to pay the highest fine.
But according to the sacred tradition, a Brāhmaṇa should be punished with the middle amercement;
or he may be banished from the kingdom, taking his wealth and his belongings with him.
But others who have committed these sins unintentionally deserve the forfeiture of all their property; however, if they did so intentionally, they deserve banishment.
Yama states: For the four offenses of a Brāhmaṇa, this is ordained:
shaving the head as punishment, and thereafter banishment from the city.
For the purpose of proclaiming his sin, the king shall cause him to depart on a donkey and have a mark branded upon his forehead, according to the prescribed rule.
I shall now declare, in due order, the bodily marks for those who violate the Guru’s bed, drink liquor, commit theft, or kill a Brāhmaṇa, just as Manu has stated.
For a twice-born man who has violated the bed of his guru, the mark of a female organ should be made;
and for a drinker of liquor, one who has consumed liquor should have the sign of a tavern flag made upon him.
In the case of theft, having fashioned a dog's foot, one should strike him with it like a peacock;
the man who has killed a Brahmin should be made headless, with the mark [of a dog's foot] upon his forehead.
But if a twice-born man forms an association with those who have fallen [from their caste], he must be made unfit to eat with;
so said Manu, the son of Svayambhū.
But those who have committed a heinous crime must be abandoned by their kinsmen, relatives, and friends.
Manu says:
"Where an ordinary person would be fined one kārṣāpaṇa, there the king should be fined one thousand; this is the established rule."
But a king should slay with various terrifying methods of execution that person of inferior caste who, out of lust, oppresses the Brahmins.
Kātyāyana says: A Śūdra who has abandoned the life of a renunciant, as well as one devoted to the muttering of prayers and burnt offerings,
the king should punish with a *tutha* fine, or else he should be fined double that amount.
For men who are untouchable Śūdras or slaves, who are evildoers,
